papers.method: Medical documents are chunked; BioBERT with SNOMED-CT and UMLS extracts entities and relations; an LLM adds broader entities and relations; the graph is stored in Neo4j and checked by medical experts. A Camel-based multi-agent system has a GP-LLM that refers a case to one of four consultant LLMs (cardiology, neurology, endocrinology, rheumatology) when its confidence is below 0.7 or the diagnosis is in a specialist set; specialist confidences are combined by weighted or simple averaging.
papers.result: No quantitative results. The paper shows knowledge graph examples for obesity (Ozempic, Wegovy, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease) and a full graph visualisation. Evaluation (a benchmark and MedQA tests against Med-PaLM, BioGPT and ESM-1b) is listed as future work.
papers.tools: Camel multi-agent framework; BioBERT for entity and relation extraction; SNOMED-CT and UMLS ontologies; unnamed LLMs for knowledge graph augmentation and agents; Neo4j graph database; PyTorch. Hardware: Not reported.
papers.gap: No experiments or metrics; LLM base models, prompts, document sources and expert validation process are not specified; how the GP confidence is produced and calibrated is not described; no imaging; no evaluation of referral accuracy.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this is a clear design for confidence-based routing between agents. A GP agent keeps a case only if its confidence is at least tau = 0.7 and the diagnosis is not in a specialist set; otherwise it refers the case on. Specialist outputs are combined by weights that sum to 1. Feedback also updates the GP knowledge. This is close to our selective-autonomy idea. We can apply the same referral rule, with a calibrated threshold, from a triage agent to tumour-specific agents, and finally to a human clinician. The expert-validated knowledge graph also offers a way to ground agent reasoning. But the confidence is not calibrated and the design is not tested, so our project must supply the calibration and the evaluation.
papers.limitations: Authors: performance depends on the quality and coverage of the knowledge graph, especially for rare or complex conditions; rapidly changing knowledge and rare disease combinations are hard; heavy need for high-quality medical data limits deployment in regions with limited data resources; coordination becomes complex as specialist domains grow. Future work: comprehensive benchmark (diagnostic accuracy, hallucination prevention, coordination efficiency), MedQA experiments versus ESM-1b, Med-PaLM and BioGPT, targeted fine-tuning of specialist agents. Additional: claims of reduced hallucination and higher precision are not supported by reported numbers.
papers.methodologyDetail: KG4Diagnosis has two parts: a knowledge graph pipeline and a hierarchical agent system. For the graph, unstructured medical documents covering 362 common diseases are split into chunks using context-based rules. BioBERT, linked to the SNOMED-CT and UMLS ontologies, extracts medical entities such as diseases, drugs and symptoms, and relation triples between them. These become nodes and edges of a graph G = (V, E), stored in Neo4j. An LLM then reads the same text and adds wider, context-aware entities and relations that BioBERT misses. In the last stage, medical experts review each relation and keep, correct or remove it. Validated knowledge expands the graph and is meant to train models later. The agent system is built on the Camel framework. A GP-LLM reads the user query and outputs a preliminary diagnosis x with a confidence between 0 and 1. If the confidence is below tau = 0.7, or if x is in a predefined set of specialist diagnoses, the case is referred. Otherwise the GP gives the diagnosis itself. The query is reformatted by a transfer function and sent to one of four consultant LLMs: cardiology, neurology, endocrinology or rheumatology. Each consultant also outputs a confidence. When several consultants are needed, the final confidence is a weighted sum of their confidences (weights sum to 1), or a plain average for complex multi-domain cases. Consultant findings are fed back to update the GP knowledge base. The paper reports no experiments. Training details, base LLMs and the source of the confidence values are not given. Evaluation on MedQA and a new benchmark is future work. To adapt it, a PhD student could use the same referral rule with a calibrated confidence (for example temperature-scaled tumour-type probabilities), tune tau on a validation set for a target error rate, and add a final referral to a human neuro-oncology clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Framework/position paper with no empirical evaluation. University of Warwick, Cranfield University, University of Cambridge and University of Oxford, UK. Not prospective or retrospective clinical study.
papers.datasets: Knowledge base of 362 common diseases across specialties built from unstructured medical documents; document sources, number of documents, entities and relations: Not reported. No patient dataset used. MedQA named only as future benchmark.
papers.preprocessing: Stage 1: each document d_i is split into m chunks by context-based segmentation rules (f_seg(d_i) -> C_i); chunk size Not reported. Stage 2: BioBERT embeddings plus SNOMED-CT/UMLS mapping for entity and relation extraction. No train/validation/test split reported.
papers.modelDetails: Knowledge graph pipeline: (1) chunking; (2) BioBERT entity extraction E and relation triples (e_i, r, e_j); (3) graph G = (V, E) with entities as nodes and relations as edges; (4) LLM-augmented extraction for broader context-aware entities and relations, stored in entity and relation databases; (5) human-guided reasoning: experts keep, correct or remove each relation, and G_expanded = G union validated entities and relations, with active learning and reinforcement learning mentioned. Agents: GP-LLM gives confidence P_GP(x|q) in [0,1]; referral if P_GP < tau (tau = 0.7) or x in X_s (diagnoses needing specialists); otherwise outputs diagnosis x. Consultant-LLMs: n = 4 (cardiology, neurology, endocrinology, rheumatology), each with P_Agent_i(y|q). Collaborative confidence: P_final = sum of w_i P_Agent_i with weights summing to 1; for complex multi-domain queries P_final = (1/n) sum of P_Agent_i. Transfer function T(A,B,q) = phi(q) reformats the query for the receiving agent. GP knowledge update K_GP(t+1) = K_GP(t) + delta K from consultants. How confidence values are obtained from LLMs: Not reported.
papers.training: Described as planned: targeted fine-tuning of specialist agents per disease category and continuous learning from agent feedback. Base models, optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size and hardware: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: None performed. Qualitative knowledge graph figures only (obesity examples and full graph). Planned benchmark on diagnostic accuracy, hallucination prevention and coordination efficiency, and MedQA.
papers.baselines: None compared. Planned: ESM-1b, Med-PaLM, BioGPT.
papers.results: No quantitative results reported. Only the referral threshold tau = 0.7, four specialist agents and 362 diseases in the knowledge base are stated.
papers.availability: Benchmark promised on the authors' GitHub repository after completion; no link given. Code, data and models: Not available.

papers.title: ArgMed-Agents: Explainable Clinical Decision Reasoning with LLM Disscusion via Argumentation Schemes
papers.authors: Hong S, Xiao L, Zhang X, Chen J
papers.venue: IEEE BIBM 2024 (International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine)
papers.aim: To make LLM clinical decision reasoning more accurate and explainable. Agents argue with each other using clinical argumentation schemes, and a symbolic solver picks a coherent, conflict-free set of arguments as the decision and its explanation.
papers.method: Three LLM agent types, all the same base model with different few-shot prompts: Generators propose arguments using the Argumentation Scheme for Clinical Discussion; a Verifier asks critical questions and, if one fails, asks for a counter-argument; a Reasoner builds an abstract argumentation graph of attacks and uses a Python symbolic solver to find acceptable decisions and the maximal explanation set. Tested zero-shot on 300 MedQA and 300 PubMedQA clinical-decision questions with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4.
papers.result: Accuracy, GPT-4: ArgMed-Agents 83.3% (MedQA) and 81.6% (PubMedQA) vs CoT 71.4% and 77.2%, direct 67.8% and 72.9%. GPT-3.5-turbo: 62.1% and 78.3% vs CoT 48.0% and 71.5%, direct 52.7% and 68.4%. Explainability (evaluator predicts decision from reasoning record, 100 MedQA cases): 0.91 with GPT-4 vs 0.73 CoT, 0.68 direct; knowledge-based CDSS 0.95. When no acceptable decision was found, 63% of cases had identifiable reasoning errors (76% conflicting knowledge, 24% insufficient domain knowledge).
papers.tools: OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 APIs; few-shot role prompts; temperature 0.0; Python 3 symbolic solver for abstract argumentation; fine-tuned LLM evaluator (model not named); in-house knowledge-based CDSS using RDF computer-interpretable guidelines as explainability benchmark.
papers.gap: Text-only multiple-choice questions, not real patient records or images; small samples (300 per dataset, 100 for explainability); explainability measured by an LLM evaluator, not clinicians; no statistical tests; the abstain signal (no acceptable decision) is only partly validated (63%); no handover to clinicians is implemented.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this gives an auditable record of how agents reach a decision. Each agent claim becomes a node in an attack graph, and a symbolic solver, not the LLM, picks the accepted decision and its explanation set. The empty-decision rule (no acceptable decision means likely reasoning error) is a natural abstain signal. It can map to our selective autonomy: if the argumentation over tumour type or surgical approach gives no acceptable decision, the case goes to the neurosurgeon. The critical-question Verifier is a pattern we can reuse for checking surgical-planning advice (for example side effects, alternatives, evidence). Our project would need to extend it to imaging inputs and calibrate the abstain rule.
papers.limitations: Authors: abstract argumentation is limited; future work should use more expressive logics (first-order, description, modal or probabilistic logic); arguments should adapt to individual user needs; interactive CDSS with patient and physician feedback. Additional: zero-shot exam questions only; general-knowledge questions excluded by the authors; repeated runs mentioned but variance not reported; Conjecture 1 (error iff no acceptable decision) is not proven; closed API models.
papers.methodologyDetail: ArgMed-Agents treats clinical reasoning as a structured debate. The authors use argumentation schemes from clinical discussion research. The main one is the scheme for decision making: given patient facts and a goal, decision D helps reach the goal, so D should be considered. It comes with four critical questions on evidence, side effects, whether the goal can be reached, and alternatives. Other schemes cover side effects and danger appeal. Three agent roles run on the same LLM (GPT-3.5-turbo or GPT-4) with different few-shot prompts and temperature 0.0. Generators propose decision arguments for the case. For a four-option MedQA question, up to four decisions are allowed. The Verifier answers the critical questions for each argument. If a question fails, for example because of a side-effect concern, the reason goes back to a Generator. The Generator writes a new argument that attacks the earlier one. Dialogue is capped at 8 turns to avoid loops. The Reasoner logs every argument and labels it as supporting a decision or a belief. It adds attack edges: rival decisions attack each other, and belief arguments can attack decisions but not the other way. A Python solver then computes which decisions are acceptable under abstract argumentation semantics. The explanation is the largest conflict-free acceptable set that contains one decision. If no decision is acceptable, the system flags a probable reasoning error. For testing, they randomly sampled 300 clinical-decision questions each from MedQA (USMLE) and PubMedQA, after removing general-knowledge items. They compared against direct answering and Chain-of-Thought. With GPT-4, accuracy rose to 83.3% on MedQA and 81.6% on PubMedQA, against 71.4% and 77.2% for CoT. For explainability, a fine-tuned LLM evaluator read the reasoning records of 100 MedQA cases and tried to predict the decision. ArgMed with GPT-4 scored 0.91, close to a rule-based RDF guideline CDSS at 0.95. A PhD student could reuse the critical-question verifier and the no-acceptable-decision rule as a deferral trigger for clinician review.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark experiment on public question-answer datasets, zero-shot setting. Hubei University of Technology, Wuhan, China. No patients or clinicians involved.
papers.datasets: MedQA (USMLE multiple-choice; full dataset 12,723 English, 34,251 simplified Chinese, 14,123 traditional Chinese questions; 4 answer options) and PubMedQA (yes/no/maybe research questions from PubMed abstracts). 300 examples randomly selected from each dataset for accuracy; biomedical general-knowledge quiz-type questions excluded so only clinical decision questions remain. 100 MedQA examples used for the explainability test. Language subset used: Not reported (examples are English).
papers.preprocessing: Random selection of 300 clinical-decision questions per dataset after removing general-knowledge questions. No training split (zero-shot). No other preprocessing reported.
papers.modelDetails: Formal basis: abstract argumentation framework <A, R>; an argument is acceptable if no argument attacks it, or every attacker is itself attacked. Argumentation schemes AS = <P, c, V> with critical questions (CQs); ASCD includes Argumentation Scheme for Decision Making (ASDM: given fact F, goal G, decision D promotes G, so D should be considered; CQ1 evidence D promotes G, CQ2 side effects, CQ3 can G be achieved by D, CQ4 alternative decisions), Side Effects (ASSE) and Danger Appeal (ASDA). Agents: (1) Generator(s) propose arguments for decisions; (2) Verifier answers CQs in a self-questioning way; if a CQ is rejected, the reason is returned and the Generator proposes a new argument that attacks the old one; the round ends when the Verifier accepts; (3) Reasoner records all dialogue, labels arguments as decision arguments Args_d or belief arguments Args_b, and builds attacks: different decision arguments attack each other, decision arguments may not attack belief arguments. A decision is optional if acceptable; the explanation set E is the maximal acceptable, conflict-free set containing one optional decision (decisions are mutually exclusive). Conjecture 1: reasoning has errors iff Args_d(E) is empty, which serves as an abstain signal. Settings: temperature 0.0; dialogue limit 8; maximum 4 decisions (MedQA has 4 options) to stop agent loops.
papers.training: No training of the agents (training-free, zero-shot with few-shot role prompts). An LLM evaluator was fine-tuned for the explainability test; its model and settings are Not reported. Hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on 300 MedQA and 300 PubMedQA clinical-decision questions, compared with direct generation and Chain-of-Thought, each with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4. Explainability: for 100 MedQA examples, the reasoning record (CoT chain, ArgMed dialogue plus argumentation graph, or CDSS RDF inference nodes) is given to a fine-tuned LLM evaluator that predicts the decision; prediction accuracy is the explainability score. Error analysis of cases with no acceptable decision. Qualitative traceability analysis.
papers.baselines: Direct generation and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4; knowledge-based CDSS (RDF guidelines and inference engine) as explainability upper benchmark.
papers.results: Accuracy (MedQA / PubMedQA): GPT-3.5-turbo direct 52.7 / 68.4; CoT 48.0 / 71.5; ArgMed-Agents 62.1 / 78.3. GPT-4 direct 67.8 / 72.9; CoT 71.4 / 77.2; ArgMed-Agents 83.3 / 81.6. Explainability prediction accuracy (100 MedQA): GPT-3.5-turbo direct 0.53, CoT 0.59, ArgMed 0.87; GPT-4 direct 0.68, CoT 0.73, ArgMed 0.91; knowledge-based CDSS 0.95. Error analysis: 63% of no-acceptable-decision cases had identifiable reasoning errors; of these 76% from conflicting knowledge and 24% from insufficient domain knowledge. Number of no-decision cases: Not reported.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals).
papers.availability: Not available (no code or data link in the paper). Datasets MedQA and PubMedQA are public.

papers.title: ClinicalLab: Aligning Agents for Multi-Departmental Clinical Diagnostics in the Real World
papers.authors: Yan W, Liu H, Wu T, Chen Q, Wang W, Chai H, Wang J, Zhao W, Zhang Y, Zhang R, Zhu L, Zhao X
papers.aim: To build a leakage-free, real-case, multi-department benchmark for end-to-end clinical diagnosis by LLMs, and to design an agent that routes each case to the best LLM for each department.
papers.method: ClinicalBench has 1,500 real de-identified cases (150 diseases x 10 cases, 24 departments) from Chinese Grade 3A hospitals and 8 tasks from department guide to treatment plan. 17 LLMs were tested with greedy decoding and four new metrics (DWR, DIFR, CDR, Acceptability). ClinicalAgent then uses a patient navigator to pick K departments and N top-ranked LLM clinicians per department, who consult, order lab and imaging reads, and give a chair-aggregated final diagnosis and plan.
papers.result: Best single LLM overall was InternLM2-20B-Chat (Avg 51.98, DWR 14.91); GPT-4 had the best CDR (33.27%) and Acceptability (11.37). ClinicalAgent variants raised CDR to 52.73 (Agent#3@1) and 54.00 (Agent#1@3), and Acceptability to 17.82 and 18.22. Human expert score was highest for Agent#1@3 (62.76 vs 55.90 for GPT-4); GPT-4o judge scored GPT-4 highest (90.93) vs Agent#1@3 89.40.
papers.tools: 17 LLMs: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini-Pro-1.0, InternLM2-20B-Chat, Yi-34B-Chat, Qwen-72B-Chat, Baichuan2-13B-Chat, Claude3, ChatGLM3-6B, BlueLM-7B-Chat, Spark-3, HuatuoGPT2-34B, WiNGPT2-14B-Chat, PULSE-20B, Taiyi-LLM, DISC-MedLLM, BianQue-2. GPT-4 for translation to English; GPT-4o as judge; bert-base-chinese for BERTScore; jieba tokeniser; API calls plus 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Code and data: https://github.com/WeixiangYAN/ClinicalLab.
papers.gap: Imaging is given only as text reports, not images. No uncertainty, calibration or deferral to clinicians. No few-shot or RAG tested. Data only from mainland China and Chinese guidelines. Automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore) disagree with human scores. No comparison with other agents such as MedAgents.
papers.relation: For O1, ClinicalLab gives a concrete pattern for care-pathway orchestration: a navigator agent routes the case, department agents backed by different LLMs consult, then lab and radiology agents report and a chair agent aggregates. The brain-tumour pathway (triage, neuroradiology, neuropathology, neurosurgery planning) maps onto this. Its benchmark-driven model-to-role assignment and end-to-end metrics such as CDR are useful for evaluation. Its data governance (two-round de-identification by doctors, watermarked application-based release) is a model for sharing Sri Lankan data. We still need to add image input, calibrated deferral and federated training.
papers.limitations: No medical agent (including MedAgents and Agent Hospital) could be compared directly because they target multiple-choice QA. Few-shot learning and RAG not tested. Data from mainland China only, so may not represent other countries. Experiments run once on Chinese samples due to cost. GPT-4o judge may prefer GPT-4's own outputs. Metrics do not fully agree with each other. Future work: combine with RAG and few-shot, better metrics.
papers.methodologyDetail: Three senior clinicians and two AI researchers chose real cases from the record databases of Chinese Grade 3A hospitals. They picked 10 cases for each of 150 common diseases across 24 departments, giving 1,500 cases of about 1,000 tokens each. Doctors checked each case for medical accuracy. They then removed names, places and other identifiers in two independent rounds, keeping only age and gender. The AI researchers checked that each record was complete. Each case holds the chief complaint, history, physical exam, lab reports and imaging reports as text, plus the doctors' reference diagnosis and treatment. The authors split the patient journey into 8 tasks. These run from choosing 1 of 24 departments, through preliminary, differential and final diagnosis, to treatment principles, the treatment plan and reading imaging reports. They ran 17 LLMs zero-shot with greedy decoding (temperature 0), through APIs and 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Choice tasks were scored by accuracy. Text tasks were scored by the mean of BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore (bert-base-chinese, jieba), after mapping synonyms to an expert-checked list. New metrics were DWR (rank-based win rate per department), DIFR (instruction following), CDR (department and diagnosis both correct) and Acceptability (CDR times text quality). No model was best in every department. So they built ClinicalAgent. A navigator (Yi-34B, picked for DIFR-N 96.23) uses the department rankings to call K departments and the N best-ranked LLMs for each one. The clinicians give first diagnoses and order tests. Biochemist and radiologist agents read the reports, and a chair agent merges the answers at each step. Agent#1@3 raised CDR from 33.27 (GPT-4) to 54.00. Seven experts with over 10 years' experience rated 20 random cases blind on a 1 to 5 scale, each case by two raters. They gave Agent#1@3 62.76 against 55.90 for GPT-4. To adapt this, a brain-tumour pathway could rank candidate models per role on local Sri Lankan cases, then route each role to the best model. A deferral rule would be added when department agents disagree.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark and agent evaluation on real hospital records. Data from officially certified Grade 3A hospitals in China (hospitals not named); ethics committee approval and notarisation reported. Work supported by Alibaba Group. Includes a blinded human expert evaluation.
papers.datasets: ClinicalBench: 1,500 real cases, 150 diseases x 10 cases each, 24 departments, average about 1,000 tokens per case, Chinese originals translated to English with GPT-4. Department shares include: Hepatobiliary and Pancreas Surgery 6.67%, Anus and Intestine Surgery 6.67%, Orthopedics 6.67%, Urinary Surgery 6.0%, Neurology 5.33%, Neurosurgery 4.67%, Respiratory Medicine 4.67%, Pediatrics 4.0%, Hematology 2.0%, Obstetrics 1.33% (and others). Each case has gender, age, chief complaint, medical history, physical exam, imaging reports (X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound as text) and lab reports (biochemical, immunological, microbiological, pathological), plus doctors' preliminary diagnosis, diagnostic basis, differential diagnosis and treatment plan. Built by 3 senior clinicians and 2 AI researchers. Cases chosen as representative of common diseases per department. Distributed 63 times by 30 Sep 2024.
papers.preprocessing: Four steps: (1) data collection of representative cases per disease from the hospital case database; (2) professional knowledge review by doctors; (3) privacy protection with two rounds of independent manual de-identification (PII, treatment region removed; gender and age kept); (4) integrity and compliance check by 2 AI researchers. Three rounds of review in total for sensitive content. Personalised watermarks embedded per applicant. Synonym list for 150 diseases built from textbooks, encyclopaedias and lists generated by the 17 models, screened by 3 medical experts, used to align terms before BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore. No train/test split; all 1,500 cases used for evaluation (zero-shot). Experiments run on the original Chinese samples.
papers.modelDetails: 8 tasks: Department Guide (DG, choose 1 of 24 departments from chief complaint); Clinical Diagnosis with 6 chain-of-thought subtasks: Preliminary Diagnosis P = PD(CC, MH, PE), Diagnostic Basis B, Differential Diagnosis D, Final Diagnosis F, Principle of Treatment G, Treatment Plan T; and Imaging Diagnosis IDR = ID(IR) from text reports. ClinicalAgent (Algorithm 1): (1) Patient navigator (Yi-34B-Chat, chosen for near-perfect instruction following: DIFR-N 96.23, DIFR-Q 99.93) reads CC and prior knowledge PK (model rankings per department from Table 2) and selects K departments and N top clinicians per department; (2) a chair clinician is chosen; each clinician LLM (for example pediatrics by GPT-4, orthopedics by InternLM2, hematology by Gemini-Pro) gives preliminary diagnosis and lab/imaging test requests; chair aggregates; (3) biochemist agent reads lab reports and gives LDR; (4) radiologist agent reads imaging text reports and gives IDR; (5) final consultation: each clinician gives B, D, F, G, T in sequence; chair aggregates; (6) nurse and pharmacist agents handle treatment. Variants: Agent#K@N, tested as Agent#3@1, Agent#1@3 and Agent#1@1. No voting, confidence score or deferral threshold.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning. Greedy decoding for all LLMs (temperature 0 or do_sample False). API calls plus 8 NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Single run per model because of cost. Training time not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Automatic: DG accuracy (Acc@1, Acc@3, Acc@5); PD and FD by accuracy; DB, DD, PT, TP and ID by the mean of BLEU (1 to 4-gram), ROUGE and BERTScore; Avg = mean of 9 scores over 8 tasks. New metrics: DWR = (1/m) sum over departments of (1/n) sum over models of (n - (rank - 1)) using Avg score ranks; DIFR = mean of DIFR-Q (share of samples where number of departments returned equals K) and DIFR-N (share of returned department names in the 24-name list); CDR = share of samples with both department guide and diagnosis correct; Acceptability = mean CDR x mean of BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore over 5 generative tasks. Human evaluation: 7 medical experts from different departments (average over 10 years' experience), 20 random cases, 7 systems, outputs anonymised, each sample graded by 2 experts double-blind, 1 to 5 scale on fluency, relevance, completeness and proficiency. GPT-4o evaluation: 150 cases (1 per disease) with the same rubric.
papers.baselines: 17 single LLMs (11 general, 6 Chinese medical) listed in tools; for the agent: top 4 single LLMs InternLM2, GPT-4, Gemini-Pro, Yi-Chat; ablation Agent#1@1. MedAgents and Agent Hospital not compared (multiple-choice design).
papers.results: Single LLMs (Avg): InternLM2 51.98 (DG Acc 64.47, PD 78.20, CDR 31.40, Acceptability 11.11, DWR 14.91); Gemini-Pro 50.63; Yi-34B 50.53; GPT-4 49.45 (FD 54.20, CDR 33.27, Acceptability 11.37); Qwen-72B 48.92; HuatuoGPT2-34B 48.42; Claude3 47.22; GPT-3.5 46.14; BianQue-2 4.50 (lowest). Imaging diagnosis best WiNGPT2 41.39. Department Guide Acc@1/3/5: Gemini-Pro 62.07/85.73/92.00; InternLM2 64.47/79.87/84.67; GPT-4 61.47/86.13/90.13 (DIFR-N 74.03). ClinicalAgent: Agent#3@1 DWR 14.30, CDR 52.73, Acceptability 17.82, Avg 54.46, Human 59.42, GPT-4o 85.61; Agent#1@3 CDR 54.00, Acceptability 18.22, Avg 51.66, Human 62.76, GPT-4o 89.40; Agent#1@1 DWR 17.00, CDR 35.13, Acceptability 12.57, Avg 53.02, Human 57.84, GPT-4o 82.46. Human scores of single LLMs: InternLM2 54.66, GPT-4 55.90, Gemini-Pro 58.84, Yi 52.42. No single LLM ranked best in all departments. General LLMs beat specialised medical LLMs. No confidence intervals.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests, confidence intervals or inter-rater agreement; double-blind dual grading used for human evaluation).
papers.availability: Code and dataset: https://github.com/WeixiangYAN/ClinicalLab; data released under the ClinicalBench Usage and Data Distribution License Agreement (application-based, watermarked).

papers.title: Tree-of-Reasoning: Towards Complex Medical Diagnosis via Multi-Agent Reasoning with Evidence Tree
papers.authors: Peng Q, Cui J, Xie J, Cai Y, Li Q
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '25), Dublin, Ireland
papers.aim: To improve complex, multi-disease medical diagnosis by LLM agents. The method makes each agent show its diagnosis, reasoning and clinical evidence as a tree, and lets agents check each other's trees.
papers.method: Four doctor agents (outpatient, laboratory, radiology, pathology) each read one type of patient data and output an evidence tree (diagnosis -> reasoning -> evidence), helped by MedRAG retrieval. A multi-agent cross-verification step (up to 2 rounds x 2 turns) lets agents review and correct each other's trees. A final step merges the trees and picks the diagnosis options.
papers.result: On 952 real inpatient cases, ToR (DeepSeek-V3 backbone) reached precision 95.70%, recall 46.60%, F1 62.68%, against 51.76% F1 for the best baseline (MMA) and 46.63% for plain DeepSeek-V3. Doctor-rated completeness was 4.0/5 (best), relevance 4.43/5 (MMA 4.47). Removing the evidence tree dropped F1 to 51.07%.
papers.tools: DeepSeek-V3 as base LLM via API; baselines via OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek APIs (GPT-4o, o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1); MedRAG with BM25 retriever over PubMed, StatPearls, textbooks and Wikipedia (top-3 documents); foundation-model comparison with GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-flash. Code: github.com/tsukiiiiiiiii/TOR. Hardware not reported.
papers.gap: No uncertainty estimate, confidence score or deferral rule is produced; agents always give an answer. Recall is still low (46.60%). Inputs are text reports only (no raw images). Single hospital in China; no prospective or external validation.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), the evidence tree gives a ready format for an auditable record of what each specialist agent concluded and why. Our brain-tumour orchestrator could store radiology, pathology and clinical agent outputs in the same diagnosis-reasoning-evidence tree, and add a calibrated confidence per node so the orchestrator can defer to clinicians. The cross-verification loop is a model for resolving conflicts between imaging and clinical agents before hand-off.
papers.limitations: The paper does not include a limitations section. Observed: single-centre retrospective data; labels built by adding random negative diseases from the same department, which makes precision easy; recall below 50%; only three doctors rated explanations, with no agreement statistics; zero-shot prompting only; no cost or latency analysis beyond token prices; no calibration or abstention. Future work is not stated explicitly.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a text-only, multi-source diagnostic benchmark from one large public tertiary hospital. They took unique patient IDs from inpatient records, anonymised private fields, and pulled four report types from the EMR: patient information, laboratory values, radiology report text (CT, MRI, X-ray, ultrasound) and pathology reports. The final set has 952 patients, 37 departments and 4,823 disease labels, stored as JSON. Diagnosis was framed as multi-label selection: every confirmed diagnosis of a patient is a correct option, and diseases drawn at random from the same department are added as wrong options. For each patient, four role-prompted agents run in parallel, all on DeepSeek-V3 through its API in zero-shot mode. Each agent sees only its own data type and can retrieve the top 3 BM25 hits from PubMed, StatPearls, textbooks and Wikipedia (MedRAG). Each agent must return an evidence tree: disease at level one, reasoning at level two and concrete evidence (for example 'glucose 9.47 mmol/L') as leaves. Next comes cross-verification. For 2 rounds of 2 turns, each agent first decides by prompt whether it disagrees with the shared trees. If it does, it picks target agents and writes opinions to them. All exchanges are logged, and at the end of each round every agent rewrites its tree from the log. A final summarising prompt merges the four trees and selects the answer options. Outputs were scored with precision, recall and F1 over the options. Three doctors rated explanation relevance and completeness from 0 to 5 using fixed rubrics. ToR scored F1 62.68% (P 95.70%, R 46.60%), against 51.76% for MMA and 46.63% for plain DeepSeek-V3. Ablations showed the radiology agent added the most (+11.23 F1), and removing the evidence tree cost 11.61 F1. To adapt this, a PhD student could keep the tree schema and the bounded 2x2 discussion loop. They could then attach calibrated confidence to each tree node and add a deferral rule, which this paper does not have.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method-development and benchmark study using real inpatient electronic medical records from one large public tertiary hospital in China (authors at South China University of Technology and Hong Kong Polytechnic University). Includes a small doctor rating study of explanations.
papers.datasets: In-house multi-source inpatient dataset (not public). 952 patients during hospitalisation, 37 clinical departments, 4,823 disease labels in total. Four data types per patient: patient information (sex, age, chief complaint, present illness, history), laboratory indicators (e.g. blood routine, carcinoembryonic markers), radiology reports (text findings from MRI, CT, X-ray, ultrasound) and pathology reports (e.g. frozen pathology, immunohistochemistry, tumour grade and stage). Top labels: hepatic cyst 2.8%, hypertension 2.3%, hypoproteinaemia 1.7%, type 2 diabetes 1.7%, chronic gastritis 1.6%. Sex: 53.9% male, 46.1% female. Age: 60-74 years 39.6%, over 75 years about 16.9%. Top departments: oncology 15.76%, gastrointestinal surgery 13.55%, thyroid surgery 8.82%. Construction: unique patient IDs taken from inpatient records, privacy-sensitive fields anonymised, then histories, lab, radiology and pathology reports pulled from the hospital EMR and stored as JSON. Inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond 'complete examination data' not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Patient identifiers anonymised; records structured as JSON with four sections. Task framed as multi-label classification: all diagnosed diseases of a patient are correct options, and other diseases randomly drawn from the same department are added as incorrect options. Number of distractor options per case not reported. No train/validation/test split, because all methods are used zero-shot; all 952 cases are used for evaluation. No images are processed; only text reports.
papers.modelDetails: Stage 1, single-agent reasoning: four role-prompted agents. Outpatient doctor reads symptoms, examination and history; laboratory doctor reads blood, urine and fluid tests; radiology doctor reads X-ray, CT, MRI and ultrasound findings; pathology doctor reads biopsy, surgical specimen, cytology and immunohistochemistry. Each agent may query MedRAG (BM25, top-3 documents from PubMed, StatPearls, textbooks, Wikipedia). Each outputs a markdown-like evidence tree: level 1 = candidate disease, level 2 = reasoning, leaves = clinical evidence items. Stage 2, multi-agent cross-verification (Algorithm 1): for k = 2 rounds and t = 2 turns per round, each agent decides via a prompt whether to participate (ShouldParticipate), chooses which agents to address (ChooseDiscussionTargets), writes opinions on their trees (GenerateOpinion), and the interactions are logged; after each round every agent updates its tree from the log (UpdateDiagnosisTree). Stage 3, final decision: a summarising prompt merges all trees into a final tree E_f and selects the diagnosis options. Prompt templates are given in Tables 5-12. No uncertainty, confidence threshold or deferral rule is used.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning. All experiments are zero-shot with API-served LLMs. DeepSeek-V3 is the base model for ToR, prompt-based and multi-agent baselines. Optimiser, learning rate, epochs and batch size not applicable. Decoding temperature, hardware and run time not reported. Token prices quoted: GPT-3.5-Turbo $1.50 per million tokens (highest), Qwen-Turbo $0.6 per million tokens (lowest).
papers.evaluation: Objective metrics on all 952 cases: precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = harmonic mean, over the selected disease options. Subjective metrics: three real doctors scored each method's diagnostic explanations for relevance and completeness on a 0-5 scale to one decimal, using written rubrics (e.g. 5.0 = completely relevant / complete; 4.0-4.9 = highly; 3.0-3.9 = moderately). Number of cases rated by doctors not reported. Ablations: removing agents one by one (their data reassigned to the outpatient agent), removing evidence tree, cross-verification or MedRAG. Foundation-model comparison over five low-cost LLMs. One qualitative case study. No cross-validation or external validation.
papers.baselines: Single LLMs: GPT-4o, o1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1. Prompt-based: chain-of-thought (CoT), tree-of-thought (ToT), MindMap. Multi-agent: MedAgents, MDAgents, MMA.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests, no confidence intervals, no inter-rater agreement for the three doctor raters).
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/tsukiiiiiiiii/TOR.git. Data: not publicly released (in-house hospital data). Prompts: in paper appendix Tables 5-12.

papers.title: AI Hospital: Benchmarking Large Language Models in a Multi-agent Medical Interaction Simulator
papers.authors: Fan Z, Tang J, Chen W, Wang S, Wei Z, Xie J, Huang F, Zhou J
papers.aim: To test whether large language models (LLMs) can act like doctors in a multi-turn consultation, where they must ask questions, order tests and then diagnose. The paper also tests whether several LLM doctors that discuss disputes can diagnose better than one.
papers.method: The authors built AI Hospital, a multi-agent simulator with a Doctor agent (the LLM being tested) and three non-player agents: Patient (GPT-3.5), Examiner (GPT-3.5) and Chief Physician (GPT-4). Each agent sees only part of a real Chinese medical record. A GPT-4 Chief Physician scores the Doctor's final report against the full record, and a Central Agent runs a dispute-resolution discussion between several Doctor agents.
papers.result: All interactive LLM doctors scored far below a one-step GPT-4 that saw the full record. For diagnostic results, interactive GPT-4 scored 29.36 versus 58.89 for one-step GPT-4. Disease-entity F1 was 30.26 for GPT-4 and 14.28 for Baichuan-13B. Three collaborating doctors with dispute resolution reached 39.60 on diagnostic results and entity F1 38.00. Agent behaviour checks were above 95% (patient relevance 100%, honesty 98.1-99.7%).
papers.tools: GPT-3.5 (Patient and Examiner agents), GPT-4 (Chief Physician, one-step upper bound, patient personalisation), Doctor LLMs tested: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Wenxin-4.0, Qwen-Max, Baichuan-13B, HuatuoGPT-II 13B and 34B; ICD-10 based disease entity linking; Tencent Questionnaire platform for expert review; bootstrap for variance. Code and data: https://github.com/LibertFan/AI_Hospital.
papers.gap: LLMs are weak at active information gathering: they do not ask the right questions or order the right tests. Entity-level metrics exist only for diseases, not symptoms or tests. The benchmark is text-only and Chinese, with no imaging and no uncertainty or deferral mechanism.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), AI Hospital gives a ready pattern for testing coordinated agents along a diagnostic pathway: role agents with restricted information views, an orchestrating moderator agent, and an LLM judge. Our brain-tumour pipeline could reuse the idea of an Examiner agent that only releases imaging or histology results when explicitly asked, and a Chief Physician style moderator that lists disagreements between specialist agents. The large drop from one-step to interactive performance shows why our orchestrator must check information completeness at each hand-off and defer to clinicians when key data are missing.
papers.limitations: Records are mainly Chinese, which limits use in other languages and health systems. Only 506 cases, so rare diseases are under-represented. Simulated agents may not copy real human nuance. The treatment-plan score does not credit valid alternative plans. Heavy use of the OpenAI API has cost and environmental burden. Future work: larger benchmark, cheaper evaluation, better agents and smaller open-source models.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team first built a test set. They collected Chinese medical records from an online case site (bingli.iiyi.com), had physicians review them, removed incomplete records and kept 506 cases across six department groups (surgery 180, internal medicine 153, obstetrics and gynaecology 94, paediatrics 29, ENT 23, others 27). Doctors from 10 departments checked 5 random cases each and judged 94% correct. Each record was split into three parts: subjective information, objective test results, and diagnosis plus treatment. These parts define what each agent may know. The Patient agent (GPT-3.5) knows only the subjective part and plays a persona that GPT-4 wrote for the case. The Examiner agent (GPT-3.5) knows only test results and releases a result only when a named test is requested; in a 50-prompt attack test it never leaked results. The Doctor agent, the model under test, knows nothing at the start. A GPT-4 chief complaint starts the chat. The Doctor asks questions and orders tests, with messages tagged by recipient. The chat stops when the Patient gets a diagnosis and outputs <END> or a round limit is hit. The Doctor then writes a five-part report. A GPT-4 Chief Physician compares each part with the full record and scores it 1-4, later scaled to 0-100 with bootstrap variance. Diagnoses are also mapped to ICD-10 entities to get precision, recall and F1. As an upper bound, GPT-4 receives all information in one step. To improve accuracy, 2 or 3 Doctor agents (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Wenxin-4.0) consult separately. A Central Agent pools their findings, re-checks disputed facts with Patient and Examiner, lists disagreements and runs discussion rounds until no dispute remains or a maximum M is reached. Three medical students checked agent behaviour on 50 dialogues per model. Results: interactive GPT-4 reached 29.36 on diagnostic results against 58.89 one-step; 3 Doctors reached 39.60. A PhD student can adapt this by replacing records with brain-tumour cases and the Examiner with MRI and histology tools.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, simulation-based benchmark study using de-identified online medical records. Authors from Alibaba Inc., Huazhong University of Science and Technology and Fudan University, China. Record review by doctors from Jiangsu Provincial People's Hospital and Tongji Medical College (tertiary Class A hospitals, China). No prospective patients.
papers.datasets: MVME (Multi-View Medical Evaluation) dataset: Chinese medical records collected online from https://bingli.iiyi.com/ and reviewed by professional physicians. After removing records with deficiencies such as incomplete information, 506 cases remained. Department counts: Surgery 180, Internal Medicine 153, Obstetrics and Gynecology 94, Pediatrics 29, Otorhinolaryngology 23, Others 27. Each record is split into Subjective information (symptoms, aetiology, history, habits), Objective information (test reports such as blood count, urinalysis, chest X-ray) and Diagnosis and Treatment (diagnostic results, rationales, treatment course). Quality check: 10 secondary departments x 5 random cases = 50 cases reviewed by department doctors with a binary correct/incorrect choice for each of three sections; 94% of records judged correct. Behaviour study: 50 randomly selected records. Failure analysis: 219 cases where GPT-4 scored 1 on diagnosis. Examiner attack test: 50 crafted prompts.
papers.preprocessing: Records were de-identified by the source before collection. Records with incomplete information were excluded. Each record was manually partitioned into subjective, objective and diagnosis/treatment parts and assigned to agents (Patient gets subjective, Examiner gets objective, Chief Physician gets all, Doctor gets none). GPT-4 generated a chief complaint for each record to start the dialogue and imagined a patient persona (background, emotions, personality). No train/test split: the whole set of 506 cases is used for evaluation only. No model training.
papers.modelDetails: Diagnostic phase: Patient agent (GPT-3.5) opens with a GPT-4-generated chief complaint; it must cooperate, use colloquial language, may omit details, shows curiosity and has a persona. Doctor agent (model under test) asks questions and recommends tests. Messages carry prefixes that show the recipient (for example <Speak to Doctor>, <Speak to Examiner>). Examiner agent (GPT-3.5) first identifies the requested test, rejects vague requests, returns results if present, else reports no abnormality. Dialogue ends when the Patient receives the diagnosis and emits <END>, or when a preset maximum number of rounds is passed (value not reported). Evaluation phase: Doctor writes a 5-part summary (symptoms, examinations, diagnostic results, rationales, treatment plan); GPT-4 Chief Physician scores each part 1-4 against the full record; scores normalised to 0-100. Entity metric: disease entities extracted from Doctor and gold diagnoses, linked to ICD-10 standard entities, set-level precision, recall, F1. Collaboration (Algorithm 1): N Doctor agents consult independently; a Central Agent (Chief Physician with no record access) collects their facts, checks disputed facts with Patient and Examiner, writes a shared summary; then in each round every Doctor gives a diagnosis given history H and dispute list d; the Central Agent summarises remaining disputes; loop stops when no dispute remains or round count exceeds M; Central Agent writes the final diagnosis. Settings: 2 Doctors (GPT-3.5 + GPT-4), 3 Doctors (+ Wenxin-4.0), and 2 Doctors without dispute resolution. No uncertainty-based deferral or confidence threshold.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning. All agents are prompted LLMs via API (prompts in appendix Tables 9-16). Temperature, maximum rounds M, hardware and cost: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: 1) Agent behaviour validation: 4 Doctor LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Wenxin-4.0, Qwen-Max) each produce 50 dialogues on 50 random records; three medical students label Patient relevance and honesty per QA pair, Examiner accuracy per test request, and Doctor report consistency (1-3 scale mapped to 0-100); two raters, third rater breaks ties. 2) Main MVME evaluation on all 506 cases with GPT-4 Chief Physician scores (1-4 per part, normalised to 0-100) and bootstrap variance. 3) Link-based disease entity metrics: average number of entities, recall, precision, F1. 4) One-step GPT-4 with full subjective and objective information as an upper bound. 5) Linear regression between information completeness (symptoms, examinations) and diagnostic quality. 6) Manual error analysis of 219 GPT-4 failure cases. 7) Discussion-round count with and without dispute resolution. 8) Adversarial test of Examiner with 50 information-extraction prompts.
papers.baselines: Interactive Doctor LLMs: Baichuan (13B), HuatuoGPT-II (13B), HuatuoGPT-II (34B), GPT-3.5, Wenxin-4.0, Qwen-Max, GPT-4. Collaboration variants: 2 Doctors without dispute resolution, 2 Doctors, 3 Doctors. Upper bound: one-step GPT-4 with all information.
papers.results: GPT-4 judge scores (0-100, bootstrap SD in brackets) for Symptoms / Examinations / Diagnostic results / Rationales / Treatment: Baichuan-13B 52.56 / 21.06 / 19.50 / 17.40 / 13.97; HuatuoGPT-II-13B 61.06 / 24.43 / 20.03 / 20.03 / 14.23; HuatuoGPT-II-34B 68.43 / 30.30 / 25.20 / 27.46 / 21.33; GPT-3.5 66.39 / 31.03 / 23.90 / 24.43 / 17.73; Wenxin-4.0 67.79 / 30.43 / 26.23 / 26.46 / 22.00; Qwen-Max 61.69 / 26.60 / 26.46 / 28.76 / 24.90; GPT-4 69.03 (1.27) / 25.10 / 29.36 (2.58) / 30.76 / 26.93; 2 Doctors w/o DR 75.49 / 43.03 / 35.56 / 38.53 / 32.40; 2 Doctors 78.06 / 47.10 / 38.06 / 41.56 / 35.90; 3 Doctors 80.26 (1.80) / 49.63 / 39.60 (2.80) / 44.23 / 37.26; one-step GPT-4 100 / 100 / 58.89 (1.63) / 66.59 / 53.16. Disease entity metrics (#, R, P, F1): Baichuan 1.58, 10.21, 23.79, 14.28; HuatuoGPT-II-13B 16.85 F1; HuatuoGPT-II-34B 22.34; GPT-3.5 25.37; Wenxin-4.0 25.91; Qwen-Max 29.56; GPT-4 1.52, 21.64, 50.26, 30.26; 2 Doctors w/o DR 33.74; 2 Doctors 35.21; 3 Doctors 3.20, 36.54, 39.58, 38.00. Agent behaviour: Patient relevance 100% for all, honesty 98.1-99.7%; Examiner accuracy 98.2-100%; Doctor consistency 98.0-100. Error types in 219 GPT-4 failures: omission of auxiliary examinations 99, focus only on complications 52, erroneous judgment 68. Examiner refused all 50 attack prompts (100%). Dispute resolution raised the share of cases reaching consensus within the first 4 discussion rounds.
papers.statistics: Bootstrap (Efron) used to estimate variance of judge scores (values in brackets). Linear regression shows positive link between information completeness and diagnostic quality (no p-values reported). Inter-rater agreement for the four behaviour questions: 99.1%, 95.6%, 99.4% and 100.0%. No significance tests reported.

papers.title: MedAgentBench: A Virtual EHR Environment to Benchmark Medical LLM Agents
papers.authors: Jiang Y, Black KC, Geng G, Park D, Zou J, Ng AY, Chen JH
papers.aim: To build a standard benchmark that tests whether LLM agents can carry out real clinical record tasks, such as reading labs and placing orders, inside a realistic electronic health record (EHR) system.
papers.method: Two internal-medicine physicians wrote 300 patient-specific tasks in 10 categories. The tasks run against a FHIR-compliant server holding de-identified profiles of 100 real Stanford patients (785,207 records). A simple agent orchestrator gives each of 12 LLMs nine FHIR functions and up to 8 rounds, and success is graded with reference answers and rule-based checks on POST payloads (pass@1).
papers.result: Best overall success rate was 69.67% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2), then GPT-4o 64.00% and DeepSeek-V3 62.67%; Mistral v0.3 7B scored 4.00%. Most models did better on query tasks than on action tasks (Claude 85.33% vs 54.00%). Hard tasks with 3 or more steps were much harder (Claude 23.33%).
papers.tools: HAPI FHIR JPA server with persistent H2 database, packaged as a Docker image (jyxsu6/medagentbench) on a Google Cloud c2d-standard-2 virtual machine; AgentBench framework for the codebase; BFCL-style function calling with JSON schemas; Python Faker for fake names and contact details; STARR Stanford clinical data warehouse; LLMs: Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, o3-mini, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5 72B, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemma2 27B, Mistral v0.3 7B (via Together AI).
papers.gap: No agent is reliable enough for unsupervised clinical action, especially for write actions and multi-step tasks. The benchmark covers only medical-record tasks, not imaging, team coordination or surgical work. Repeatability of actions and advanced agent designs were not tested.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), MedAgentBench gives a ready, open FHIR test bed and a task-success metric for agents that read and write clinical records. Our brain-tumour orchestrator could be tested on similar FHIR tasks (fetch prior MRI reports, record tumour grade, place referral to neurosurgery). Its finding that write actions fail far more often than reads supports our design choice to let agents read freely but route every record-changing action to a clinician for approval (selective autonomy).
papers.limitations: Does not capture the full complexity of real care that needs coordination between teams. All patients come from Stanford Hospital and are not representative of the general population. Does not cover all clinical tasks; focus is medical records only. Only GET requests sent to the live server to avoid restarting it (POST checked offline). Only a simple baseline agent used. Future work: surgery and nursing tasks, repeatability of action tasks, many-shot in-context learning and meta-prompting.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first defined clinical work that an agent could automate inside an EHR. Two Stanford internal-medicine physicians wrote 300 tasks in 10 categories, such as finding a patient's MRN, reading the latest magnesium level, averaging glucose over 24 hours, recording a blood pressure, ordering an HbA1c test if the last one is over a year old, ordering a referral, and ordering potassium by a dosing rule. Half of the tasks (150) only read data and half (150) must write data. Each task has a clinician instruction plus hospital context, such as a LOINC, NDC or SNOMED code and a fixed current time of 2023-11-13 10:15 UTC. Next they built the patient data. They sampled 100 patients from the STARR de-identified warehouse who had a sodium test on the morning of 13 Nov 2023, and pulled five years of labs, six vital signs, procedures, diagnoses and medication orders (785,207 records). They created fake MRNs and used Faker for names and addresses, cleaned missing values and removed PRN medication orders. These data were loaded into a HAPI FHIR JPA server and shipped as a Docker image on a Google Cloud c2d-standard-2 VM. For testing, a simple orchestrator built on the AgentBench code gave each LLM a prompt, nine FHIR functions as JSON schemas and the task. In each of up to 8 rounds the model had to output one GET, one POST or a finish call. GET results went back to the model; POST payloads were only checked for valid JSON so the server never had to restart. Twelve LLMs ran once each (pass@1) with temperature 0 except o3-mini. Answers were graded with reference solutions and rule-based payload checks. Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 led with 69.67%, but action and multi-step tasks stayed weak. A PhD student could reuse the Docker server and add brain-tumour tasks, such as retrieving MRI reports or ordering a neurosurgery referral, with a deferral step before any POST.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark development and retrospective evaluation study using de-identified, time-jittered real patient data from Stanford Hospital (STARR), USA. Tasks written by two internal-medicine physicians at Stanford University. No prospective patients and no clinician user study.
papers.datasets: Patient profiles: 100 patients randomly sampled from a STARR cohort who had an inpatient sodium lab test ordered on the morning of 13 November 2023. Data from the last five years (cut-off 13 November 2018). Age 58.15 +/- 19.82 years, 47% female. Total records 785,207: Observation 563,426, Procedure 124,969, Condition 74,821, MedicationRequest 21,991. Data types: lab results (taken time, result time, base name, value, unit, flag), six vital signs (heart rate, SpO2, respiratory rate, FiO2, blood pressure, temperature), procedure orders (date, CPT code, description, quantity), diagnoses (name, ICD-10 code, start date), medication orders (date, description, route, frequency, dosage, unit). Tasks: 300 clinician-written tasks in 10 categories (grouped into 7 broad categories: patient information retrieval, lab result retrieval, patient data aggregation, recording patient data, test ordering, referral ordering, medication ordering); 150 query-only tasks and 150 action tasks. Difficulty split by steps: easy (1 step), medium (2 steps), hard (3 or more steps); per-level counts not given directly.
papers.preprocessing: Protected health information was already removed in STARR and timestamps jittered per patient. Fake 7-digit MRNs prefixed with the letter S were generated (deduplicated). Faker library produced US names, phone numbers and addresses. Procedures with missing quantity were imputed with 1; procedures missing CPT code or description were removed. Diagnosis records with any missing value were removed. Medication orders with PRN frequency were removed to approximate real administrations. Data were uploaded as FHIR resources by parallel POST requests. Task context added hospital-specific codes (LOINC, NDC, SNOMED, flowsheet IDs) and a fixed current time of 2023-11-13T10:15:00+00:00. No train/test split: all 300 tasks are for evaluation only.
papers.modelDetails: Workflow: (1) clinician gives a high-level task to the agent orchestrator; (2a) the LLM plans function calls; (2b) it sends requests to the FHIR server; (3) the orchestrator returns a summary. Baseline orchestrator (inspired by BFCL) exposes nine FHIR functions as JSON schemas: condition.search, lab.search, vital.search, vital.create, medicationrequest.search, medicationrequest.create, procedure.search, procedure.create, patient.search. In each round the LLM must output exactly one of: a GET request (GET url?param=value), a POST request (POST url plus JSON payload), or finish([answers]). GET responses are returned raw to the model. POST payloads get a JSON-loadable sanity check and a success message. Maximum 8 rounds per task. Invalid action or more than 8 rounds counts as failure. Gemini tool_code block markers are stripped before parsing. Temperature set to 0 for all models except o3-mini. No uncertainty estimate, confidence threshold or deferral rule.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning; all models used zero-shot through APIs or Together AI serverless API. Environment: Docker container on a Google Cloud c2d-standard-2 VM; FHIR server takes about 90 seconds to start. Cost and runtime: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Metric: task success rate with pass@1 (single attempt) to reflect low error tolerance in healthcare. Query tasks: agent answer compared with answers from manually written reference solutions. Action tasks: manually written rule-based checks of POST payload correctness. Subgroups: query SR (150 tasks) vs action SR (150 tasks); difficulty SR for easy, medium and hard. Qualitative error-pattern analysis (invalid action format, answer in full sentence instead of value). No human clinician comparison.
papers.baselines: 12 LLMs compared with the same baseline orchestrator: Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 (685B), Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o-mini, o3-mini, Qwen2.5 (72B), Llama 3.3 (70B), Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemma2 (27B), Gemini 2.0 Pro, Mistral v0.3 (7B).
papers.statistics: Not reported (no confidence intervals or significance tests; single pass@1 run per model).

papers.title: MedRAX: Medical Reasoning Agent for Chest X-ray
papers.authors: Fallahpour A, Ma J, Munim A, Lyu H, Wang B
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267 (arXiv:2502.02673v2)
papers.aim: To build a training-free AI agent that combines many specialised chest X-ray (CXR) models with a large language model so it can answer complex, multi-step CXR questions. The paper also creates a new benchmark, ChestAgentBench, to test this kind of reasoning.
papers.method: MedRAX uses GPT-4o as a reasoning engine in a ReAct loop (observe, think, act) built on LangChain and LangGraph. The LLM picks and calls specialised tools (visual QA, segmentation, grounding, report generation, classification, image generation, DICOM utilities) through JSON calls, keeps tool outputs in short-term memory and stops when it can answer, needs user input or hits a time limit. It was tested on ChestAgentBench (2,500 six-choice questions from 675 Eurorad cases), CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR report generation and SLAKE VQA.
papers.result: MedRAX reached 63.1% overall accuracy on ChestAgentBench versus 57.9% (Llama-3.2-90B), 56.4% (GPT-4o), 39.5% (CheXagent) and 28.7% (LLaVA-Med). On CheXbench it scored 68.1% overall. On MIMIC-CXR report generation it had mF1-14 79.1% and mF1-5 64.9% but lower macro F1 (MF1-14 34.2%). On SLAKE CXR VQA it reached 90.35% accuracy and 91.23% recall.
papers.tools: GPT-4o with vision (backbone LLM, via Azure OpenAI with data logging opt-out); LangChain and LangGraph; Gradio interface; CheXagent and LLaVA-Med (visual QA); MedSAM and a PSPNet trained on ChestX-Det (segmentation); MAIRA-2 (grounding); SwinV2 Transformer with two-layer BERT decoder trained on CheXpert Plus (report generation); DenseNet-121 from TorchXRayVision (18-class classification); RoentGen (CXR generation); single NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU. Benchmark generation and quality checks with GPT-4o.
papers.gap: No uncertainty quantification, so the agent cannot say when it is unsure or hand over to a clinician. It struggles when tools disagree. Benchmark questions are generated by GPT-4o and checked automatically, with no radiologist reader study. Only chest X-ray, no CT or MRI, and no clinical validation.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), MedRAX is a close template for a tool-routing orchestrator: an LLM that calls specialised imaging models through typed JSON tool definitions, caches results and can ask the user for input. For brain MRI we could swap in tumour segmentation (for example nnU-Net or MedSAM), tumour classification and report generation tools. Its stated weakness, no uncertainty quantification and poor handling of conflicting tool outputs, is exactly the gap our calibrated selective-autonomy layer targets: we would add confidence scores per tool and a deferral rule at each hand-off.
papers.limitations: Sometimes fails to resolve contradictory tool outputs, especially between classification and segmentation in fine-grained visual tasks. Running many tools adds computational overhead and slower responses than end-to-end models. Lacks robust uncertainty quantification. Future work: study optimal balance of tool use, prompting for critical tool evaluation, reinforcement learning to improve reasoning and reduce hallucination, uncertainty-aware reasoning, expansion to other imaging modalities, and full clinical validation.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first set up a toolbox of existing chest X-ray models and wrapped each as a tool with a class that states its inputs, outputs and purpose. The tools were CheXagent and LLaVA-Med for visual question answering, MedSAM and a PSPNet trained on ChestX-Det for segmentation, MAIRA-2 for grounding phrases to image regions, a SwinV2-BERT model trained on 223K CheXpert Plus reports for report writing, a TorchXRayVision DenseNet-121 for 18 disease labels, RoentGen for image synthesis, and DICOM and plotting utilities. GPT-4o was the reasoning engine, run through LangChain and a LangGraph state machine on one RTX 6000 GPU. For each user question and image, the agent observes the input and memory, reasons about what is needed, then either asks the user for more input, answers, or picks tools. Tools are called with JSON arguments, independent tools run in parallel, and outputs plus thoughts are stored in memory so they are not recomputed. Tool errors come back as messages so the LLM can try another tool. A time limit tmax stops endless loops. To test it, they built ChestAgentBench. They took 675 chest cases with X-rays from Eurorad, then prompted GPT-4o to write six-choice questions for five question types that mix seven skills (detection, classification, localization, comparison, relationship, diagnosis, characterization). GPT-4o then screened each question for format, grounding and verifiability, and weak items were dropped, giving 2,500 questions. MedRAX and four baselines answered all items; the letter was extracted by regex with up to three retries. They also ran CheXbench (618 questions), MIMIC-CXR findings generation on 3,858 test images with CheXbert F1, and 114 SLAKE CXR questions. MedRAX scored 63.1% on ChestAgentBench, 68.1% on CheXbench and 90.35% on SLAKE. To adapt it for brain tumours, a student would replace the tools with MRI segmentation, grading and report models and add per-tool confidence and deferral rules.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective technical development and benchmark evaluation study. University of Toronto, Vector Institute, University Health Network and Cohere, Toronto, Canada. Uses public, de-identified case data (Eurorad) and public benchmarks. No prospective patients and no reader study.
papers.datasets: ChestAgentBench (new): 675 chest cases with CXRs and full documentation from Eurorad (European Society of Radiology peer-reviewed case database), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; 53 unique areas of interest (lung 51.2%, thorax 42.8%, mediastinum 15.8%); 55.4% male, 44.1% female, 0.45% unknown; mean age 46.0 years (SD 20.4, median 47.0); settings: ER 133 (19.7%), ICU 33 (4.9%), other 509 (75.4%); 20 findings, for example mass 26.3%, effusion 24.6%, pleural effusion 21.5%, consolidation 21.3%, nodule 17.2%, calcification 10.7%, pneumothorax 7.6%, lymphadenopathy 7.6%, pneumonia 7.2%, emphysema 7.1%, cardiomegaly 1.5%. 2,500 six-choice questions over 7 categories (detection, classification, localization, comparison, relationship, diagnosis, characterization). CheXbench subsets: 238 visual QA questions (Rad-Restruct and SLAKE) and 380 fine-grained image-text reasoning questions (OpenI). MIMIC-CXR test set: 3,858 images for single-image findings generation. SLAKE VQA: 114 English close-ended CXR test samples filtered from 2,094 SLAKE test samples. Tool training data (from cited works): CheXinstruct 8.5M samples (CheXagent), 600K PMC-15M pairs plus 60K instructions (LLaVA-Med), 1,570,263 image-mask pairs (MedSAM), ChestX-Det 3,578 NIH images with 13 classes, 223K CheXpert Plus reports, NIH/CheXpert/MIMIC-CXR/PadChest for the 18-class DenseNet-121.
papers.preprocessing: Eurorad cases were preprocessed (with help acknowledged) and filtered to cases with chest X-rays and complete clinical documentation. Questions were made by prompting GPT-4o per case and per question type (five types: detailed finding analysis, pattern recognition and relations, spatial understanding, clinical decision making, diagnostic characterization) to write a six-choice question verifiable from the case findings and discussion. GPT-4o then checked each question for six-choice structure with one correct answer, grounding in the case, and verifiability; failing questions were removed, plus a further quality check removing ungrounded or incomplete questions. Image resolution and normalisation for tools: Not reported (tools used with official configurations). No training, so no train/validation/test split; all benchmarks used as test sets.
papers.modelDetails: Algorithm 1 (ReAct): inputs are user query Q, CXR images I, tool set T, memory M and maximum time tmax. Step 0: record start time and observe Q, I and M. Loop while time is below tmax: (1) LLM reasons over state and memory; (2) if more user input is needed, return a prompt to the user; (3) if an answer can be given, return it; (4) otherwise select tools, run independent tools in parallel, add (thoughts, tools, results) to memory and observe again. If time runs out, return a timeout response. Tool calls are structured JSON with arguments such as image path and text prompt. Tool errors are returned as tool messages so the LLM can try another tool, ask the user or state limits. Memory caches tool outputs to avoid repeat work. Tools can be quantized and placed on CPU or GPU. New tools need only a class definition of input/output and capability; no retraining. Implemented as a LangGraph state machine with reasoning and action nodes and conditional edges. Value of tmax: Not reported. No confidence threshold or uncertainty-based deferral.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning of MedRAX; all tools are pre-trained models used off the shelf. Deployed on a single NVIDIA RTX 6000 GPU with GPT-4o as backbone. Answer parsing by regex to extract the letter choice; unclear responses, errors or timeouts retried up to 3 times; still-invalid answers counted wrong. Temperature, runtime per query and cost: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Four benchmarks. (1) ChestAgentBench: accuracy over 2,500 six-choice questions, reported per category and overall. (2) CheXbench: accuracy on 238 VQA (Rad-Restruct, SLAKE) and 380 OpenI fine-grained image-text reasoning questions. (3) MIMIC-CXR report generation on 3,858 test images: CheXbert-based micro F1 and macro F1 for 14 observations (mF1-14, MF1-14) and 5 key findings (cardiomegaly, edema, consolidation, atelectasis, pleural effusion; mF1-5, MF1-5). (4) SLAKE VQA on 114 CXR samples: exact-match accuracy and recall of ground-truth words. Baselines run with official implementations; literature baselines for benchmarks 3 and 4 taken from the M4CXR paper. Two qualitative case studies (Eurorad cases 17576 and 16703). No external clinical validation or radiologist comparison.
papers.baselines: Run by authors: LLaVA-Med (LLaVA-13B), CheXagent (Vicuna-13B based), GPT-4o, Llama-3.2-90B Vision. From literature (M4CXR paper): RadFM, MAIRA-1, LLaVA-Rad, Med-PaLM M 84B, M4CXR, CheXagent.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no confidence intervals, significance tests or inter-rater agreement).
papers.availability: Code and data: https://github.com/bowang-lab/MedRAX. ChestAgentBench released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

papers.title: CXRAgent: Director-Orchestrated Multi-Stage Reasoning for Chest X-Ray Interpretation
papers.authors: Lou J, Yang Y, Yu Z, Fu Z, Han W, Huang Q, Yu J
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (accepted version read: arXiv:2510.21324v2)
papers.aim: To build a chest X-ray (CXR) agent in which a central director LLM calls many CXR tools, checks each tool output against visual evidence, and then forms a virtual expert team, so that conflicting tool outputs are resolved and the final answer is evidence-backed.
papers.method: A multimodal LLM director (GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-Max) runs three stages: ReAct tool invocation with an Evidence-driven Validator (EDV) that lists supporting and refuting image evidence and rates each tool claim High, Medium or Low confidence; diagnostic planning that picks one of four collaboration modes (Skip, Relay, Dispatch, Probe); and collaborative decision-making where a recruited team of role agents answers sub-tasks before the director synthesises a final answer from team output and memory. It was tested on CheXbench, Medical-CXR-VQA and MIMIC-CXR report generation, with ablations and a blinded radiologist study.
papers.result: CXRAgent (Qwen) reached 67.0% overall accuracy on CheXbench and 75.6% on Medical-CXR-VQA; CXRAgent (GPT-4o) reached 66.3% and 71.7%. On MIMIC-CXR report generation (GPT-4o director) it got RaTEScore 0.569, GREEN 0.359, RadGraph 0.251 and LLMScore 3.267. EDV raised accuracy by 1.9 to 5.7 points under simulated 3:1 conflicting tool outputs. Five radiologists preferred CXRAgent reports on average 65.8% (completeness), 67.2% (accuracy) and 69.6% (clinical usability) of pairwise comparisons.
papers.tools: Director LLMs: GPT-4o, Qwen-VL-Max (low-temperature decoding). CXR tools: MedGemma-4B (Gemma3 with SigLIP encoder), LLaVA-Rad, CheXagent, LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-2, MedVLM-R1. ReAct framework. Hardware: two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Metrics toolkit for RaTEScore, GREEN and RadGraph-F1; GPT-4o for LLMScore and for ranking case complexity.
papers.gap: Confidence from EDV is a qualitative LLM judgement (High/Medium/Low), not a calibrated probability, and there is no formal deferral rule to a clinician. Only chest X-ray. Heavy compute and large LLM needs. No prospective or real-workflow validation.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), CXRAgent is the closest design to our planned orchestrator: a director agent that validates each tool hand-off (EDV), re-invokes alternative tools on low confidence, chooses a team mode by case difficulty, and issues a cautious interpretation that flags discrepancies for the radiologist. For brain-tumour MRI, we could reuse EDV as a hand-off check between segmentation, classification and surgical-planning agents, but replace the qualitative High/Medium/Low label with calibrated uncertainty and an explicit threshold for clinician deferral. The paper itself notes GPU and cost barriers in low-resource or rural hospitals, which supports our focus on lighter models for Sri Lanka.
papers.limitations: Multi-stage orchestration, iterative tool reasoning and EDV add computation and latency compared with single-loop agents; quantization may be needed. Needs a large multimodal LLM and several tools, with substantial GPU memory, which may not be available in low-resource or rural hospitals. Must meet regulatory needs for traceability, auditability, fail-safe mechanisms, physician oversight, privacy and stability. Failure case shows mislocalised pleural effusion and missed opacification due to overlapping appearance of pathologies. Future work: Not explicitly listed beyond these deployment challenges.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built an inference-only agent with a multimodal LLM as director (GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-Max, low temperature, on two RTX A6000 GPUs) and six existing CXR tools: MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Rad, CheXagent, LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-2 and MedVLM-R1. For each image and question, the director first runs a ReAct loop. It reasons over the image, question and a memory log, selects one or more tools, stores their outputs, and repeats until it has enough information. Every tool statement then passes through the Evidence-driven Validator. The director itself writes a short conclusion, lists image signs that support it and signs that refute it, and gives a High, Medium or Low confidence. A claim without visible support, or with clear contradiction, is marked Low and not used directly. On Low confidence the director calls a different tool with a similar job, compares tools, and, if doubt remains, writes a cautious note that flags the discrepancy for the radiologist. Next, the director plans the collaboration mode: Skip for clear cases, Relay for step-by-step refinement, Dispatch for parallel sub-tasks to role agents such as a cardiologist and pulmonologist, or Probe for targeted questions in ambiguous cases. It recruits k role agents, each with a role and mission, runs them, and synthesises a final answer from team output and memory. Evaluation used CheXbench (11 sub-tasks), 1,000 Medical-CXR-VQA questions (594 presence, 256 abnormality, 150 view) and the full MIMIC-CXR test split (3,858 reports) with RaTEScore, GREEN, RadGraph-F1 and a GPT-4o 1-5 LLMScore. Ablations removed tools, EDV, team and memory. A stress test fed 1 correct and 3 wrong tool answers. Five radiologists compared 100 blinded report pairs. CXRAgent reached 67.0% on CheXbench, 75.6% on Medical-CXR-VQA and RaTEScore 0.569. A PhD student could adapt this by using brain MRI tools and replacing the qualitative confidence label with calibrated scores and a deferral threshold.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective technical development and benchmark study with ablations plus a blinded pairwise reader study by five certified radiologists. Institutions: Hangzhou Dianzi University, Tsinghua University, Zhejiang Cancer Hospital, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen), China. Public datasets only; no prospective patients.
papers.datasets: 1) CheXbench (public): image perception and image-text reasoning tasks used: single disease identification (SDI) on MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert, multiple disease identification (MDI) on MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert, VQA on Rad-Restruct and SLAKE, fine-grained reasoning (FGR) on OpenI, binary disease classification (BDC) on CheXpert, SIIM and RSNA, view classification (VC) on MIMIC-CXR; per-task sample counts Not reported. 2) Medical-CXR-VQA: randomly sampled 594 Presence, 256 Abnormality and 150 View binary questions (1,000 total). 3) MIMIC-CXR: 377,110 CXRs with 227,835 reports; entire test split used for report generation (3,858 reports). Complexity subsets: 200 most complex and 200 simplest test cases, ranked by GPT-4o for ambiguity and complexity (complex = intricate anatomy, post-surgical hardware or ambiguous conclusions). Reader study: 100 randomly selected samples. EDV stress test: SDI task of CheXbench (MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert) with all candidate options treated as tool outputs (1 correct, 3 misleading).
papers.preprocessing: No model training, so no train/validation/test split; all data are used as test sets. Medical-CXR-VQA questions randomly sampled per official task type. Tool outputs are normalised by EDV into a common structure (conclusion, supportive evidence, refuting evidence, confidence). Image resolution and normalisation: Not reported (tools used as released). Answer extraction rules: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Stage 1, Tool invocation (ReAct): Thought_i = Plan(Log_{i-1}, I, q) decides whether more tools are needed; Action_i selects a set of tools from T (MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Rad, CheXagent, LLaVA-Med, MAIRA-2, MedVLM-R1); observations are added to the log (Log_i = Log_{i-1} U Obs_i); loop ends when enough information is gathered. Evidence-driven Validator (run by the director LLM itself, no extra vision model): for each tool statement it writes a conclusion, supportive evidence, refuting evidence and a confidence rating of High, Medium or Low. Evidence must be visible in the image, map clearly to the finding, have no clear contradiction, and be sufficient for downstream use; otherwise the statement is Low and not used directly. On Low confidence or strong refuting evidence the director (a) re-invokes an alternative tool with similar function but different architecture, (b) cross-checks tools to resolve conflict, and (c) if ambiguity remains, writes a cautious interpretation that flags discrepancies to the radiologist. Stage 2, Diagnostic planning: director chooses by in-context reasoning (no trained policy) one of Skip (clear case, no team), Relay (experts refine sequentially), Dispatch (parallel sub-tasks to domain experts, for example cardiologist and pulmonologist), Probe (targeted probing questions to each member for complex or ambiguous cases). Stage 3, Collaborative decision-making: Team = {(agent_i, role_i, mission_i)} for i = 1..k = R(I, q, s); Algorithm 1 runs the team by mode and concatenates outputs; final Diagnose(q, I, s, Memory, TeamOutput). Team size k chosen dynamically (value not fixed). Low-temperature decoding (exact value not reported).
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning; inference-only agent. Deployed on two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs with GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-Max as director via API. Low-temperature decoding to reduce run-to-run variation. Latency, cost and number of runs: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy for CheXbench tasks and Medical-CXR-VQA (average over all samples; overall = average over tasks). Report generation on the full MIMIC-CXR test split with RaTEScore (entity-level NER-based), LLMScore (GPT-4o rating 1-5 on ITU five-point scale), GREEN (LLM-based) and RadGraph-F1 (entities and relations), computed with a public toolkit. Subgroup analysis on 200 simple vs 200 complex reports. Ablations: None, Tools, Tools+EDV, Full model, for both directors; memory vs memory-less; EDV under simulated 3:1 misleading tool outputs; EDV on 200 complex cases. Significance: McNemar's test for accuracy (CheXbench, Medical-CXR-VQA) and paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for report metrics. Reader study: 5 certified radiologists, 100 random samples, blinded randomised pairwise comparison of CXRAgent vs one of MedRAX, CheXagent, MedGemma or LLaVA-Rad, with image and reference report shown; judged on completeness, accuracy and clinical utility; win and tie rates reported.
