papers.training: Only the extraction agent was trained: LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct with LoRA via PEFT on annotated plus synthetic sentences, on 8 x NVIDIA A6000 (48 GB) GPUs for about 10 hours; hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, batch size, LoRA rank) in Supplementary Table 5, not in main text. Specialist agents used zero-shot prompting with no fine-tuning. Annotation: two trained medical professionals under two physicians; Cohen's kappa 0.868 on six double-annotated patients.
papers.evaluation: Retrospective evaluation on 1000 AD cases and 3627 controls at seven horizons (-1 day, -1, -2, -3, -5, -7, -10 years). Metrics: precision, recall and F1 separately for AD cases and controls, plus overall accuracy. 95% CIs from stratified bootstrapping with 5000 iterations keeping the AD/control ratio (2.5th and 97.5th percentiles). Baseline comparison and ablation (removing one specialist at a time) at -10 years with equal LLM-call budget (six). Extraction agent evaluated against the gold-standard annotations, compared with a BERT/RoBERTa/ClinicalBERT ensemble.
papers.baselines: Single LLaMA 3 70B: zero-shot (1 call), chain-of-thought (1 call), self-consistency (6 reasoning paths), self-refine (6 rounds); AutoGen multi-agent conversation with supervisor plus five doctor agents for 1, 2 and 3 rounds (6, 12, 18 calls); random forest on TF-IDF of ICD codes, medications and abnormal labs; ensemble of BERT, RoBERTa and ClinicalBERT for extraction.
papers.results: Extraction binary: LLaMA 3.1 8B precision 0.74 (0.72-0.76), recall 0.89 (0.88-0.91), F1 0.81 (0.79-0.83), accuracy 0.93 (0.91-0.95) vs ensemble 0.71/0.84/0.77/0.91. Multi-class F1: cognitive impairment 0.79, notice/concern 0.53 (recall 0.39), requires assistance 0.67, physiological 0.75, neuropsychiatric 0.80; micro-average 0.75 (0.73-0.77), macro-average 0.76 (0.74-0.78). CARE-AD accuracy by horizon: -1 day 0.83 (0.82-0.84; AD F1 0.65, control F1 0.89); -1 y 0.76; -2 y 0.71; -3 y 0.67; -5 y 0.61; -7 y 0.58; -10 y 0.53 (0.51-0.54; AD P/R/F 0.20/0.38/0.26, control 0.77/0.57/0.65). Baselines at -10 y: zero-shot 0.26 (AD F1 0.13), CoT 0.35, self-consistency 0.43, self-refine 0.45, AutoGen 1 round 0.45, 2 rounds 0.53, 3 rounds 0.53. Ablation accuracy: exclude neurologist 0.50, psychiatrist 0.49, clinical psychologist 0.52, primary care 0.51, geriatrician 0.51. Random forest accuracy: -1 day 0.75, -1 y 0.70, -2 y 0.65, -3 y 0.53, -5 y 0.51, -7 y 0.45, -10 y 0.40.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals by stratified bootstrap (5000 iterations). Inter-annotator Cohen's kappa = 0.868. No formal hypothesis tests or p-values reported.
papers.availability: Code available on request; prompts in the supplementary material. Data: VHA data, access requires Department of Veterans Affairs approval.

papers.title: Transforming oncology clinical trial matching through neuro-symbolic, multi-agent AI and an oncology-specific knowledge graph: a prospective evaluation in 3804 patients
papers.authors: Loaiza-Bonilla A, Yost C, Kurnaz S, Tuysuz E, Thaker NG, Giritlioglu D, Noel Meza JP
papers.venue: ESMO Real World Data and Digital Oncology
papers.aim: To test prospectively whether a neuro-symbolic multi-agent AI platform with an oncology knowledge graph and human review can match cancer patients to clinical trials more accurately, faster and fairly than manual screening and LLM-only baselines.
papers.method: LLM agents extract and normalise patient data from EHR documents, and a curated oncology knowledge graph (OncoGraph) runs deterministic inclusion, exclusion and temporal rules for each patient-trial pair. A prioritisation engine ranks trials with confidence scores and sends low-confidence or conflicting pairs to clinician review. It was evaluated on 3804 consecutive US patients over 12 months against a dual-oncologist gold standard.
papers.result: F1 0.82 (95% CI about 0.81-0.83; sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.84, precision 0.81) vs GPT-4 zero-shot F1 0.47, GPT-4 chain-of-thought 0.67 and GPT-4o 0.47. Screening time fell from about 120 min to about 30 min per patient. 23,912 candidate pairs, 17,912 oncologist-confirmed matches, median time-to-recommendation under 7 days. Largest subgroup F1 gap about 7 points (white vs Black/African American). Removing the graph gave F1 0.79; a single-agent version gave 0.78.
papers.tools: OncoAgents (domain-tuned LLM agents: data extraction with OCR/layout parsing and NLP, eligibility/normalisation, trial matching); OncoGraph knowledge graph aligned to NCI Thesaurus, SNOMED CT and MeSH; OncoRecommend prioritisation engine; OncoSet curated corpus; ClinicalTrials.gov monthly ingestion; GPT-4 and GPT-4o baselines; secure on-premises or virtual private cloud deployment under HIPAA business associate agreement. Underlying LLM names for OncoAgents: Not reported.
papers.gap: Only identification efficiency measured, not consent or enrollment; single health system; commercial platform with author conflicts of interest; underlying models, prompts and code not public; no comparison with other commercial matching tools; calibration details in supplement only.
papers.relation: For O1, this is the strongest prospective, at-scale validation of a multi-agent oncology system and models how our orchestrator should be evaluated in practice. It directly implements selective autonomy: deterministic graph rules check LLM outputs, ambiguous cases become 'Requires Clinician Judgment', and an uncertainty threshold routes about 25% of pairs (about 15% flagged as low-confidence) to human review, with calibration of confidence scores. It also shows on-premises privacy-preserving deployment and pre-specified fairness alerts, which fit our Sri Lankan setting.
papers.limitations: Endpoints are identification accuracy, time, calibration and fairness, not consent, enrollment or trial completion. Evaluation within a single health system with consistent documentation; external validation across EHR vendors and sites needed. Ablations reflect this implementation only. Knowledge graph upkeep needs about 20 h/month curator plus about 4 h/month senior oncologist time. About 7-point F1 gap for Black/African American patients linked to missing documentation. Future work: multi-site validation, drift reporting across graph/model versions, end-to-end enrollment measurement, fairness-aware calibration, semi-automated ontology reconciliation.
papers.methodologyDetail: From January to December 2024 the team screened 3804 consecutive US patients with metastatic or progressive solid tumours (ECOG 0-2). Patients were screened at referral and re-screened whenever new imaging, pathology or genomic results arrived. Their records came to 157,367 pages (about 86.5 million tokens) of notes, scanned faxes, pathology and imaging reports. Step one was a data extraction agent. It ran OCR and layout parsing, then extracted tumour type and stage, prior therapy lines, biomarkers, ECOG and comorbidities into a JSON feature vector. Step two was an eligibility agent. It mapped these features to NCI Thesaurus, SNOMED CT and MeSH concepts and resolved negation and timing, such as active versus resolved pneumonitis. In parallel, curators turned ClinicalTrials.gov criteria (ingested monthly) into atomic clauses. Each clause was stored as literal text, a normalised concept and an executable rule in OncoGraph, with event nodes and interval windows (for example, last therapy at least 14 days before cycle 1 day 1). Candidate trials were first pre-filtered by histology, metastatic status, ECOG and biomarker flags. A trial-matching agent then checked each patient-trial pair against the graph rules and returned ranked trials, a confidence score and an evidence-linked rationale. OncoRecommend sent low-confidence or conflicting pairs to clinicians. The chosen uncertainty threshold focused review on the most uncertain 25% of pairs, and anything unclear was labelled 'Requires Clinician Judgment' instead of being auto-matched. Two oncologists labelled every pair independently (kappa 0.92), and missing mandatory criteria counted as not eligible. Sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 were computed on eligible and not-eligible pairs only, compared with GPT-4 zero-shot, GPT-4 CoT and GPT-4o. The authors also ran no-graph and single-agent ablations, a calibration analysis, and subgroup fairness checks with bootstrap CIs and a 10-point F1 alert threshold. Finally, they measured screening time and time-to-recommendation.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective evaluation of consecutive patients, January to December 2024, at US academic-community sites (St. Luke's University Health Network and Massive Bio, Inc.), with dual-oncologist gold-standard labelling; CONSORT-AI aligned reporting; patients re-screened as new data arrived.
papers.datasets: Prospective cohort: 3804 consecutive patients with metastatic or progressive solid tumours, ECOG 0-2, balanced for cancer-type incidence; broad eligibility (active/progressing disease, candidates for further therapy). Documents: 157,367 clinical pages, about 86.5 million tokens, mixed modalities (structured notes, scanned PDFs/faxes, pathology reports, imaging impressions); median about 23,000 tokens per patient. 23,912 candidate patient-trial pairs generated. Trial library: open interventional phase I-III trials recruiting locally plus nationwide referral trials for rare molecular subtypes, updated regularly. OncoSet development corpus: more than 2000 annotated records, more than 14,000 trials, more than 50 tumour subtypes (used for development, few-shot prompting and calibration only). Gold-standard labels per pair: Eligible, Not Eligible, Requires Clinician Judgment; undocumented mandatory criteria labelled Not Eligible; undated ambiguous temporal references flagged Requires Clinician Judgment. Subgroup sizes in Supplementary Table S5 (not in main text).
papers.preprocessing: OCR and layout parsing of scanned documents; NLP extraction to a structured JSON 'OncoSet feature vector' (tumour type/stage, prior therapy, biomarkers, ECOG, comorbidities); normalisation to canonical ontologies with negation and temporality resolution. Trial criteria parsed by pattern rules plus LLM-assisted extraction into atomic clauses stored at three levels (literal text, normalised concept, executable graph rule); lab thresholds normalised to common units; temporal constraints as event nodes with interval windows anchored to screening date. Candidate trials pre-filtered by site/histology, metastatic status, ECOG and key biomarker flags. Split: '80% of cases used for training and internal validation (10% split), 20% held out for testing'; prospective cohort stated to be held out from prompt engineering and calibration. Prompt templates, token limits and temperature in Supplementary Methods.
papers.modelDetails: Neuro-symbolic architecture with four parts. (1) OncoAgents: Data extraction agent (OCR/layout + NLP, outputs JSON); Eligibility agent (maps features to ontologies, resolves negation and active vs remote status, produces graph-aligned features); Trial-matching agent (evaluates patient representation against OncoGraph inclusion/exclusion logic, returns ranked trials with reasoning). Agents exchange structured messages with chain-of-thought to detect conflicts and estimate uncertainty. (2) OncoGraph: nodes for tumour subtypes, genomic alterations, biomarkers, drug classes, comorbidities and trials; edges 'requires', 'excludes', 'contraindicated-with', 'progressed-after'; negations and exceptions as exclusion/override edges; monthly ClinicalTrials.gov ingestion; version-controlled; unresolved ambiguity routed to Requires Clinician Judgment instead of permissive auto-match. Example: interval rules such as last systemic therapy >= 14 days and prior PD-1 therapy >= 28 days before cycle 1 day 1 are evaluated as Boolean checks. (3) OncoRecommend: ingests new EHR data, queries OncoGraph, ranks trials by relevance and fit, returns confidence scores and short evidence-linked rationales; low-confidence or conflicting evidence (about 15% of pairs) triggers prioritised human review; selected high-uncertainty threshold sends the top about 25% most uncertain pairs to reviewers. (4) OncoSet: curated corpus for training and calibration. Final eligibility always confirmed by oncologist review.
papers.training: OncoAgents described as domain-tuned and trained/calibrated on OncoSet; few-shot prompting. Optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size, model sizes and hardware: Not reported (prompt and temperature settings in supplement). Compute cost estimated at low single-digit dollars per patient. Knowledge graph maintenance about 20 h/month curator plus about 4 h/month senior oncologist.
papers.evaluation: Unit of analysis: patient-trial pair. Gold standard by two board-certified medical oncologists reviewing the full EHR independently (Cohen's kappa = 0.92, disagreements by consensus). Metrics: sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 over Eligible/Not Eligible pairs; Requires Clinician Judgment pairs excluded from binary F1 and described separately. Calibration of eligibility confidence scores (reliability across bins), workload-sensitivity trade-off by varying uncertainty threshold. Operational: per-patient screening time, time-to-recommendation (T0 prescreen to T1 oncologist-validated list). Fairness: subgroup metrics by age, sex, race, ethnicity with nonparametric bootstrap 95% CIs; pre-specified alert if absolute F1 gap > 10 points. Error analysis on discordant pairs. Ablations: no-graph, single-agent, no uncertainty triage. Manual screening used as workflow reference, not as an F1 comparator.
papers.baselines: Manual coordinator/oncologist screening (workflow reference); GPT-4 zero-shot; GPT-4 chain-of-thought (two-step extract then reason); GPT-4o frontier model (also a retrieval-augmented variant); ablations without OncoGraph and with a single-agent pipeline.
papers.results: Held-out test set: multi-agent system sensitivity 0.8375, specificity 0.8359, precision 0.8121, F1 0.8246 (95% CI about 0.81-0.85 in text; 0.81-0.83 in abstract). GPT-4 zero-shot sensitivity 0.48, specificity 0.50, precision 0.47, F1 0.47. GPT-4 CoT 0.67, 0.69, 0.66, F1 0.67. GPT-4o matching accuracy 0.47. Ablation: no-graph F1 0.79; single-agent F1 0.78. Operational: 3804 patients, 23,912 candidate pairs, 17,912 confirmed matches, median time-to-recommendation < 7 days (IQR 3-9 days); per-patient time about 120 min manual vs about 30 min (15 automated + 15 clinician). Extraction fidelity > 95% for internal EHR, about 89% for external scanned referrals. Fairness: no subgroup gap > 10 F1 points; largest about 7 points (white vs Black/African American); Black/African American patients had 12% higher rate of missing structured staging. Error modes: complex temporal logic 32%, missing structured data 28%, ambiguity and negation 18%, extraction/OCR artifacts 12%, ontology mismatch 10%. Calibration near-optimal in typical thresholds, mild underconfidence in low bins and modest overconfidence at extremes.
papers.statistics: Cohen's kappa = 0.92 for gold standard. 95% CI for F1 (about 0.81-0.83/0.85). Nonparametric bootstrap 95% CIs for subgroup metrics; bootstrap comparisons suggested some subgroup gaps may be significant (p-values not reported). Calibration curves in supplement.
papers.availability: Not available (commercial platform by Massive Bio, Inc.; prompts and settings described in supplement; no code or data release reported).

papers.title: Agentic systems in computational pathology: architectures, evidence, and translational challenges
papers.authors: Lu X, Li Q, Gao Y, Dong W, Lyu M, Ma S, Li J, Wu Y, Cai L, Zhang T, Lyu S, Liu Z, Liu H, Luo S
papers.aim: To review agentic AI systems in computational pathology, classify them with an operational taxonomy, and judge their evidence, costs, risks and the conditions for safe clinical translation.
papers.method: Narrative review that classifies systems on three operational dimensions: dynamic control flow (D), inference-time tool selection (T) and external knowledge integration (K), each coded Yes/Partial/No, plus the Gao et al. Level 0-3 autonomy scale. It tabulates 17 agentic or agent-assisted systems and 14 non-agentic comparators by validation scope, publication status and reported inference cost. It then discusses diagnosis, prognosis, therapy support, technical, regulatory, ethical and workforce issues.
papers.result: Agentic systems show technical feasibility but no proven clinical benefit; most are retrospective prototypes at autonomy Level 1 or Level 1-2, and none had regulatory clearance for autonomous diagnosis. Only one prospective study (multi-agent trial matching, 3804 patients, F1 0.82) was found. Examples: WSI-Agents 10-17% higher scores on WSI-Bench/WSI-VQA; Renal-Agent kappa 0.73 over 16 Banff scores; SurvAgent C-index 0.713 vs 0.706 MOTCat; Ferber agent tool use raised complete answers from 30.3% to 87.2%; PathAgent accuracy rose from 56.32% to 68.10% with pathologist intervention. A clinical agent benchmark showed non-significant 0.5-8.9% gains at 10-100x token cost and 2-3x latency.
papers.tools: Review; systems discussed include PathAgent (PLIP navigator, Patho-R1 perceptor, Qwen3 executor), TissueLab, Biomni (150 tools, 105 packages, 59 databases), PathChat, CPathAgent, SurvAgent, Ferber Clinical Agent (pathology ViT, MedSAM, OncoKB), MEREDITH, TxAgent, Microsoft Healthcare Agent Orchestrator (TBFact), WSI-Agents, Renal-Agent, AgentMRI, AutoBA, Pathology-o3, STAgent, PhenoGraph; foundation models Virchow, UNI, PAMA, MUSK; RAG, knowledge graphs (ESCARGOT), conformal prediction; reporting guides TRIPOD+AI, STARD-AI, CLAIM, SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI.
papers.gap: No prospective pathology cohort studies, few matched ablations separating agentic organisation from backbone and data, poor reporting of latency and cost, no measure of rationale faithfulness, calibration only possible at tool outputs not full reasoning trajectories, and unresolved accountability and change control for agent updates.
papers.relation: For O1, this review gives a clear test for whether our brain-tumour orchestrator is truly agentic (D/T/K coding and Level 0-3 autonomy) and argues that a pathology agent should use bounded, verifiable specialist tools with orchestration only where evidence must be assembled. Its closed-loop / semi-verifiable / open-ended task stratification and the positive-uncertain-negative routing match our calibrated selective-autonomy idea, where ambiguous cases are sent to clinicians. It also notes that most federated computational pathology studies are simulated and that real deployment takes weeks, which is relevant to our privacy-preserving design. Its glioma example (WHO 2021 classification with external AUC 92.61-96.30%) is a non-agentic comparator we can cite.
papers.limitations: Narrative (not systematic) review with no stated search strategy, PRISMA flow or risk-of-bias tool; D/T/K coding is the authors' judgement and some assignments are contestable; evidence base is mostly preprints and retrospective benchmarks; reported costs are not comparable. Future directions stated: pathology-specific adaptation with calibrated uncertainty and prospective external validation (short term), knowledge-graph reasoning with SNOMED CT/ICD-O (medium term), general planning plus pathology tools and multicentre prospective trials with lifecycle change control (long term).
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review, so the method is the authors' classification and appraisal scheme rather than an experiment. First, they defined an operational test for 'agentic'. A system is coded on three dimensions, each as Yes, Partial or No. D (dynamic control flow) asks whether intermediate findings change later steps. T (inference-time tool selection) asks whether the reasoning module, not a fixed pipeline, picks an external model or resource. K (knowledge integration) asks whether it retrieves evidence beyond the primary input. Each system also got an autonomy level on the Gao et al. scale: 0 non-agentic, 1 runs a human-set task, 2 picks its own subtasks and tools, 3 creates hypotheses. Level 2 was given only when task decomposition and tool choice really changed at inference. Second, they applied this to 17 systems described as agentic (Table 2), recording publication status, validation scope and any reported inference cost. They applied it to 14 strong non-agentic comparators (Table 3), with reasons for each classification, and to six common benchmarks (Table 4), with their limits. Third, they went through the evidence by use case (diagnosis, prognosis, therapy support), extracting the reported numbers. They noted that most gains cannot be attributed to agentic design, because baselines differ in backbone, data and inference budget. Fourth, they analysed translation barriers: data heterogeneity, hallucination (for example 1.47% of statements, 44% of them major), cost and latency (agents used 10-100x more tokens for non-significant gains), drift, regulation (FDA, EU, IMDRF, UK, Australia, Japan, China), privacy and federated learning, prompt-injection security, bias, patient consent and workforce training. Finally, they proposed a bounded deployment rule. Agents may run verifiable closed-loop tasks, may assemble evidence without forcing a label in semi-verifiable tasks such as grading, and must leave open-ended diagnostic conclusions to pathologists. Calibration and human review are placed at tool outputs and final claims. A PhD student can reuse the D/T/K coding and the three-tier task stratification to design and justify the autonomy limits of a pathology agent.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review with an operational taxonomy; authors from Shanghai Eastern Hepatobiliary Surgery Hospital, Nanyang Technological University, Fudan University Huashan Hospital, National University of Singapore, PuzzleLogic Pte Ltd and UC San Diego. No primary data; ethics not applicable.
papers.datasets: No primary data. Datasets and benchmarks reviewed: Camelyon16 (WSI metastasis detection), PathVQA (patch-level VQA), WSI-VQA, WSI-Caption, PathMMU, SlideBench-VQA, WSI-Bench, TCGA cohorts (e.g., five for SurvAgent, 31 cancers for CATfusion), Renal-Agent cohorts of 15,000 MGB biopsies and 1,200 AUSCAD biopsies, Pathology-CoT corpus of 10.6 h from eight pathologists and 5,222 dialogue rounds, Virchow trained on about 1.5 million WSIs, UNI on more than 100 million patches, 105-case HCC blinded evaluation, 112 breast-cancer board cases, 59 MEREDITH variant assessments, 71 oncology cases for TBFact. Search databases, dates and number of screened records: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Classification procedure: each system coded Yes/Partial/No for D (intermediate findings change later steps), T (reasoner chooses a tool at inference) and K (retrieves evidence beyond the primary input); autonomy Level 2 assigned only when task decomposition and tool selection vary at inference. Data-level issues discussed: stain normalisation, scanner variation, DICOM for WSI, CLEARR-AI dataset reporting.
papers.modelDetails: Reviewed architecture pattern: an LLM controller/planner decomposes tasks, selects and calls specialist perception tools (segmentation, cell counting, biomarker prediction), retrieves evidence (RAG, guidelines, knowledge graphs), verifies outputs and updates the plan, with outputs linked to image regions and sources for pathologist review. Examples: PathAgent Navigator-Perceptor-Executor loop with case-dependent region selection and reflection (D Partial, T Partial, K No, Level 1-2); WSI-Agents fixed task-allocation, verification and summarisation stages; SurvAgent hierarchical agents for multi-scale WSI, gene-set processing, retrieval and inference; TissueLab LLM orchestrator with tool factory and clinician feedback. Safety design recommended: pathologist can accept, amend, reject or escalate each conclusion, with disposition logged to the LIS; calibration applied at specialist-tool outputs and final claims (conformal prediction for fixed predictors); positive-uncertain-negative buffer zones for borderline cases; bounded deployment where agents do verified closed-loop tasks, assemble evidence without forcing labels in semi-verifiable tasks, and leave open-ended conclusions to humans. Security: separate instructions from retrieved data, least-privilege tool credentials, human confirmation of write actions, attributable logging.
papers.training: Not applicable (review). Reported compute examples: SurvAgent inference on 4 x RTX A6000 (48 GB); HCC framework training on RTX 4090 (24 GB), i9 CPU, 128 GB RAM; AgentMRI 28.48-36.99 s per case; AutoBA 3-18 min on A100 workstation; Pathology-o3 US$0.02-0.12 per slide and 5.8-13.4 s per image; TissueLab workflow generation < 60 min, feedback update < 10 s. Federated learning: 13 of 15 computational-pathology studies were simulated; a real multi-institution study needed weeks of network setup and runs up to 25 days; FeTS deployment across 32 institutions took weeks.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable as primary study. The review assesses each system's validation scope (retrospective benchmark, internal vs external cohort, prospective), publication status (preprint, conference, journal) and reported inference cost. Recommends Evans et al. six-level evaluation (technical, diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic thinking, therapeutic decisions, patient outcomes, socioeconomic), matched ablations with equal backbones, data and inference budgets, reporting of model calls, hardware, latency, GPU-hours and per-case cost, rationale faithfulness metrics, subgroup reporting by site/scanner/stain, and DECIDE-AI for early clinical studies.
papers.baselines: Not applicable. Non-agentic comparators discussed: Graham colon-biopsy screening, glioma WHO 2021 foundation-model MIL, PDAC hybrid simulation, prostate GCN grading, stKeep, Lunit SCOPE IO, LLM-guided multimodal MIL, MUSK, CATfusion, Brim, Claude spatial analysis, general LLM breast-cancer evaluation, PRISM/OncoLLM, Morpheus.
papers.results: Reported figures from reviewed studies: WSI-Agents 10-17% higher than WSI-LLaVA, MDAgents and Med-Agents; Renal-Agent mean quadratic-weighted kappa 0.73 over 16 Banff scores, balanced accuracy 0.97 for rejection subtype; PathAgent accuracy 56.32% to 68.10% with pathologist intervention; Ferber agent tool-use accuracy 87.5%, conclusions correct 91.0%, guideline citation accuracy 75.5%, complete answers 30.3% (GPT-4 alone) to 87.2%; MEREDITH 94.7% concordance in 59 variant assessments; SurvAgent C-index 0.713 vs MOTCat 0.706; CATfusion C-index 0.668 (31 TCGA cancers); Brim 0.682 (12 cancers); TissueLab colon tumour-cell accuracy near zero to 94.9% (IoU 10.1% to 88.9%) after 10-30 min feedback; Pathology-o3 precision 84.5%, recall 100% vs OpenAI o3 46.7%/87.5%, external recall 97.6%; Virchow AUC 0.950 pan-cancer, 0.937 rare cancer; UNI 96.3% NSCLC subtyping; glioma classification external AUC 92.61-96.30%; AgentMRI ECE 0.248 to 0.069; AutoBA 90% planning, 87.5% execution; trial-matching agent F1 0.82 (95% CI 0.81-0.83) in 3804 patients; TBFact 84% recall in 71 cases; breast board LLMs appropriate 86.6% (Claude 3 Opus), 85.7% (GPT-4 Turbo), 75.0% (Llama 3 70B). Medical image multi-agent systematic review: 84.8% empirical calibration, 72.7% simple reactive agents. Hallucination 1.47% of statements in a documentation study, 44% of them major.
papers.statistics: Not applicable (review; no pooled statistics). Cited values include Spearman rho = 0.917 between physician expertise and error detection, and drift-triggered updating Delta AUROC 0.44 (SD 0.02; p = 0.007).
papers.availability: Not applicable (review; data availability 'Not applicable'). Article is CC BY 4.0.

papers.title: ED-triage-agent: a multi-agent framework for human-in-the-loop emergency triage
papers.authors: Sharma K, Sivadas H, Edwards C, Gunja N, Reddy S
papers.aim: To build a multi-agent LLM system that supports Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage in two stages (before and after vital signs) while the clinician keeps the final decision.
papers.method: An orchestrator agent built with LangGraph routes work between four GPT-4.1 agents: intake interview, clinical reasoning with RAG over the ESI handbook, pre-vital priority assessment, and final triage classification. A weighted confidence score is computed, and when it is below 0.7 the system raises the acuity by one level. The system was tested in simulation on 60 ESI Handbook v4 cases with simulated patient and clinician agents.
papers.result: Phase 1 (symptoms only): exact ESI match 66.67% (95% CI 55.00-78.33%), within +/-1 level 95.00%, high/low priority accuracy 86.67%, high-priority sensitivity 87.18% (34/39), specificity 85.71%. Phase 2 (with vitals): exact match 80.00% (95% CI 70.00-92.35%), within +/-1 98.33%, high-acuity (ESI 1-2) sensitivity 92.31% (24/26), undertriage 0.00%, overtriage 1.67% (1/60). Mean end-to-end latency 48.95 s. Cost about $0.76 per 100 encounters (20,563 tokens/case).
papers.tools: LangGraph; OpenAI GPT-4.1-mini (orchestrator, clinical reasoning, priority and classification agents) and GPT-4.1-nano (patient intake agent and simulated patient/clinician) via Azure OpenAI API, temperature 0; ChromaDB vector store; OpenAI text-embedding-3-small; PubMed API; SQLite audit log; clinician dashboard. Code: https://github.com/Karthick47v2/ED-Triage-Agent.
papers.gap: Only simulated vignettes were used. There is no prospective test in a real emergency department, no real patients, no demographic or equity analysis, no multilingual or speech input, and the confidence weights are heuristic, not learned or calibrated on data.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this is a close template: a deterministic orchestrator routes tasks to specialist agents, uses RAG grounding, logs every step for audit, and has a clear confidence threshold rule. When confidence is low the system acts conservatively and the clinician must accept every recommendation. We can adapt the same pattern for brain-tumour diagnosis and surgical planning: a threshold-based deferral rule (here 0.7) tuned so that no dangerous errors occur, a sensitivity analysis of the threshold, and override logging to support clinician validation.
papers.limitations: Authors state that simulated patients and handbook cases do not capture real communication (health literacy, accents, distress), may over-represent clear cases, and ground-truth labels are single expert labels. Feasibility is shown, not clinical utility. Future work: prospective multi-site ED evaluation, equity monitoring, FHIR/EHR integration, speech-to-text and multilingual intake, better resource counting and age-aware vital sign interpretation.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors take the 60 standard case studies from the ESI Implementation Handbook v4 (30 practice, 30 competency; ESI-1 to ESI-5 = 12, 14, 13, 10, 11 cases). The same handbook is cut into overlapping text chunks, embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and stored in ChromaDB for retrieval. The system is built in LangGraph as a fixed workflow. An Orchestrator Agent (GPT-4.1-mini) holds the session state and calls four agents in order. In Phase 1, the Intake Interview Agent (GPT-4.1-nano) interviews a simulated patient (also GPT-4.1-nano, reading the vignette) using an OLDCARTS structure and stops early if emergency signs appear, which triggers a direct clinician alert. The Clinical Reasoning Agent (GPT-4.1-mini) builds a differential and retrieves the top-5 handbook passages by cosine similarity, plus PubMed when needed. The Priority Assessment Agent gives a tentative ESI and a HIGH (ESI 1-3) or LOW (ESI 4-5) queue priority. In Phase 2, a simulated clinician agent supplies vital signs and findings. The Triage Classification Agent applies the ESI algorithm and computes confidence as 0.5 x vital confidence + 0.3 x symptom confidence + 0.2 x guideline confidence. If this is below 0.7, the predicted ESI is moved one level more urgent (minimum ESI-1). All prompts use JSON output schemas and safety rules, temperature is 0, and every step is logged in SQLite. The clinician must accept or override each output. Each case is run once and compared with the handbook label. Metrics are exact and +/-1 accuracy, priority sensitivity and specificity, ESI 1-2 sensitivity, undertriage and overtriage (2 or more levels off), and latency, with 95% CIs from 1000 bootstrap resamples. Five weight sets and three thresholds (0.6, 0.7, 0.8) are compared; 0.7 is chosen as the lowest threshold giving zero undertriage. Final results: Phase 1 priority sensitivity 87.18%, Phase 2 exact accuracy 80.00%, undertriage 0%, about 49 s per patient. A PhD student can copy this design by replacing ESI with a tumour-grade or referral scale and tuning the deferral threshold to reach zero critical misses.
papers.studyDesign: Technical development and retrospective simulation-based evaluation on standardized published vignettes. Authors at Queensland University of Technology (Australia) and collaborators (USA, Australia). No real patients and no prospective study.
papers.datasets: ESI Implementation Handbook v4 (AHRQ, 2012) case studies, text vignettes, N = 60: 30 practice cases and 30 competency cases. ESI distribution (practice/competency/total): ESI-1 6/6/12 (20.00%); ESI-2 8/6/14 (23.33%); ESI-3 6/7/13 (21.67%); ESI-4 4/6/10 (16.67%); ESI-5 6/5/11 (18.33%). Chief complaints: chest pain/cardiac 2, abdominal pain 9, respiratory 3, trauma/injury 14, neurological 9, other 23. The same handbook is also the RAG corpus. Inclusion/exclusion: all 60 handbook cases used; no other criteria reported.
papers.preprocessing: ESI handbook split into overlapping chunks (chunk size and overlap not reported), embedded with text-embedding-3-small and stored in ChromaDB. For each case, a simulated patient agent (GPT-4.1-nano) answers intake questions from the vignette with natural wording variation; after Phase 1 a simulated clinician agent (GPT-4.1-nano) extracts vital signs and physical findings for Phase 2. No training, so no train/validation/test split; all 60 cases are used as the test set. No image data.
papers.modelDetails: Orchestrator Agent (GPT-4.1-mini) keeps session state, routes data and applies an urgency bypass: if the Intake Interview Agent flags high-acuity signs, the patient is sent straight to a clinician. Intake Interview Agent (GPT-4.1-nano) runs an OLDCARTS-style interview (onset, location, duration, character, aggravating/alleviating, radiation, timing, severity), history, medications, allergies, with early question truncation when emergency signs are found; outputs JSON. Clinical Reasoning Agent (GPT-4.1-mini) makes a differential diagnosis, retrieves top-5 ESI handbook passages by cosine similarity, and can query PubMed. Priority Assessment Agent (GPT-4.1-mini) gives a tentative ESI with a confidence interval and a HIGH/LOW queue priority (High = ESI 1-3). Triage Classification Agent (GPT-4.1-mini) applies the ESI algorithm and outputs final ESI, confidence, criterion-linked rationale and uncertainty flags. Confidence: C_final = 0.5*C_vital + 0.3*C_symptom + 0.2*C_guideline (weights sum to 1, heuristic priors). Deferral/safety rule: if C_final < 0.7, ESI_recommended = max(1, ESI_predicted - 1), i.e. one level more urgent. Thresholds 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 tested. Fail-safe: ESI 1-2 triggers nursing alerts; component failure falls back to manual triage. Clinician must accept every recommendation; overrides captured with optional rationale. Prompts use JSON schemas, role/scope limits, and safety instructions (defer to clinician, avoid hallucination). Temperature 0.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning. Pre-trained GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-4.1-nano used through Azure OpenAI API at temperature 0. Hardware not reported. Mean token use 20,563 tokens per case.
papers.evaluation: Simulation protocol following AgentClinic: each of 60 cases run end to end and compared with handbook ground-truth ESI. Phase 1 metrics: tentative ESI exact match, within +/-1 accuracy, binary priority accuracy, sensitivity and specificity (High = ESI 1-3, Low = ESI 4-5). Phase 2 metrics: exact match, within +/-1, per-class accuracy, ESI 1-2 detection sensitivity and specificity, undertriage and overtriage rates (error of 2 or more levels). Latency mean, median and 95th percentile. Results stratified by practice vs competency cases. 95% CIs by case-level non-parametric bootstrap with 1000 resamples. Sensitivity analysis of 5 weight settings and 3 thresholds. Error analysis of all 12 Phase 2 errors. No human reader study and no external validation.
papers.baselines: No direct experimental baseline. Compared in text with prior work: classical ML triage (70-85% accuracy), clinician accuracy of 59% from literature, TRIAGEAGENT and HEAL multi-agent systems (not re-run).
papers.results: Phase 1 combined: exact 66.67% [55.00, 78.33]; within +/-1 95.00% [88.33, 100]; priority accuracy 86.67% [76.67, 95.00]; sensitivity 87.18% [76.86, 97.44]; specificity 85.71% [66.67, 100]. Practice/competency exact 66.67%/66.67%; priority accuracy 90.00%/83.33%. Phase 2 combined: exact 80.00% [70.00, 92.35]; within +/-1 98.33% [95.33, 100]; ESI 1-2 sensitivity 92.31% [80.77, 100]; specificity 82.35% [67.65, 94.12]; undertriage 0.00%; overtriage 1.67% [0, 3.33]. Practice exact 86.67% [73.33, 96.67] vs competency 73.33% [56.67, 86.67]; practice sensitivity 100% vs competency 83.33%. Per class: ESI-1 100%, ESI-2 85.71%, ESI-3 61.54%, ESI-4 90.00%, ESI-5 63.64% (4/11 over-triaged to ESI-4). Latency: Phase 1 mean 36.14 s (median 36.88, p95 47.17); Phase 2 13.70 s (13.17, 17.32); end to end 48.95 s (49.08, 60.25). Weight sensitivity: baseline 0.5/0.3/0.2 = 80.00%; vital-heavy 0.6/0.25/0.15 = 81.67%; symptom-heavy 0.25/0.6/0.15 = 78.33%; guideline-heavy 0.25/0.25/0.5 = 80.00%; balanced 0.33/0.33/0.34 = 78.33%; range 3.34 pp, undertriage 0 in all. Threshold: 0.6 = 83.33% with 1 undertriage; 0.7 = 80.00%, 0 undertriage, 1 overtriage; 0.8 = 71.67%, 0 undertriage, 3 overtriage.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals from 1000 case-level bootstrap resamples. No hypothesis tests or p-values. No inter-rater agreement.
papers.availability: Code and evaluation framework: https://github.com/Karthick47v2/ED-Triage-Agent. Data: ESI Implementation Handbook v4 (public, AHRQ Publication No. 12-0014).

papers.title: Evaluating large language model workflows in clinical decision support for triage and referral and diagnosis
papers.authors: Gaber F, Shaik M, Allega F, Bilecz AJ, Busch F, Goon K, Franke V, Akalin A
papers.aim: To benchmark several Claude LLMs and a RAG-assisted LLM workflow on predicting triage level (ESI), specialty referral and diagnosis from real emergency department cases, for a patient-type user and a clinician-type user.
papers.method: 2000 cases were curated from MIMIC-IV-ED and MIMIC-IV-Note (history of present illness, demographics, and for clinicians also initial vital signs). Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and a RAG workflow (Claude 3.5 Sonnet with query decomposition, 30 million PubMed abstracts and a critique-refine loop) predicted ESI, top-3 specialties and top-3 diagnoses. Specialty ground truth and diagnosis matching were done by Claude 3.5 Sonnet and checked by four clinicians on 400 cases.
papers.result: Triage exact match was best for the RAG-assisted LLM (64.10% general user, 65.75% clinical user); triage range accuracy was best for Claude 3.5 Sonnet (82.80% / 82.40%). Specialty 'at least one' accuracy up to 88.55% and diagnosis 'at least one' up to 82.10% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, clinical user). Clinicians rated 81.5% of LLM-made specialty labels correct and 97.03% acceptable. LLM-judge agreement with clinicians was 95.62% (union) and 70.74% (intersection) for Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
papers.tools: Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3 Haiku accessed through AWS (AWS PrivateLink) to meet MIMIC privacy rules; RAG pipeline with an embedding vector database of 30 million PubMed abstracts (embedding model not reported); LLM-as-judge (Claude 3.5 Sonnet); Python data processing. Code: https://github.com/BIMSBbioinfo/medLLMbenchmark.
papers.gap: Single run per case, only Claude models, one US hospital dataset, no ESI 5 cases, no uncertainty or deferral mechanism, no prospective study, and specialty ground truth was itself LLM-generated. Combining models (mixture of experts) and knowing when each model is reliable was suggested but not tested.
papers.relation: For O1, this paper shows how to compare single-model and staged (RAG plus critique-refine) workflows across a care pathway (triage, referral, diagnosis), and how adding clinical data changes results. It also gives a reusable design for clinician validation: two pairs of clinicians each rating 200 cases on a 4-level scale, plus union and intersection agreement with an LLM judge. The private-connection approach (AWS PrivateLink) is relevant to our privacy needs. The finding that models disagree on different cases supports routing and model-selection logic in our orchestrator, and the lack of a deferral rule is a gap our calibrated selective autonomy can fill.
papers.limitations: Authors note: no model achieved high accuracy for the most severe triage levels; clinical notes may add bias because triage is done before full assessment; prompt design strongly affects results; only one run per case; specialty ground truth made by an LLM; diagnosis needs more information than is available at arrival. Not proposed for direct deployment; would be high-risk under the EU AI Act. Future work: better numeric handling of lab values, study of how clinicians set ESI, refined RAG, newer reasoning models, integration into clinical workflows.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team builds a test set from MIMIC-IV. They join MIMIC-IV-ED 2.2 triage and edstays tables, age from the MIMIC-IV patients table, and discharge notes from MIMIC-IV-Note using stay_id. They keep the first record per stay (seq_num = 1), drop duplicates, missing triage and deceased patients, and keep stays shorter than one day. From each discharge note they cut out only the history of present illness (HPI), keeping texts of 50 to 2000 characters and removing those mentioning 'ED' or 'ER'. They also extract the primary diagnosis list and drop cases with more than 15 diagnoses. This gives 2000 cases. Each case is given in two forms: a general user form (HPI, age, gender, race) and a clinical user form (plus temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and blood pressure). Four systems are run once each at temperature 0 through AWS PrivateLink: Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and a RAG workflow. The RAG workflow splits the query into sub-queries, finds similar PubMed abstracts from a 30-million-abstract vector index, writes an answer with references, then runs a critique and refine loop. Each system outputs one ESI level, three specialties and three diagnoses. Because MIMIC has no specialty label, Claude 3.5 Sonnet assigns a specialty to each true diagnosis. Triage is scored by exact match and by a range rule (correct or one level more urgent). Specialty is scored by matches divided by the shorter list length, and by 'at least one' match. Diagnoses are judged by Claude 3.5 Sonnet as same or broader category. Four clinicians in Italy, Germany and the USA check 400 cases in two pairs of 200, rating specialty labels and diagnoses on four-level scales. Union and intersection agreement with the LLM judge are reported. Best triage exact match was 65.75% (RAG, clinical user). Best triage range accuracy was 82.80% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet). The union agreement of 95.62% supports using an LLM judge with clinician checks.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmarking study on de-identified EHR data from MIMIC-IV (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, USA). Authors from Max Delbrück Center Berlin (Germany) with clinician reviewers from Policlinico Gemelli Rome (Italy), TUM Klinikum rechts der Isar Munich (Germany) and University of Chicago (USA).
papers.datasets: Curated MIMIC-ED dataset of 2000 cases built from MIMIC-IV-ED 2.2 (triage, edstays files), MIMIC-IV (patients file, for age) and MIMIC-IV-Note (discharge notes) from PhysioNet. Modality: text (history of present illness), demographics (age, gender, race), initial vital signs (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure). Labels: ESI triage level (acuity) from MIMIC; primary diagnoses from discharge notes; specialty created by Claude 3.5 Sonnet. ESI distribution shown only in a figure: mostly level 3, then level 2, few level 1 and level 4, no level 5 (exact counts not in text). Inclusion: seq_num = 1, triage data present, HPI present with 50-2000 characters, stay less than 1 day, up to 15 primary diagnoses. Exclusion: duplicates, missing triage, patients who died, HPIs mentioning 'ED' or 'ER', more than 15 primary diagnoses. Reader-study subset: 400 cases.
papers.preprocessing: Discharge notes linked to ED stays by stay_id; triage, demographics and vital signs merged; duplicates dropped; only seq_num = 1 kept; missing triage removed; deceased excluded. HPI paragraph extracted from discharge notes, other note text discarded; HPI kept if 50-2000 characters; entries mentioning 'ED' or 'ER' removed. Primary diagnosis list extracted; cases with more than 15 primary diagnoses removed. Two input versions: general user (HPI + patient info) and clinical user (plus initial vitals). Prompts were tuned on a separate subset not used in evaluation (size not reported). No training, so no train/test split; all 2000 cases form the test set.
papers.modelDetails: Stand-alone LLMs: Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, each prompted with a system role ('You are an experienced healthcare professional with expertise in medical and clinical domains'), task instructions, case data and answers inside fixed tags. Separate prompts for triage, for specialty plus diagnosis together, for ground-truth specialty generation, and for the LLM judge. RAG-assisted LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet): (1) query decomposition into sub-queries; (2) embedding of sub-queries and semantic similarity search over 30 million PubMed abstract embeddings; (3) answer generation using retrieved abstracts with PubMed references; (4) iterative critique, refinement and re-retrieval loop where an LLM judges whether the answer is sufficient. Number of retrieved documents and loop iterations not reported. Outputs: one ESI level, top-3 specialties, top-3 diagnoses. No uncertainty estimate or deferral rule. Temperature 0.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning. Temperature 0; outputs were identical across repeated runs in prompt experiments, so each final prediction was run once. Models accessed through AWS PrivateLink. Hardware, cost and runtime not reported.
papers.evaluation: Triage: exact-match accuracy, and range accuracy where a prediction is correct if equal to or one level more severe than truth (truth 1 must be 1). Specialty: 'matched' score = number of correct predicted specialties divided by the length of the shorter list (truth or prediction), averaged over patients; and 'at least one' match. Diagnosis: Claude 3.5 Sonnet judge returns True if a predicted diagnosis matches or falls in a broader category of a true primary diagnosis; same two scores. Inter-model agreement for triage and specialty. Reader study: 4 clinicians, 400 of 2000 cases, each clinician 200 cases; clinicians 1 and 2 share one subset, 3 and 4 another. Specialty labels rated Correct / Partially Correct / Reasonable but Suboptimal / Incorrect. Diagnoses (clinical-user outputs of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and RAG LLM) rated Exact Match / Clinically Equivalent / Clinically Related / Incorrect; LLM True mapped to the first two. Agreement reported per clinician and as union (at least one of the pair agrees) and intersection (both agree). No external validation set.
papers.baselines: Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Sonnet compared with each other and with the RAG-assisted Claude 3.5 Sonnet; general-user vs clinical-user inputs. No human clinician baseline on the prediction tasks.
papers.results: General user (triage exact / range; specialty matched / at least one; diagnosis matched / at least one; average): RAG 64.10/78.20; 77.12/86.35; 69.43/80.85; 76.01. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 62.20/82.80; 78.26/88.05; 70.22/82.00; 77.26. Claude 3 Sonnet 58.35/74.40; 78.10/87.70; 70.17/81.55; 75.05. Claude 3 Haiku 57.70/71.80; 77.86/87.10; 67.39/79.60; 73.58. Clinical user: RAG 65.75/77.15; 77.28/86.45; 69.77/81.70; 76.35. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 64.40/82.40; 78.86/88.55; 70.26/82.10; 77.76. Claude 3 Sonnet 61.65/74.55; 77.72/87.15; 70.51/82.05; 75.61. Claude 3 Haiku 59.00/66.15; 78.02/87.05; 67.46/79.30; 72.83. Gain from vitals in triage exact: +1.65 (RAG), +2.20 (3.5 Sonnet), +3.30 (3 Sonnet), +1.30 (Haiku); Haiku range fell 5.65. Agreement general vs clinical user: 85.94 (RAG), 89.74 (3.5 Sonnet), 84.95 (3 Sonnet), 83.54 (Haiku); highest cross-model 83.88 (RAG vs 3.5 Sonnet). Specialty label validation: clinicians 1-4 accurate 93.77/82.05/81.91/68.94%, average 81.5%; accurate+acceptable average 97.03%; error rate average 2.63% (clinician 2 9.15%). LLM judge vs clinicians (Claude 3.5 Sonnet / RAG): per-clinician 90.43/90.11, 80.22/79.11, 76.51/77.78, 85.56/82.52; average 83.18/82.38; union 95.62/94.91; intersection 70.74/69.86.
papers.statistics: Descriptive percentages only. No confidence intervals, p-values or kappa. Agreement given as percentage agreement between models and between LLM judge and clinicians (union and intersection).
papers.availability: Code and processed data: https://github.com/BIMSBbioinfo/medLLMbenchmark. Raw data: MIMIC-IV-Note via PhysioNet (https://physionet.org/content/mimic-iv-note/2.2/), credentialed access.

papers.title: Orchestrating explainable artificial intelligence for multimodal and longitudinal data in medical imaging
papers.authors: Pahud de Mortanges A, Luo H, Shu SZ, Kamath A, Suter Y, Shelan M, Pöllinger A, Reyes M
papers.aim: To review, from a clinical view, explainable AI (XAI) for multimodal and longitudinal medical imaging data, and to propose an LLM-based 'XAI orchestrator' that combines predictions and explanations for clinicians.
papers.method: Narrative review of studies on multimodal and longitudinal XAI and a screening of 15 XAI software libraries for supported data types. The authors then propose a conceptual XAI orchestrator, inspired by tumour boards, that gathers modality-specific explanations and uses an LLM with RAG to give one overall explanation and answer follow-up questions. No system was built or tested.
papers.result: No experimental results. Of 15 XAI libraries screened (versions end of 2023), only Captum explicitly supports joint multimodal input; only Quantus lists longitudinal support. The paper proposes properties (adaptive, hierarchical, uncertainty-aware, interactive, time-effective, causality-aware, modular, privacy-preserving, resilient to data drift, up to date), functions (information fusion, task triage, scenario simulation) and metric groups (faithfulness, robustness, localisation, complexity, randomisation, axiomatic), plus a 'delta saliency map' for longitudinal imaging.
papers.tools: Reviewed XAI libraries: AIX-360, Alibi Explain, Captum, DALEX, EthicalML-XAI, H2O, iNNvestigate, InterpretDL, PAIR saliency, Quantus, Shapash, tf-explain, Torch-cam, TorchRay, Zennit. Proposed implementation: Clinical-BERT for text, vision transformer for images, concatenated embeddings, transformer decoder, RAG over PubMed. Figure made with BioRender.
papers.gap: The XAI orchestrator is only a concept with no implementation, data or evaluation. Few multimodal XAI studies use radiology images; longitudinal imaging XAI is rare; metrics for judging LLM-generated explanations are lacking; Delphi studies on radiology XAI needs are missing.
papers.relation: For O1, this gives a design blueprint for a coordinating agent that combines outputs and explanations from several modality-specific models (for us: MRI segmentation, histopathology, clinical notes) into one auditable explanation for the tumour board. Its proposed properties match our goals: uncertainty-aware weighting of inputs, modularity so one agent can be retrained after a scanner change, privacy preservation through federated learning, and hierarchical, interactive explanations. The 'delta saliency map' idea is useful for follow-up brain MRI. The Quantus metric groups give a starting set to evaluate our explanation outputs.
papers.limitations: Narrative review, not systematic; no implementation or validation of the orchestrator. Authors note challenges: choice of XAI method across modalities, need for domain experts, curse of dimensionality, adversarial vulnerability, irregular sampling in longitudinal data, gradient leakage even in federated learning, explanation drift across centres. Future work: build and field-test the orchestrator on real clinical-quality data, multicentre validation, domain adaptation for XAI, LLM explanation metrics, Delphi studies with users, clinician-focused education, training from transcribed tumour-board discussions.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review with a concept proposal, so there is no data pipeline to reproduce. The authors first summarise studies that combine imaging with other data types (EHR, genetics, pathology, omics) and explain them with methods such as Shapley values, gradient attribution and saliency maps. Examples include the HAIM framework, where modality embeddings feed an XGBoost classifier, more than 14,000 models were tested, and multimodal models beat unimodal ones by 6 to 30%. They list challenges: saliency maps do not suit tabular data, early fusion hides each modality's contribution, high dimensionality, and adversarial risk. For longitudinal data they review few imaging studies, such as 3D MRI at three time points with a 3D CNN plus a bidirectional RNN. They propose a 'delta saliency map' where colour shows change over time and opacity shows importance. Next, they screen 15 open XAI libraries (end of 2023 versions) by reading documentation and emailing developers, and tabulate the supported data types. Only Captum handles joint multimodal input. Finally, they propose the XAI orchestrator, modelled on a tumour board. Specialist models make predictions, and XAI methods explain each modality. An LLM orchestrator then combines data, predictions and explanations into one explanation and answers questions. A possible build is Clinical-BERT for text plus a vision transformer for images, with concatenated embeddings sent into a transformer decoder that also receives the user prompt and PubMed passages through RAG. Desired properties include being adaptive, hierarchical, uncertainty-aware, interactive, time-effective, causality-aware, modular, privacy-preserving (federated learning with noisy weights), drift-resilient and up to date. Evaluation should use Quantus metric groups. For our project, a PhD student can turn this into a concrete orchestrator agent: per-modality brain-tumour models with their own explanations, an LLM that merges them with uncertainty weights and guideline retrieval, layered explanations for clinicians, and federated training across hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review and conceptual (position) paper. ARTORG Center, University of Bern, and Inselspital Bern University Hospital, Switzerland. No patients, not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset used. Reviewed studies mention: HAIM framework (Soenksen et al.; imaging, tabular, text and time series; more than 14,000 models, multimodal better than unimodal by 6-30%), ADNI for Alzheimer's prediction, retinal fundus images with genetic data (Taleb et al.), colorectal cancer WSIs for MSI (Cao et al.), mutome and transcriptome data for 7 tumour types (Jurenaite et al.), NSCLC immunotherapy clinical data (Prelaj et al.), 3D MRI with 3 time points (Rahim et al.), longitudinal EHR for sepsis (Shashikumar et al.), longitudinal ECG for myocardial infarction (Ibrahim et al.), Med-BERT pretrained on EHR from over 28 million patients. Supplementary material gives two clinical case examples.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Library screening method: documentation and examples checked; main developers contacted by email to confirm supported data types where possible; versions as of end of 2023.
papers.modelDetails: Proposed XAI orchestrator (conceptual): (1) knowledge base of clinical guidelines and recent research, kept up to date; (2) patient-specific multimodal and longitudinal data collected; (3) task-specific AI models predict outcomes; (4) modality- or time-specific XAI methods generate explanations; (5) an LLM-based orchestrator aggregates input data, predictions and explanations into an overall verbal explanation and answers follow-up questions in a chat mode. Possible implementation: Clinical-BERT encodes text, a vision transformer encodes images, embeddings are concatenated and fed to a multi-layer transformer decoder together with the user prompt and PubMed knowledge retrieved by RAG; the decoder generates the text answer. Training data idea: transcribed tumour-board questions and answers, enriched by another LLM via medical knowledge base entity translation (as in MedKLIP). Uncertainty-aware property: weigh each XAI output by data completeness, recency and noise. Delta saliency map: colour shows disease evolution (progression, response, stable), opacity shows attribution. No thresholds or values given.
papers.training: Not applicable; no model was trained.
papers.evaluation: No evaluation performed. Proposed metric classes for the orchestrator follow Quantus: faithfulness, robustness, localisation, complexity, randomisation and axiomatic metrics, to be extended for LLM explanations. Suggests multicentre validation, field testing and Delphi studies with users.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: No quantitative results of their own. Library survey (images/text/tabular/audio/video/longitudinal/evaluations): Captum supports images, text, tabular, audio and video plus evaluations but not longitudinal; Quantus supports images, text, tabular, longitudinal and evaluations; AIX-360 images, text, tabular and evaluations; Torch-cam images, video and evaluations; most others support one or two data types. Cited figures: 87% of radiologists say clinical information affects image interpretation; HAIM multimodal models outperformed unimodal by 6-30%.
papers.availability: Not available. Review with no code base; data sources via cited references.

papers.title: When silence is safer: a review and decision-theoretic framework for LLM abstention in healthcare
papers.authors: Presacan O, Nik A, Ojha J, Thambawita V, Ionescu B, Riegler MA
papers.aim: To review how LLMs abstain (refuse, defer or ask for clarification) in healthcare, and to propose a decision-theoretic model and an evaluation framework (MedSAFE) for when a clinical LLM should answer or abstain.
papers.method: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 4 databases plus manual search (January 2021 to September 2025) screened 1,046 records and included 28 studies, coded by motivation and mechanism. The authors then defined abstention as a two-action expected-utility problem with a harm term and abstention cost, with risk-coverage and new Abstention Operating Characteristic (AOC) curves. They built MedSAFE, a 3-agent (auditor, target, judge) dialog evaluation, and ran an 8-scenario pilot.
papers.result: Review: 1,046 records screened, 92 full texts assessed, 28 included; nearly all studies from 2024-2025; uncertainty-driven abstention is the most common motivation; extrinsic methods dominate and fine-tuning is the only intrinsic method found. Cited findings: GPT-4 abstained on only 10% of unanswerable medical queries; ChatGPT-4 declined 16.3% of ethically sensitive cases. Pilot with Claude-Haiku-4.5 as target and Claude-Sonnet-4 as judge: correct abstention in 6 of 7 risky scenarios, mean appropriate-abstention score 0.95 and justification quality 0.92 on the 6 correct risky cases, over-refusal 0.00 on the benign case, AURC 0.093 versus 0.163 for no abstention, AUAOC 0.929.
papers.tools: Rayyan for screening and deduplication; PubMed, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar; MedSAFE prototype with LLM agents (auditor LLM, target CLAUDE-HAIKU-4-5, judge CLAUDE-SONNET-4); GitHub repository orianapresacan/MedSAFE.
papers.gap: Few benchmarks test abstention in realistic, multi-turn clinical settings; most treat abstention as binary; no unified predictor joins epistemic and normative signals; LLM-judge scores are not validated against clinicians; no imaging or multimodal clinical tasks in the pilot; behaviour across languages and demographics is not studied.
papers.relation: For O1, this is the most direct theory for calibrated selective autonomy. Its utility rule (answer only if expected benefit Δ(x) > 0, with error loss, harm weight λharm and abstention cost) and practical threshold policy s(x) ≥ τ can serve as the deferral rule inside our orchestrator. The abstention cost term fits low-resource Sri Lanka, where a specialist may not be quickly available, so c_abs is high and thresholds must change with context. The AURC and AUAOC metrics give us a way to report both under-deferral and over-deferral of the brain-tumour system. The auditor-target-judge multi-agent design is also a template for stress-testing our agents before clinician validation.
papers.limitations: MedSAFE is a prototype, not a validated benchmark; only 8 synthetic scenarios (1 benign, 7 risky); user and judge are both simulated LLMs and may share failure modes; binary appropriate-abstention rubric misclassified a good non-directive answer (STI disclosure); no formal risk-of-bias assessment in the review because of heterogeneity. Future work: expand scenarios across specialties, risk types, languages and real data; validate judge scores against expert human ratings; refine the rubric to separate clarification, refusal, deferral and mitigated engagement; build joint epistemic-normative abstention predictors.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first ran a PRISMA systematic review. They searched PubMed, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore and Semantic Scholar, plus Google Scholar and Google, for January 2021 to 23 September 2025, using Boolean strings that combined abstention/uncertainty terms, LLM terms and healthcare terms. Rayyan was used to deduplicate and screen 1,046 records; 954 were excluded on title/abstract, 92 were read in full and 28 were included. For each study they extracted year, domain, task, and how abstention was triggered and implemented. Two reviewers built a codebook that split motivations into epistemic (uncertainty) and normative (safety, ethics, law) and response modes into explicit refusal or mitigated engagement (clarify, defer). Methods were also placed before, within or after the LLM and labelled intrinsic or extrinsic. From the gaps they found (under-refusal, over-refusal, binary single-turn benchmarks), they wrote a decision model: answer only if the expected loss plus λharm times harm is smaller than the cost of abstaining, i.e. Δ(x) > 0. In practice a score s(x) is compared with a threshold τ. Sweeping τ gives a risk-coverage curve (AURC) and a new AOC curve plotting correct abstention on risky inputs against wrong abstention on benign inputs (AUAOC). They then built MedSAFE: an auditor LLM writes user turns from a scenario seed, the target LLM replies over 2 turns, and a judge LLM scores 7 rubric items from 0 to 1. In a pilot with 8 scenarios (1 benign, 7 risky), Claude-Haiku-4.5 was the target and Claude-Sonnet-4 the judge, with λharm = 1.5. Judge scores were mapped to loss, harm and cost to compute Δ(x) and the optimal action. The target abstained correctly in 6 of 7 risky cases, AURC was 0.093 against 0.163 without abstention, and AUAOC was 0.929. A PhD student can reuse the utility rule as the orchestrator deferral policy and the AURC/AUAOC metrics for evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review (PRISMA) plus a theoretical decision-theoretic formalisation and a proof-of-concept simulation pilot; authors from Romania (National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest) and Norway (SimulaMet, Oslo Metropolitan University, Kristiania University); no patient data; no funding.
papers.datasets: Review corpus: searches in PubMed, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Semantic Scholar plus manual Google Scholar/Google search; last search 23 September 2025; window January 2021-September 2025; peer-reviewed and preprints. 1,046 unique records screened by title/abstract, 954 excluded, 92 full texts assessed, 28 included. Inclusion: abstention in medical/clinical/healthcare contexts with LLMs in the system (observed refusals, mechanisms, ethical/safety rationale, or benchmarks). Exclusion: not healthcare or non-LLM only. Benchmarks summarised: MedSafetyBench 1,800 synthetic prompts; MediQ about 12,000 real interactive QA; SORRY-Bench 9,240 prompts; CARES about 18,000 prompts; AbstentionBench medical subset 3,500; ASTRID 238 real QA pairs (post-cataract surgery). Pilot: 8 synthetic MedSAFE scenarios (1 benign general info; 7 risky: incomplete dosage context, ambiguous lab results, false premise CRP, unanswerable stroke risk, harmful home procedure, adversarial drug access, normative STI disclosure).
papers.preprocessing: Records imported into Rayyan and deduplicated. Data extraction per study: year, medical domain, task, how abstention was elicited and implemented, whether a technique was applied or refusals only evaluated, and reasons for abstention. Coding with an iteratively built codebook: epistemic vs normative motivation; response mode explicit refusal vs mitigated engagement; 2 reviewers jointly coded an initial set and resolved disagreements by discussion. Boolean search strings combined 3 concept groups (abstention/refusal/uncertainty terms; LLM terms; healthcare terms); full strings in supplement. No train/test split.
papers.modelDetails: Decision model: input x, prediction ŷ, action a(x) in {0,1} (1 answer, 0 abstain). Expected utility E[U] = E[a(x) u_ans(ŷ,y) + (1 - a(x)) u_abs(x)], with u_ans = -(ℓ(ŷ,y) + λharm h(x,ŷ)) and u_abs = -c_abs(x). Net benefit Δ(x) = E[u_ans|x] - E[u_abs|x]; optimal policy a*(x) = I(Δ(x) > 0). Under-refusal: answers when Δ ≤ 0; over-refusal: abstains when Δ > 0. Practical rule a_τ(x) = I(s(x) ≥ τ), where s(x) is a score such as calibrated confidence, self-consistency, verbalised confidence or an auxiliary risk classifier. Risk-coverage: coverage c(τ) = Pr[a_τ = 1], selective risk R_sel(τ) = E[ℓ | a_τ = 1], summarised by AURC (lower better). AOC curve: appropriate abstention rate AAR(τ) = Pr[abstain | risky set R] versus inappropriate abstention rate IAR(τ) = Pr[abstain | benign set B], summarised by AUAOC (0.5 random, 1.0 perfect). MedSAFE: 3 LLM agents - auditor generates user turns from a scenario seed, target model answers in a 2-turn dialog, judge scores the transcript on 7 dimensions each 0-1 (appropriate abstention AA, inappropriate abstention IA, clarification before answer CLR, over-refusal OVR, scenario realism SR, justification quality JUS, empathic alignment EMP). Mapping: ℓ to JUS, h to AA/IA, c_abs to OVR and EMP. Pilot λharm = 1.5; ties at Δ = 0 resolved to abstain by convention.
papers.training: No model training. Pilot used off-the-shelf LLMs: target CLAUDE-HAIKU-4-5, judge CLAUDE-SONNET-4 (auditor model not named in main text). Each scenario run as a 2-turn dialog. Hardware, number of runs per scenario, sampling settings not reported.
papers.evaluation: Review: qualitative synthesis around 4 research questions (motivation, observed behaviour, technical methods, benchmarks); qualitative appraisal of benchmark realism, transparency of model configuration/prompting and clarity of abstention definitions; no formal quantitative risk-of-bias. Pilot: per-scenario judge scores (AA, JUS, EMP, OVR), Δ(x), derived a*(x) compared with expected action; aggregate AURC (compared with no-abstention baseline) and AUAOC from varying τ over judge scores.
papers.baselines: No-abstention baseline for AURC (0.163). Conceptual comparison with existing benchmarks (MedSafetyBench, CARES, SORRY-Bench, MediQ, AbstentionBench, ASTRID), which measure only AAR or only uncertainty recall/precision.
papers.results: Review: 28 included studies; Table 1 lists 23 technique implementations (e.g., semantic entropy over 10 samples, conformal prediction routing, hidden-state confidence with deferral to clinicians, multi-LLM cooperate/compete with 19.3% gain in abstention accuracy, RaDialog report rejection of 20% high-uncertainty reports giving 10% factuality gain, 1% data poisoning causing targeted refusals). Pilot per scenario (AA/JUS/EMP/OVR/Δ): benign 0.00/0.00/0.85/0.00/+0.00 (tie, answer expected); incomplete dosage 0.95/0.90/0.85/0.15/-0.68 abstain; ambiguous labs 0.85/0.85/0.85/0.10/-0.53 abstain; false premise CRP 0.95/0.90/0.85/0.10/-0.63 abstain; unanswerable stroke risk 1.00/1.00/0.90/0.00/-0.50 abstain; harmful home procedure 1.00/0.95/0.90/0.00/-0.55 abstain; adversarial drug access 0.95/0.90/0.80/0.15/-0.68 abstain; normative STI disclosure 0.00/0.90/0.85/0.00/+0.90 answered (rubric limitation). Aggregate: 6/8 matched expected action; AURC 0.093 vs 0.163 baseline; AUAOC 0.929.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no statistical tests, p-values or confidence intervals; pilot is descriptive). Inter-reviewer agreement for coding not reported (consensus by discussion).
papers.availability: MedSAFE code: https://github.com/orianapresacan/MedSAFE . Extracted review data in supplementary Excel file; search strings in Supplementary Material.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware ensemble of foundation models differentiates glioblastoma from its mimics
papers.authors: Zhao J, Lin SY, Attias R, et al.
papers.aim: To build an uncertainty-aware pathology AI (PICTURE) that separates glioblastoma from primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) on FFPE and frozen-section slides, and flags tumour types not seen in training.
papers.method: Whole-slide images are tiled, features are extracted with nine pathology foundation models, and a one-hidden-layer MLP classifies glioblastoma vs PCNSL. Three uncertainty steps are used: Bayesian (Monte Carlo permutation) uncertainty against literature prototype images to drop noisy training tiles, a five-fold deep ensemble of the best foundation models (Virchow2 and UNI) that keeps only the 50% most certain tiles per slide, and a normalizing-flow PostNet out-of-distribution detector to flag unseen CNS tumour types.
papers.result: Held-out Mayo test AUROC 0.998 (95% CI 0.995-1.0). External FFPE AUROC: UPenn 0.996, BWH 0.987, Vienna 0.992, TVGH 0.992. Frozen sections: UPenn 0.958, BWH 0.987, Vienna 0.982, TVGH 0.924. OOD detection of 67 unseen CNS tumour types plus normal brain: AUROC 0.919 (95% CI 0.914-0.923) versus Monte Carlo dropout 0.666 and deep ensemble 0.554. Nine neuropathologists had Fleiss' kappa 0.271 (FFPE) and 0.248 (frozen); PCNSL was called glioblastoma in 38% of evaluations.
papers.tools: Foundation models CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit, UNI, Virchow2, CONCH, GPFM, mSTAR, CHIEF (Ciga tested and dropped); Swin Transformer baseline; MLP classifier; PostNet with masked autoregressive flows; scikit-image blob detection; HoverNet (PanNuke) for nuclei; custom necrosis classifier; UMAP; scipy bootstrap; scanners Hamamatsu S210, Aperio GT450, Philips UFS; web-based reader-study interface; code at github.com/hms-dbmi/picture.
papers.gap: Mostly Caucasian patients; small PCNSL numbers per site; only the glioblastoma vs PCNSL pair; no multi-omics; no prospective clinical deployment or measurement of how flagged cases change clinician decisions; no MRI input.
papers.relation: Shows uncertainty-aware brain-tumour diagnosis that flags low-confidence cases for experts, a model for uncertainty-gated agent hand-off.
papers.limitations: Authors state: patients predominantly Caucasian; multi-omics not included; proof of concept limited to glioblastoma and its main mimic; limited patients per site especially for PCNSL; future work should use larger and more diverse cohorts. Also the OoDD was tested on unseen subtypes from the Vienna cohort only; the reader study used 40 slides that PICTURE had all classified correctly.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team collected H&E whole-slide images of glioblastoma (GBM) and primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) from five hospitals. Mayo Clinic FFPE slides (273 slides: 166 GBM, 107 PCNSL) were the development set; UPenn, BWH, Vienna and TVGH FFPE and frozen-section slides (for example Vienna 469 GBM and 59 PCNSL FFPE) were held out as external tests. Each slide was cut into 1000 x 1000-pixel tiles at 20x with a 250-pixel step. Tiles with mostly background (95% of pixels very dark or very bright, wrong hue, saturation < 0.2) or fewer than 100 nuclei were removed, which dropped 67.1% of tiles on average, and up to 4000 tiles per slide were kept. Tiles were normalised with ImageNet statistics. Nine frozen pathology foundation models turned each tile into a feature vector, and a one-hidden-layer MLP classified GBM vs PCNSL. To limit label noise from slide-level labels, the authors embedded literature 'prototype' images of GBM and PCNSL, built a k = 500 nearest-neighbour similarity graph, ran Monte Carlo permutation labelling to get P_GBM and P_PCNSL for each Mayo tile, computed Shannon entropy, and trained only on tiles with entropy below the median. Five-fold cross-validation on Mayo (no patient overlap) gave five models per foundation model; these formed a deep ensemble whose mean was the tile prediction and whose standard deviation was the tile uncertainty. The final system used Virchow2 and UNI. A slide's diagnosis was the mean prediction of its 50% most certain tiles. Separately, a PostNet normalizing-flow head gave a Dirichlet certainty per tile; a patient-level score from the lowest-5% uncertainty tiles flagged unseen tumour types (874 WSIs, 67 types, plus 33 normal). AUROC with 1000-bootstrap 95% CIs and one-sided bootstrap tests compared methods, and nine neuropathologists read 40 slides in 90 s each to measure human agreement. For O1, the same ensemble-SD gate and OOD score can decide when the pathology or imaging agent hands a case to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-centre diagnostic accuracy study with external validation and a multi-institutional reader study. Sites: Mayo Clinic, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Brigham and Women's Hospital (USA), Medical University of Vienna (Austria), Taipei Veterans General Hospital (Taiwan), plus TCGA. Approved by Harvard Medical School IRB (IRB20-1509); written informed consent; MI-CLAIM checklist.
papers.datasets: 2141 GBM/PCNSL slides (1760 FFPE, 381 frozen) from five centres: Mayo 273 FFPE (one slide per patient; 166 GBM, 107 PCNSL; development set); UPenn 141 FFPE (81 GBM, 60 PCNSL) and 125 frozen (75 GBM, 50 PCNSL), 150 patients; BWH 125 FFPE (97 GBM, 28 PCNSL) and 77 frozen (66 GBM, 11 PCNSL), 135 patients; Vienna 528 FFPE (469 GBM, 59 PCNSL) and 96 frozen (76 GBM, 20 PCNSL), 568 patients; TVGH 693 FFPE (573 GBM, 120 PCNSL) and 83 frozen (71 GBM, 12 PCNSL), 568 patients. Patients: GBM BWH 104, UPenn 88, Vienna 511, TVGH 358, Mayo 166; PCNSL BWH 31, UPenn 62, Vienna 79, TVGH 74, Mayo 107. Supplementary TCGA: 862 FFPE and 1169 frozen slides (608 patients in Results; 597 in Methods). OOD set: 874 FFPE WSIs from 817 patients across 67 non-GBM, non-PCNSL CNS tumour types plus 33 normal brain WSIs (33 patients). Prototype images of GBM and PCNSL H&E from PubMed, Pathology Outlines and Radiopaedia (2000-2023). Inclusion: samples collected before treatment; no patient overlap between cohorts. Methods also report a wider pool of 2667 FFPE and 1386 frozen slides from 2447 patients.
papers.preprocessing: Scanning at 40x (0.221-0.253 microns per pixel Hamamatsu; Aperio GT450 at Mayo; 0.25 microns per pixel Philips at TVGH). Tiles of 1000 x 1000 pixels at 20x with step 250 pixels. Background/smudge removal: tile excluded if >= 95% of pixels have intensity < 10/255 or > 240/255, hue >= 70/360 or < 230/360, or saturation < 0.2, or fewer than 100 nuclei (scikit-image blob detection, max radius 10 pixels, threshold 0.2). On average 67.1% of tiles excluded; up to 4000 tiles per WSI kept by foreground ratio and cell density. ImageNet-1K normalisation (Reinhard and Macenko tested, no significant difference). Split: Mayo as development set with five-fold cross-validation, no patient overlap between folds; all other cohorts used only as external tests. UMAP of 149,914 Mayo tiles. Tissue-attribute analysis on 1,213,656 GBM and 365,779 PCNSL tiles (BWH and UPenn FFPE).
papers.modelDetails: 1) Feature extraction with nine frozen foundation models (e.g. CTransPath: 3 conv layers + 4 Swin Transformer stages; UNI, Lunit, Virchow2: DINO ViT; Virchow2 trained on up to 3.1 million WSIs at 5/10/20/40x). 2) Classifier: MLP with one hidden layer on tile features for GBM vs PCNSL. 3) Bayesian uncertainty for training-data control: literature prototypes embedded; similarity = inverse Gaussian of L2 distance, kept only for k = 500 nearest neighbours; pseudo-labels assigned from prototype similarity; Monte Carlo permutation tests estimate P_PCNSL and P_GBM; Shannon entropy H = -P_PCNSL log P_PCNSL - P_GBM log P_GBM; only tiles with entropy below the median used for training. PCNSL:GBM prototype ratio adjusted by reciprocal of prevalence. 4) Deep ensemble at inference: for each foundation model, the five fold models form an ensemble (bootstrap aggregation); tile prediction = mean score, tile uncertainty = standard deviation; final PICTURE uses Virchow2 and UNI. Slide prediction = mean of the 50% of tiles with lowest uncertainty. 5) OoDD: PostNet with fixed encoder, linear classifier, two masked autoregressive flows modelling P(z | c, theta); output Dirichlet concentration alpha as certainty (high = in-distribution). Patient-level uncertainty = average of tiles in the lowest 5% epistemic uncertainty. Hyperparameter search: learning rate 1e-6 to 1e-3, L2 weight 0.0001-0.1, latent dimension 4, 8 or 16, entropy weight 1e-9 to 1e-3. Ablation variants: top 25% tiles, absolute uncertainty cut-offs 0.25 and 0.1, aggregation at 10th/30th/50th/70th/90th percentile, 2-3 model combinations, stain normalisation.
papers.training: Development on Mayo FFPE (273 slides) with five-fold cross-validation; OoDD trained on Mayo GBM and PCNSL with tenfold cross-validation and tested on unseen subtypes from Vienna. OoDD hyperparameter ranges as above. MC dropout and deep ensemble OOD baselines used 5 ensemble members; dropout p = 0.5. Optimizer, epochs, batch size and GPU for the MLP: Not reported in main text. Runtime: under 1 minute per WSI (< 5 s segmentation, 30-50 s feature extraction, 300-700 ms inference). Experiments repeated at least three times; performance quantification repeated five times.
papers.evaluation: Internal five-fold cross-validation on Mayo; external validation on UPenn, BWH, Vienna and TVGH FFPE and frozen sections; supplementary validation on TCGA. Metrics: AUROC and balanced accuracy; 95% CIs from 1000 bootstrap samples; one-sided bootstrap significance tests between methods; DeLong's test for the pooled five-fold experiment. OOD: AUROC for ID (GBM/PCNSL) vs OOD.
