papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy versus guideline prompting and physicians.
papers.baselines: Standard and guideline-based prompting; physicians alone.
papers.results: Improved accuracy over prompting baselines; MACD-human workflow +18.3 percentage points over physician-only diagnosis on text vignettes.

papers.title: Empowering Medical Multi-Agents with Clinical Consultation Flow for Dynamic Diagnosis
papers.authors: Sihan Wang, Suiyang Jiang, Yibo Gao, Boming Wang, Shangqi Gao, Xiahai Zhuang
papers.aim: To teach a doctor agent to gather information step by step before diagnosing, as in a real consultation.
papers.method: Diagnosis is a multi-turn game with a simulated patient and an examiner; the doctor agent's actions follow consultation flow and are trained with reinforcement learning.
papers.result: State-of-the-art results on a public dynamic diagnosis benchmark.
papers.tools: Doctor, patient and examiner agents in a partially observable Markov game;
papers.gap: Simulated patients; no calibrated confidence or clinician handover.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single benchmark; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Diagnosis is framed as a multi-turn game between a doctor agent, a simulated patient and an examiner that returns test results. The doctor agent's possible actions are organised hierarchically following real consultation flow, and reinforcement learning teaches it to keep collecting information rather than diagnosing too early. The approach was evaluated on a public dynamic diagnosis benchmark.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public dynamic-diagnosis benchmark (Fudan University).
papers.datasets: Public multi-turn dynamic diagnosis benchmark (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Hierarchical action set derived from clinical consultation flow and a medical textbook.
papers.modelDetails: Doctor, patient and examiner agents in a partially observable Markov game; the doctor agent chooses actions from the hierarchical set and is optimised with reinforcement learning to avoid premature diagnosis.
papers.training: RL training of the doctor policy (settings in paper).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy and interaction efficiency on the benchmark.
papers.baselines: Foundation models and prior agent methods.
papers.results: Improved over baselines and reached state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark.

papers.title: A Structured Debate-Mixture-of-Agents Framework for Complex Clinical Diagnostic Decision Support
papers.authors: Chang Xia, Leilei Ouyang, Huimin Wang, Yong Zhao, Kang Li
papers.aim: To improve diagnosis of rare and difficult cases with a structured debate between agents.
papers.method: DMoA: presenter and rebutter agents debate each diagnostic direction and an aggregator combines the revised ideas; tested on 2,016 hard cases with ablations.
papers.result: Most-likely-diagnosis accuracy +10.2 points and safety rate +11.4 points over GPT-4o, not explained by extra compute alone.
papers.tools: GPT-4o
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty; no clinician escalation; case-report text only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; reference diagnoses from published cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: DMoA organises diagnosis as a structured debate: in each Debater a Presenter proposes a diagnostic direction and a Rebutter critiques it, the Presenter revises, and an Aggregator combines the revised hypotheses from several Debaters. It was evaluated on 2,016 rare and challenging cases for most-likely and top-three diagnoses and a safety rate, with ablations showing that the structured workflow, not just more compute, drove the improvement. Fixed role topology contrasts with open-ended agent chat.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark study with ablations, reliability, error and cost analyses (IEEE JBHI submission, preprint).
papers.datasets: Clinical case dataset of Li et al.: 297 rare-disease cases (297 diseases, 33 categories) and 1,719 challenging cases (32 specialties); supplementary clinical knowledge questions.
papers.preprocessing: Structured or semi-structured case text; reference diagnoses extracted from the case reports; an Information Editor tool helps prepare inputs.
papers.modelDetails: Debate-Mixture-of-Agents: fixed role topology of Debaters (each a Presenter and a Rebutter that generate, rebut and revise hypotheses) feeding an Aggregator that integrates revised hypotheses into the final diagnosis; best with 4x2 structure.
papers.training: No training; varied base models and token budgets.
papers.evaluation: Most-likely-diagnosis accuracy, top-3 accuracy, safety rate, reliability and cost.
papers.baselines: GPT-4o and other base models alone; ablations with more models or longer outputs.
papers.results: Across both datasets DMoA improved most-likely-diagnosis accuracy by 10.21 points and safety rate by 11.36 points over GPT-4o; gains not explained by more models or tokens alone.

papers.title: From Analytics to Tumor Boards: An Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Workflow for Oncology Feature Extraction
papers.authors: Daniel Kang, Michelle Hu, Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Shayan Vassef, Yufan Wang, Anit Kumar Sahu, Munmun De Choudhury, Vedant Das Swain, Christian Poellabauer, Li Yan Khor, et al.
papers.aim: To speed up cancer-registry data extraction with agents that show the evidence for every value.
papers.method: A 328-field oncology schema is split across specialised agents that extract values from reports and attach the supporting text; tested on 230 documents from 40 patients against clinician review.
papers.result: High precision on present fields, and evidence links let clinicians verify each value before the tumour board.
papers.tools: nMAS: separates clinician-defined fields across specialised agents, links each extracted value to its source evidence, and normalises values for…
papers.gap: Small single-site set; no uncertainty score per field.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Evaluated only on fields present; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Manual cancer-registry abstraction can take about 27 minutes per case. This workflow splits a 328-field oncology schema across specialised agents that extract values from heterogeneous reports and attach the supporting text to every value, so a clinician can verify each one before a tumour board. It was evaluated on 230 documents from 40 patients against clinician review. Evidence linking is a practical form of the audit trail this study requires.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective evaluation of an evidence-linked multi-agent extraction workflow (ML4H 2026 submission).
papers.datasets: 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients (pathology, radiology, cytology, clinical notes) from one academic medical centre; clinician-informed schema of 328 attributes.
papers.preprocessing: Direct identifiers replaced by placeholders; evaluation restricted to fields clinicians identified as present.
papers.modelDetails: nMAS: separates clinician-defined fields across specialised agents, links each extracted value to its source evidence, and normalises values for tumour-board use.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Rank-weighted value-level precision and related extraction metrics on clinician-reviewed fields.
papers.baselines: Single-pass LLM extraction.
papers.results: High rank-weighted value-level precision on present fields (exact figures in paper); evidence links support review.

papers.title: CoMMa: Contribution-Aware Medical Multi-Agents for Decentralized Oncology Decision Support
papers.authors: Yichen Wu, Kailong Fan, Sangjoon Park, Yuhan Liu, Zhiyi Shi, Sekeun Kim, Dania Daye, Hana Farzaneh, Xiang Li, Raul Uppot, et al.
papers.aim: To combine evidence held separately by specialist agents and show how much each contributes.
papers.method: CoMMa: each data type has its own specialist agent (frozen LLM encoder plus small head); a gating network trained with Shapley-based estimates weights each agent per patient.
papers.result: Better than single- and role-play multi-agent baselines, with stable, interpretable agent contributions.
papers.tools: fine-tuning
papers.gap: Attribution is not uncertainty; no deferral to clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; benchmark tasks.
papers.methodologyDetail: CoMMa keeps each type of patient evidence separate and assigns it to a specialist agent, as in a decentralised setting where data cannot be pooled. Each specialist is a frozen language-model encoder with a small trainable head, the specialists exchange information, and a gating network trained with a Shapley-based estimate decides how much each contributes to the final prediction for that patient. The result is an explicit credit assignment over agents rather than narrative consensus.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on oncology benchmarks (Harvard/MGH, preprint).
papers.datasets: Multiple oncology decision benchmarks with partitioned evidence streams (imaging findings, labs, staging, history).
papers.preprocessing: Patient evidence partitioned into separate streams, each given to one specialist.
papers.modelDetails: CoMMa: each stream encoded by a frozen open-source LLM plus a trainable specialty projection; cross-agent collaborative reasoning; contribution-aware aggregation with a sample-specific fusion gate regularised by a Shapley contribution estimator.
papers.training: Agent-specific fine-tuning of projection modules.
papers.evaluation: Prediction accuracy and stability; agent-level attribution.
papers.baselines: Single-agent and role-play multi-agent LLM frameworks.
papers.results: Outperformed single- and role-play multi-agent baselines with stable, interpretable agent contributions.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Intelligence for Multidisciplinary Decision-Making in Gastrointestinal Oncology
papers.authors: Rongzhao Zhang, Junqiao Wang, Shuyun Yang, Mouxiao Bian, Chihao Zhang, Dongyang Wang, Qiujuan Yan, Yun Zhong, Yuwei Bai, Guanxu Zhu, et al.
papers.aim: To support gastrointestinal oncology MDT decisions with one agent per data type.
papers.method: Modality agents extract findings into a shared evidence store, conflicts are detected and a core agent writes the MDT report; compared with one model reading everything, rated by experts.
papers.result: Clearly better than the single agent, especially for reasoning logic and medical accuracy.
papers.tools: Qwen, fine-tuning
papers.gap: No calibrated confidence or deferral; expert scoring only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single region; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Each modality of a gastrointestinal oncology case is handled by its own agent, which extracts structured findings into a shared evidence container; conflicts between modalities are detected, and a core agent writes the MDT report. Compared with one model reading all inputs concatenated, with the same fine-tuning, the multi-agent design avoided context dilution and was rated better by experts. It supports modality-specific agents feeding a coordinating agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and expert evaluation of a hierarchical multi-agent MDT system for GI oncology (Shanghai hospitals, preprint).
papers.datasets: GI oncology cases with EMR text, 5-10 endoscopic frames per case, radiology reports and laboratory results, with target MDT diagnostic reports.
papers.preprocessing: Inputs split by modality; cross-modal conflict detection before final reasoning.
papers.modelDetails: Specialist agents for text, endoscopy, radiology and laboratory (Qwen-3 32B; Intern S1 Mini for endoscopy) write to an evidence container; an MDT-Core agent produces the standardised report.
papers.training: Supervised fine-tuning on the training set (same for baseline).
papers.evaluation: Expert panel scoring of reasoning logic, medical accuracy and other dimensions.
papers.baselines: Single-agent Qwen-3 32B with concatenated inputs and identical fine-tuning; real-world clinical benchmarks.
papers.results: Substantial improvements over the single agent across all dimensions, largest in reasoning logic and medical accuracy.

papers.title: MTBBench: A Multimodal Sequential Clinical Decision-Making Benchmark in Oncology
papers.authors: Kiril Vasilev, Alexandre Misrahi, Eeshaan Jain, Phil F Cheng, Petros Liakopoulos, Olivier Michielin, Michael Moor, Charlotte Bunne
papers.aim: To create a benchmark that simulates a molecular tumour board with multimodal, time-ordered patient data.
papers.method: MTBBench: agents receive patient histories with pathology, IHC, blood and genomic data and answer validated questions; many models were tested, with and without modality-specific tools.
papers.result: Large models were unreliable over time and across modalities; giving agents specialist tools improved performance by up to 9-11%.
papers.tools: Open and closed LLMs/VLMs evaluated as agents;
papers.gap: Measures answer accuracy, not calibrated confidence or deferral; oncology broadly, not neuro-oncology.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Benchmark questions, not live boards.
papers.methodologyDetail: MTBBench simulates a molecular tumour board: an agent receives a patient's history as a sequence of clinical events with pathology images, immunohistochemistry, blood results and genomics, and must answer clinically validated questions about diagnosis, prognosis and biomarkers. The authors benchmarked many models, analysed their failure modes, and showed that giving agents foundation-model tools for each modality improves multimodal and longitudinal reasoning. It is a relevant benchmark design for longitudinal brain-tumour cases.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and evaluation of LLM agents for molecular tumour board decisions (ETH Zürich, EPFL, HUG; NeurIPS 2025).
papers.datasets: MTBBench: multimodal, longitudinal oncology questions built from patient data (H&E, IHC, haematology, genomics, temporally ordered clinical events); ground truth validated by clinicians through a co-developed app.
papers.preprocessing: Patient histories presented as time-ordered events with multimodal attachments; multiple-choice and true/false question formats.
papers.modelDetails: Open and closed LLMs/VLMs evaluated as agents; an agentic framework adds foundation-model tools for pathology, IHC and text and access to knowledge bases.
papers.training: No training of the benchmarked models.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on diagnosis, prognosis (e.g. 2-year recurrence) and biomarker questions; analysis of hallucination, temporal reasoning and conflicting evidence.
papers.baselines: LLMs without tools.
papers.results: Models at scale lacked reliability (hallucinations, poor time-resolved reasoning, failure to reconcile conflicting modalities); the tool-based agent framework improved task performance by up to 9.0% (multimodal) and 11.2% (longitudinal).
papers.availability: Benchmark on GitHub (bunnelab/MTBBench) and Hugging Face.

papers.title: TumorBoard: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Decision Support for Longitudinal Neuro-Oncology
papers.authors: Yantong Liu, Zheyu Zhang, Runpeng Liu, Mu Xitang, Seong-Yoon Shin, Hyun-Ae Lee
papers.aim: To build an evidence-grounded multi-agent system for longitudinal brain-tumour decisions that can defer when evidence is weak.
papers.method: TumorBoard: specialist agents add source-linked claims to a shared time-stamped ledger, a critic checks contradictions and a safety governor releases, qualifies or defers each recommendation; tested on 360 clinician-built cases.
papers.result: Action F1 0.772 and harmful releases 3.9% vs 6.8%; the governor cut harmful releases by 7.8 points at the cost of 4.3 points of false deferral.
papers.tools: Specialist agents (radiology, neuropathology, molecular diagnosis, guidelines, therapy planning) write atomic claims with provenance to a shared case…
papers.gap: Deferral based on evidence sufficiency rules rather than calibrated model uncertainty; no imaging models; synthetic benchmark.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; no prospective clinical evaluation.
papers.methodologyDetail: TumorBoard keeps one shared, time-stamped state for each brain-tumour patient. Specialist agents add small factual claims, each linked to its source evidence, to a ledger; a critic agent looks for contradictions; and a safety governor decides whether a recommendation is released, released with qualification, or deferred because evidence is insufficient or out of date. On a 360-case benchmark built by clinicians it beat several budget-matched agent designs, and ablations showed that the ledger, critic and governor each produced the expected benefit. It is the closest published design to this study's orchestrator and audit trail.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with a 360-case hidden benchmark built by clinical authors; perturbation, ablation and expert-rating studies (Kunsan National University, preprint).
papers.datasets: Longitudinal neuro-oncology case packets (serial MRI, pathology, molecular markers, treatment history, performance status, guideline versions); 360-case hidden test set balanced for common and difficult states, incomplete cases included.
papers.preprocessing: Two-pass case construction: one clinical author builds the chronological packet, a second independently creates the action graph and decisive evidence; disagreements adjudicated before model runs.
papers.modelDetails: Specialist agents (radiology, neuropathology, molecular diagnosis, guidelines, therapy planning) write atomic claims with provenance to a shared case state and claim-evidence ledger; an adversarial critic exposes contradictions; a safety governor releases, qualifies or defers recommendations by evidence sufficiency and temporal validity.
papers.training: No training; matched token budget across systems.
papers.evaluation: Action-graph F1, evidence entailment, recommendation-to-evidence coverage, harmful-release and deferral rates; robustness to evidence deletion, conflict, guideline version shift, role corruption and prompt injection.
papers.baselines: Direct LLM, RAG agent, plan-critique, free-chat council and typed council (budget-matched).
papers.results: Action F1 0.772 (95% CI 0.754-0.790), entailment 0.914, harmful release 0.039 vs 0.068 for the typed council; gain over best baseline 0.031 (Holm p=0.0012); governor reduced harmful release by 7.8 points at 4.3 points false deferral; 14,220 tokens and 21.8 s per case.
papers.statistics: Paired case-level bootstrap CIs; mixed-effects ordinal models for expert ratings; exact paired tests; weighted kappa/ICC; Holm correction.
papers.availability: All prompts, retrieved passages, messages, ledger states and outputs retained for audit.

papers.title: OMGs: A multi-agent system supporting MDT decision-making across the ovarian tumour care continuum
papers.authors: Yangyang Zhang, Zilong Wang, Jianbo Xu, Yongqi Chen, Chu Han, Zhihao Zhang, Shuai Liu, Hui Li, Huiping Zhang, Ziqi Liu, et al.
papers.aim: To support ovarian tumour MDT decisions with a multi-agent system and test it in real cohorts.
papers.method: OMGs: five specialist agents with an orchestrator and services for extraction, evidence and provenance; evaluated on retrospective and prospective cohorts and in paired clinician studies.
papers.result: The system improved clinicians' recommendations most in evidence and robustness, where MDT expertise is often missing.
papers.tools: OMGs: an orchestrator coordinates five specialty LLM agents (chair, oncologist, radiologist, pathologist, nuclear medicine) through structured MDT…
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty or explicit deferral; gynaecologic oncology.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; Chinese centres.
papers.methodologyDetail: OMGs reproduces an ovarian tumour board with five specialist agents coordinated by an orchestrator and supported by services for data extraction, evidence retrieval and provenance. It was evaluated on multicentre retrospective and prospective cohorts by expert raters using a five-dimension scale with a safety gate, and in paired studies where clinicians made recommendations with and without the system. It shows a staged evaluation including prospective cohorts and human-AI comparison.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre retrospective and prospective evaluation with paired human-AI studies; five tertiary hospitals in Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang; IRB approvals at all centres.
papers.datasets: Retrospective and prospective ovarian tumour cohorts with demographics, pathology, imaging, labs, molecular and genetic profiles, treatment and follow-up.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified data; agent servers extract data, assemble context and track provenance.
papers.modelDetails: OMGs: an orchestrator coordinates five specialty LLM agents (chair, oncologist, radiologist, pathologist, nuclear medicine) through structured MDT deliberation, with evidence retrieval and provenance tracking.
papers.training: No training reported.
papers.evaluation: Five SPEAR dimension scores and a safety-gated overall score from three senior gynaecologic oncologists; paired human-AI studies.
papers.baselines: Clinician recommendations without AI; single-agent LLMs.
papers.results: OMGs enhanced clinicians' recommendations most in Evidence and Robustness, the dimensions weakest when multidisciplinary expertise is lacking.
papers.statistics: Pre-specified endpoints, two-sided alpha 0.05; ICC(2,k) for inter-rater agreement.

papers.title: SurvAgent: Hierarchical CoT-Enhanced Case Banking and Dichotomy-Based Multi-Agent System for Multimodal Survival Prediction
papers.authors: Guolin Huang, Wenting Chen, Jiaqi Yang, Xinheng Lyu, Xiaoling Luo, Sen Yang, Xiaohan Xing, Linlin Shen
papers.aim: To predict cancer survival from pathology and genomics with agents that reason over similar past cases.
papers.method: SurvAgent: agents analyse slides at several magnifications and gene groups to build a case bank, then retrieve similar cases and reason about survival for new patients.
papers.result: Best C-index on all five datasets, with interpretable reports.
papers.tools: chain-of-thought
papers.gap: Survival prediction, not diagnosis; no deferral; no clinician evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; public cohorts only.
papers.methodologyDetail: SurvAgent first builds a bank of analysed historical cases: a pathology agent explores each slide at increasing magnification, including low-confidence patches, and writes structured reports with reasoning, while a genomics agent summarises gene groups. For a new case it retrieves similar cases and uses expert agents to reason about survival, producing a prediction with an explanation. It shows agents using case memory and confidence-guided exploration in pathology.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on five public cancer survival datasets (preprint).
papers.datasets: Five TCGA-type cohorts with whole-slide images and genomic data and survival times.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs analysed hierarchically at x2.5, x10 and x20; genes grouped into six functional categories.
papers.modelDetails: SurvAgent: case bank built by a PathAgent (low-magnification screening, similarity-aware and confidence-aware patch mining, checklist reports, chain-of-thought with self-critique) and a GenAgent; at inference similar cases are retrieved and dichotomy-based multi-expert agents predict survival.
papers.training: Not detailed in extract.
papers.evaluation: Concordance index; interpretability of reports.
papers.baselines: Multimodal survival models (e.g. MCAT, pathomic fusion) and pathology agents.
papers.results: Best C-index across all five datasets with interpretable multimodal reports.

papers.title: Demo: Healthcare Agent Orchestrator (HAO) for Patient Summarization in Molecular Tumor Boards
papers.authors: Matthias Blondeel, Noel Codella, Sam Preston, Hao Qiu, Leonardo Schettini, Frank Tuan, Wen-wai Yim, Smitha Saligrama, Mert Öz, Shrey Jain, et al.
papers.aim: To summarise patient histories for molecular tumour boards with every statement linked to its source.
papers.method: The PatientHistory agent builds a cited timeline and summary; tested on 71 real board patients by checking whether key facts appear, judged by an LLM.
papers.result: Specialised prompts captured 84% of high-importance facts vs 66% with generic prompts.
papers.tools: Healthcare Agent Orchestrator coordinating agents;
papers.gap: Recall only, no assessment of decisions; no uncertainty flags.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Proprietary data from one partner; LLM-based judging.
papers.methodologyDetail: For molecular tumour boards, the PatientHistory agent compiles a patient's records into a timeline and summary in which every statement cites its source. The team evaluated it on 71 real board patients by breaking reference summaries into facts and checking, with an LLM judge, whether each important fact appeared in the agent's summary, a method they propose for local, data-free evaluation. Specialised prompts that prioritise biomarkers, treatment lines and imaging status improved recall. Citation-backed summaries are relevant to the audit trail.
papers.studyDesign: System demonstration with retrospective evaluation on a proprietary corpus (Microsoft Health and Life Sciences, preprint).
papers.datasets: TB-Bench: de-identified longitudinal materials for 71 oncology patients discussed at molecular tumour boards (board transcripts, EHR exports with imaging, biomarkers, diagnoses, medications, procedures, social history, clinician summaries).
papers.preprocessing: Reference summaries standardised by LLM into a narrative plus timeline; evaluation restricted to dataset-verifiable facts.
papers.modelDetails: Healthcare Agent Orchestrator coordinating agents; the PatientHistory agent builds a citation-backed clinical timeline and summary using Universal Abstraction prompt templates.
papers.training: No training; generic vs specialised prompting.
papers.evaluation: TBFact: fact-level recall of high-importance and all facts under strict and partial entailment, a data-free evaluation framework deployable locally.
papers.baselines: Generic prompting baseline.
papers.results: Specialised prompting gave TBFact recall 0.84 for high-importance facts (0.71 all) vs 0.66 and 0.56 generic; 94% of high-importance information included with partial credit.
papers.availability: Orchestrator code released by Microsoft (open source); TB-Bench proprietary.

papers.title: Multi-Agent AI System for Radiology Report Structuring and Quality Assurance with Independent Radiologist Evaluation
papers.authors: Iryna Hartsock, Cesar Lam, Christopher Otteni, Aliya Qayyum, Robert Gatenby, Cyrillo Araujo, Ghulam Rasool
papers.aim: To structure radiology reports and check their quality with a tiered multi-agent system that runs inside the hospital.
papers.method: Sentences go first to simple rules, then a local LLM, and only ambiguous ones to a reasoning model; further agents do quality checks; radiologists judged the output.
papers.result: Rules handled 83% of sentences, the local LLM 12.3% and the reasoning model 4.7%, with favourable radiologist ratings.
papers.tools: Llama, DeepSeek
papers.gap: Escalation by rule failure rather than calibrated confidence; report text only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single institution; CT reports only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiology reports were split into sentences and passed through a cascade: cheap rules first, then a local LLM, then a reasoning model only for sentences that remained ambiguous, to sort findings into standard anatomical sections; further agents performed quality checks. Independent radiologists judged the output. Escalating hard items to a more capable component is a simple example of tiered routing, and all processing stayed inside the hospital.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and independent radiologist evaluation, Moffitt Cancer Center; IRB approved, consent waived; models run locally behind the firewall.
papers.datasets: 638 CT chest/abdomen/pelvis reports by 15 radiologists (2023-2024), 146-1,594 words; 22,270 sentences.
papers.preprocessing: Findings extracted by rule-based section detection; custom sentence segmentation; follow-up fragments merged with preceding sentences.
papers.modelDetails: Cascade of agents: Agent 1 regex rules, Agent 2 LLaMA 3, Agent 3 DeepSeek-R1 for harder sentences, assigning sentences to standardised anatomical sections; separate QA agents check report quality.
papers.training: No training; local open models.
papers.evaluation: Share of sentences classified at each stage; radiologist evaluation of structuring accuracy and QA findings.
papers.baselines: Radiologist reference.
papers.results: Regex classified 83.0% of sentences, LLaMA 3 12.3%, DeepSeek-R1 4.7%; <0.04% unclassified (headers); favourable radiologist ratings.

papers.title: MARCH: Multi-Agent Radiology Clinical Hierarchy for CT Report Generation
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Yihao Ding, Yonghui Wu, Yifan Peng
papers.aim: To generate chest CT reports with agents that mimic a radiology department hierarchy.
papers.method: MARCH: a resident agent drafts, a retrieval agent finds similar cases, fellow agents revise and an attending agent resolves disagreements; tested on a large public CT dataset.
papers.result: Better clinical accuracy and language scores than state-of-the-art methods.
papers.tools: Llama, LoRA, GPT-4, GPT-4o
papers.gap: No uncertainty passed to a human; consensus may hide disagreement; chest CT only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Automatic metrics; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: MARCH mirrors a radiology department hierarchy for chest CT reporting. A resident agent trained on paired CTs and reports writes a draft using region-level features; a retrieval agent finds similar previous cases; fellow agents revise the draft with that evidence; and an attending agent resolves disagreements through a structured consensus discussion. It was trained and tested on a large public CT dataset with language and clinical-accuracy metrics.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on a public chest CT report dataset (Weill Cornell, preprint).
papers.datasets: RadGenome-ChestCT: 25,692 chest CT scans from 21,304 patients with reports; official split 24,128 train / 1,564 test.
papers.preprocessing: CT partitioned into ten anatomical subregions with the SAT segmentation model.
papers.modelDetails: Resident Agent (frozen RadFM ViT3D + LLaMA-2-Chat-7B with LoRA) drafts the report; Retrieval Agent finds similar cases (image-image, image-text, logits-based over 18 abnormalities); Fellow Agents (GPT-4.1) revise; Attending Agent (GPT-4o) runs stance-based consensus.
papers.training: AdamW, lr 1e-5, batch 1, 10 epochs (~40 h) on one H100; temperature 0 for LLM agents.
papers.evaluation: BLEU, ROUGE-L, METEOR and clinical efficacy precision/recall/F1 over 18 abnormalities via RadBERT.
papers.baselines: R2GenPT and other 3D report-generation models.
papers.results: Significantly better clinical fidelity and linguistic scores than state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: A Multimodal Multi-Agent Framework for Radiology Report Generation
papers.authors: Ziruo Yi, Ting Xiao, Mark V. Albert
papers.aim: To generate more accurate radiology reports by splitting the work between agents.
papers.method: Five agents retrieve similar reports, draft, extract findings, read the image directly and write the final report; compared with a single-model baseline.
papers.result: More accurate and structured reports than the baseline on automatic and LLM-judged metrics.
papers.tools: CLIP
papers.gap: No clinician evaluation or uncertainty; X-ray only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: LLM-based evaluation; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Report generation is split into five steps handled by separate agents: retrieve similar prior reports, draft from them, extract key findings, describe the image directly with a vision-language model, and synthesise a final report. Separating retrieval from direct image reading reduces copying of irrelevant text. Evaluated against a single-model baseline with automatic and LLM-judged metrics.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on chest X-ray report generation (University of North Texas, preprint).
papers.datasets: Public chest X-ray report dataset (MIMIC-CXR style) with image-report pairs.
papers.preprocessing: Image and report embeddings for CLIP-style cross-modal retrieval.
papers.modelDetails: Five agents in sequence: Retrieval (top-k similar reports), Draft, Refiner (key findings), Vision (image description by a VLM) and Synthesis (final report), communicating through structured intermediate outputs.
papers.training: No training beyond retrieval embeddings.
papers.evaluation: Automatic NLG metrics and LLM-based evaluation of accuracy, structure and interpretability.
papers.baselines: Strong single-model RAG baseline.
papers.results: Outperformed the baseline on automatic metrics and LLM-based evaluation, with more accurate and structured reports.

papers.title: How Well Can Modern LLMs Act as Agent Cores in Radiology Environments?
papers.authors: Qiaoyu Zheng, Chaoyi Wu, Weike Zhao, Pengcheng Qiu, Lisong Dai, Ya Zhang, Yanfeng Wang, Weidi Xie
papers.aim: To measure how well modern LLMs work as the core of radiology agents, with ideal and with real tools.
papers.method: A synthetic benchmark with perfect simulated tools plus 165 real 2D and 3D cases with real tools, comparing many models by task difficulty.
papers.result: Success fell sharply on hard tasks, and agents with real tools were about 15% below their ideal performance.
papers.tools: DeepSeek, Claude, Gemini, GPT-4o, GPT-4
papers.gap: No measure of agent confidence or safe handover; mostly synthetic records.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Model versions change rapidly; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The benchmark separates two questions: how well an LLM plans and reasons when tools are perfect, using a large synthetic set of radiologist-checked records and simulated tools, and how well agents perform with real, imperfect tools on 165 real 2D and 3D cases for grounding, diagnosis and report generation. Many recent models were compared by task difficulty. The gap between idealised and real performance highlights tool failure and long chains as the main weaknesses of radiology agents.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of LLMs as agent cores in radiology (Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Renmin Hospital, preprint).
papers.datasets: RadA-BenchPlat synthetic layer: 2,200 clinician-verified patient records over 22 anatomy-modality combinations, 24.2k QA pairs and 10 tool categories; real-environment layer: 165 2D/3D cases (e.g. Chest ImaGenome, RadGenome-MRI) with executable tools.
papers.preprocessing: Records generated by GPT-4 from templates and polished for over a month by a radiologist (97.32% information-valid, 96.73% clinically consistent); 550 records reviewed by three further clinicians.
papers.modelDetails: LLM agent cores (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Gemini-3.0-Pro, GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, o3) planning and calling tools for grounding, diagnosis and report generation under varied tool availability.
papers.training: No training; prompting strategies compared.
papers.evaluation: Task completion by difficulty; Dice/Jaccard for grounding; accuracy for diagnosis; RadGraph F1, RaTE, LLM and human ratings for reports.
papers.baselines: Upper-bound idealised tools versus real tools.
papers.results: Completion falls with difficulty (Claude-Sonnet-4.5 0.691 regular to 0.327 high); real-environment agents trail their idealised upper bound by about 15%.

papers.title: AgentRx: A Benchmark Study of LLM Agents for Multimodal Clinical Prediction Tasks
papers.authors: Baraa Al Jorf, Farah E. Shamout
papers.aim: To benchmark LLM agents, alone and in teams, on multimodal clinical prediction.
papers.method: AgentRx: MIMIC encounters with notes, ICU signals, X-rays and reports; single and multi-agent LLMs predicted mortality and length of stay and were compared with trained models.
papers.result: LLM agents were worse than supervised models, and multi-agent teamwork did not reliably close the gap.
papers.tools: LLaVA-Med, LLaVA
papers.gap: No uncertainty or deferral; ICU prediction rather than diagnosis.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small backbones; single data source.
papers.methodologyDetail: AgentRx builds a large multimodal benchmark from MIMIC data, aligning a patient summary, ICU time series, chest radiograph and radiology reports per encounter, and tests whether LLM agents, alone or as a team of modality-specific agents, can predict mortality and length of stay. Four comparable-size vision-language backbones were used and compared with trained multimodal models. The negative finding is important: agent collaboration did not automatically handle heterogeneous data well.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study (CHIL 2026, PMLR) of single and multi-agent LLM systems for multimodal clinical risk prediction, NYU Abu Dhabi.
papers.datasets: MIMIC-IV EHR time series, MIMIC-CXR images, MIMIC-IV-Note radiology reports and patient summaries; mortality task 17,773 train / 4,925 test encounters (CXR subset 4,259/1,174); length-of-stay task of similar size.
papers.preprocessing: Modalities aligned per encounter; images 224x224; EHR serialised for LLM input.
papers.modelDetails: Single-agent and multi-agent (modality-specific agents with collaboration) frameworks with four ~7-8B VLM backbones: Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, LLaVA-Med-v1.5.
papers.training: Batch size 3-4 (16 for supervised models, 1 for LLaVA-Med); supervised multimodal baselines trained.
papers.evaluation: AUROC, AUPRC and related metrics for in-hospital mortality and length of stay, unimodal and multimodal.
papers.baselines: Supervised multimodal fusion models; single-agent LLMs.
papers.results: LLM agents lagged supervised models on multimodal prediction, and multi-agent collaboration did not reliably close the gap, showing a need for better collaboration over heterogeneous inputs.

papers.title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
papers.authors: Semil Eminovic, Robin Schmidt, Bogdan Levita, Maximilian Lindholz, Tobias Penzkofer, Jawed Nawabi
papers.aim: To test whether rule-based and LLM-based checks stop radiology agents from writing false information into records.
papers.method: Six LLM agents wrote documentation in a simulated system, some with misleading inputs; every write passed a safety gate with permissions, rules, or rules plus an LLM checker.
papers.result: Serious errors occurred in 7-27% of episodes; layered checks reduced but did not prevent them.
papers.tools: Claude, TRIPOD, CLAIM
papers.gap: Verification is rule- and LLM-based, not calibrated uncertainty; synthetic data.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Simulated environment; future model versions may differ.
papers.methodologyDetail: Six LLM agents were asked to write radiology documentation in a simulated information system; in some scenarios an external document contained misleading information. Every action that would change the record had to pass a safety gate configured with permissions only, deterministic rules, or rules plus an LLM checker. A separate evaluator scored every executed statement against a hidden reference. Results quantify how often agents record false information and how much layered verification helps, which informs the safeguards around the orchestrator in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled computational study in a simulated radiology information environment with synthetic patients (Charité Berlin); protocol, scenarios and analysis fixed in advance; reported to TRIPOD-LLM and CLAIM.
papers.datasets: 48 synthetic base scenarios in three documentation modules; 48 clean and 43 misleading-information variants (91 variants); six agents; 1,638 episodes.
papers.preprocessing: Reference standard stored separately and hidden from the agent and checker.
papers.modelDetails: Tool-using LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) with read-only tools; each state-changing action passes a safeguard gate: permissions only, plus deterministic rules, plus an LLM checker; blocked actions can be revised twice within 40 tool calls.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Proportion of episodes with a high-severity error, task success, justified vs unnecessary blocks, scored by a deterministic evaluator.
papers.baselines: Permissions-only configuration.
papers.results: With permissions only, high-severity errors in 7.3% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to 27.1% (GLM-5.3) of episodes; average 14.9% clean and 25.0% with misleading information; task success 49.0-77.1%; layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors.
papers.statistics: Within-scenario risk differences with stratified t-intervals (Satterthwaite) and cluster bootstrap; no hypothesis tests.

papers.title: Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Agents for Clinical Decision Making in Oncology
papers.authors: Dyke Ferber, Omar S. M. El Nahhas, Georg Wölflein, Isabella C. Wiest, Jan Clusmann, Marie-Elisabeth Leßman, Sebastian Foersch, Jacqueline Lammert, Maximilian Tschochohei, Dirk Jäger, et al.
papers.aim: To show that an LLM agent with validated tools can make better oncology decisions than an LLM alone.
papers.method: An LLM agent with specialist tools and guideline retrieval worked through 20 realistic multimodal cancer cases; clinicians assessed tool use and recommendations.
papers.result: Decision accuracy rose from about 30% (GPT-4 alone) to about 87% with tools, and most answers cited guidelines.
papers.tools: GPT-4, MedSAM
papers.gap: Only 20 cases; no uncertainty or deferral; tool errors can propagate silently.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Retrospective proof of concept.
papers.methodologyDetail: An LLM agent was given a set of validated specialist tools and a retrieval system over oncology guidelines and asked to work through 20 realistic multimodal cancer cases, deciding which tool to call, combining results and citing evidence. Clinicians assessed tool use, conclusions and recommendations against GPT-4 alone. The authors argue that validating each tool separately simplifies regulation, a principle relevant to separately validated agents in this framework.
papers.studyDesign: Preprint version of the autonomous oncology agent study (Heidelberg, Dresden, TUM and others), later published in Nature Cancer.
papers.datasets: Knowledge base of about 6,800 documents from MDCalc, UpToDate, MEDITRON guidelines, ASCO, ESMO and Onkopedia; 20 realistic multimodal patient cases (histology, radiology, genomics, clinical history).
papers.preprocessing: Guideline documents keyword-filtered and embedded for retrieval.
papers.modelDetails: GPT-4 as central agent calling tools: vision transformers predicting mutations from histology, MedSAM for radiology segmentation, OncoKB, PubMed search and guideline retrieval.
papers.training: No LLM training; tools are pre-trained models.
papers.evaluation: Correct tool use, correctness of conclusions and completeness of recommendations, citation of guidelines, judged by clinicians.
papers.baselines: GPT-4 without tools.
papers.results: Decision accuracy rose from about 30% (GPT-4 alone) to about 87% with tools; most tool calls correct; most answers cited guidelines.

papers.title: MedOpenClaw and MedFlowBench: Auditing Medical Agents in Full-Study Workflows
papers.authors: Weixiang Shen, Chengzhi Shen, Yanzhu Hu, Che Liu, Junde Wu, Jiayuan Zhu, Xiao Han, Zongyue Li, Jingpei Wu, Min Xu, et al.
papers.aim: To audit medical agents working on complete imaging studies in real viewer software.
papers.method: MedOpenClaw/MedFlowBench: agents must open full studies (brain MRI, PET/CT, pathology), find lesions and record visual evidence; answers and evidence are scored.
papers.result: Brain MRI tasks were easiest (localisation 0.96), but longitudinal comparison, small lesions and self-checking remained weak.
papers.tools: 3D Slicer, QuPath, Gemini, Claude
papers.gap: No uncertainty or deferral measure; agents not clinically validated.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Public datasets; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of answering questions about pre-cropped images, agents in MedOpenClaw must open complete studies in real imaging software, navigate them, find the lesion and record auditable visual evidence. The benchmark covers brain MRI, longitudinal MRI, PET/CT and pathology slides and scores both answers and the evidence produced. It shows that brain-tumour localisation is within reach of frontier models but that longitudinal reasoning and verification remain weak.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark and runtime development for full-study imaging agents (TUM, LMU, Imperial, Oxford, NVIDIA and others, preprint).
papers.datasets: Full imaging studies from public sets including UCSF-PDGM (brain MRI), longitudinal MRI, NSCLC-Radiogenomics (PET/CT), BRACS and CAMELYON17 (pathology).
papers.preprocessing: Complete volumes or slides loaded in viewers; tasks defined with evidence requirements.
papers.modelDetails: MedOpenClaw: a controlled, replayable runtime in which VLM agents operate 3D Slicer and QuPath (navigate slices and magnifications, measure, annotate); MedFlowBench tasks in radiology and pathology tracks.
papers.training: No training; evaluated general and medical VLMs (GPT-5.x, Gemini 3.x, Claude, Qwen3.5) and baselines M3D and RadFM.
papers.evaluation: Task accuracy, strict evidence-grounded accuracy and localisation, under MCQ or structured-answer protocols.
papers.baselines: Direct VLM answering on pre-selected images.
papers.results: Brain MRI easiest (Gemini 3.1 Pro task 0.73, strict 0.73, localisation 0.96); performance dropped sharply for longitudinal comparison and small lesions (e.g. lung PET/CT); tools help when they simplify procedures, but agents struggle to choose inputs, manage viewer state and verify intermediate results.
papers.availability: Runtime and benchmark released; dataset licences listed.

papers.title: A Modular Agent for Reliable and Auditable Spatial Relation Verification in CT Scans
papers.authors: Simon Vincent Abel, Heiko Hillenhagen, Michael Götz, Timo Ropinski, Ayhan Can Erdur, Daniel Santak Wolf
papers.venue: Published at the MICCAI 2026 Agentic AI for Medicine Workshop
papers.aim: To answer spatial questions about CT scans reliably by using detection and geometry instead of guessing.
papers.method: A modular agent routes each question to an anatomy detector and a geometry module so every answer is traceable; compared with vision-language models answering directly.
papers.result: 94.1% accuracy, 42.5 points better than direct prompting.
papers.tools: LangChain, YOLO
papers.gap: Single 2D task; detector errors not expressed as uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: CT slices only; workshop scale.
papers.methodologyDetail: The agent keeps a normal question-answer interface but, instead of letting the vision-language model guess spatial relations, it routes the question to a detector that finds the anatomical structures and a geometry module that computes the relation, so each answer is traceable to detections and rules. Compared directly with the same models answering end to end, the modular design was far more accurate. It supports delegating verifiable sub-tasks to specialised, auditable components.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and controlled comparison (Ulm University and TUM; MICCAI 2026 Agentic AI workshop).
papers.datasets: MIRP RQ1 benchmark of axial CT slices with binary spatial-relation questions; held-out test set of 938 image-question pairs; anatomical detector trained on the training cohort plus AMOS and BTCV (61 classes, 421,023 instances).
papers.preprocessing: Segmentation-derived bounding boxes; strict patient-level separation between detector training and test.
papers.modelDetails: Hybrid agent: a VLM controller (MedGemma 4B or Qwen2-VL 7B, orchestrated with LangChain) extracts the spatial query and routes it to a pathway where a YOLO detector localises structures and deterministic geometry computes the answer.
papers.training: Detector trained on the training cohort (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and F1 on binary spatial questions.
papers.baselines: Direct end-to-end VLM prompting with the same interface.
papers.results: Best hybrid configuration 94.1% accuracy and 94.2% F1, 42.5 points more accurate than direct Qwen2-VL prompting.

papers.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Uncertainty-Aware and Abstention-Enabled Acute Ischemic Stroke Imaging Decisions
papers.authors: Md Rashadul Islam
papers.aim: To design a stroke imaging AI that separates perception, uncertainty and decision, and can abstain.
papers.method: Separate agents analyse lesions, estimate slice-level reliability and apply a safety policy that may abstain, with visual explanations; qualitative evaluation.
papers.result: Abstention happened in ambiguous and low-information slices; no quantitative benchmark.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: Fixed thresholds, no calibration analysis or clinician evaluation; no quantitative results.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single-author conceptual study.
papers.methodologyDetail: The framework separates perception, uncertainty estimation and decision into distinct agents for stroke imaging: one agent analyses lesions, another estimates how reliable each slice prediction is, and a decision agent applies a safety policy that can abstain, with visual explanations for both outcomes. The evaluation is qualitative, showing where abstention occurs. It illustrates the design principle of this study but without quantitative validation.
papers.studyDesign: Conceptual framework with qualitative case-based evaluation (Daffodil International University, Bangladesh, preprint).
papers.datasets: Representative acute ischaemic stroke CT/MRI slices (public data; no new cohort reported).
papers.preprocessing: Slice-wise analysis.
papers.modelDetails: Perception agent for lesion-aware analysis; uncertainty estimation agent computing slice-level predictive reliability; decision agent applying a safety policy that predicts or abstains by predefined uncertainty thresholds; explainability module for both predictions and abstentions.
papers.training: Not reported in detail.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative and behavioural evaluation of uncertainty and abstention patterns.
papers.baselines: None quantitative.
papers.results: Abstention arose in diagnostically ambiguous regions and low-information slices; no new performance benchmark claimed.

papers.title: WSI-Agents: A Collaborative Multi-Agent System for Multi-Modal Whole Slide Image Analysis
papers.authors: Xinheng Lyu, Yuci Liang, Wenting Chen, Meidan Ding, Jiaqi Yang, Guolin Huang, Daokun Zhang, Xiangjian He, Linlin Shen
papers.aim: To analyse whole-slide pathology images with a team of agents that combine general and specialist models.
papers.method: WSI-Agents: decides the task type, routes to the right pathology model, then verifies answers for consistency and with external knowledge before summarising.
papers.result: Better than current whole-slide multimodal models and medical agent frameworks.
papers.tools: WSI-Agents: a task agent classifies the question and allocates specialised expert agents;
papers.gap: Verification scores not calibrated; no clinician handover.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Benchmarks only; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: WSI-Agents answers questions about whole-slide images by first deciding what kind of task a question is and which specialised pathology model should answer it, then checking the preliminary answers with verification steps based on consistency and external knowledge before summarising. It balances the versatility of general models with the accuracy of task-specific ones, which is the same trade-off as the Pathology Agent in this framework.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmark evaluation (Shenzhen University and partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: Multi-modal WSI benchmarks with WSIs paired with questions and reports (e.g. WSI-VQA and report generation sets).
papers.preprocessing: WSIs processed by pathology feature encoders.
papers.modelDetails: WSI-Agents: a task agent classifies the question and allocates specialised expert agents; verification mechanisms (internal consistency and external knowledge checks) assess answers; a summary module produces the final response.
papers.training: Expert agents are existing pathology MLLMs and task-specific models.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on WSI VQA, report generation metrics and multi-task performance.
papers.baselines: Single pathology MLLMs and task-specific models.
papers.results: Outperformed current WSI MLLMs and medical agent frameworks across tasks.

papers.title: LungNoduleAgent: A Collaborative Multi-Agent System for Precision Diagnosis of Lung Nodules
papers.authors: Cheng Yang, Hui Jin, Xinlei Yu, Zhipeng Wang, Yaoqun Liu, Fenglei Fan, Dajiang Lei, Gangyong Jia, Changmiao Wang, Ruiquan Ge
papers.aim: To diagnose lung nodules with a multi-agent system from detection to malignancy assessment.
papers.method: Detection models propose nodules checked by vision-language judges; a radiologist agent writes local reports; doctor agents use a knowledge graph to decide malignancy.
papers.result: Better than baselines for nodule description and diagnosis.
papers.tools: Nodule Spotter (mixture of detection foundation models, mask clustering, VLM judging panel), Simulated Radiologist (local CT report generation with…
papers.gap: Class scores not calibrated; no deferral; 2D slices.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Partly private data; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: LungNoduleAgent works in three stages: several detection models propose nodule masks that are clustered and validated by a panel of vision-language judges; a simulated radiologist writes a local report for each nodule from global and close-up features; and a doctor-agent system retrieves knowledge from a medical knowledge graph and discusses the case to give a malignancy diagnosis with reasons. Generated descriptions were checked with attribute-level yes/no questions, including negative questions that catch fabricated details.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on private and public lung CT data (Hangzhou Dianzi University and partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: Two private sets of 1,616 and 386 axial lung CT slices (512x512) with nodule boxes, morphology and malignancy class (pre-invasive, minimally invasive, invasive adenocarcinoma); LIDC-IDRI (1,018 scans) with masks, attributes and malignancy ratings 1-5.
papers.preprocessing: CT volume split into slices; attribute-level yes/no questions (positive and negative) built from annotations to verify generated reports.
papers.modelDetails: Nodule Spotter (mixture of detection foundation models, mask clustering, VLM judging panel), Simulated Radiologist (local CT report generation with gated cross-attention of global and focal features), Doctor Agent System (knowledge-graph retrieval, multi-agent discussion, final diagnosis with class scores).
papers.training: Training details per module in the paper.
papers.evaluation: Detection metrics, attribute QA accuracy (Pos/Neg QA), malignancy classification accuracy.
papers.baselines: General and medical MLLMs and prior nodule analysis models.
papers.results: Outperformed baselines in nodule description and diagnosis; region-level alignment and multi-agent collaboration both contributed.

papers.title: Evidence-based diagnostic reasoning with multi-agent copilot for human pathology
papers.authors: Luca L. Weishaupt, Chengkuan Chen, Drew F. K. Williamson, Richard J. Chen, Guillaume Jaume, Tong Ding, Bowen Chen, Anurag Vaidya, Long Phi Le, Guillaume Jaume, et al.
papers.aim: To build a pathology copilot that explores whole slides like a pathologist and explains its diagnosis.
papers.method: PathChat+ assistant model plus SlideSeek agents that zoom and collect evidence before diagnosing; tested on several benchmarks and a new 150-slide diagnostic set.
papers.result: PathChat+ clearly outperformed earlier and general models across benchmarks.
papers.tools: PathChat+ multimodal pathology copilot and SlideSeek multi-agent system that navigates WSIs, gathers evidence across magnifications and reasons to an…
papers.gap: No calibrated confidence or defer-to-pathologist mechanism; brain tumours not specific.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single-institution slides; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built PathChat+, a pathology assistant model, and SlideSeek, a multi-agent system that explores a whole slide like a pathologist, zooming and collecting regional evidence before reasoning to a diagnosis with an explanation. Evaluation covered region-level question answering, classification and captioning benchmarks and a new 150-slide diagnostic benchmark with many rare diagnoses, with bootstrap intervals and permutation tests. It shows agentic navigation of gigapixel slides with evidence collection.
papers.studyDesign: Model and agent development with ROI-level and slide-level benchmarking (Brigham and Women's / MGH / Harvard, preprint).
papers.datasets: ROI benchmarks: PathMMU (validation 710 Q&A, test 9,677 Q&A; expert-level subset 1,156), PathBenchQA, BRACS, UniToPatho, HiCervix; slide-level DDxBench: 150 H&E WSIs from BWH archives with report-derived diagnoses verified by a pathologist, 55 categories (14 common, 41 rare) across 19 tissues.
papers.preprocessing: Diagnoses mapped to OncoTree codes; rarity defined as <6 per 100,000 per year.
papers.modelDetails: PathChat+ multimodal pathology copilot and SlideSeek multi-agent system that navigates WSIs, gathers evidence across magnifications and reasons to an evidence-based diagnosis.
papers.training: PathChat+ trained on large pathology instruction data (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: VQA accuracy, classification accuracy, captioning, slide-level diagnostic accuracy for common and rare diseases.
papers.baselines: Prior PathChat, state-of-the-art general and pathology MLLMs.
papers.results: PathChat+ substantially outperformed PathChat and general and pathology-specific models across benchmarks.
papers.statistics: 95% CIs by bootstrap (1,000 replicates); two-sided paired permutation tests (1,000 permutations).

papers.title: Trust but Verify:Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Clinical Information Extraction in Pathology
papers.authors: Yufan Wang, Anit Kumar Sahu, Yan Fei Ng, Daniel Kang, Shayan Vassef, Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Koustuv Saha, Piyum Zonooz, Navin Kumar, Chee Leong Cheng, et al.
papers.aim: To extract information from pathology reports with the supporting text shown for every answer.
papers.method: Clinicians define the fields; agents return each value with the exact source text; tested on 54 gastric biopsy reports against another system.
papers.result: 98.6% correct, with every correct answer linked to verbatim evidence; value lies in traceability.
papers.tools: nMAS: configurable workflow separating clinician-defined field specifications from extraction models;
papers.gap: Tiny pilot; no uncertainty output.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Dummy reports; four fields only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The workflow lets clinicians define the fields they need and returns, for each field, a prediction plus the exact text in the report that supports it. On 54 gastric biopsy reports it was compared with an independent extraction system; both made the same three errors, so the authors argue the value lies in traceability and workflow integration rather than accuracy. Source-linked evidence is a practical way to make agent outputs auditable.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective pilot technical evaluation of an evidence-linked multi-agent extraction workflow (Nimblemind with Singapore General Hospital, preprint).
papers.datasets: 54 dummy gastric biopsy pathology reports (2022) from a tertiary system in Singapore; four binary target fields chosen with four clinicians; 216 feature-case decisions.
papers.preprocessing: Identifiers replaced with dummy placeholders; full report records (coded and narrative fields) processed.
papers.modelDetails: nMAS: configurable workflow separating clinician-defined field specifications from extraction models; returns predictions with verbatim source-linked evidence spans.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 per field against two reviewers (Cohen's kappa 0.975); evidence-span verification.
papers.baselines: External UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator.
papers.results: 213/216 correct (98.61%); biopsy fields 100%, H. pylori positivity 98.15%, H. pylori gastritis 96.30%; all evidence spans for correct predictions verbatim in source; comparator identical at label level.

papers.title: The Optimization Paradox in Clinical AI Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Suhana Bedi, Iddah Mlauzi, Daniel Shin, Sanmi Koyejo, Nigam H. Shah
papers.aim: To show that combining the best model for each step does not give the best clinical multi-agent system.
papers.method: Diagnosis was split into three steps; single-model, multi-agent and best-of-breed systems were compared on 2,400 real cases for outcome, process and cost.
papers.result: The best-of-breed system had good information accuracy (85.5%) but lower diagnostic accuracy (67.7%) than a top multi-agent system (77.4%).
papers.tools: Single-agent systems (one model for all steps) vs multi-agent systems (specialised models per step), including a best-of-breed system assembled from…
papers.gap: No uncertainty passed between steps; text cases.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Four abdominal conditions; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors split clinical diagnosis into three steps and built systems either with one model doing everything or with a specialised model per step, including one assembled from the best model for each step. Evaluated on 2,400 real cases with outcome, process and cost metrics, the component-optimised system did worse overall, showing that information flow and compatibility between agents matter. End-to-end validation of the whole chain is therefore required.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective comparative evaluation on MIMIC-CDM (Stanford, preprint).
papers.datasets: 2,400 real patient cases with appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis or diverticulitis (MIMIC-CDM).
papers.preprocessing: Diagnosis decomposed into information gathering, interpretation and differential diagnosis.
papers.modelDetails: Single-agent systems (one model for all steps) vs multi-agent systems (specialised models per step), including a best-of-breed system assembled from top components.
papers.training: No training; various LLMs.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, process adherence (information accuracy) and cost efficiency.
papers.baselines: Single-agent systems.
papers.results: Multi-agent systems generally outperformed single agents, but the best-of-breed system with 85.5% information accuracy had lower diagnostic accuracy (67.7%) than a top multi-agent system (77.4%).

papers.title: RadFabric: Agentic AI System with Reasoning Capability for Radiology
papers.authors: Wenting Chen, Yi Dong, Zhaojun Ding, Yucheng Shi, Yifan Zhou, Fang Zeng, Yijun Luo, Tianyu Lin, Yihang Su, Yichen Wu, et al.
papers.aim: To combine several chest X-ray models through a reasoning agent that reconciles their outputs.
papers.method: RadFabric links classifiers and report generators via a tool protocol; a reasoning agent reads all outputs and resolves conflicts, optionally trained with reinforcement learning.
papers.result: Near-perfect fracture detection and better overall diagnosis than the separate models.
papers.tools: RadFabric: built on the Model Context Protocol;
papers.gap: Aggregation does not use calibrated confidence; no clinician deferral; CXR only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; benchmark evaluation.
papers.methodologyDetail: RadFabric connects several chest X-ray classifiers and report-generation models through a standard tool protocol, then a reasoning agent reads all their scores and texts and reconciles them, catching findings that one model misses or misattributes. Case examples show classifiers detecting opacities that report generators omit. The reasoning agent can be further trained with reinforcement learning. It is an example of aggregating heterogeneous specialist outputs, though without calibrated uncertainty.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on chest X-ray data (CityU HK, MGH, CUHK and others, preprint).
papers.datasets: Public chest X-ray datasets with multi-label pathology annotations (e.g. MIMIC-CXR/CheXpert-style labels including lung opacity, pneumonia, fractures).
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed in extract.
papers.modelDetails: RadFabric: built on the Model Context Protocol; multiple CXR classification agents and report-generation models (e.g. CAMMAL, CheXagent) feed a reasoning agent that reconciles their outputs; reasoning agent optionally trained with GRPO.
papers.training: Reasoning agent trained with GRPO reinforcement learning (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Per-pathology detection accuracy and overall diagnostic performance.
papers.baselines: Individual CXR agents and report generators; prior systems.
papers.results: Near-perfect fracture detection (1.000 accuracy) and better overall diagnosis than baselines; trained reasoning agent improved further.

papers.title: Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents
papers.authors: Frederik Hauke, Patrick Wienholt, Christiane Kuhl, Dyke Ferber, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
papers.aim: To test whether passing uncertainty from an image model to an LLM agent improves its decisions.
papers.method: A chest X-ray classifier with Monte Carlo dropout gave outputs to an LLM agent with or without uncertainty, as numbers or as a simple high-risk flag.
papers.result: Only the simple flag changed the agent's behaviour, cutting confident misdiagnoses from 8.5% to 2.7%.
papers.tools: DINOv2, ViT, Monte Carlo dropout
papers.gap: Chest X-ray only; agent simulated; no human clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single dataset; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: A chest-radiograph classifier was trained at ten data scales with Monte Carlo dropout to show that its epistemic uncertainty tracks overfitting and flags confident errors. In a factorial experiment, a language-model decision-support agent received the classifier's outputs either with or without uncertainty, presented either as raw numbers or as a simple 'high error risk' flag. Only the flag changed the agent's behaviour, halving confident misdiagnoses. This directly informs how uncertainty should be communicated between agents in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective experimental study with a 2x2 factorial agent experiment (RWTH Aachen, Heidelberg, Dresden; preprint).
papers.datasets: TAIX-Ray Thorax public cohort: 137,593 training, 34,860 validation, 42,928 test radiographs (patient-stratified); ordinal grades for eight findings (heart size, congestion, effusion, opacities, atelectasis left/right).
papers.preprocessing: Grades binarised at >0 for training, raw grades kept; centre-cropped 448x448, z-normalised; augmentations: random crop, vertical flip, axis transposition.
papers.modelDetails: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 (~21M parameters) fine-tuned with a linear head; Monte Carlo dropout for epistemic uncertainty; an LLM clinical-decision-support agent receives predictions with uncertainty as raw scores or as a binary error-risk flag.
papers.training: Per-class BCE; AdamW, lr 1e-6, weight decay 1e-2; FP16; ten training-set fractions for scaling analysis.
papers.evaluation: Error-detection AUROC; relation of uncertainty to validation loss; agent confident-misdiagnosis rate across 2x2 conditions.
papers.baselines: Point prediction alone; raw uncertainty scores.
papers.results: Uncertainty raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 (+0.023, 95% CI +0.014 to +0.033); the agent used uncertainty only as a binary error-risk flag, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%.

papers.title: Why Specialist Models Still Matter: A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Paradigm for Medical Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Yanan Wang, Shuaicong Hu, Jian Liu, Guohui Zhou, Aiguo Wang, Cuiwei Yang
papers.aim: To show that generalist LLMs should coordinate specialist models rather than replace them.
papers.method: HetMedAgent: an orchestrator sends each data type to a specialist that reports a confidence, conflicts are weighted, a reasoning agent integrates them, and uncertain cases go to a clinician.
papers.result: AUROC 0.866/0.801/0.727 vs 0.823/0.751/0.692 for the best multi-agent baseline; generalist plus specialists beat either alone.
papers.tools: Transformer
papers.gap: Confidence calibration and clinician workload not rigorously measured; cardiology rather than neuro-oncology.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; limited datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: HetMedAgent argues that generalist LLMs should coordinate rather than replace specialist models. An orchestrator sends each data type to a trained specialist that reports findings with a confidence; conflicting findings are weighted; a reasoning agent integrates them with clinical information; and when the overall decision is uncertain, a clinician is asked to intervene, with thresholds adjusted adaptively. It was compared with medical LLMs and multi-agent frameworks on three tasks. Its structure is very close to this study's design, though calibration is not deeply evaluated.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on three real-world clinical decision tasks (preprint, China).
papers.datasets: Three clinical decision datasets with multimodal data including echocardiography and ECG plus clinical information (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Modality-specific data dispatched to specialist models.
papers.modelDetails: HetMedAgent: an orchestrator dispatches each modality to specialist models (transformer-based ECHO and ECG models) that return findings with generation confidence; conflict-aware weighting; a reasoning LLM integrates evidence; decision uncertainty triggers clinician intervention; adaptive threshold calibration.
papers.training: Specialist models trained per modality (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUROC and F1 for each task; BERTScore and conflict scores for specialist outputs; with and without clinician intervention.
papers.baselines: Medical LLMs (PMC-LLaMA, Meditron, BioMistral, others) and multi-agent systems (MedAgents, AgentClinic, AutoGen, MetaGPT).
papers.results: Without clinician: AUROC 0.866/0.801/0.727 vs best multi-agent 0.823/0.751/0.692; generalist-specialist synergy beat either alone; transformer specialists had best BERTScore and lowest conflict.

papers.title: Trustworthy Agents for Electronic Health Records through Confidence Estimation
papers.authors: Yongwoo Song, Minbyul Jeong, Mujeen Sung
papers.aim: To make EHR question-answering agents trustworthy by measuring accuracy only on confident answers.
papers.method: The agent estimates confidence at each database step and combines them; a new metric scores accuracy at strict confidence thresholds on two ICU databases.
papers.result: Up to 25 points better than baselines at strict thresholds, where baselines failed completely.
papers.tools: TrustEHRAgent: a confidence-aware LLM agent with step-wise confidence estimation during multi-step EHR querying and…
papers.gap: Confidence not checked for calibration; EHR text tasks only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; benchmark questions.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors propose measuring an agent's accuracy only on answers it is confident about, at a series of confidence thresholds, which rewards agents that know when to abstain. Their agent estimates confidence at each step of querying an EHR database and combines these into an answer confidence. On two ICU databases it maintained useful accuracy at strict thresholds where baselines did not. HCAcc@k% is a variant of the selective-risk measures used in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Method and metric development on EHR question answering (Kyung Hee University and Upstage AI, preprint).
papers.datasets: MIMIC-III and eICU EHR question-answering benchmarks.
papers.preprocessing: Questions over structured EHR databases.
papers.modelDetails: TrustEHRAgent: a confidence-aware LLM agent with step-wise confidence estimation during multi-step EHR querying and answering; new metric HCAcc@k% (hallucination-controlled accuracy at k% confidence threshold).
papers.training: No training reported.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and HCAcc@k% at varying thresholds.
papers.baselines: Baseline EHR agents without confidence estimation.
papers.results: TrustEHRAgent beat baselines by up to 25.34 points at HCAcc@70%, where baselines failed completely.

papers.title: CRC-Router: Risk-Constrained Routing for Medical Agentic AI Systems
papers.authors: Xueyang Li, Mingze Jiang, Gelei Xu, Jun Xia, Ching-Hao Chiu, Mengzhao Jia, Danny Z. Chen, Yiyu Shi
papers.aim: To decide for each chest X-ray finding whether to accept the AI or escalate, with a guaranteed error limit.
papers.method: CRC-Router combines ensemble score, disagreement, aleatoric uncertainty and out-of-distribution distance, predicts the risk of a wrong acceptance, and sets thresholds with conformal risk control (5% target).
papers.result: Best risk-coverage trade-off of all methods, meeting the 5% risk target on more findings, alone and inside an agent.
papers.tools: ResNet, DenseNet, conformal risk control, radiomics, ensemble
