papers.results: CIFAR-10 ResNet-110 (AURC / AUROC): baseline 9.94 / 90.76; mixup 15.05 / 86.93; LS 24.50 / 81.89; focal 10.70 / 90.70; CS-KD 18.02 / 85.89. WideResNet baseline AURC 4.89, AUROC 93.24; LS 16.69 / 85.30. FMFP had higher AUROC than baseline (e.g. +3.00 and +2.24 points on two settings for ResNet-110) and the best results on most metrics.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard deviation over repeated runs.

papers.title: Revisiting the Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.authors: Matthias Minderer, Josip Djolonga, Rob Romijnders, Frances Hubis, Xiaohua Zhai, Neil Houlsby, Dustin Tran, Mario Lucic
papers.aim: To re-check whether newer, more accurate image classifiers are worse calibrated, using recent architectures such as Vision Transformers and MLP-Mixer.
papers.method: Systematic study of calibration (ECE) vs accuracy for many recent ImageNet models (ViT, MLP-Mixer, BiT, ResNeXt-WSL, SimCLR, CLIP, AlexNet, etc.), in-distribution, under ImageNet-C corruptions and on natural OOD datasets, with and without temperature scaling; analyses effect of model size, pre-training amount and architecture.
papers.result: The most recent non-convolutional models (ViT, MLP-Mixer) are among the best calibrated; calibration degrades less under distribution shift than in older models; models Pareto-optimal on ImageNet stay Pareto-optimal on OOD sets; architecture matters more than size or pre-training for calibration.
papers.tools: Pre-trained ImageNet models (ViT, MLP-Mixer, BiT, ResNeXt-WSL, SimCLR, CLIP, AlexNet), temperature scaling, ImageNet-C, ImageNet-v2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, ObjectNet.
papers.gap: Natural images only; calibration measured, not used for deferral.
papers.relation: Re-examines calibration of modern architectures, including transformers, in and out of distribution, which informs backbone choice for calibrated agents.
papers.limitations: Image classification only; ECE estimator choices affect comparisons.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors revisit the widely cited claim (from Guo et al. 2017) that modern networks are badly calibrated. They take a large set of published ImageNet classifiers - from AlexNet and ResNets to BiT, ResNeXt-WSL, SimCLR, CLIP, Vision Transformers and MLP-Mixer, in different sizes and with different amounts of pre-training - and measure ECE against error on the ImageNet validation set, on ImageNet-C corruptions at increasing severity, and on natural out-of-distribution sets such as ImageNet-R and ObjectNet, both before and after temperature scaling. The newest non-convolutional models are among the best calibrated, lose less calibration under shift, and remain on the accuracy-calibration Pareto front on OOD data; model size and pre-training data do not explain the differences, so architecture is the main factor. For our PhD this is evidence for considering transformer backbones in the imaging agents when good calibration across hospitals is needed, while still checking calibration on local data.
papers.studyDesign: Large empirical study of pre-trained image models (no new method).
papers.datasets: ImageNet validation set; ImageNet-C (corruptions); natural out-of-distribution sets: ImageNet-v2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, ObjectNet.
papers.preprocessing: Models used as published; temperature scaling fitted on held-out ImageNet data for recalibrated results.
papers.modelDetails: Model families compared: Vision Transformer (ViT), MLP-Mixer, Big Transfer (BiT) ResNets, ResNeXt WSL, SimCLR, CLIP zero-shot, AlexNet and others, across sizes and pre-training sets (ImageNet, ImageNet-21k, JFT-300M).
papers.training: Not applicable (pre-trained models evaluated).
papers.evaluation: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) vs classification error; ECE under corruption severity; Pareto analysis of accuracy vs calibration on OOD datasets; effect of temperature scaling.
papers.baselines: Older convolutional models (e.g. ResNets, AlexNet) as the reference trend.
papers.results: Non-convolutional models (MLP-Mixer, ViT) had the best calibration among accurate models; their calibration was more robust to ImageNet-C shift; accuracy and calibration were strongly correlated on OOD datasets; within families, larger models were not necessarily worse calibrated; differences remained after temperature scaling. Values shown in figures (Table 1 lists model details).

papers.title: Deep Deterministic Uncertainty: A New Simple Baseline
papers.authors: Jishnu Mukhoti, Andreas Kirsch, Joost van Amersfoort, Philip H. S. Torr, Yarin Gal
papers.aim: To get reliable epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty from a single forward pass of one network, matching deep ensembles without their cost.
papers.method: Deep Deterministic Uncertainty (DDU): train a standard softmax network with a well-regularised feature space (residual connections + spectral normalisation); after training, fit Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (one Gaussian per class) on the features. Feature density = epistemic uncertainty (OOD detection); softmax entropy = aleatoric uncertainty.
papers.result: DDU beat the single-pass methods DUQ and SNGP on OOD detection and matched 5-member deep ensembles on CIFAR-10/100 vs SVHN / Tiny-ImageNet, and on ImageNet vs ImageNet-O; it also worked well for active learning.
papers.tools: Wide-ResNet-28-10, ResNet-50, Wide-ResNet-50-2, VGG-16; spectral normalisation; GDA density; PyTorch.
papers.gap: Classification only; OOD detection on natural images; not tested for medical segmentation or deferral.
papers.relation: Separates epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty in a single forward pass, a cheap uncertainty signal for compute-limited deployment.
papers.limitations: Needs spectral normalisation and residual architecture; density in feature space may not capture all shifts.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors want ensemble-quality uncertainty from one network and one forward pass. They argue the key ingredient of earlier single-pass methods is a well-behaved feature space, which they obtain with residual connections and spectral normalisation in an ordinary softmax classifier. After normal training they fit one Gaussian per class to the penultimate-layer features of the training data; for a new input, low density under these Gaussians signals an unfamiliar (out-of-distribution) case, while softmax entropy signals an ambiguous case. They test on CIFAR-10/100 with a Wide-ResNet-28-10 over 25 runs (OOD sets SVHN, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) and on ImageNet vs ImageNet-O with ResNet-50, Wide-ResNet-50-2 and VGG-16, comparing with DUQ, SNGP, energy scores and ensembles. DDU is the best single-pass method and matches or beats ensembles (ImageNet-O AUROC 59.4 vs 55.5 for a 3-ensemble with ResNet-50). For our PhD, DDU lets each agent separate 'this scan is ambiguous' from 'this scan is unlike anything I was trained on', and both can trigger escalation at almost no extra cost.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with benchmark experiments on OOD detection and active learning.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (in-distribution) vs SVHN, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet (OOD); ImageNet vs ImageNet-O; active learning on MNIST / Dirty-MNIST type benchmarks.
papers.preprocessing: Standard augmentation for each dataset; results averaged over 25 runs for CIFAR experiments.
papers.modelDetails: Backbone with residual connections and spectral normalisation (sensitivity + smoothness of features). After training, class-conditional Gaussians fitted to penultimate features (GDA). Epistemic score = feature log-density; aleatoric score = softmax entropy. Compared with DUQ (Jacobian penalty, kernel distance), SNGP (spectral norm + GP output layer), energy-based scores, 5-member ensembles (predictive entropy and mutual information).
papers.training: Standard softmax cross-entropy training; GDA fitting is a cheap post-training step; settings per dataset in appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, ECE and AUROC for OOD detection; active learning curves.
papers.baselines: Softmax entropy, energy-based model, DUQ, SNGP, 3- and 5-member deep ensembles.
papers.results: CIFAR-10 Wide-ResNet-28-10: softmax accuracy 95.98, ECE 0.85, AUROC vs SVHN 94.44 / CIFAR-100 89.39 / Tiny-ImageNet 88.42; DUQ 93.71 / 85.92 / 86.83; SNGP 94.0 / 91.13 / 89.97; DDU comparable to 5-ensembles (best single-pass). ImageNet vs ImageNet-O AUROC: ResNet-50 softmax entropy 50.65, energy 53.88, DDU 59.44, 3-ensemble MI 55.46; Wide-ResNet-50-2 DDU 63.15 vs 57.98 ensemble MI.

papers.title: Plex: Towards Reliability using Pretrained Large Model Extensions
papers.authors: Dustin Tran, Jeremiah Liu, Michael W. Dusenberry, et al.
papers.aim: To define and measure the reliability of large pre-trained models across uncertainty, robust generalisation and adaptation tasks, and to build model extensions that improve reliability out of the box.
papers.method: Defines 10 types of reliability tasks over 40 vision and language datasets (selective prediction, open-set recognition, calibration under covariate and subpopulation shift, label uncertainty, active learning, few-shot uncertainty). Builds ViT-Plex and T5-Plex: large pre-trained models with efficient ensembling (BatchEnsemble) and a Gaussian-process last layer, fine-tuned per task.
papers.result: Plex greatly improved the state of the art across reliability tasks without designing task-specific scores; reliability improved with model size (up to 1B parameters) and pre-training data (up to 4B examples); strong zero-shot open-set recognition and uncertainty in conversational language understanding.
papers.tools: ViT and T5 backbones (up to 1B parameters), BatchEnsemble, GP output layer (SNGP-style), JFT pre-training, TPUs; new ImageNet ReaL-H label-uncertainty dataset.
papers.gap: Very large compute; no medical imaging tasks; preprint.
papers.relation: Benchmarks reliability of large pretrained models, including selective prediction and uncertainty under shift, which are design references for trustworthy agents.
papers.limitations: Requires large-scale pre-training resources; evaluation tasks mostly natural images and text.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors argue a deployed model should be judged on reliability, not only accuracy: it should know when it is unsure, handle shifted data, and adapt with few labels. They assemble 10 kinds of reliability tasks over 40 datasets in vision and language, including selective prediction, open-set recognition, calibration under covariate and subpopulation shift, agreement with human label uncertainty (a new ImageNet ReaL-H dataset built from individual rater votes), active learning and few-shot uncertainty. They then extend large pre-trained Vision Transformers and T5 language models with two cheap uncertainty components - a BatchEnsemble (several low-cost ensemble members sharing most weights) and a Gaussian-process output layer - and fine-tune them per task. Across model sizes up to 1 billion parameters and pre-training data up to 4 billion examples, these Plex models improve nearly every reliability metric over standard fine-tuning and common uncertainty methods. For our PhD this supports building agents on pre-trained foundation backbones with a light ensemble/GP head, so the uncertainty used for escalation is strong without heavy per-task design.
papers.studyDesign: Large empirical study defining a reliability benchmark and proposing model extensions.
papers.datasets: 40 datasets. Vision: CIFAR-10/100 with CIFAR-10-C/100-C, SVHN, CIFAR-10H (label uncertainty), subpopulation-shift CIFAR; ImageNet-1K with ImageNet-A, -C, -R, ImageNetV2, ImageNet-Vid-Robust, ObjectNet, YTBB Robust; new ImageNet ReaL-H built from raw ImageNet ReaL rater data. Text: natural language inference, toxic comment detection, conversational language understanding.
papers.preprocessing: Label distributions for ReaL-H built from individual human ratings per image.
papers.modelDetails: Plex = pre-trained ViT or T5 + efficient ensemble (BatchEnsemble, rank-1 members) + Gaussian process last layer; fine-tuned on downstream tasks; compared across model sizes and pre-training dataset sizes.
papers.training: Pre-training on up to 4 billion examples; fine-tuning per task; details in appendix (large TPU budgets).
papers.evaluation: Per task: selective prediction (AUROC / oracle collaboration), open-set recognition AUROC, accuracy, NLL, ECE under covariate shift, label-uncertainty metrics on ReaL-H, active learning curves, few-shot uncertainty.
papers.baselines: Deterministic ViT/T5, MC dropout, deep ensembles, SNGP, BatchEnsemble alone, task-specific methods.
papers.results: Plex was best or near best on most of the 10 task types; gains increased with scale; reliability did not require task-specific tuning. Detailed numbers in many tables and figures of the 100+ page report.

papers.title: Conformal Risk Control
papers.authors: Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates, Adam Fisch, Lihua Lei, Tal Schuster
papers.aim: To extend conformal prediction from controlling coverage to controlling the expected value of any monotone loss, such as the false negative rate of a segmentation.
papers.method: Conformal risk control: on n calibration points compute the loss L_i(lambda) as a function of a threshold lambda; choose the smallest lambda such that (n/(n+1)) * mean loss + B/(n+1) <= alpha (B = maximum loss). This guarantees expected loss <= alpha on new data, tight to O(1/n). Extensions to distribution shift, quantile risk, multiple risks and U-statistics.
papers.result: Worked examples controlled the target risk at alpha = 0.1: polyp segmentation false negative rate mean 0.0987 (SD 0.0114) over 1,000 random splits; MS COCO multilabel FNR 0.0996 (SD 0.0052); also hierarchical ImageNet graph distance and open-domain QA token-level F1.
papers.tools: PraNet (polyp segmentation), TResNet (MS COCO), ResNet (hierarchical ImageNet), retrieval QA model; Python.
papers.gap: Guarantee is marginal (on average), not per patient; assumes exchangeable data.
papers.relation: Bounds any monotone clinical loss, such as false-negative rate in tumour segmentation, with distribution-free guarantees, which can set deferral thresholds.
papers.limitations: Loss must be monotone in lambda and bounded; marginal guarantee only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Standard conformal prediction guarantees that a prediction set contains the true answer with a chosen probability. Many medical tasks need a different guarantee, such as missing no more than 10% of a tumour. The authors generalise the method: for each calibration case they compute how the loss (here, the fraction of true tumour pixels missed) changes with the decision threshold, then pick the most permissive threshold whose adjusted average calibration loss stays below the target alpha. They prove the expected loss on a new case is then at most alpha, with very little slack. In a polyp segmentation example they pool five public endoscopy datasets, use a pre-trained PraNet, calibrate on 1,000 images and test on 781, repeating 1,000 random splits; the realised false negative rate averages 0.0987 for a 0.1 target. Similar control is shown for 80-class COCO labels, hierarchical ImageNet distance and question answering. For our PhD this allows the segmentation and classification agents to carry explicit error guarantees (for example on missed tumour volume) fitted on local Sri Lankan calibration cases, with uncertain cases escalated.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological / statistical paper with worked examples in vision and language.
papers.datasets: Gut polyp segmentation pooled from Kvasir, Hyper-Kvasir, CVC-ColonDB, CVC-ClinicDB and ETIS-Larib (n = 1,000 calibration, 781 evaluation); MS COCO 80-class multilabel (n = 4,000 calibration, 1,000 evaluation); hierarchical ImageNet; open-domain question answering (Natural Questions).
papers.preprocessing: Random calibration / evaluation splits repeated 1,000 times.
papers.modelDetails: Base model f outputs scores; a threshold lambda turns them into a set (pixels predicted as tumour, labels predicted present). Loss L(lambda) = false negative rate (non-increasing in lambda for larger sets). Calibrated lambda-hat = inf{lambda: (n/(n+1)) R_hat_n(lambda) + B/(n+1) <= alpha}. Theorem: E[L_{n+1}(lambda-hat)] <= alpha, and >= alpha - 2B/(n+1) under continuity.
papers.training: No retraining of the base model; calibration step only.
papers.evaluation: Realised risk (e.g. FNR) and set size over 1,000 random calibration/test splits at alpha = 0.1.
papers.baselines: Split conformal prediction (coverage special case); uncalibrated thresholds.
papers.results: Polyp segmentation FNR 0.0987 +/- 0.0114 (target 0.1); MS COCO FNR 0.0996 +/- 0.0052; the realised risk tightly matched alpha with reasonable set sizes in all examples.
papers.statistics: Distribution of realised risk over 1,000 independent splits (mean and SD); theoretical finite-sample guarantee.

papers.title: Learn then Test: Calibrating Predictive Algorithms to Achieve Risk Control
papers.authors: Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates, Emmanuel J. Candes, Michael I. Jordan, Lihua Lei
papers.aim: To calibrate any trained model so that its predictions meet explicit finite-sample statistical guarantees on one or several risks, without refitting the model.
papers.method: Learn then Test (LTT): turn the choice of model parameters (thresholds lambda) into multiple hypothesis testing. For each candidate lambda test H_lambda: risk(lambda) > alpha using p-values from concentration inequalities (e.g. Hoeffding-Bentkus) on a calibration set; select lambdas whose null is rejected with family-wise error control (Bonferroni, fixed-sequence or graph-based testing). Allows non-monotone losses and several risks at once.
papers.result: Worked examples achieved the target guarantees: false discovery rate control in multi-label classification, intersection-over-union control in instance segmentation, simultaneous control of outlier-detection type-1 error and set coverage, and selective classification / risk control on tabular medical data. Multiple-testing approaches were less conservative than uniform-concentration bounds.
papers.tools: Pre-trained vision models (e.g. TResNet for MS COCO, detection/segmentation networks), tabular medical prediction model, Python implementations.
papers.gap: Marginal guarantees; requires exchangeable calibration data and enough calibration size.
papers.relation: Turns threshold selection, such as abstention cut-offs, into multiple hypothesis testing with finite-sample guarantees on error risk.
papers.limitations: Guarantee is with high probability over calibration data, not per patient; conservative with small calibration sets.
papers.methodologyDetail: Many safety requirements are not simple coverage: a clinician may want the false discovery rate below 10%, the segmentation overlap above a level, and the escalation rate under a budget at the same time. The authors frame the choice of a model's decision thresholds as multiple hypothesis testing. For each candidate threshold on a grid they test the null hypothesis 'this threshold's risk is above alpha' using a p-value computed from the calibration data with concentration inequalities, then apply a family-wise error control procedure (Bonferroni, or testing thresholds in order). Every threshold that passes is guaranteed, with probability at least 1 - delta, to have risk at most alpha; with several risks a graph-based procedure handles them together. They show it on simulated loss curves, multi-label image classification, instance segmentation, outlier detection with coverage, and tabular medical data. For our PhD, LTT is the tool to set each agent's escalation threshold so that missed findings and clinician workload both meet stated limits, with a formal statement of confidence for the ethics and clinical evaluation documents.
papers.studyDesign: Statistical methodology paper with simulations and worked examples.
papers.datasets: Synthetic autoregressive loss processes (V-shaped risk) for numerical comparison; MS COCO multi-label classification; MS COCO instance segmentation; ImageNet-type classification with outlier detection; tabular medical data example.
papers.preprocessing: Random calibration / test splits repeated many times.
papers.modelDetails: Risk R(lambda) over a grid Lambda of parameters; valid p-values p_lambda from Hoeffding, Bentkus or Hoeffding-Bentkus bounds on the calibration risk; multiple testing with family-wise error rate delta (Bonferroni; fixed-sequence testing along an ordered grid; graph-based procedures for multiple risks). Output: a set of lambdas for which P(R(lambda) <= alpha) >= 1 - delta.
papers.training: No refitting; only calibration on held-out data.
papers.evaluation: Realised risk distribution over random splits vs alpha; fraction of violations vs delta; utility (e.g. set size, recall) of the selected lambda.
papers.baselines: Uniform concentration bounds; conformal risk control (monotone special case); naive empirical-risk thresholding.
papers.results: In simulations, multiple-testing LTT gave valid control with less conservativeness than uniform concentration; in worked examples, realised FDR, IoU-based risk and type-1 error stayed below targets with the stated probability. Detailed values in figures.
papers.statistics: Finite-sample guarantees: P(risk <= alpha) >= 1 - delta; empirical distributions over repeated splits.

papers.title: Fair Conformal Predictors for Applications in Medical Imaging
papers.authors: Charles Lu, Andreanne Lemay, Ken Chang, Katharina Hobel, Jayashree Kalpathy-Cramer
papers.aim: To show how conformal prediction sets can express uncertainty for clinicians in medical imaging and to check fairness of these sets across patient subgroups.
papers.method: Field interviews with four clinicians about useful uncertainty; then compares conformal methods (APS, RAPS) with group-conditional versions (GAPS, GRAPS) on skin lesion classification for rule-in and rule-out of malignancy, measuring coverage and set size per Fitzpatrick skin type, and links set size to epistemic uncertainty.
papers.result: At alpha = 0.1 all methods gave similar accuracy and set size; group-conditional methods reduced coverage disparity between skin types (at the cost of larger set-size disparity); prediction set size correlated strongly with epistemic uncertainty (max softmax and entropy).
papers.tools: CNN classifier on Fitzpatrick17k, conformal APS / RAPS / GAPS / GRAPS, clinician interviews.
papers.gap: Dermatology photographs only; small interview sample; no prospective use.
papers.relation: Applies conformal prediction sets with coverage across subgroups to medical imaging, giving a principled uncertainty signal for referral.
papers.limitations: Group labels (skin type) required at calibration; only four clinicians interviewed.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first interviewed four clinicians working with medical imaging to learn what form of uncertainty would help them, and found that a short list of possible diagnoses that contains the right one with a known probability is intuitive. They then trained a CNN on Fitzpatrick17k, 16,577 dermatology photographs grouped into benign, malignant and non-neoplastic conditions and labelled by skin tone (Fitzpatrick types 1-6). Using a held-out calibration set they built conformal prediction sets at 90% coverage with APS and RAPS, and group-conditional versions that calibrate separately for each skin type, and studied ruling malignancy in or out. Group-conditional calibration made coverage more equal across skin tones, though set sizes became less equal, and larger sets went with higher model uncertainty. For our PhD this supports presenting the agent's output to clinicians as a calibrated set of possible diagnoses, escalating when the set is large, and checking coverage separately for hospitals, scanners and patient groups.
papers.studyDesign: Mixed: qualitative field interviews plus retrospective quantitative evaluation on a public dataset.
papers.datasets: Fitzpatrick17k: 16,577 clinical photographs from two dermatology atlases, 114 skin conditions grouped into 3 categories (benign, malignant, non-neoplastic) and annotated with Fitzpatrick skin types 1-6. Interviews with four clinicians (roles and years of experience in Table 1).
papers.preprocessing: Split into training, calibration and test sets; calibration per skin-type group for group methods.
papers.modelDetails: Naive softmax top-k sets; Adaptive Prediction Sets (APS); Regularized APS (RAPS, penalises large sets); group-conditional GAPS and GRAPS calibrated separately per Fitzpatrick skin type. Rule-in (malignant in set) and rule-out (malignant not in set) use cases.
papers.training: Base CNN trained on training split; conformal calibration at alpha = 0.1.
papers.evaluation: Marginal and subgroup coverage, average set size, coverage disparity and set-size disparity across skin types, correlation of set size with epistemic uncertainty.
papers.baselines: Naive (non-conformal) prediction sets; aggregate conformal methods vs group-conditional ones.
papers.results: Similar overall accuracy and set size at alpha = 0.1; GAPS/GRAPS slightly better at ruling in and worse at ruling out malignancy for skin types 1-2; lower subgroup coverage disparity and higher set-size disparity with group methods (Table 3); strong correlation between set size and uncertainty (Figure 6).
papers.statistics: Coverage and disparity metrics; correlation analysis.

papers.title: Pitfalls of Conformal Predictions for Medical Image Classification
papers.authors: Hendrik Alexander Mehrtens, Tabea-Clara Bucher, Titus J. Brinker
papers.venue: UNSURE Workshop at MICCAI 2023 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science)
papers.aim: To show the limitations and assumptions of conformal prediction that practitioners must know before using it in medical image classification.
papers.method: Trains ResNet-34 models on dermatology and histopathology data and demonstrates, with controlled experiments, how conformal guarantees fail under input (domain) shift and label shift, when used to select predictions, for subgroups (classes, patient attributes), and with few classes.
papers.result: Conformal predictions were unreliable under distribution shift in inputs and labels; they should not be used to select confident predictions to improve accuracy; coverage was not guaranteed for subsets such as individual classes or patient attributes; with few classes (e.g. binary) prediction sets give limited information.
papers.tools: ResNet-34 (x5 per dataset), HAM10000, CAMELYON17, split conformal / APS-type methods.
papers.gap: Points out problems; does not provide a fix for shift.
papers.relation: Shows where conformal guarantees break down under distribution shift and class imbalance in medical images, which are key risks for deployment in Sri Lanka.
papers.limitations: Two datasets; illustrative experiments.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors train five ResNet-34 models each on HAM10000 skin lesions and on CAMELYON17 histopathology patches (training on three clinics and testing on two others) and apply standard split conformal prediction, calibrated on data from the training distribution. They then probe the method's assumptions one by one. When test images come from new clinics or the class mix changes, coverage drops below the promised level. Even when overall coverage is correct, coverage for individual classes or patient attributes can be far off, because the guarantee is only on average. Using conformal sets to pick 'safe' cases (for example only those with a single label) does not carry a guarantee of higher accuracy, and with two classes the sets are rarely informative. For our PhD this defines how conformal methods must be used: recalibrate on each hospital's data, check coverage per tumour type and per subgroup, and combine conformal sets with other shift detectors rather than relying on them alone for escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical demonstration study (retrospective) on two public medical image datasets.
papers.datasets: HAM10000 (7 skin-lesion classes) and CAMELYON17 (50 whole-slide images with annotated tumour regions from 5 clinics, cut into 256x256 non-overlapping patches); trained on CAMELYON17 centres 1, 3, 5 and tested on centres 2 and 4 for domain shift.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs tiled into 256x256 patches; augmentations and hyper-parameters as in prior work; five training runs per dataset; calibration set sizes listed in Table 1.
papers.modelDetails: ResNet-34 classifiers; split conformal prediction with standard scores (e.g. LAC / APS) calibrated on in-distribution data; experiments on covariate shift (new clinics), label shift (changed class prevalence), class-conditional and attribute-conditional coverage, and selective use of singleton sets.
papers.training: Following Mehrtens et al. 2023 setup; 5 evaluations per dataset.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage vs nominal 1 - alpha overall, per class and per subgroup; coverage under domain and label shift; accuracy of singleton-set selection.
papers.baselines: Nominal coverage targets; in-distribution vs shifted results.
papers.results: Coverage fell below the nominal level on shifted CAMELYON17 centres and under label shift; per-class and per-attribute coverage varied widely even when marginal coverage held; selecting only singleton sets did not give a guaranteed accuracy gain; binary tasks gave mostly uninformative sets.

papers.title: RR-CP: Reliable-Region-Based Conformal Prediction for Trustworthy Medical Image Classification
papers.authors: Yizhe Zhang, Shuo Wang, Yejia Zhang, Danny Z. Chen
papers.venue: UNSURE Workshop at MICCAI 2023 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science)
papers.aim: To make conformal prediction actually meet very small user-specified error rates (e.g. 0.5%) in medical image classification.
papers.method: Reliable-Region-Based Conformal Prediction (RR-CP): estimates on the calibration set a 'reliable region' of the score space where the set-valued prediction meets the error constraint, and builds prediction sets from it, accepting somewhat larger sets to satisfy the strict error rate.
papers.result: With alpha = 0.5%, RR-CP met the target error rate on 4 of 5 MedMNIST datasets while classic CP, RAPS and ERAPS failed on most; e.g. BloodMNIST actual error 0.39% vs 0.85% (CP), 0.59% (RAPS), 0.74% (ERAPS).
papers.tools: ResNet-18 (official MedMNIST weights), conformal prediction methods CP, RAPS, ERAPS.
papers.gap: Small 2D MedMNIST images; no distribution shift; larger set sizes.
papers.relation: Proposes conformal prediction with stronger error guarantees for medical classifiers, which can serve as the basis for deciding when to escalate.
papers.limitations: Failed on OrganCMNIST (no method met 0.5%); trades set size for error.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors note that in clinical use the allowed error is tiny (here 0.5%), and standard conformal methods often miss such targets in practice. They take ResNet-18 classifiers released for five MedMNIST datasets (abdominal organs in three CT views, blood cells, skin lesions), use each validation set for calibration and the test set for evaluation. RR-CP looks at the calibration data to find the region of prediction scores where set predictions are reliable enough, and builds sets so the error constraint holds, accepting larger sets where needed. Compared with classic CP, RAPS and ERAPS, RR-CP achieved the 0.5% error target on four of five datasets (for example 0.42% vs 0.78% on OrganAMNIST) with moderate set sizes, while the others mostly failed. For our PhD this supports setting very strict error levels for automated outputs and treating larger prediction sets as the trigger for clinician escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper evaluated on five public medical image datasets.
papers.preprocessing: Validation set used as calibration set; test set for evaluating actual error rate and set size.
papers.modelDetails: ResNet-18 classifier trained on each training set (official MedMNIST release weights). RR-CP estimates a reliable region of predicted probabilities using the calibration data so that the error of the set prediction stays below alpha, then forms sets; compared with classic split CP, RAPS and ERAPS.
papers.training: Pre-trained ResNet-18 per dataset; conformal calibration only.
papers.evaluation: Actual error rate (AER, % of test cases whose set misses the true label) vs alpha = 0.5%, and average prediction set size (PSS).
papers.baselines: Classic CP, RAPS, ERAPS.
papers.statistics: Single evaluation per dataset on test sets.

papers.title: Soft Dice Confidence: A Near-Optimal Confidence Estimator for Selective Prediction in Semantic Segmentation
papers.authors: Bruno Laboissiere Camargos Borges, Bruno Machado Pacheco, Danilo Silva
papers.aim: To give a single, well-founded confidence score for a whole segmentation, so the model can abstain on images whose segmentation is likely poor (image-level selective prediction).
papers.method: Derives the optimal image-level confidence estimator under the Dice metric when pixel posteriors are known (intractable for real images), then proposes Soft Dice Confidence (SDC), a tractable approximation with a proven bound on its error, computed from the model's pixel probabilities without tuning.
papers.result: In simulations SDC's risk-coverage curve was almost identical to the optimal estimator. On six medical segmentation tasks (including BraTS 2020 brain tumour with 3D nnU-Net), SDC beat earlier image-level confidence measures in-distribution and on out-of-distribution test sets, often matching or beating tunable methods without needing extra data.
papers.tools: 3D nnU-Net (BraTS 2020), UNeXt (BUSI, ISIC 2018), 3D U-Net (MS lesions), Segtran (optic cup), Polyp-PVT (polyps).
papers.gap: Binary or per-class Dice; image-level abstention only, not region-level escalation.
papers.relation: Gives an image-level confidence score for selective prediction in segmentation, which applies directly to deciding when to refer a tumour segmentation.
papers.limitations: Assumes the model's pixel probabilities are reasonably calibrated; Dice-specific.
papers.methodologyDetail: For segmentation, the question 'should the model abstain?' is usually answered pixel by pixel, but a clinician reviews whole images. The authors therefore seek one confidence number per image that best predicts its Dice score. They prove what the optimal estimator is when the pixel-wise posterior probabilities are known - the expected Dice of the predicted mask - and show it is impossible to compute for real image sizes. They then derive Soft Dice Confidence, which is simply the soft Dice between the predicted binary mask and the probability map, and bound how far it can be from the optimum; small simulations confirm it is almost optimal. Finally they apply it, unchanged, to six published segmentation models including a 3D nnU-Net on BraTS 2020 brain tumours, with in-distribution and out-of-distribution test sets for several tasks, and compare risk-coverage curves with other image-level scores. SDC is consistently among the best and needs no extra data. For our PhD, SDC is a ready escalation score for the tumour segmentation agent: low SDC means the whole segmentation goes to the radiologist.
papers.studyDesign: Theory plus simulation and retrospective evaluation on six public medical segmentation tasks with in-distribution and OOD test sets.
papers.datasets: Brain tumour: BraTS 2020 (3D nnU-Net); breast ultrasound: BUSI (UNeXt); skin lesions: ISIC 2018 (UNeXt); multiple sclerosis white-matter lesions: ISBI + MSSEG-1 (ID) and PubMRI (OOD) (3D U-Net); optic cup: REFUGE (ID) and ORIGA + G1020 (OOD) (Segtran); polyps: Kvasir-SEG + ClinicDB (ID) and ETIS + ColonDB + EndoScene (OOD) (Polyp-PVT).
papers.preprocessing: ID data split into training and test sets exactly as in the original model papers (no test data in training); OOD data used entirely for testing; for tunable estimators the test sets were further split into tuning and test parts.
papers.modelDetails: Image-level confidence g(x) used to rank images; optimal estimator = expected Dice of the predicted mask under the posterior; SDC = soft Dice between the predicted mask and the pixel-probability map. Compared with average pixel confidence/entropy, other aggregation scores and tunable (learned) estimators.
papers.training: Segmentation models used as trained by original authors; SDC needs no training.
papers.evaluation: Risk-coverage curves and AURC with 1 - Dice as risk; empirical bounds on the gap to the optimal estimator; ID and OOD performance.
papers.baselines: Mean max-probability, mean entropy, other image-level aggregation scores, learned/tunable confidence estimators.
papers.results: Simulation: SDC risk-coverage nearly identical to the optimal IDC. Real data: SDC was the best or near-best non-tunable estimator on all six tasks, robust on OOD sets, and competitive with tunable methods (values in Tables 3-5).
papers.statistics: Bounds on relative error; comparisons over multiple random tuning/test partitions.

papers.title: Region-based evidential deep learning to quantify uncertainty and improve robustness of brain tumor segmentation
papers.authors: Hao Li, Yang Nan, Javier Del Ser, Guang Yang
papers.aim: To get reliable voxel-wise uncertainty maps and accurate brain tumour segmentation in one forward pass, robust to noise and image corruption.
papers.method: Region-based evidential deep learning (EDL): the network outputs evidence parameterising a Dirichlet distribution per voxel (Subjective Logic); trained with new region-based losses (Dice and weighted Dice) instead of cross-entropy/MSE so EDL works for segmentation; uncertainty = Dirichlet vacuity.
papers.result: Region-based EDL reached Dice 0.791-0.793 (best among EDL variants) with the highest uncertainty-error overlap (sUEO 0.420) and BraS score (0.875), while ensembles and MC dropout had slightly higher Dice (0.807, 0.804) and lowest ECE (0.009-0.010) at much higher cost; EDL was more robust to noise and corruptions.
papers.tools: nnU-Net base network, evidential Dirichlet output layer, BraTS 2020, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Single dataset (BraTS 2020); not tested on clinical deployment data.
papers.relation: Produces single-pass evidential uncertainty maps for brain tumour segmentation that could feed a referral decision.
papers.limitations: Slightly lower Dice and calibration than ensembles; synthetic corruptions.
papers.methodologyDetail: Ensembles and MC dropout give good uncertainty for brain tumour segmentation but need many forward passes. Evidential deep learning gets uncertainty from one pass by having the network output 'evidence' that defines a Dirichlet distribution for each voxel, so the total evidence tells how sure the model is; however it had performed poorly for segmentation. The authors make it work by training the evidential nnU-Net with region-based Dice and weighted-Dice losses. Using BraTS 2020 (369 labelled cases split 236/59/74, four MRI sequences resampled to 1 mm and cropped), they compare their models with ensembles, MC dropout and evidential models trained with older losses, measuring Dice, calibration, how well the uncertainty map overlaps actual errors (sUEO), and the QU-BraTS filtering score, also under synthetic noise and corruption. Their method gives the best error-overlap and robustness with only a small Dice cost. For our PhD it offers a cheap way for the segmentation agent to produce voxel-level uncertainty maps that show radiologists where to look.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method study on a public brain tumour MRI dataset with robustness tests.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 training set with labels (369 cases) split into 236 train / 59 validation / 74 test; four MRI sequences (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR), 240x240x155, multi-scanner.
papers.preprocessing: Co-registered, interpolated to 1 mm^3, skull-stripped; cropped to 160x192x128; intensity normalisation; on-the-fly data augmentation as in nnU-Net.
papers.modelDetails: nnU-Net backbone configured as in the original; evidential output layer producing non-negative evidence -> Dirichlet alpha per voxel; losses compared: cross-entropy-based, MSE-based, and proposed Dice and weighted Dice (wDice) region-based EDL losses with KL regulariser. Labels: enhancing tumour, oedema, necrotic/non-enhancing core; evaluated as ET, TC, WT.
papers.training: nnU-Net-style optimisation (details in paper); same splits for all methods.
papers.evaluation: Dice per region; ECE; uncertainty-error overlap (sUEO); BraTS uncertainty score (BraS, from QU-BraTS filtering); robustness under added noise and image corruptions.
papers.baselines: Deep ensembles, MC dropout, EDL with CE or MSE loss, deterministic nnU-Net.
papers.results: Dice: ensemble 0.807, dropout 0.804, EDL-Dice 0.791, EDL-wDice 0.793 (region losses +0.01 over CE/MSE EDL). ECE: ensemble 0.009, dropout 0.010 (lowest). sUEO best for proposed EDL (0.420); BraS best 0.875. Proposed EDL kept higher performance under noise and corruption.
papers.statistics: Mean values on the 74-case test set (Table 1).

papers.title: Understanding calibration of deep neural networks for medical image classification
papers.authors: Abhishek Singh Sambyal, Usma Niyaz, Narayanan C. Krishnan, Deepti R. Bathula
papers.venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine
papers.aim: To study how training regime, architecture and dataset affect the calibration (not just accuracy) of medical image classifiers.
papers.method: Empirical study of ResNet-18, ResNet-50 and WideResNet trained three ways - fully supervised from random initialisation, fully supervised with pre-training, and rotation-based self-supervised pre-training then fine-tuning - on three medical datasets, measured with six calibration metrics; analysis of weight distributions and representation similarity (CKA).
papers.result: Rotation-based self-supervised pre-trained models were significantly better calibrated with comparable or better accuracy than fully supervised models; weight distributions and similarity of learned representations correlated with calibration trends; different calibration metrics sometimes disagreed.
papers.tools: ResNet-18, ResNet-50, WideResNet; rotation-prediction self-supervision; ECE, MCE, adaptive ECE, classwise ECE, NLL, Brier; CKA.
papers.gap: Classification only; one self-supervised method; small COVID dataset.
papers.relation: Studies how training choices affect calibration of medical image classifiers, which O2 relies on for trustworthy confidence.
papers.limitations: Limited architectures and SSL methods; no distribution-shift tests.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors ask whether how a medical image classifier is trained changes how trustworthy its confidence is. They train three architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, WideResNet) on three contrasting datasets - 35,000 retinal fundus photographs graded 0-4 for diabetic retinopathy, 220,000 lymph-node histology patches labelled tumour or not, and only 317 COVID-19 chest X-rays - using three regimes: supervised from scratch, supervised with ImageNet pre-training, and pre-training with a rotation-prediction self-supervised task before fine-tuning. They measure accuracy and six calibration metrics, and examine weight distributions and how similar the learned representations are (CKA). Self-supervised pre-training produced clearly better-calibrated models with similar or better accuracy, and representation similarity tracked the calibration differences. For our PhD, where local labelled data are small, this supports self-supervised pre-training on unlabelled Sri Lankan scans before fine-tuning, and reporting several calibration metrics.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective empirical comparison on three public medical imaging datasets.
papers.datasets: Diabetic Retinopathy (EyePACS, 35K high-resolution fundus images, 5 severity classes, varied cameras); Histopathologic Cancer (modified PatchCamelyon, 220K 96x96 patches, tumour vs not); COVID-19 chest X-ray (317 high-resolution images, 3 classes).
papers.preprocessing: Standard resizing and augmentation per dataset (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: Training regimes: FS_r (fully supervised, random init), FS_p (fully supervised, ImageNet pre-training), SSL_p (rotation-based self-supervision with pre-training, then fine-tuning). Architectures ResNet-18, ResNet-50, WideResNet.
papers.training: Each architecture x regime x dataset trained with comparable schedules (supplement).
papers.evaluation: Accuracy plus six calibration metrics (e.g. ECE, MCE, adaptive/classwise ECE, NLL, Brier score); weight distribution analysis; CKA similarity of representations between regimes.
papers.baselines: Fully supervised training with and without pre-training.
papers.results: SSL_p gave the lowest calibration errors on most metrics and datasets with equal or higher accuracy; differences in mean CKA between SSL_p and FS_p correlated with calibration differences; mixed metric results show the need for several calibration metrics (values in figures and supplementary tables).
papers.statistics: Comparisons across repeated runs; some differences reported as not highly significant.

papers.title: Trustworthy clinical AI solutions: A unified review of uncertainty quantification in Deep Learning models for medical image analysis
papers.authors: Benjamin Lambert, Florence Forbes, Senan Doyle, Harmonie Dehaene, Michel Dojat
papers.aim: To review uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for deep learning in medical image classification and segmentation, how they are evaluated, and the open challenges.
papers.method: Systematic literature search (Google Scholar and PubMed, June 2022) for supervised DL studies with UQ in medical image classification or segmentation published 2015 - June 2022, then a unified taxonomy of UQ methods and evaluation protocols.
papers.result: Groups methods into Bayesian (variational inference, MC dropout, SWAG/Laplace), ensemble, test-time augmentation, deterministic single-pass (evidential, distance-aware) and post-hoc approaches; catalogues evaluation metrics (calibration, uncertainty-error overlap, OOD detection, referral curves); highlights challenges: no standard evaluation, label uncertainty from inter-rater variability, computational cost, multi-site shift, and clinical integration.
papers.tools: Literature review; keywords Deep Learning, Uncertainty, MRI, CT, PET, X-ray, Medical image.
papers.gap: Review up to mid-2022; no quantitative meta-analysis.
papers.relation: Surveys uncertainty-quantification methods for medical imaging and how they are used to flag cases for clinicians.
papers.limitations: Authors partly employed by a company (Pixyl); non-systematic synthesis of results.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors performed a systematic search of Google Scholar and PubMed in June 2022 for deep-learning studies on medical images (MRI, CT, PET, X-ray) published from 2015 that reported a measure of uncertainty for classification or segmentation, excluding non-peer-reviewed work. From the selected corpus they build a unified overview of how uncertainty is produced - Bayesian approximations such as MC dropout and Laplace, ensembles, test-time augmentation, evidential and other single-pass methods, and post-hoc calibration - and of how it is evaluated, from calibration error and uncertainty-error overlap to out-of-distribution detection and referral curves. They close with open problems: inconsistent evaluation, uncertainty in the ground-truth labels themselves, computational cost, robustness to different sites, and the lack of studies on how clinicians use uncertainty. For our PhD this review is the reference for choosing UQ methods per agent and for justifying the evaluation plan (calibration + error overlap + referral curves) in the methodology chapter.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic search plus narrative / taxonomic review.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (review of published studies on MRI, CT, PET, X-ray and other imaging).
papers.preprocessing: Inclusion: supervised DL for medical image classification or segmentation with a quantification of uncertainty; exclusion: non-peer-reviewed work (with stated exceptions).
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy covers: Bayesian neural networks (variational, MC dropout, Laplace, SWAG), deep ensembles and cheaper ensemble variants, test-time augmentation, evidential deep learning, deterministic distance-aware methods, conformal/post-hoc calibration, and aleatoric vs epistemic decomposition.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Summarises evaluation protocols: calibration (ECE, reliability diagrams), correlation of uncertainty with error (uncertainty-error overlap, QU-BraTS filtering score), OOD detection AUROC, referral/rejection curves, qualitative uncertainty maps.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Uncertainty quantification is an active field with many methods but no agreed evaluation standard; uncertainty arises from noisy images, imperfect labels, missing data and inter-site variability; integration into clinical workflow and user studies remain rare.

papers.title: Uncertainty-informed deep learning models enable high-confidence predictions for digital histopathology
papers.authors: Dolezal JM, Srisuwananukorn A, Karpeyev D, Ramesh S, et al.
papers.aim: To give whole-slide histopathology classifiers a clinically usable uncertainty measure with pre-set thresholds separating high- and low-confidence predictions.
papers.method: MC dropout on an Xception tile classifier; uncertainty and prediction thresholds determined on training data by nested cross-validation; slides/patients above the uncertainty threshold are labelled low-confidence. Tested on unannotated slides from two large external cohorts and on out-of-distribution non-lung cancers.
papers.result: High-confidence predictions clearly beat predictions without uncertainty: cross-validation AUROC 0.981 vs 0.960; CPTAC external patient-level AUROC 0.99 (accuracy 97.5%) vs 0.93 (85.3%) without UQ, with 66-100% of patients high-confidence; Mayo Clinic AUROC 1.0 vs 0.98. Thresholds remained reliable under domain shift.
papers.tools: Xception (ImageNet pre-trained) with 2 dense layers (1024) and dropout 0.1, Slideflow 1.1 (TensorFlow), MC dropout, nested cross-validation.
papers.gap: Binary lung cancer subtype task; dropout-based uncertainty only; high-confidence share drops with class imbalance.
papers.relation: Uses uncertainty thresholds set on training data to separate high-confidence predictions from low-confidence cases that go to a pathologist, a working version of selective prediction.
papers.limitations: UQ did not help with highly imbalanced data (1:10); thresholds set on TCGA may need local re-tuning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors train Xception-based tile classifiers with dropout to separate lung adenocarcinoma from squamous cell carcinoma on 941 TCGA whole-slide images, keeping dropout active at test time to get an uncertainty estimate for every tile, then aggregating to slide and patient level. Crucially, both the uncertainty cut-off and the class decision threshold are fixed in advance using nested cross-validation on the training data only, so external testing mimics real deployment on unannotated slides. On 1,306 CPTAC slides from 416 patients the high-confidence group (66-100% of patients depending on training size) reached AUROC 0.99 and 97.5% accuracy versus 0.93 and 85.3% for the same model without uncertainty; low-confidence cases had AUROC 0.75. Results held at Mayo Clinic, with other architectures, and on non-lung tumours, but not with severe class imbalance (1:10). For our PhD this is the model for the pathology agent's escalation: thresholds set before deployment from training data, high-confidence slides reported, low-confidence slides sent to the neuropathologist.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective model development with nested cross-validation and external multi-institution validation (IRB approved, University of Chicago and Mayo Clinic).
papers.datasets: Training: TCGA 941 H&E WSIs (467 lung adenocarcinoma LUAD, 474 squamous cell carcinoma LUSC), one slide per patient. External 1: CPTAC 1,306 slides (644 LUAD, 662 LUSC) from 416 patients. External 2: Mayo Clinic institutional cohort. Out-of-distribution: non-lung adenocarcinoma / squamous cancers. Adenosquamous tumours removed.
papers.preprocessing: Slides tiled; tile-level predictions aggregated per slide and per patient; augmentation with random flips/rotations, JPEG compression and Gaussian blur; category-level mini-batch balancing.
papers.modelDetails: Xception backbone + two hidden layers of width 1024 with dropout p = 0.1 after each; MC dropout at inference gives tile uncertainty; slide uncertainty aggregated; uncertainty threshold and prediction threshold chosen by nested cross-validation on training data; slides above the uncertainty threshold are low-confidence. Also tested InceptionV3, ResNet50V2, InceptionResNetV2, EfficientNetV2M.
papers.training: 276 standard and 504 UQ-enabled models trained across dataset sizes; one epoch with early stopping (pilot showed 1 epoch optimal); hyper-parameters from prior work without tuning.
papers.evaluation: Patient-level AUROC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and Youden's index for high-confidence vs all predictions; share of patients high-confidence; effect of dataset size and class imbalance; OOD cohorts.
papers.baselines: Same models without uncertainty thresholding (non-UQ).
papers.results: Cross-validation (941 slides): non-UQ AUROC 0.960 +/- 0.008; high-confidence UQ 0.981 +/- 0.004 (P < 0.001); 79-94% slides high-confidence. CPTAC: non-UQ AUROC 0.93, accuracy 85.3%, sens 91.1%, spec 79.8%; high-confidence AUROC 0.99, accuracy 97.5%, sens 98.4%, spec 96.7%; low-confidence best AUROC 0.75. Mayo: non-UQ AUROC 0.98, accuracy 94.1%; high-confidence AUROC 1.0, accuracy 100%. Benefit held at 1:3 imbalance but not at 1:10.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- SD across cross-validation folds; P values for AUROC differences.
papers.availability: Code: Slideflow (https://github.com/jamesdolezal/slideflow); data from TCGA and CPTAC public portals.

papers.title: Estimating diagnostic uncertainty in artificial intelligence assisted pathology using conformal prediction
papers.authors: Olsson H, Kartasalo K, Mulliqi N, Capuccini M, et al.
papers.aim: To use conformal prediction to detect unreliable AI predictions in prostate biopsy diagnosis and grading, including on data from new scanners and labs.
papers.method: Conformal predictor (Mondrian, class-conditional) on top of a CNN-based prostate pathology AI system (trained on STHLM3 biopsies). Outputs prediction sets at a chosen confidence; multi-label or empty sets are flagged as unreliable. Evaluated on six test datasets including external scanners, labs and pathology assessment and atypical tissue.
papers.result: Same lab/scanner: with conformal prediction only 1 in 794 (0.1%) cancer-detection predictions was wrong vs 14 errors (2%) without, while 175 (22%) predictions were flagged unreliable. Systematic external differences were detected with small samples (N = 49 external scanner, N = 10 external lab and scanner, N = 12 external lab, scanner and pathology). Atypical tissue: 3 errors (2%) with conformal prediction vs 44 (25%) without, with 143 (80%) flagged.
papers.tools: CNN-based AI system (Strom et al. 2020), Hamamatsu C9600-12 and Aperio ScanScope AT2 scanners, Mondrian conformal prediction.
papers.gap: Prostate biopsies, not brain tumours; basic conformal predictor (larger sets than advanced methods).
papers.relation: Uses conformal prediction to flag unreliable AI pathology diagnoses for human review, with error-rate guarantees that can drive escalation.
papers.limitations: Authors note more advanced conformal methods could give smaller sets; flagged rate high on atypical tissue.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors take an existing deep-learning system for prostate biopsy diagnosis and Gleason/ISUP grading, trained on 7,788 biopsies from 1,192 men in the STHLM3 screening study, and wrap it with a class-conditional conformal predictor calibrated on held-out STHLM3 data. For each new biopsy the predictor returns a set of labels at a chosen confidence; if the set has exactly one label the prediction is treated as reliable, otherwise it is flagged for the pathologist. They test on 3,059 biopsies from 676 men in six settings: the same lab and scanner, a different scanner, a different lab and scanner, a different lab, scanner and pathology panel, and atypical tissue the model was not designed for. Conformal prediction cut cancer-detection errors from 2% to 0.1% while flagging 22% of cases, cut errors on atypical tissue from 25% to 2% while flagging 80%, and could reveal that a new site's data behaved differently using only 10-49 samples. For our PhD this is the template for the pathology agent and for site monitoring: calibrate a conformal predictor locally, auto-report single-label slides, escalate the rest, and use the flagged rate on a small local batch to detect a new scanner or lab problem.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective diagnostic study using a population screening trial cohort (STHLM3) plus external datasets.
papers.datasets: Training: 7,788 H&E prostate biopsies from 1,192 STHLM3 participants (men 50-69, Stockholm 2012-2015), scanned on Hamamatsu C9600-12 (n = 5,124) or Aperio AT2 (n = 2,664). Testing: 3,059 biopsies from 676 men across six datasets: same lab/scanner, external scanner, external lab and scanner, external lab + scanner + pathology (ISUP Imagebase expert panel), and atypical prostate tissue.
papers.preprocessing: Whole-slide digitisation; tiling and preprocessing as in Strom et al. (2020); calibration set held out from training data.
papers.modelDetails: Ensemble of CNNs (Strom et al.) gives class scores for cancer vs benign and ISUP grade groups; Mondrian (class-conditional) inductive conformal predictor builds prediction sets at significance level epsilon; single-label sets = reliable; sets with two labels or empty = unreliable, flagged for review.
papers.training: AI system training as in Strom et al. (2020); conformal calibration on held-out STHLM3 biopsies.
papers.evaluation: Validity (error rate not above significance level), efficiency (fraction of correct single-label predictions), number of unreliable predictions, detection of systematic differences in external data with small samples; cancer detection and ISUP grading.
papers.baselines: Same AI system without conformal prediction (point predictions).
papers.results: Cancer detection, same lab/scanner: errors 1/794 (0.1%) with CP vs 14 (2%) without; 175 (22%) flagged. External data: shifts detected with N = 49, 10 and 12 samples. Atypical tissue: errors 3 (2%) vs 44 (25%); 143 (80%) flagged. Similar patterns for ISUP grading (in paper).
papers.statistics: Conformal validity guarantees; error rates with counts.
papers.availability: Code linked in the paper; STHLM3 data under restricted access.

papers.title: Machine learning with asymmetric abstention for biomedical decision-making
papers.authors: Gandouz M, Holzmann H, Heider D
papers.venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
papers.aim: To show that asymmetric abstention intervals (different reject ranges on each side of the decision boundary) suit imbalanced biomedical data better than symmetric ones.
papers.method: Logistic regression classifiers with a reject option; abstention interval around the decision threshold chosen either symmetrically or asymmetrically (separate lower/upper bounds) to maximise Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) on accepted samples; tested on imbalanced and down-sampled balanced versions of three datasets.
papers.result: Both symmetric and asymmetric abstention significantly improved MCC on accepted cases; asymmetric abstention rejected as many or fewer samples than symmetric, so it is preferred for imbalanced data.
papers.tools: Logistic regression, MCC, UCI biomedical datasets, R/Python.
papers.gap: Simple tabular models and small datasets; no imaging.
papers.relation: Proposes abstention with class-asymmetric thresholds, which matches making escalation depend on the unequal clinical cost of different errors.
papers.limitations: Only logistic regression; small UCI datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: Most reject-option methods drop cases whose predicted probability falls in a band centred on the decision threshold. In medicine, classes are usually imbalanced, so errors cluster on one side. The authors fit logistic regression models on three UCI datasets - breast cancer, prostate cancer and cardiotocography - in their natural imbalanced form and in a down-sampled balanced form, and compare symmetric abstention bands with asymmetric ones whose lower and upper limits are tuned separately to maximise the Matthews correlation coefficient of the accepted predictions. Both kinds of abstention improve MCC, but the asymmetric band reaches the same or better MCC while rejecting fewer patients on imbalanced data. For our PhD this suggests tuning escalation thresholds separately for each class or error direction, for example being stricter about uncertain 'high-grade' predictions than about uncertain 'low-grade' ones.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective methodological comparison on three public biomedical datasets.
papers.datasets: UCI Machine Learning Repository: breast cancer (wdbc), prostate cancer (pc), cardiotocography (ctg); sizes from 72 samples upward; different class imbalance levels.
papers.preprocessing: Two scenarios: imbalanced data as is, and down-sampled balanced data; train/test splitting with repeated runs.
papers.modelDetails: Logistic regression gives probability p; reject if p is in [t_low, t_high]. Symmetric: interval centred on the decision boundary. Asymmetric: t_low and t_high chosen independently to maximise MCC on accepted samples for a given rejection budget.
papers.training: Standard logistic regression fitting; abstention bounds searched on training data.
papers.evaluation: Matthews correlation coefficient on accepted samples, number of rejected samples, confusion matrices.
papers.baselines: No abstention; symmetric abstention.
papers.results: Baseline MCC without abstention: wdbc 0.925 (imbalanced) / 0.93 (balanced); pc 0.483 / 0.438; ctg 0.963 / 0.955. Abstention raised MCC on accepted samples for all datasets; asymmetric abstention rejected equal or fewer samples than symmetric for the same or better MCC in imbalanced data.
papers.statistics: Significance of MCC improvements reported in the paper (repeated evaluation).

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware deep learning in healthcare: A scoping review
papers.authors: Loftus TJ, Shickel B, Ruppert MM, Balch JA, et al.
papers.aim: To evaluate methods for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning for healthcare and to propose a conceptual framework for specifying the certainty of predictions to build trust.
papers.method: PRISMA-compliant scoping review of Embase, MEDLINE and PubMed; study quality rated with validated tools; data extracted with modified CHARMS criteria; synthesis into a conceptual framework of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
papers.result: 30 studies included (24 imaging, 6 non-imaging). All imaging models used CNNs; Monte Carlo dropout was the dominant uncertainty method; conformal prediction performed similarly well and was easy to interpret and apply to any model. Uncertainty was rarely used to build trust among patients, caregivers or clinicians.
papers.tools: Systematic database search, PRISMA, CHARMS extraction, quality appraisal tools.
papers.gap: Few studies used uncertainty to support clinical trust or decisions; heterogeneous non-imaging methods.
papers.relation: Maps how uncertainty-aware deep learning has been used in clinical settings, including uncertainty-triggered clinician review.
papers.limitations: Scoping review (no meta-analysis); 30 studies only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched Embase, MEDLINE and PubMed following PRISMA guidelines for studies that used deep learning in healthcare and quantified the uncertainty of its predictions, rated study quality, and extracted model and outcome data with a modified CHARMS checklist. Thirty studies met the criteria, mostly imaging applications built on convolutional networks. MC dropout was the most common way to estimate uncertainty, while conformal prediction gave similarly strong results, was easier to interpret, and works with any model. The authors propose a framework linking epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty to when a model's output can be trusted, and note that almost no studies used uncertainty to help clinicians or patients decide whether to rely on the model. For our PhD this justifies combining MC dropout or ensembles with conformal sets and shows that our clinician-facing evaluation of uncertainty and escalation (O4) addresses a real gap.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review following PRISMA guidelines.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (30 included studies: 24 imaging, 6 non-imaging).
papers.preprocessing: Inclusion of deep-learning healthcare studies that quantified uncertainty; quality rating and CHARMS-based extraction.
papers.modelDetails: Framework: epistemic uncertainty (model knowledge, reducible with data) vs aleatoric (noise in data); methods reviewed: MC dropout, ensembles, Bayesian networks, conformal prediction, test-time augmentation; proposed use of uncertainty to decide when a model output can be entrusted.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative synthesis of methods, performance and uses of uncertainty across included studies.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Imaging: CNN models; MC dropout most common; conformal prediction comparably strong and more interpretable. Non-imaging: heterogeneous models, generally strong performance, uncertainty useful for comparing models. Uncertainty-based entrustment of clinicians was largely unexplored.

papers.title: Privacy-preserving Federated Learning and Uncertainty Quantification in Medical Imaging
papers.authors: Koutsoubis N, Waqas A, Yilmaz Y, Ramachandran RP, et al.
papers.aim: To review federated learning (FL), privacy-preserving FL and uncertainty quantification within FL for medical imaging, and identify gaps.
papers.method: Narrative review of FL algorithms, privacy threats from shared gradients and defences (differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation), and UQ methods adapted to FL with non-IID, class-imbalanced client data.
papers.result: FL lets institutions train jointly without sharing data, but gradients can leak information; privacy defences trade off against performance; UQ in FL is hard because client data differ, and standard calibration and UQ methods need modification; few studies combine privacy-preserving FL with UQ in medical imaging.
papers.tools: Review of FedAvg, FedProx, personalised FL, DP-SGD, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation, MC dropout / ensembles / conformal methods in FL.
papers.gap: Lack of studies combining privacy-preserving FL with uncertainty quantification on real multi-site medical data.
papers.relation: Covers uncertainty quantification together with federated learning in radiology, linking the escalation objective to the PhD's privacy-preserving setting.
papers.limitations: Narrative review without systematic search or quantitative synthesis.
papers.methodologyDetail: This review surveys how federated learning lets hospitals train a shared imaging model by exchanging model updates instead of patient images, why those updates can still leak private information, and the main defences - differential privacy, homomorphic encryption and secure aggregation - each of which can cost accuracy. It then focuses on uncertainty quantification inside federated systems, explaining that different hospitals have different scanners, patient mixes and class balance (non-IID data), so calibration and uncertainty methods designed for one dataset must be adapted, for example federated ensembles, Bayesian federated learning, federated calibration and federated conformal prediction. The authors conclude that combining privacy-preserving FL with reliable uncertainty is still rare in medical imaging. For our PhD this frames a specific requirement: when agents are trained federatedly across Sri Lankan hospitals, their uncertainty must be calibrated per site (or with federated conformal methods) before it is used for escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (review).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Covers FL aggregation (FedAvg and variants), privacy attacks (gradient inversion, membership inference), privacy-preserving FL (differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation), and UQ in FL (federated ensembles, Bayesian FL, federated calibration, federated conformal prediction).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative comparison of methods and challenges.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Identifies key gaps: privacy-performance trade-off, UQ under non-IID client data and class imbalance, need for calibrated outputs from FL models, and need for clinical validation of PPFL + UQ.

papers.title: Bridging the clinical gap: Confidence informed IDH prediction in brain gliomas using MRI and deep learning
papers.authors: Bangalore Yogananda CG, Truong NCD, Wagner BC, et al.
papers.aim: To predict glioma IDH mutation status non-invasively from MRI and give each prediction a calibrated confidence score that clinicians can act on.
papers.method: Multi-contrast 2D voxel-wise segmentation network (MC-net, nnU-Net pipeline) classifies each tumour voxel as IDH-mutant or wildtype; percentage of mutant voxels per patient feeds a Bayesian logistic regression (BLR) fitted only on held-out test data to give an IDH status and a confidence score.
papers.result: On 2,481 gliomas from eight institutions, MC-net + BLR reached 96.4% and 95.1% accuracy on diverse test groups, AUC 0.98; confidence scores were well calibrated (Brier score 0.0125).
papers.tools: PyTorch, nnU-Net preprocessing/augmentation, in-house MC-net, Bayesian logistic regression, 5-fold cross-validation.
papers.gap: IDH only (not full WHO 2021 integrated diagnosis); US/European cohorts; retrospective.
papers.relation: Uses confidence to decide when MRI-based IDH predictions in glioma are reliable enough for clinical use and when to fall back to tissue testing.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; BLR calibrated on test data; class imbalance (577 mutant vs 1,904 wildtype).
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors collected 2,481 pre-operative glioma MRI studies with known IDH status from ten sources (TCIA, IvyGAP, UCSF, EGD, UPenn, three UT Southwestern cohorts, NYU and UW-Madison). Using the nnU-Net preprocessing and augmentation pipeline, they trained a multi-contrast 2D network (MC-net) with 5-fold cross-validation on four sources to label every tumour voxel as IDH-mutant or wildtype. For each patient the share of voxels called mutant separates the two classes well, and a Bayesian logistic regression turns that share into an IDH call plus a confidence score; the regression is fitted on held-out test data so it is independent of training. On external test groups from six other sources the system reached about 95-96% accuracy, AUC 0.98, and a Brier score of 0.0125 for the confidence scores. For our PhD this is a strong template for the MRI marker agent: a voxel-level network for the molecular marker, a calibrated patient-level confidence, and escalation of low-confidence cases to tissue testing or MDT review.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-institution development and external testing study.
papers.datasets: 2,481 pre-operative glioma cases with multi-contrast MRI and IDH status from 5 public sources (TCIA, EGD, UCSF, UPenn, IvyGAP) and in-house/collaborators (UTSW-1/2/3, NYU, UWM); 577 IDH-mutant and 1,904 wildtype. Training: TCIA + UTSW-1 + IvyGAP + UCSF. Testing: NYU, UWM, EGD, UPenn (TG-1), UTSW-2, UTSW-3.
papers.preprocessing: nnU-Net preprocessing and data augmentation; only pre-operative studies with multi-contrast MRI and known IDH status included.
papers.modelDetails: MC-net: multi-contrast 2D network trained to label tumour voxels as IDH-mutant or wildtype; subject-level feature = percentage of mutant voxels (bimodal distribution between classes); BLR maps this to probability of IDH-wildtype with posterior uncertainty, giving a confidence score per patient.
papers.training: 5-fold training-only cross-validation on shuffled training data; architecture and hyper-parameters from the authors' prior IDH work (Supplementary Table 2).
papers.evaluation: Subject-wise accuracy, ROC AUC per database and overall; Brier score and calibration of confidence scores.
papers.baselines: MC-net output without BLR confidence.
papers.results: TG-1 subject-wise AUC: NYU 0.9705, UWM 0.9599, EGD 0.9867, UPenn 0.9801, overall 0.9755; accuracies 96.4% and 95.1% on test groups; overall AUC 0.98; Brier score of confidence scores 0.0125.
papers.statistics: ROC analysis per site; Brier score for calibration.

papers.title: CONSeg: Voxelwise Uncertainty Quantification for Glioma Segmentation Using Conformal Prediction
papers.authors: Elyassirad D, Gheiji B, Vatanparast M, Ahmadzadeh AM, et al.
papers.aim: To apply conformal prediction to voxel-wise glioma segmentation and use the resulting uncertainty to flag cases with poor segmentation.
papers.method: U-Net segmentation trained on UCSF gliomas; conformal threshold chosen from nonconformity scores on an internal or external calibration set; defines an uncertainty ratio (UR) per case and tests its relation to Dice; splits cases into certain/uncertain by a UR threshold; also applied to the BraTS fusion model's segmentations.
papers.result: Base Dice 0.8628 (internal UCSF test) and 0.8257 (external UPenn). Conformal coverage 0.9982 internal and 0.9977 external. UR correlated strongly and negatively with Dice (r = -0.827, p < 0.001). Uncertain cases (20.4%, UR > 0.0314) had Dice 0.7090 vs 0.9023 for certain cases (p < 0.001); same pattern for the BraTS fusion model.
papers.tools: U-Net, conformal prediction (split CP with nonconformity scores), UCSF-PDGM and UPenn-GBM datasets, BraTS fusion model.
papers.gap: Two datasets; whole-tumour style segmentation; retrospective.
papers.relation: Applies conformal prediction to glioma MRI segmentation so that uncertain cases can be flagged for neuroradiologist review.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; single architecture; UR threshold chosen on data.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors train a U-Net to segment gliomas on 495 UCSF patients (70% train, 10% validation, 10% calibration, 10% test) and test it externally on 147 UPenn glioblastoma patients, 30% of which are used to recalibrate. Conformal prediction is applied at voxel level: nonconformity scores on the calibration scans set a threshold so each voxel gets a prediction set, and voxels whose set contains both 'tumour' and 'not tumour' are uncertain. Coverage reached 99.8% internally and externally. They summarise each case by an uncertainty ratio and show it tracks segmentation quality closely (r = -0.83 with Dice): the 20% most uncertain cases had Dice 0.71 versus 0.90 for the rest, and the same held for the BraTS fusion model. For our PhD this gives a concrete, brain-tumour-validated escalation rule for the segmentation agent: calibrate CP on local scans, compute the uncertainty ratio, and send high-ratio cases to the radiologist.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development with internal and external validation.
papers.datasets: UCSF glioma dataset (495 patients; WHO grade 2: 56, grade 3: 43, grade 4: 396) split 70/10/10/10 into train/validation/calibration/test; UPenn dataset (147 patients, all grade 4) split 30% external calibration / 70% external test.
papers.preprocessing: Standard multi-sequence MRI preprocessing of public datasets; prediction normalisation so the optimal threshold is 0.5.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net producing voxel probabilities; nonconformity score per voxel; conformal threshold (NCST) from calibration set; voxel prediction sets; uncertainty ratio = share of voxels with uncertain (both-label) sets relative to segmentation; UR threshold separates certain vs uncertain cases.
papers.training: U-Net trained on UCSF training split, best model by validation Dice (0.8745).
papers.evaluation: Dice score; conformal coverage; Spearman/Pearson correlation of UR with Dice; Dice comparison between certain and uncertain groups (p-values); same analysis on BraTS fusion model segmentations.
papers.baselines: Base U-Net without CP; BraTS fusion model segmentations.
papers.results: UCSF test: NCST 0.8874, coverage 0.9982, UR-Dice correlation -0.827 (p < 0.001); uncertain 10 cases (20.4%) Dice 0.7090 vs certain 0.9023 (p < 0.001). UPenn external: Dice 0.8257, coverage 0.9977, significant negative correlation. BraTS fusion model: higher UR linked to lower Dice; certain cases higher Dice (p < 0.001).
papers.statistics: Correlation tests and group comparisons with p < 0.001.

papers.title: Method to Minimize the Errors of AI: Quantifying and Exploiting Uncertainty of Deep Learning in Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Lee J, Shin D, Oh SH, Kim H
papers.aim: To detect and automatically correct incorrect brain tumour segmentations using uncertainty measures, especially for small lesions.
papers.method: Computes four MC-dropout uncertainty maps (aleatoric, epistemic, entropy, mutual information) from a baseline 3D CNN, then feeds uncertainty into an Uncertainty Attention Module (UAM) plugged into the network so it re-weights features in uncertain regions and corrects errors.
papers.result: Adding UAM raised Dice for enhancing tumour by 3.15 points and tumour core by 0.58 (DMFNet 80.12 -> 83.27 and 84.54 -> 85.12) with a slight whole-tumour drop (-0.34), at almost no extra compute (params 3.88 -> 3.89 M).
papers.tools: MFNet and DMFNet 3D CNNs, MC dropout, uncertainty attention module, BraTS 2018, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Uses uncertainty to self-correct rather than to refer to clinicians; BraTS only.
papers.relation: Uses uncertainty to find and reduce errors in brain-tumour segmentation, supporting the idea of sending uncertain outputs to a human.
papers.limitations: Small whole-tumour drop; single public dataset; MDPI journal (check quality).
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors start from two efficient 3D brain tumour segmentation networks (MFNet and DMFNet) trained on BraTS 2018 (285 glioma patients, four MRI sequences from 19 centres). Using MC dropout they compute four voxel-wise uncertainty maps - aleatoric, epistemic, entropy and mutual information - and show these highlight where the baseline segmentations are wrong. They then add a small Uncertainty Attention Module that takes these maps as input and re-weights the network's features in uncertain areas, so the model corrects itself. This improved the clinically important enhancing tumour and tumour core Dice by 3.15 and 0.58 points with almost no extra parameters or computation. For our PhD the uncertainty maps can serve two roles in the segmentation agent: improving the model and showing the radiologist which regions need checking before the result is accepted.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method development on a public challenge dataset.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018: 285 patients (210 high-grade glioma, 75 low-grade), 3T multimodal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) from 19 institutions, expert neuroradiologist annotations.
