papers.preprocessing: BraTS preprocessing: co-registration to a common template, interpolation to 1 mm^3, skull stripping.
papers.modelDetails: Baseline MFNet / DMFNet (multi-fibre 3D CNNs). MC dropout T samples give: aleatoric uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty (variance of predictions), predictive entropy, mutual information. UAM: attention module that takes uncertainty maps and re-weights decoder features; plugged into baseline networks.
papers.training: Standard BraTS training of baselines then with UAM; details in the paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice per region (ET, TC, WT); parameters and FLOPs; qualitative uncertainty maps; small-lesion performance.
papers.baselines: MFNet and DMFNet without UAM.

papers.title: Post-operative glioblastoma multiforme segmentation with uncertainty estimation
papers.authors: Holtzman Gazit M, Faran R, Stepovoy K, Peles O, Shamir RR
papers.aim: To segment post-operative glioblastoma for TTFields treatment planning, with uncertainty estimation and an editing tool for physicians.
papers.method: Ensemble of segmentation networks with a Kullback-Leibler divergence agreement term in the loss to estimate label uncertainty and handle noisy labels/inter-observer variability; integrates surgery type (total, partial resection, biopsy) and co-segments ventricles/CSF to reduce confusion with the resection cavity; uncertainty map shown in an interactive editing tool.
papers.result: Validation Dice (mean, SD): whole tumour 0.81 (0.11), resection 0.71 (0.24), necrotic core 0.64 (0.25), enhancing tissue 0.68 (0.19). Three physicians rated 72% (26/36) of segmentations acceptable for treatment planning, 22% needed a short edit and 6% significant editing.
papers.tools: Ensemble of 3D segmentation networks (nnU-Net-style), KL-divergence agreement loss, custom visualisation and editing tool (Novocure).
papers.gap: Single-company dataset; T1 contrast only; edema not segmented.
papers.relation: Adds uncertainty estimates to post-operative glioblastoma segmentation to flag unreliable results in a neurosurgical workflow.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; small physician review (12 scans x 3 physicians); authors are company employees.
papers.methodologyDetail: After surgery, glioblastoma scans contain a resection cavity, residual tumour and post-surgical enhancement, which confuse models trained on pre-operative scans. Using 340 post-operative contrast T1 scans from TTFields patients (270 for training, 70 for testing), the authors train an ensemble of segmentation networks whose loss includes a Kullback-Leibler agreement term so the members model label uncertainty and noisy annotations. They add the surgery type as prior information and also segment the ventricles so cerebrospinal fluid in the cavity and ventricles is not confused. The ensemble's disagreement gives an uncertainty map, shown to users in an editing tool. Three physicians graded 36 segmentations: 72% were usable for treatment planning, 22% needed a short edit. For our PhD this supports presenting uncertainty maps with quick editing in the surgical-planning workflow so neurosurgeons validate AI outlines efficiently.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and physician validation study.
papers.datasets: 340 contrast-enhanced T1 MRI scans of patients treated with TTFields (270 train, 70 test); voxel size about 1x1x1-2 mm^3; manual labels: enhancing tissue, necrotic core, resection cavity, validated by a radiologist; physician review of 12 scans by 3 physicians (36 ratings).
papers.preprocessing: Annotation by a trained team; enhancing tissue unified (tumour and post-surgical enhancement); surgery type used as meta-data (partial resection when unknown).
papers.modelDetails: Ensemble of segmentation networks; loss includes Kullback-Leibler divergence agreement score between members to model label uncertainty; post-processing integrates surgery type; ventricle (CSF) segmentation added to separate cavity from ventricles; voxel uncertainty from ensemble disagreement.
papers.training: Trained on 270 scans; details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice per tissue class; confusion between structures (mislabelling rates); physician grading on a 1-7 scale of usability for treatment planning.
papers.baselines: Pre-operative GBM segmentation methods; ablations without surgery type, CSF segmentation or uncertainty fine-tuning.
papers.results: Dice 0.81 / 0.71 / 0.64 / 0.68 (whole tumour / resection / necrotic core / enhancing). Using surgery type and CSF segmentation sharply reduced confusion between CSF, cavity and necrotic core; uncertainty fine-tuning reduced it further. Physicians: 72% acceptable (grade 5-7), 22% short edit (grade 3-4), 6% significant editing.
papers.statistics: Mean and SD of Dice; descriptive physician ratings.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Classification of Adamantinomatous Craniopharyngioma from Preoperative MRI
papers.authors: Prince EW, Ghosh D, Gorg C, Hankinson TC
papers.aim: To add predictive uncertainty and an abstention mechanism to a deep learning classifier that diagnoses adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (ACP) from preoperative MRI.
papers.method: Re-trains and calibrates the authors' earlier ACP classifier with a Bayesian deep learning approach (predictive distributions instead of point estimates, one-vs-all for paediatric suprasellar tumours); uses the variance of the predictive distribution to abstain on uncertain cases.
papers.result: The calibrated model under-performed the earlier published results, showing the original model was over-fit; the mean of predictive distributions was not informative but the variance was. With abstention, accuracy rose from 80.8% to 95.5% at a 34.2% abstention rate. Clinical experts reach about 86% accuracy from MRI.
papers.tools: Bayesian deep learning (variational layers), LazyAdam optimiser with decoupled weight decay, stochastic weight averaging; random forest and XGBoost…
papers.gap: Small cohort (86 patients); paediatric suprasellar tumours only; high abstention rate.
papers.relation: Classifies a brain tumour from preoperative MRI with an uncertainty measure that indicates when a prediction should not be trusted.
papers.limitations: Small multi-institutional dataset; one tumour type vs others; MDPI journal.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors revisit their earlier deep learning classifier that distinguishes adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma from other paediatric suprasellar tumours on preoperative MRI (86 patients from several institutions). They rebuild it as a Bayesian network that outputs a full predictive distribution per patient, trained with LazyAdam and stochastic weight averaging, and find the calibrated model scores lower than their previously published accuracy - evidence the old model was over-fit. The spread (variance) of each patient's predictive distribution, not its mean, signals when the model is unsure. Using predicted value and variance together they define an abstention rule: the model abstains on about 34% of patients and accuracy on the rest rises from 80.8% to 95.5%, above the roughly 86% reported for expert radiologists. For our PhD this is a brain-tumour MRI example of the accuracy-referral trade-off at the heart of O2 and a reminder that calibrating models can expose over-fitting.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-institution model development and evaluation.
papers.datasets: Preoperative MRI from 86 paediatric suprasellar tumour patients across multiple institutions (same dataset as the authors' prior ACP study).
papers.preprocessing: Same pipeline as the prior study (multi-institutional MRI); one-vs-all labels (ACP vs other suprasellar tumours).
papers.modelDetails: Original CNN classifier recast as a Bayesian deep learning model producing a predictive distribution per patient; uncertainty = variance of the distribution; abstention algorithm combines predicted value and variance to decide predict vs abstain.
papers.training: LazyAdam optimiser with decoupled weight decay, smoothed by stochastic weight averaging; comparison models random forest and XGBoost.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy with and without abstention, abstention rate; comparison to random forest, XGBoost and clinical expert accuracy (86%).
papers.baselines: Previously published (non-Bayesian) classifier, random forest, XGBoost.
papers.results: Accuracy 80.8% without abstention -> 95.5% with abstention (34.2% of cases abstained); predictive variance indicated uncertainty while mean did not; original classifier beat random forest and XGBoost; calibrated model lower than earlier published (over-fit) results.

papers.title: Uncertainty quantification in the radiogenomics modeling of EGFR amplification in glioblastoma
papers.authors: Hu LS, Wang L, Hawkins-Daarud A, Eschbacher JM, et al.
papers.aim: To build a radiogenomics model that predicts regional EGFR amplification in glioblastoma from MRI and quantifies the uncertainty of each prediction.
papers.method: Transductive Gaussian Process (GP) model on image-localised biopsies with spatially matched multi-parametric MRI; predictive distributions per sample give uncertainty; transductive learning uses unlabelled regions to reduce uncertainty; compared with a standard GP by leave-one-patient-out cross-validation and on a separate validation set.
papers.result: Overall accuracy 75% (n = 95 biopsies). Lowest-uncertainty predictions were 83% accurate (n = 72) vs 48% for higher-uncertainty ones (n = 23); on the separate validation set (24 biopsies, 7 patients) the lowest-uncertainty predictions were 78% accurate. Uncertainty mainly reflected extrapolation beyond training data.
papers.tools: Transductive Gaussian Processes, multi-parametric MRI features, image-localised stereotactic biopsies, leave-one-patient-out cross-validation.
papers.gap: Small cohorts; single biomarker (EGFR); feature-based GP rather than deep learning.
papers.relation: Shows that restricting glioblastoma radiogenomic predictions to low-uncertainty cases raises accuracy, a form of selective prediction in neuro-oncology.
papers.limitations: 25 + 7 patients only; regional biopsy matching required; not externally validated at scale.
papers.methodologyDetail: Glioblastomas are genetically mixed, so one biopsy may not represent the whole tumour. The authors collected 95 stereotactic biopsies from 25 untreated glioblastoma patients, recorded each biopsy's exact location on multi-parametric MRI, and measured EGFR amplification in each sample. They extracted MRI features around each biopsy site and trained a Gaussian Process model that gives both a prediction and its uncertainty, using a transductive version that also learns from unlabelled image regions to reduce uncertainty. Leave-one-patient-out cross-validation gave 75% accuracy overall; the 72 lowest-uncertainty predictions were 83% accurate while the 23 most uncertain were only 48%, and on 24 biopsies from 7 other patients the confident predictions reached 78%. High uncertainty mostly marked cases outside the training data. For our PhD this supports reporting MRI-based molecular predictions only when uncertainty is low and sending other cases for tissue testing or MDT review.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective radiogenomics study with image-localised biopsies (IRB approved), leave-one-patient-out cross-validation and separate validation set.
papers.datasets: 95 image-localised biopsies with spatially matched MRI from 25 untreated glioblastoma patients (training / LOPO CV); separate validation set of 24 image-localised biopsies from 7 high-grade glioma patients.
papers.preprocessing: Biopsy locations co-registered to multi-parametric MRI; regional texture and intensity features extracted around each biopsy site; EGFR amplification measured on each biopsy.
papers.modelDetails: Gaussian Process classifier giving a predictive mean and variance per biopsy; transductive variant adds unlabelled image regions to shape the GP and reduce uncertainty; uncertainty threshold used to stratify predictions.
papers.training: Leave-one-patient-out cross-validation for model fitting and comparison (standard GP vs transductive GP).
papers.evaluation: Accuracy overall and within low- vs high-uncertainty strata; validation accuracy in the low-uncertainty group.
papers.baselines: Standard (non-transductive) Gaussian Process.
papers.results: Accuracy 75% (n = 95); lowest uncertainty 83% (n = 72) vs higher uncertainty 48% (n = 23); validation set 78% accuracy among lowest-uncertainty predictions; transductive learning reduced overall uncertainty vs standard GP.
papers.statistics: Leave-one-patient-out cross-validation; accuracy by uncertainty strata.

papers.title: Uncertainty quantification in multi-parametric MRI-based meningioma radiotherapy target segmentation
papers.authors: Wang L, Yang Z, LaBella D, Reitman Z, Ginn J, et al.
papers.aim: To improve meningioma radiotherapy target (GTV) segmentation on MRI and provide pixel-wise uncertainty using a spherical-projection U-Net.
papers.method: SPU-Net: U-Net with spherical image projection that maps 2D slices onto a sphere from multiple projection centres, giving several segmentation predictions per image; pixel-wise entropy of these predictions = uncertainty; Otsu's method aggregates them into the final segmentation.
papers.result: SPU-Net vs standard U-Net: sensitivity 0.758 vs 0.746, Dice 0.760 vs 0.742, mean Hausdorff 0.612 vs 0.744 cm, HD95 2.682 vs 2.912 cm, plus an uncertainty map that U-Net lacks.
papers.tools: SPU-Net (spherical projection U-Net), entropy, Otsu thresholding, T1 and T1ce MRI.
papers.gap: Single centre, single annotator, 76 patients; meningioma rather than glioma.
papers.relation: Uncertainty maps for brain-tumour (meningioma) target delineation that point clinicians to regions needing manual review in treatment planning.
papers.limitations: Small single-institution dataset; contours by one radiation oncologist.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors study radiotherapy target segmentation for 76 supratentorial meningioma patients at Duke, using T1 and contrast T1 MRI with targets drawn by one experienced radiation oncologist. They propose SPU-Net, which projects each 2D image onto a sphere from several centre points before a U-Net segments it; each projection centre gives a slightly different prediction, so the spread between them measures uncertainty at each pixel (via entropy), and Otsu's method combines them into one final contour. SPU-Net matched or slightly beat a standard U-Net (Dice 0.760 vs 0.742, HD95 2.68 vs 2.91 cm) while adding an uncertainty map. For our PhD this gives another way to produce contour uncertainty for the surgical-planning agent, so neurosurgeons can see which tumour boundaries are least certain.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-institution development study (Duke University).
papers.datasets: 76 supratentorial meningioma patients treated with radiotherapy; GTVs contoured by one experienced radiation oncologist on high-resolution contrast-enhanced T1 MRI; T1 and T1ce used as inputs.
papers.preprocessing: Spherical projection of 2D slices from multiple projection centres (a non-linear transform enhancing local detail while keeping the global field of view).
papers.modelDetails: SPU-Net produces a prediction for each projection centre; variance between predictions measured by pixel-wise entropy; final segmentation by Otsu thresholding of aggregated predictions.
papers.training: Details in the paper (train/test split of the 76 patients).
papers.evaluation: Sensitivity, Dice, mean Hausdorff distance, 95% Hausdorff distance; qualitative uncertainty maps.
papers.baselines: Standard U-Net.
papers.results: Sensitivity 0.758 vs 0.746; Dice 0.760 vs 0.742; mHD 0.612 vs 0.744 cm; HD95 2.682 vs 2.912 cm (SPU-Net vs U-Net); uncertainty maps highlighted ambiguous tumour boundaries.
papers.statistics: Comparison of mean metrics on the test set.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Selective Prediction in Brain-Tumour MRI Classification: Selective Risk Reduction and Component-Wise Reliability Findings
papers.authors: Alshamlan H
papers.aim: To measure whether confidence- and entropy-based selective prediction reduces risk in a brain-MRI vision-language classifier, and at what coverage cost, within a multi-module brain-MRI framework.
papers.method: LoRA-fine-tuned LLaVA-Med classifier with a disjunctive rejection rule (reject if softmax confidence low OR predictive entropy high); companion modules evaluated for reliability: nnU-Net v2 3D segmentation (3-fold ensemble), DenseNet-121 glioma grading, and Llama 3.2 3B report generation fine-tuned with QLoRA. Pre-specified analysis plan with 95% Wilson intervals.
papers.result: Withholding 1.80% of predictions (95% CI 1.14-2.83) raised selective accuracy to 97.76% (96.63-98.52) and cut selective risk from 3.40% to 2.24% (34.1% relative reduction). Withheld cases were strongly enriched for errors (66.7% vs 2.24%; OR 87.3, p = 4.6e-15), capturing 35.3% of all errors while keeping 99.38% of correct predictions.
papers.tools: LLaVA-Med (LoRA), nnU-Net v2 3D full-resolution, DenseNet-121, Meta Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (QLoRA), BRISC2025, BraTS 2020.
papers.gap: Single operating point (continuous score AUROC not identifiable); 2D classification dataset; modules not evaluated together clinically.
papers.relation: Applies selective prediction with abstention directly to brain-tumour MRI classification and evaluates risk-coverage trade-offs.
papers.limitations: Per-sample probabilities not retained, so only one threshold analysed; balanced accuracy of the rejection rule 67.34%; MDPI journal.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study evaluates a brain-MRI analysis framework module by module, focusing on whether letting the classifier abstain makes it safer. A LLaVA-Med vision-language model, fine-tuned with LoRA, classifies 1,000 test images from BRISC2025; any prediction with low softmax confidence or high entropy is withheld. Only 1.8% of cases were withheld, but two thirds of them were errors, so selective accuracy rose to 97.8% and risk fell by a third, while almost all correct answers were still issued. The authors also report reliability evidence for an nnU-Net v2 segmentation ensemble on 74 BraTS 2020 cases, a DenseNet-121 high/low-grade glioma classifier and a Llama 3.2 3B report generator, all with pre-specified analyses and Wilson confidence intervals, and they are careful to note what a single threshold cannot show (the AUROC of the score). For our PhD this is a closely matching design and a model for how to report escalation: coverage, selective risk, error enrichment of escalated cases, all with confidence intervals and a pre-registered analysis plan.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective evaluation on public datasets with a pre-documented analysis plan.
papers.datasets: BRISC2025 brain MRI classification test partition (1,000 images); BraTS 2020 for segmentation (74 held-out cases) and glioma grading (high vs low grade).
papers.preprocessing: Multi-slice representations for grading; structured findings for report generation; standard nnU-Net preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Classifier: LLaVA-Med fine-tuned with LoRA; rejection rule: withhold if max softmax < threshold or entropy > threshold. Segmentation: nnU-Net v2 3D full-res, 3-fold ensemble. Grading: DenseNet-121. Reports: Llama 3.2 3B Instruct with QLoRA.
papers.training: LoRA / QLoRA fine-tuning; nnU-Net default training; details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Coverage, selective accuracy, selective risk, error enrichment among withheld cases (odds ratio, Fisher exact test), balanced accuracy of the rejection decision; 95% Wilson score intervals.
papers.baselines: Same classifier without abstention (full coverage).
papers.results: Coverage 98.2%; selective accuracy 97.76% vs 96.60% full coverage; selective risk 3.40% -> 2.24%; withheld error rate 66.7%; OR 87.3; 35.3% of errors captured; 99.38% of correct predictions issued; rejection-rule balanced accuracy 67.34%; underlying score AUROC bounded only to [0.351, 0.996].
papers.statistics: 95% Wilson score intervals; Fisher exact test; odds ratio.

papers.title: Conformal selective prediction with cost aware deferral for safe clinical triage under distribution shift
papers.authors: Kwon H, Kim DJ
papers.aim: To build a clinical triage system that gives set-valued predictions with coverage guarantees and defers low-confidence cases to clinicians when this lowers the expected clinical cost, robustly under distribution shift.
papers.method: Calibrated probabilistic model + split conformal prediction (plus group-conditional Mondrian for gender-stratified coverage and importance-weighted conformal for shift) + a single cost-aware deferral threshold chosen by minimising expected clinical cost on a held-out calibration set.
papers.result: For early sepsis prediction, at 80% coverage selective deferral reduced error on retained cases by 49.6% (in-distribution) and 46.7% (out-of-distribution); low ECE on both splits; near-perfect NPV at 95% sensitivity; coverage near the 90% target ID and slightly lower OOD (weighted method most robust); Mondrian reduced the gender coverage gap to 1.4 percentage points.
papers.tools: Calibrated gradient-boosting / probabilistic classifier, split, Mondrian and weighted conformal prediction, expected-cost optimisation.
papers.gap: Tabular EHR sepsis task, not imaging; single deferral threshold; costs assumed.
papers.relation: Combines conformal selective prediction with cost-aware deferral to clinicians under distribution shift, closely matching the O2 escalation design.
papers.limitations: Single clinical task; assumed cost values; temporal shift only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors design triage that is safe by construction. A probabilistic model for early sepsis is first calibrated; split conformal prediction then turns its outputs into prediction sets with a guaranteed 90% coverage, with a gender-wise (Mondrian) version to equalise coverage across groups and an importance-weighted version to stay valid when the patient population drifts over time. A single deferral threshold is chosen on a held-out calibration set by minimising an explicit expected clinical cost that weighs missed sepsis, false alarms and clinician review. Testing on a later time period (out-of-distribution) as well as the original period, deferring 20% of cases roughly halved the error on the cases kept (-49.6% ID, -46.7% OOD), calibration stayed good, negative predictive value was near perfect at 95% sensitivity, and coverage degraded only slightly under shift. For our PhD this is the most direct template for the escalation mechanism: calibrate each agent, form conformal sets (group- and shift-aware), and pick the escalation threshold that minimises the clinical cost of errors plus clinician time.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development with temporally separated in-distribution and out-of-distribution test splits.
papers.datasets: Early sepsis prediction EHR data with temporally separated ID and OOD test splits (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Temporal splitting into training, calibration, ID test and later OOD test periods; gender groups for Mondrian conformal; importance weights for shifted data.
papers.modelDetails: Base model outputs calibrated probabilities; conformal prediction sets at nominal 90% coverage (split, Mondrian by gender, importance-weighted); deferral rule: defer when the prediction set is uncertain and deferral reduces expected cost (cost matrix of false negatives, false positives and clinician review); single threshold chosen on calibration data.
papers.training: Model trained on the training period; calibration and threshold selection on a held-out calibration set.
papers.evaluation: Risk-coverage curves, error on retained cases, expected clinical cost, ECE, NPV at 95% sensitivity, empirical coverage overall and by gender, ID vs OOD.
papers.baselines: No deferral; confidence-only deferral; unweighted vs weighted vs Mondrian conformal.
papers.results: Retained-case error reduced 49.6% (ID) and 46.7% (OOD) at 80% coverage; expected cost low on both splits, moderate increase under shift; low ECE; near-perfect NPV at 95% sensitivity; coverage close to 90% ID, slightly lower OOD; weighted conformal most robust; gender coverage gap 1.4 pp with Mondrian.
papers.statistics: Finite-sample conformal coverage guarantees; empirical comparisons across splits.

papers.title: Conformal Triage for Medical Imaging AI Deployment
papers.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Pomerantz S, Do S, Bates S, et al.
papers.aim: To deploy a black-box medical imaging AI model safely in a new hospital by sorting patients into low-risk, high-risk and uncertain groups with statistical guarantees on predictive value.
papers.method: Conformal triage: using a representative calibration set from the deployment site, choose two thresholds on the AI score so the high-risk group has guaranteed high positive predictive value and the low-risk group guaranteed high negative predictive value; cases in between are 'uncertain' and go to radiologists. No prediction sets are built.
papers.result: On a previously developed head CT model applied at Massachusetts General Hospital (a different setting from training), false positives fell from 233 (45%) to 8 (5%) while abstaining on only 14% of exams.
papers.tools: Head CT AI model (Do and colleagues), conformal risk control / Learn-then-Test style threshold selection.
papers.gap: Requires a labelled representative sample from the new site; preprint; single head CT task.
papers.relation: From a strong conformal-prediction group: uses conformal risk control to triage imaging cases between autonomous AI output and radiologist review, with statistical guarantees.
papers.limitations: Validity depends on the local calibration sample being representative; not yet peer reviewed.
papers.methodologyDetail: AI models often lose accuracy when moved to a new hospital. The authors take an existing head CT model built by another group and apply it at Massachusetts General Hospital. Using a labelled sample of local exams, they use conformal techniques to pick two cut-offs on the model's score: above the upper cut-off a case is 'high risk' with a guaranteed high positive predictive value, below the lower cut-off it is 'low risk' with a guaranteed high negative predictive value, and everything in between is 'uncertain' and left to radiologists. On the MGH test data false positives in the high-risk group dropped from 233 (45%) to 8 (5%) while only 14% of exams were left uncertain. For our PhD this is the deployment procedure for agents developed on BraTS or foreign data: collect a small labelled Sri Lankan calibration set, set conformal triage thresholds with guaranteed PPV/NPV, and route the uncertain middle group to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective deployment simulation at a new hospital (preprint).
papers.datasets: Head CT exams from Massachusetts General Hospital, scored by a head CT AI model developed previously by Do and colleagues (trained in a different environment).
papers.preprocessing: Split of MGH data into a calibration set and a test set; labels from radiology ground truth.
papers.modelDetails: Black-box classifier score s(x). Two thresholds lambda_low and lambda_high selected with conformal / risk-control techniques so that P(disease | s > lambda_high) >= target PPV and P(no disease | s < lambda_low) >= target NPV with high probability; exams between thresholds labelled uncertain.
papers.training: No retraining of the AI model; calibration only on deployment-site data.
papers.evaluation: Number and percentage of false positives in the high-risk group, PPV and NPV of groups, abstention rate.
papers.baselines: Using the AI model's original operating point without recalibration.
papers.results: False positives 233 (45%) -> 8 (5%); abstention (uncertain group) 14% of exams; guarantees held in a setting different from training.
papers.statistics: Finite-sample conformal guarantees on PPV and NPV.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction in Clinical Medical Sciences
papers.authors: Vazquez J, Facelli JC
papers.aim: To review how conformal prediction has been used to assess the accuracy of individual predictions in clinical applications.
papers.method: Comprehensive SCOPUS search for papers reporting conformal prediction in clinical applications; description of methods and results of the included papers.
papers.result: 14 clinical CP papers identified. CP can give useful insight into the reliability of individual predictions, but studies were mostly isolated, lacked input from practising clinicians, did not compare different CP approaches, and ignored socio-technical factors needed for clinical adoption.
papers.tools: SCOPUS literature search; narrative synthesis.
papers.gap: Small evidence base; no clinician involvement or comparative evaluation in included studies.
papers.relation: Reviews clinical uses of conformal prediction as a distribution-free way to decide when a model's output is reliable enough to act on.
papers.limitations: Single database; only 14 studies; descriptive.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched SCOPUS for papers that applied conformal prediction to clinical problems and found 14. For each they describe the clinical task, the underlying model and conformal variant (usually split or class-conditional CP on top of random forests, SVMs or neural networks) and what the prediction sets showed about reliability of individual predictions. Across studies, CP did provide meaningful per-patient confidence, but almost none involved clinicians in design or evaluation, compared CP methods with each other, or considered how clinicians would actually use prediction sets in workflow. For our PhD this supports our plan to evaluate conformal-based escalation together with neurosurgeons, radiologists and pathologists, including usability and trust, rather than only statistical validity.
papers.studyDesign: Literature review (single-database search, narrative).
papers.datasets: Not applicable (14 included clinical CP studies).
papers.preprocessing: Search of SCOPUS for conformal prediction in clinical applications; screening for clinical use.
papers.modelDetails: Summarises CP variants used: inductive/split CP, Mondrian (class-conditional) CP, CP with random forests, SVMs and neural networks for diagnosis and prognosis tasks.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative comparison of reported validity, efficiency and clinical relevance.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: CP reliably quantified individual-prediction uncertainty in the reviewed applications; however studies rarely involved clinicians, rarely compared CP approaches, and did not address adoption factors.

papers.title: Impact of uncertainty quantification through conformal prediction on volume assessment from deep learning-based MRI prostate segmentation
papers.authors: Gade M, Nguyen KM, Gedde S, Fernandez-Quilez A
papers.aim: To estimate the uncertainty of a deep learning prostate segmentation with conformal prediction and test its effect on prostate volume calculation.
papers.method: Deep learning prostate segmentation on T2 MRI; pixel-wise conformal prediction at 85% confidence flags unreliable pixels; prostate volume recalculated excluding uncertain pixels (PV_CP) and compared with the DL volume (PV_DL) and the PI-RADS 2.1 ellipsoid reference (PV_ref).
papers.result: CP significantly reduced relative volume difference (RVD -2.81 +/- 8.85 vs -8.01 +/- 11.50 for DL alone). PV_CP agreed better with the reference: mean difference 1.27 mL (95% LoA -13.64 to 16.17) vs 6.07 mL (-14.29 to 26.42); ICC 0.97 (95% CI 0.97-0.98).
papers.tools: Deep learning segmentation model, pixel-wise conformal prediction, ICC, Bland-Altman analysis, Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
papers.gap: Prostate, not brain; volume assessment only; retrospective.
papers.relation: Shows that conformal uncertainty on MRI segmentation can screen out unreliable volume estimates before they reach clinical use.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; reference volume from ellipsoid formula, not manual 3D contours.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors use 377 multi-centre prostate MRI exams with a radiologist's ellipsoid volume as reference. A deep learning model segments the prostate, and pixel-wise conformal prediction calibrated at 85% confidence marks pixels whose label is uncertain. Recomputing volume with only confident pixels reduced the average relative volume error from -8.0% to -2.8%, narrowed Bland-Altman bias from 6.1 mL to 1.3 mL and gave an ICC of 0.97 with the reference. For our PhD this suggests reporting tumour volumes and margins from the segmentation agent together with conformal flags, and excluding or highlighting uncertain voxels before measurements are used for surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-centre study.
papers.datasets: 377 multi-centre 3T axial T2-weighted prostate MRI exams of biopsied men at risk of prostate cancer (age 66.64 +/- 7.47 years) with PI-RADS 2.1 ellipsoid prostate volume available.
papers.preprocessing: Segmentation from a trained DL model; calibration set for conformal thresholds.
papers.modelDetails: Pixel-wise split conformal prediction at 85% confidence level: pixels whose prediction set contains both labels are uncertain; volume recomputed from certain pixels only.
papers.training: DL segmentation model as described in the paper; conformal calibration on held-out exams.
papers.evaluation: Relative volume difference (RVD), ICC, Bland-Altman limits of agreement vs PV_ref; Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p < 0.05).
papers.baselines: DL-based volume without conformal flagging (PV_DL).
papers.results: RVD -2.81 +/- 8.85 (CP) vs -8.01 +/- 11.50 (DL), significant; mean difference 1.27 mL vs 6.07 mL; ICC 0.97 for PV_CP.
papers.statistics: ICC with 95% CI, Bland-Altman, Wilcoxon signed-rank (p < 0.05).

papers.title: Predictive uncertainty estimation for out-of-distribution detection in digital pathology
papers.authors: Linmans J, Elfwing S, van der Laak J, Litjens G
papers.aim: To benchmark common uncertainty estimation methods for detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) whole-slide images in digital pathology.
papers.method: Patch-based classifiers with several uncertainty methods (e.g., MC dropout, deep ensembles, multi-head ensembles trained for diversity) whose patch uncertainties are aggregated to slide-level scores; evaluated on near-OOD and far-OOD detection for lymph-node metastasis and prostate cancer tasks.
papers.result: Deep ensembles best for far-OOD detection; multi-head ensembles with optimised diversity beat them on the harder near-OOD task; slide-level uncertainty separated in-distribution and OOD slides with high AUC; OOD data clearly harmed deployed model performance; findings from natural-image benchmarks did not always transfer.
papers.tools: CNN patch classifiers, MC dropout, deep ensembles, multi-head ensembles, slide-level aggregation, AUROC.
papers.gap: OOD types must be anticipated to tune thresholds; pathology only.
papers.relation: Tests whether uncertainty estimates can catch out-of-distribution pathology slides that should be referred rather than auto-classified.
papers.limitations: Specific OOD scenarios; thresholds dataset-dependent.
papers.methodologyDetail: A pathology model will meet slides it was never trained on - other cancers or unexpected tissue - and should say 'I don't know' rather than fail silently. The authors trained patch classifiers for breast cancer lymph-node metastases (CAMELYON) and prostate cancer (Radboud/PANDA), added uncertainty methods such as MC dropout, deep ensembles and multi-head ensembles, and combined patch uncertainties into a slide-level score. They then tested whether this score could separate normal test slides from 'far' outliers (a different organ) and 'near' outliers (similar-looking tissue such as colon within prostate slides). Deep ensembles were best for far outliers, diverse multi-head ensembles for near outliers, and outlier slides clearly reduced accuracy when not flagged. For our PhD it supports ensemble-based uncertainty in the biopsy agent to flag unusual brain tumour slides for neuropathologist review.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study on public and institutional datasets.
papers.datasets: Lymph node task: CAMELYON16 (train 270, test 129 WSIs) and CAMELYON17 as in-distribution; lymphoma and prostate slides as OOD. Prostate task: Radboud PANDA slides (train 4,342, validation 482 WSIs), Prostate-520 test set as in-distribution; prostate slides with colon tissue (near-OOD) and C16 (far-OOD) as OOD.
papers.preprocessing: Patches 279x279 at 20x (0.48 um per pixel), tumour/normal sampling ratio 4:1 for lymph node; manual confirmation of colon tissue cases.
papers.modelDetails: Patch-level CNN classifiers; uncertainty from predictive entropy or variance across MC dropout samples, ensemble members or heads; slide-level aggregation of patch uncertainty.
papers.training: Models trained per method with validation-based checkpoint selection.
papers.evaluation: Slide-level AUROC for in-distribution vs near-OOD and far-OOD; effect of OOD on task performance; benign-subset analyses.
papers.baselines: Single deterministic network (softmax confidence).
papers.results: Ensembles strongest overall; multi-head diverse ensembles best for near-OOD; high AUC for OOD discrimination; OOD slides degraded task metrics.
papers.availability: Code on GitHub (DIAGNijmegen, cited in paper).

papers.title: Benchmarking common uncertainty estimation methods with histopathological images under domain shift and label noise
papers.authors: Mehrtens HA, Kurz A, Bucher TC, Brinker TJ
papers.aim: To evaluate common uncertainty and robustness methods for whole-slide image classification, focusing on selective classification under domain shift and label noise.
papers.method: Comparison of Deep Ensembles, Monte-Carlo Dropout, Stochastic Variational Inference, Test-Time Augmentation and ensembles of these at tile level (domain shift across clinics/scanners, induced label noise) and slide level; rejection of the most uncertain samples.
papers.result: Ensembles of methods generally gave the best uncertainty estimates and the most robustness to domain shift and label noise; other methods showed no systematic gain (unlike natural-image benchmarks); rejecting the most uncertain samples reliably and significantly raised accuracy on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.
papers.tools: CNN classifiers, Deep Ensembles, MC dropout, SVI, TTA, selective classification curves; open-source framework released.
papers.gap: Tasks limited to tumour detection in specific cancers; label-noise simulated.
papers.relation: Benchmarks uncertainty methods for selective classification on pathology images under domain shift, which matters for multi-site deployment in low-resource settings.
papers.limitations: Compute cost of ensembles; limited slide-level datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: This benchmark asked which uncertainty method a pathology classifier should use so it can refuse to answer when it is likely wrong. Using CAMELYON17 lymph-node slides from five clinics and three scanners (so the test data differ from training data) and TCGA slides, the authors compared deep ensembles, MC dropout, variational Bayesian layers, test-time augmentation and combinations, and also added increasing amounts of label noise. Ensembles - especially ensembles that combine methods - gave the most useful uncertainty and were most robust; the other methods did not consistently help. Across all methods, setting aside the most uncertain cases clearly increased accuracy on the remaining cases, both on familiar and on shifted data. For our PhD this is strong support for selective classification with ensemble-based uncertainty in the pathology agent, especially across Sri Lankan labs with different scanners.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study with controlled domain-shift and label-noise experiments.
papers.datasets: Tile level: CAMELYON17 lesion-level annotated set - 50 breast lymph-node WSIs from 5 clinics and 3 scanners (realistic domain shift). Slide level: TCGA tissue slides (tumour classification).
papers.preprocessing: Tiling of annotated regions; leave-centre-out splits for domain shift; synthetic label noise of increasing levels and types at tumour annotation edges.
papers.modelDetails: Base CNN classifier with uncertainty variants: Deep Ensembles, MC Dropout, SVI (Bayesian layers), TTA, and combinations (ensembles of MC dropout/TTA models).
papers.training: Each method trained under identical settings; multiple runs.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, calibration (ECE), AUROC, accuracy versus rejection rate (selective classification) on in-distribution and shifted data, robustness to label noise.
papers.baselines: Plain deterministic network.
papers.results: Ensemble combinations best; no systematic advantage for MC dropout, SVI or TTA alone; rejection of uncertain tiles/slides consistently improved accuracy in and out of distribution; ensembles most robust to label noise.
papers.statistics: Repeated runs with mean and spread; significance of rejection gains.
papers.availability: Code framework published by the authors (DKFZ, GitHub).

papers.title: Generalisation effects of predictive uncertainty estimation in deep learning for digital pathology
papers.authors: Poceviciute M, Eilertsen G, Jarkman S, Lundstrom C
papers.aim: To test whether uncertainty estimates add clinical value in digital pathology, by improving predictions or detecting mispredictions under domain shift.
papers.method: Compares model-integrated uncertainty (MC dropout, deep ensembles) with model-agnostic test-time augmentation (TTA), and four uncertainty metrics, for breast cancer metastasis detection in lymph-node WSIs under two shifts: a different medical centre and an under-represented cancer subtype.
papers.result: Uncertainty estimates increased reliability by making performance less sensitive to the classification threshold and by detecting 70-90% of the model's mispredictions; deep ensembles performed best, closely followed by TTA.
papers.tools: CNN patch classifiers, MC dropout, deep ensembles, test-time augmentation; entropy, variance and other uncertainty metrics.
papers.gap: Lymph-node metastasis task; patch-level; no clinician study.
papers.relation: Evaluates whether uncertainty-based filtering of pathology predictions still works on external data, which bears on dependable escalation at new hospitals.
papers.limitations: Single task; two shift scenarios.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors train deep learning classifiers to detect breast cancer metastases in lymph-node whole-slide images and add uncertainty in three ways - MC dropout, an ensemble of independently trained networks, and test-time augmentation that perturbs each input - scoring uncertainty with four different metrics. They test on two realistic shifts: slides from a medical centre not seen in training, and an under-represented cancer subtype. Uncertainty made the system less sensitive to where the decision threshold is set and flagged 70-90% of wrong predictions, with ensembles best and TTA, which works on any existing model, close behind. For our PhD this supports using ensembles (or TTA when retraining is not possible) for the histopathology agent, and confirms uncertainty is most valuable exactly when slides come from a new lab or rare tumour subtype.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective experimental study with domain-shift test sets.
papers.datasets: Whole-slide images of lymph-node sections for breast cancer metastasis detection (Camelyon-type data) from multiple centres, with a held-out centre and an under-represented cancer subtype as shifted test sets.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs tiled into patches; standard augmentation; TTA transforms at test time.
papers.modelDetails: Patch-level CNN classifiers; uncertainty methods: MC dropout, deep ensembles, TTA; uncertainty metrics include predictive entropy, variance, and others (four compared).
papers.training: Models trained on source-centre data; details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification performance across thresholds, misprediction detection rate, comparison of methods and metrics under centre shift and subtype shift.
papers.baselines: Deterministic model without uncertainty.
papers.results: Uncertainty detected 70-90% of mispredictions; reduced sensitivity of performance to threshold choice; ranking deep ensembles > TTA > MC dropout overall.
papers.statistics: Comparisons across repeated runs (details in paper).

papers.title: Statistical uncertainty quantification to augment clinical decision support: a first implementation in sleep medicine
papers.authors: Kang DY, DeYoung PN, Tantiongloc J, Coleman TP, Owens RL
papers.aim: To show that uncertainty from an automated classifier can drive targeted clinician review (human in the loop) to improve accuracy at lower effort than full manual review.
papers.method: Automated single-channel sleep staging with per-epoch Shannon entropy as uncertainty; epochs above an entropy threshold are flagged for clinician review; compared with automated scoring alone and full manual scoring.
papers.result: Across 20 sleep studies, entropy-guided review improved agreement with the gold standard over automated scoring alone (average Cohen's kappa +0.28) while needing about 60% less scoring time than full manual review.
papers.tools: Statistical (Bayesian/state-space) sleep staging classifier on single-channel EEG, Shannon entropy, clinician review interface.
papers.gap: Sleep staging, not imaging; 20 studies; single centre.
papers.relation: An implemented clinical decision-support system that shows uncertainty to clinicians so they can judge when to override automated output.
papers.limitations: Small sample; one task; reviewer behaviour not fully studied.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors stage sleep automatically from a single EEG channel with a probabilistic classifier that gives, for each 30-second epoch, a probability for each sleep stage. The Shannon entropy of these probabilities measures how unsure the model is. Instead of reviewing a whole night, the clinician reviews only the epochs above an entropy threshold, and the corrected labels replace the automated ones. In 20 sleep studies this raised agreement with gold-standard scoring by an average Cohen's kappa of 0.28 compared with automation alone, while taking about 60% less time than full manual scoring. For our PhD this is direct evidence for the selective-autonomy principle: let clinicians review only uncertain outputs, and measure both accuracy gain and time saved in the clinical evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective implementation study with clinician review (single centre).
papers.datasets: 20 overnight polysomnography sleep studies with gold-standard manual scoring.
papers.preprocessing: Single-channel EEG segmented into 30-second epochs.
papers.modelDetails: Automated classifier outputs posterior probabilities over sleep stages per epoch; uncertainty = Shannon entropy of the posterior; epochs above threshold flagged for human re-scoring; final hypnogram = automated + reviewed epochs.
papers.training: Model training as described in the paper; entropy threshold chosen to balance review load and accuracy.
papers.evaluation: Cohen's kappa vs gold standard; scoring time compared with full manual review.
papers.baselines: Automated scoring alone; full manual scoring.
papers.results: Average kappa improvement +0.28 over automated alone; scoring time reduced by about 60% vs full manual review.

papers.title: Identifying normal mammograms in a large screening population using artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Lang K, Dustler M, Dahlblom V, Akesson A, Andersson I, Zackrisson S
papers.aim: To evaluate whether AI can identify normal mammograms in a screening population so they can be removed from radiologist reading.
papers.method: Retrospective analysis of double-read screening exams with a commercial deep learning AI system that gives a cancer risk score 1-10; simulated removal of exams below different risk thresholds from human reading; panel review of cancers with low scores.
papers.result: Excluding scores 1-2 would remove 1,829 exams (19.1%, 95% CI 18.3-19.9) including 10 false positives (5.3%) and no cancers. Scores <= 5 covered 5,082 exams (53.0%) including 7 cancers (10.3%) and 52 false positives (27.8%); 6 of 7 such cancers were clearly visible.
papers.tools: Commercial deep learning mammography AI (risk score 1-10); radiologist panel review.
papers.gap: Retrospective; breast screening; single trial cohort.
papers.relation: Studies AI confidence thresholds for autonomously clearing normal exams while sending the rest to radiologists, a real-world selective autonomy design.
papers.limitations: Subcohort of one trial; AI vendor system; no prospective workflow test.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using 9,581 exams from the Malmo breast screening trial that had been double-read (68 cancers, 187 false positives), the authors ran a commercial AI system that rates each exam from 1 (very low risk) to 10. They then simulated removing exams below each score from radiologist reading and counted how many exams, cancers and false positives would be removed, with confidence intervals, and had three breast radiologists review any cancers the AI rated low. Removing scores 1-2 would cut 19% of reading with no missed cancers and fewer false positives, but going up to score 5 would remove 53% of exams while missing 7 cancers, most of them clearly visible. For our PhD this illustrates how to set the 'autonomous normal' threshold: choose it on local data so no clinically important finding is missed, and report workload saved with confidence intervals.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective study within the prospective population-based Malmo Breast Tomosynthesis Screening Trial.
papers.datasets: 9,581 double-read digital mammography screening exams, including 68 screen-detected cancers and 187 false positives (Malmo trial subcohort).
papers.preprocessing: Each exam scored by the AI system (1 = lowest, 10 = highest cancer risk).
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning-based commercial AI system producing an exam-level risk score 1-10; thresholds tested for excluding exams from radiologist reading.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial pre-trained system).
papers.evaluation: Proportion of exams, cancers and false positives below each threshold with 95% CI; radiologist panel review of appearance and visibility of low-score cancers.
papers.baselines: Standard double reading of all exams.
papers.results: Scores 1-2: 19.1% of exams removed, 0 cancers, 10 false positives (5.3%). Scores <= 5: 53.0% of exams, 7 cancers (10.3%), 52 false positives (27.8%); 6/7 low-score cancers clearly visible.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction
papers.authors: Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates
papers.venue: Foundations and Trends® in Machine Learning
papers.aim: To give a practical, self-contained introduction to conformal prediction and related distribution-free uncertainty quantification.
papers.method: Tutorial/monograph: split conformal prediction with any pre-trained model, score functions for classification and regression (e.g., adaptive prediction sets), conditional coverage checks, extensions (conformal risk control, distribution shift, outlier detection), with worked code examples.
papers.result: Conformal methods produce prediction sets or intervals that contain the true answer with a user-chosen probability (e.g., 90%) without distributional or model assumptions, using only a held-out calibration set; set size naturally grows for harder inputs.
papers.tools: Split conformal prediction, adaptive prediction sets (APS), conformalised quantile regression, conformal risk control; Python notebooks.
papers.gap: Guarantees are marginal (on average), not per-patient; exchangeability assumption can break under site shift.
papers.relation: Core method for O2: calibrate each agent with conformal prediction and defer to clinicians when the prediction set is too large or contains clinically different classes.
papers.limitations: Tutorial; needs exchangeable calibration data per site.
papers.methodologyDetail: Conformal prediction turns any trained model's scores into a set of possible answers with a guaranteed hit rate. You keep aside a calibration set, compute how 'non-conforming' the true label looks for each case, and pick the cut-off that achieves the rate you want, for example 90%; at test time all labels under that cut-off form the prediction set. No assumptions about the model or data distribution are needed beyond calibration and test cases being exchangeable. The tutorial covers classification and regression versions, checks for whether coverage holds across subgroups, and extensions such as risk control and handling distribution shift, with code. For our PhD it is the main technique for O2: if the set for a tumour type or grade contains more than one clinically different option, the case is deferred to a clinician, and calibration must be repeated per hospital.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological tutorial / monograph.
papers.datasets: Illustrative examples (e.g., ImageNet classification, regression and medical-style examples).
papers.preprocessing: Hold-out calibration split from data not used for training.
papers.modelDetails: Model-agnostic wrapper: compute conformity scores on calibration data, take the (1-alpha) adjusted quantile, include all labels below the threshold in the set.
papers.training: No retraining; post-hoc calibration.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage, set size, conditional coverage diagnostics (e.g., size-stratified coverage).
papers.baselines: Raw softmax thresholding without guarantees.
papers.results: Demonstrates valid coverage and informative set sizes across examples.
papers.statistics: Finite-sample coverage guarantee P(Y in C(X)) >= 1 - alpha.

papers.title: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods
papers.authors: Eyke Hüllermeier, Willem Waegeman
papers.aim: To introduce the distinction between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning and review methods to represent and quantify each.
papers.method: Conceptual and methodological review: sources of uncertainty, version-space learning, Bayesian inference, calibration, ensembles, Gaussian processes, deep networks, likelihood-based methods, credal sets, conformal and set-valued prediction, generative models.
papers.result: Aleatoric uncertainty comes from inherent randomness or noise in the data and cannot be reduced by more data; epistemic uncertainty comes from lack of knowledge about the best model and can be reduced; several methods (e.g., Bayesian posteriors, ensembles, credal sets) can separate the two, but formal and practical challenges remain.
papers.tools: Review of probabilistic and set-based uncertainty methods.
papers.gap: Few validated ways to separate the two uncertainties in deep networks; little application-specific evidence.
papers.relation: Theory for O2: epistemic uncertainty (unfamiliar cases, new scanners) should trigger deferral or more data, while aleatoric uncertainty (ambiguous images) may call for additional tests or expert review.
papers.limitations: Conceptual; no medical experiments.
papers.methodologyDetail: This review explains two kinds of uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty comes from noise or genuine ambiguity in the data - for example, a blurry scan - and does not go away with more training data. Epistemic uncertainty comes from the model not knowing enough - for example, a tumour type or scanner it has rarely seen - and can be reduced with more data. The authors survey ways to represent and estimate these, including Bayesian methods, ensembles, Gaussian processes, credal sets and conformal prediction, and discuss calibration. For our PhD it gives the reasoning for different escalation actions in O2: high epistemic uncertainty means the case is outside the system's experience and should go to a specialist, while high aleatoric uncertainty may mean further tests are needed.
papers.studyDesign: Review / tutorial.
papers.datasets: Not applicable.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable. Methods reviewed: Bayesian neural networks, deep ensembles, MC dropout, Gaussian processes, credal classifiers, conformal prediction.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Discussion of calibration and evaluation of uncertainty.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Conceptual framework and method taxonomy.

papers.title: Generalized Out-of-Distribution Detection: A Survey
papers.authors: Jingkang Yang, Kaiyang Zhou, Yixuan Li et al.
papers.aim: To unify out-of-distribution (OOD) detection with related problems and review methods and benchmarks.
papers.method: Survey proposing 'generalised OOD detection' covering anomaly detection, novelty detection, open-set recognition, OOD detection and outlier detection; categorises methods (classification-, density-, distance- and reconstruction-based) and benchmarks, and discusses challenges.
papers.result: The five problems differ mainly in what counts as in-distribution and whether labels are used; the unified view clarifies settings and evaluation; open issues include near-OOD detection, evaluation realism and foundation-model era methods.
papers.tools: Taxonomy, benchmark review (later OpenOOD benchmark by the same group).
papers.gap: Mostly natural-image benchmarks; limited medical evaluation.
papers.relation: Helps O2 choose methods to flag cases unlike the training data (rare tumours, artefacts, other scanners) before an agent output is trusted.
papers.limitations: Survey; method performance varies by domain.
papers.methodologyDetail: Detecting inputs that a model was never trained for is studied under several names - anomaly detection, novelty detection, open-set recognition, out-of-distribution detection and outlier detection. This survey puts them in one framework, explaining how they differ in what is considered 'normal' and whether labels are available, and groups methods into those using classifier scores, distances in feature space, density estimates or reconstruction errors. It discusses metrics and benchmarks and highlights the hard 'near-OOD' case where unusual inputs look similar to normal ones. For our PhD it guides the choice of an OOD check in front of each agent so unfamiliar Sri Lankan cases are flagged for clinicians rather than given confident outputs.
papers.studyDesign: Survey.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (reviews CIFAR, ImageNet and other OOD benchmarks).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable. Method families: softmax/logit scores, energy scores, Mahalanobis and kNN distances, density and reconstruction models, outlier exposure.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Discussion of AUROC, FPR@95%TPR and benchmark design.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Unified framework and taxonomy; list of open challenges.
papers.availability: Paper list and OpenOOD benchmark (GitHub Jingkang50).

papers.title: Improving Learning-to-Defer Algorithms Through Fine-Tuning
papers.authors: Naveen Raman, Michael Yee
papers.aim: To personalise a learning-to-defer system to the specific person it hands cases to.
papers.method: A model of human skill trained on other people is fine-tuned with a few examples from the target person (two fine-tuning methods), tested on a synthetic driving task and an image task with real annotators.
papers.result: Fine-tuning captured simple skill patterns and helped with synthetic experts, but did not consistently improve accuracy with real annotators.
papers.tools: fine-tuning
papers.gap: Non-medical tasks; small gains with real humans.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Workshop-scale study.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study asks whether a deferral system can be personalised to the particular human it hands cases to. Starting from a model of human skill trained on other people, two fine-tuning methods adapt it with a few examples from the target person, in a synthetic driving task and an image task with real annotators. Fine-tuning captured simple skill patterns but not nuanced ones. Personalising deferral to specific clinicians is relevant when only a few specialists are available.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental study with synthetic and image data (University of Maryland, MIT Lincoln Lab; workshop preprint).
papers.datasets: Synthetic driving-time simulation (drivers with Poisson mean times under rain and darkness); image classification with synthetic and real annotators (CIFAR-10H-style human labels).
papers.preprocessing: For each target individual, data split equally between fine-tuning and testing; extra unlabelled samples provided.
papers.modelDetails: Learning-to-defer with a human performance model, adapted to a specific individual by two fine-tuning algorithms.
papers.training: Fine-tuning on k samples from the target individual (details in appendix).
papers.evaluation: Human-model accuracy, system accuracy, average trip duration.
papers.baselines: No fine-tuning; known-mean and ideal oracles.
papers.results: Fine-tuning reduced average trip time by 30 s (oracle 2 min 30 s) and improved human-model accuracy for synthetic experts, but did not consistently improve system accuracy with real annotators.

papers.title: Why Ask One When You Can Ask $k$? Learning-to-Defer to the Top-$k$ Experts
papers.authors: Yannis Montreuil, Axel Carlier, Lai Xing Ng, Wei Tsang Ooi
papers.aim: To let a deferral system send a case to the best k experts instead of only one.
papers.method: Learning-to-defer extended to choose the k most cost-effective experts and combine them, or learn how many experts each case needs, with consistency proofs.
papers.result: Deferring to the top-k experts beat single-expert deferral, with better accuracy for the same cost.
papers.tools: selective prediction
papers.gap: Simulated experts and non-medical data; no calibration of expert costs.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Requires expert labels for training.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of deferring each case to one expert, the method chooses the k most cost-effective experts and aggregates them, or learns how many experts a case needs. It comes with consistency proofs and shows better accuracy for a given budget on standard datasets. In clinical terms it formalises when a case needs one versus several reviewers, relevant to multidisciplinary escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and empirical machine-learning study (NUS, Toulouse, A*STAR; ICLR 2026).
papers.datasets: California Housing (two-stage regression), CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN (classification) with simulated experts and query costs.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits.
papers.modelDetails: Top-k Learning-to-Defer: allocates each query to the k most cost-effective entities (model or experts) with a k-independent consistent surrogate; Top-k(x) learns the number of experts per query from input difficulty, expert quality and cost; unifies one-stage and two-stage L2D, selective prediction and cascades.
papers.training: Details in appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy or RMSE vs expected budget and expected number of queried entities.
papers.baselines: One-stage and two-stage single-expert L2D methods (Mozannar & Sontag; Mao et al.; Narasimhan et al.).
papers.results: Top-k and Top-k(x) consistently outperformed single-expert deferral, with better accuracy-cost trade-offs.

papers.title: Learning to Complement and to Defer to Multiple Users
papers.authors: Zheng Zhang, Wenjie Ai, Kevin Wells, David Rosewarne, Thanh-Toan Do, Gustavo Carneiro
papers.aim: To decide for each case whether the AI decides alone, works with humans, or defers fully to humans.
papers.method: LECODU learns which of the three options to use, charging a cost for each human involved, trained on consensus labels from noisy multi-rater data; tested on natural images and colon pathology.
papers.result: Higher accuracy than earlier methods with equal or fewer human reviewers.
papers.tools: learning to defer
papers.gap: Uniform user cost; no asymmetric error costs or calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Small medical dataset; patch-level classification.
papers.methodologyDetail: LECODU unifies three options for each case: let the AI decide, combine the AI with one or more humans, or defer fully to humans, and learns which option to use while charging a cost for each human involved. Training uses consensus labels estimated from noisy multi-rater data. Tested on natural images and a colon pathology dataset with real pathologist labels, it reduced human workload while keeping accuracy. This is a cost-aware deferral formulation close to O2.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with real multi-rater datasets (University of Surrey, Royal Wolverhampton NHS, Monash; ECCV-style paper).
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10N (train) and CIFAR-10H (test, ~51 human labels per image, up to three users per case); CIFAR10-IDN with synthetic instance-dependent noise 0.2-0.5; Chaoyang colon pathology patches (6,160, three pathologist labels, 4 classes).
papers.preprocessing: Consensus labels and quality scores from CROWDLAB; samples with quality >0.5 kept.
papers.modelDetails: LECODU: a Human-AI Selection Module predicts a distribution over collaboration scenarios (AI alone, AI complemented by one or more users, defer to users) and a Collaboration Module combines AI and user predictions; trained to maximise accuracy and minimise user-involvement cost.
papers.training: Pre-trained learning-with-noisy-labels AI model; selection module trained with cost penalty.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy vs number of users involved (collaboration cost).
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art human-AI collaboration methods (learning to complement, learning to defer, LECOMH).
papers.results: Higher accuracy than prior methods at equal or lower user involvement; often matched multi-user accuracy with fewer users.

papers.title: Realizable $H$-Consistent and Bayes-Consistent Loss Functions for Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Anqi Mao, Mehryar Mohri, Yutao Zhong
papers.aim: To find training losses that guarantee a joint predictor and defer decision reach the best policy.
papers.method: Theoretical study of realizable H-consistent and Bayes-consistent surrogate losses for learning to defer, with proofs and experiments.
papers.result: New losses matched or beat earlier ones and resolved an open theoretical question.
papers.tools: learning to defer
papers.gap: No medical evaluation; uniform costs.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Theoretical focus.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper studies which training losses guarantee that learning a predictor and a defer decision together converges to the best possible policy, both in idealised and realistic hypothesis classes. It proposes a broad family of such losses with proofs and confirms them empirically. It provides theoretical grounding for training a deferral model jointly with a classifier.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical learning-theory paper with experiments (NYU Courant, Google Research).
papers.datasets: Standard benchmarks with simulated experts (e.g. CIFAR-10, SVHN) for empirical validation.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: A family of surrogate losses for learning to defer parameterised by a non-increasing function, proven realizable H-consistent and, for classification-error costs, H-consistent and Bayes-consistent.
papers.training: Standard training of predictor and rejector with the surrogate.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy; theoretical bounds.
papers.baselines: Earlier L2D surrogates (Mozannar & Sontag, Verma & Nalisnick, realizable surrogate).
papers.results: New losses matched or improved prior surrogates and resolved an open question on realizable consistency.

papers.title: In Defense of Softmax Parametrization for Calibrated and Consistent Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Yuzhou Cao, Hussein Mozannar, Lei Feng, Hongxin Wei, Bo An
papers.aim: To fix softmax-based learning to defer so its deferral probabilities are valid and calibrated.
papers.method: An asymmetric softmax loss that is both consistent and calibrated, tested with synthetic and real human experts under deferral budgets.
papers.result: Similar or lower error with much higher coverage (e.g. 98.2% vs 77.7%) and the best error within a budget.
papers.tools: learning to defer
papers.gap: Uniform error costs; non-medical benchmarks.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Needs expert labels for training.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors show why softmax-based learning-to-defer estimators had produced invalid deferral probabilities and propose an asymmetric softmax loss that is both consistent and calibrated. On synthetic and real human experts it gave lower error under deferral budgets and higher coverage. Calibrated estimates of whether to defer are exactly what a budget-limited escalation policy needs.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and empirical machine-learning study (NTU Singapore, MIT, SUSTech; NeurIPS 2023).
papers.datasets: CIFAR-100 with synthetic experts (correct on first k in {20,40,60} classes with p=94% or 75%); real experts: CIFAR-10H, HateSpeech, ImageNet-16H; 5 trials.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis showing that unbounded deferral-probability estimates come from symmetric softmax surrogates, and a new statistically consistent asymmetric softmax surrogate (A-SM) giving valid, bounded probability estimates of deferral.
papers.training: Details in appendix F.
papers.evaluation: System error, coverage, ECE of the deferral estimate, budgeted error at 10/20/30% deferral budgets.
papers.baselines: Symmetric softmax (S-SM), one-vs-all (S-OvA), asymmetric OvA (A-OvA).
papers.results: A-SM matched or beat baselines in error with much higher coverage (e.g. 98.16% vs 77.72% for S-SM at k=20, p=94%), competitive ECE and best budgeted error.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard error over 5 trials; t-tests at 5%.

papers.title: A Unifying Post-Processing Framework for Multi-Objective Learn-to-Defer Problems
papers.authors: Mohammad-Amin Charusaie, Samira Samadi
papers.aim: To decide between predicting and deferring when several constraints must hold at once (expert budget, error limits, fairness).
papers.method: Derives the optimal rule under multiple constraints and applies it as a post-processing step on trained scores.
papers.result: Fewer constraint violations than baselines at similar accuracy.
papers.tools: d-GNP: a d-dimensional generalisation of the Neyman-Pearson lemma giving the Bayes-optimal learn-to-defer solution under multiple constraints…
papers.gap: Non-medical datasets; constraint levels assumed.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Requires good probability estimates.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper derives the optimal way to decide between predicting and deferring when several constraints must hold at once, such as a limit on how many cases go to the expert, limits on particular error types, or fairness. A post-processing algorithm applies this to trained scores. Constraints on expert budget and on specific error types map directly to clinician capacity and asymmetric clinical costs in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and empirical study (Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems; NeurIPS 2024).
papers.datasets: COMPAS (7,214 defendants, 1,000 real human assessments) and ACSIncome.
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing; 10 random seeds.
papers.modelDetails: d-GNP: a d-dimensional generalisation of the Neyman-Pearson lemma giving the Bayes-optimal learn-to-defer solution under multiple constraints (fairness, expert-intervention budget, anomaly deferral, error-type limits), with a post-processing estimation algorithm.
papers.training: One-layer feed-forward networks for classifier and rejector scores.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy vs constraint violation (demographic parity, TPR/TNR constraints).
papers.baselines: Madras et al. (2018) regularised L2D; Mozannar et al. (2020) with threshold shifting.
papers.results: Lower constraint violation at comparable accuracy than baselines.

papers.title: Coverage-Constrained Human-AI Cooperation with Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Zheng Zhang, Cuong Nguyen, Kevin Wells, Thanh-Toan Do, David Rosewarne, Gustavo Carneiro
papers.aim: To share cases between AI and several human experts while guaranteeing a set share handled by the AI alone.
papers.method: CL2DC chooses AI alone, one expert, or AI plus that expert for each case, learning from noisy multi-expert labels with a fixed AI-only coverage.
papers.result: Better than baselines at the same coverage on all datasets.
papers.tools: learning to defer
papers.gap: Coverage constraint but no asymmetric error costs; limited medical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: CL2DC chooses, for each case, between the AI alone, a specific human expert, or the AI combined with that expert, while guaranteeing that a chosen fraction of cases is handled by the AI alone. It learns from data with several noisy expert labels and no clean ground truth. Specifying the AI-only coverage in advance corresponds to setting a clinician workload target in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with multi-rater datasets (University of Surrey, Monash, Royal Wolverhampton NHS; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multi-rater noisy-label datasets including CIFAR-10H/CIFAR-10N-style sets and medical images (e.g. Chaoyang colon pathology) with several expert labels and no clean labels.
papers.preprocessing: Training sets with multiple noisy expert annotations.
papers.modelDetails: CL2DC: an AI classifier, a gating model choosing AI alone, defer to one of M experts, or AI plus one expert (complement), and a complementary aggregation module; trained with a coverage constraint so a target fraction of cases is handled by AI alone.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy at fixed coverage levels; cooperation cost.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art human-AI cooperative classification methods (L2D, L2C, LECODU).
papers.results: Outperformed baselines at matched coverage across datasets.

papers.title: Reliable uncertainty quantification for 2D/3D anatomical landmark localization using multi-output conformal prediction
papers.authors: Jef Jonkers, Frank Coopman, Luc Duchateau, Glenn Van Wallendael, Sofie Van Hoecke
papers.aim: To give guaranteed uncertainty regions around anatomical landmarks in 2D and 3D images.
papers.method: Several multi-output conformal prediction variants were applied on top of two landmark models, using a separate calibration set.
papers.result: Conformal regions reached the target coverage, whereas normal-distribution methods underestimated uncertainty.
papers.tools: conformal prediction, ResNet, EfficientNet
papers.gap: Marginal guarantees; small datasets; not brain anatomy.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint; private canine data.
papers.methodologyDetail: Landmark predictions are wrapped with conformal prediction so that each landmark comes with a region guaranteed to contain the true position with a chosen probability. Several conformal variants were tested on top of two landmark models in 2D and 3D datasets, using a separate calibration set. Normal-distribution assumptions under-covered, while conformal regions met their targets. This is relevant to giving guaranteed uncertainty regions around anatomical structures in surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with three landmark datasets (Ghent University, preprint).
papers.datasets: ISBI 2015 cephalometric challenge (400 radiographs, 19 landmarks; four folds: two train, one calibration, one test; junior annotator labels); private Canine Hip Dysplasia set (472 radiographs: 207 train, 103 calibration, 162 test; 12 landmarks); a 3D mandibular molar landmark dataset.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits with a dedicated calibration set.
papers.modelDetails: Model-agnostic multi-output conformal prediction for landmark regions (including M-R2CCP and M-R2C2R methods), applied to SpatialConfigurationNet with learned aleatoric uncertainty and a one-hot heatmap classification approach (2D UNet with ResNet-34; 3D UNet with EfficientNet-B0 and MedicalNet weights).
papers.training: SCN trained as in Payer et al. (2020); other settings in paper.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage at nominal levels and size of prediction regions.
papers.baselines: Normality-based uncertainty (Gaussian) and other UQ methods.
papers.results: Conformal regions achieved valid coverage where normality-based methods systematically underestimated total uncertainty, with informative region sizes in 2D and 3D.

papers.title: Federated Conformal Predictors for Distributed Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Charles Lu, Yaodong Yu, Sai Praneeth Karimireddy, Michael I. Jordan, Ramesh Raskar
papers.aim: To apply conformal prediction in federated learning without sharing hospital data.
papers.method: FCP: each site computes calibration scores locally and shares only a compressed summary, from which a global threshold with a guarantee is estimated; tested with deliberately different sites.
papers.result: Coverage close to target with set sizes similar to centralised conformal prediction, even with heterogeneous sites.
papers.tools: conformal prediction, federated learning
papers.gap: Coverage only on average across sites; per-site guarantees weaker; 2D benchmarks.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Simulated federations.
papers.methodologyDetail: FCP extends conformal prediction to federated learning: each hospital computes calibration scores locally and shares only a compressed summary, from which a global threshold is estimated with a guarantee that holds under a weaker form of exchangeability suited to heterogeneous sites.
