Tested on vision and medical datasets with deliberately heterogeneous clients. It offers a way to calibrate escalation thresholds across hospitals without sharing data.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological and empirical study (MIT, UC Berkeley; ICML 2023).
papers.datasets: FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and MedMNIST (DermaMNIST, PathMNIST, TissueMNIST) partitioned by class across clients; Fitzpatrick17K (114 skin conditions in 3 categories) partitioned by disease category or skin type.
papers.preprocessing: Clients created with label or skin-type heterogeneity.
papers.modelDetails: Federated Conformal Prediction (FCP): train a federated model (e.g. TCT), compute conformal scores on each client's validation data, send sketches of scores, estimate the global quantile by distributed quantile estimation; theory based on partial exchangeability.
papers.training: Federated optimisation details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage and set size; selective classification on skin lesions; ablations of score function and quantile method.
papers.baselines: Local conformal prediction and centralised conformal prediction.
papers.results: FCP achieved coverage close to the target with set sizes similar to centralised conformal prediction under heterogeneity, and supported selective classification.

papers.title: Empirical Validation of Conformal Prediction for Trustworthy Skin Lesions Classification
papers.authors: Jamil Fayyad, Shadi Alijani, Homayoun Najjaran
papers.aim: To test whether conformal prediction gives more trustworthy uncertainty than other methods for skin-lesion classification.
papers.method: Conformal prediction, Monte Carlo dropout and evidential learning were compared on skin-lesion and blood-cell classifiers with clean, noisy and shifted test data.
papers.result: Conformal prediction kept its coverage most consistently; the other methods were less reliable under shift.
papers.tools: conformal prediction, Monte Carlo dropout, evidential deep learning
papers.gap: Classification only; no decision or deferral evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Public datasets; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors applied conformal prediction, Monte Carlo dropout and evidential learning to skin-lesion and blood-cell classifiers and compared how well each quantified uncertainty when test data were clean, noisy or shifted. Conformal prediction kept its coverage most consistently. It is an empirical argument for conformal methods in medical imaging.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical comparison study (University of British Columbia, University of Victoria; preprint).
papers.datasets: HAM10000 (>10,000 images, 7 classes), Dermofit (~1,200 images, 7 classes) and a blood-cell microscopy set (~17,000 images, 8 classes); split 50/20/30 with a reserved calibration portion.
papers.preprocessing: Class balancing by augmentation (flips, rotations, crops).
papers.modelDetails: Conformal prediction (several score functions) compared with Monte Carlo dropout and evidential deep learning on CNN classifiers.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Coverage, set size, accuracy under in-distribution, noisy and shifted test conditions.
papers.baselines: MC dropout, evidential deep learning.
papers.results: Conformal prediction gave robust and consistent coverage across testing conditions, whereas the other methods were less reliable under shift.

papers.title: Robust Conformal Volume Estimation in 3D Medical Images
papers.authors: Benjamin Lambert, Florence Forbes, Senan Doyle, Michel Dojat
papers.aim: To keep conformal tumour-volume intervals valid when test scans differ from calibration scans.
papers.method: Calibration cases are weighted by similarity to the test case, estimated from the segmentation network's features; tested on synthetic shifts and glioblastoma-to-meningioma shift in BraTS.
papers.result: Lower coverage error under shift while keeping useful interval widths.
papers.tools: conformal prediction
papers.gap: Volume only, not voxel-level or decision-level; shift types limited.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Density-ratio estimates can be unstable with few calibration cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: Conformal prediction gives a volume interval around a segmented tumour, but its guarantee breaks when test scans differ from calibration scans. The authors weight calibration samples by how similar they are to the test case, estimating that similarity cheaply from the segmentation network's internal features, and tested it on synthetic shifts and on glioblastoma versus meningioma shift in BraTS. It is directly relevant to keeping tumour-volume uncertainty valid on Sri Lankan scans that differ from training data.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with synthetic and real brain-tumour experiments (Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Inria, Pixyl; MICCAI 2024).
papers.datasets: Synthetic: 4,000 32x32x32 volumes of spheres; 3,000 high-SNR in-distribution (1,000 train, 1,000 calibration, 1,000 ID test) and 1,000 low-SNR shifted test. Real: BraTS 2023 glioblastoma and meningioma subjects (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR) with necrosis, oedema and enhancing labels.
papers.preprocessing: Calibration and test drawn from different distributions to create covariate shift (SNR in synthetic data; tumour type in real data).
papers.modelDetails: Weighted conformal prediction for volume prediction intervals, with density-ratio estimation computed from the segmentation model's compressed latent representations.
papers.training: Segmentation network trained per experiment (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Coverage error of volume prediction intervals and interval width under shift.
papers.baselines: Standard split conformal prediction.
papers.results: Reduced coverage error under covariate shift in both synthetic and real brain-tumour settings while keeping useful interval widths.

papers.title: A conformalized learning of a prediction set with applications to medical imaging classification
papers.authors: Roy Hirsch, Jacob Goldberger
papers.aim: To produce smaller sets of possible diagnoses while keeping the conformal guarantee.
papers.method: A small network learns a case-specific threshold, then conformal calibration adjusts it so coverage still holds.
papers.result: Smaller prediction sets than current methods at the required coverage.
papers.tools: conformal prediction
papers.gap: Classification only; no deferral or clinical study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Benchmark datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: Most conformal classifiers use one threshold for all cases. Here a small network learns a case-specific threshold and conformal calibration then adjusts it so the coverage guarantee still holds, producing tighter sets of candidate diagnoses. Smaller sets mean fewer options for the clinician to check while keeping the guarantee.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on medical image classification datasets (Bar-Ilan University).
papers.datasets: Several standard medical imaging classification datasets (MedMNIST-type collections).
papers.preprocessing: Standard train/validation/calibration/test splits.
papers.modelDetails: A network predicts an instance-specific conformal threshold (rather than a single global threshold as in APS/RAPS); the learned threshold is then conformalised to guarantee coverage.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage at a target (e.g. 90%) and average prediction-set size.
papers.baselines: APS, RAPS and other conformal methods.
papers.results: Smaller average prediction sets than current approaches while maintaining the required coverage.

papers.title: Three Applications of Conformal Prediction for Rating Breast Density in Mammography
papers.authors: Charles Lu, Ken Chang, Praveer Singh, Jayashree Kalpathy-Cramer
papers.aim: To show three practical uses of conformal prediction for breast-density rating in mammography.
papers.method: A breast-density model trained on a large multi-site trial was tested internally and externally; conformal sets were used to detect data shift, give per-case uncertainty and send ambiguous cases to a radiologist.
papers.result: Set size grew under data shift and flagged uncertain cases, supporting monitoring and selective review.
papers.tools: conformal prediction
papers.gap: Ordinal task with inter-rater variability; no workload or outcome evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Workshop study.
papers.methodologyDetail: A breast-density model was trained on a large multi-site screening trial and tested internally and on an external hospital set. Conformal prediction sets were used in three ways: as a signal that incoming data had shifted, as calibrated uncertainty for each case, and as a basis for sending ambiguous cases to a radiologist. It illustrates conformal sets as an operational monitoring and triage tool.
papers.studyDesign: Applied methodological study with internal and external data (MGH / Harvard; ICML workshop preprint).
papers.datasets: DMIST: 108,230 mammograms from 33 sites read by 92 radiologists (60/10/30 split); external MGH set of 8,603 mammograms (IRB approved); BI-RADS density in four categories.
papers.preprocessing: Largest connected component kept to remove burnt-in artefacts; intensities scaled to [0,1]; vertical flip augmentation; ImageNet initialisation; class-weighted cross-entropy.
papers.modelDetails: Deep breast-density classifier with conformal prediction sets used for three applications: detecting distribution shift, quantifying uncertainty under shift, and identifying cases for review or abstention.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa; coverage and set size internally and externally.
papers.baselines: Softmax confidence.
papers.results: Conformal set size increased under distribution shift and flagged uncertain cases, demonstrating practical uses for monitoring and selective review.

papers.title: Quantifying Volumetric Risk: Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction for 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Shadi Alijani, Fereshteh Aghaee Meibodi, Homayoun Najjaran
papers.aim: To give guaranteed, class-specific volume intervals for tumour subregions under data shift.
papers.method: A three-headed segmentation model gives lower and upper volumes; conformal prediction reweights calibration cases for shift and widens each side according to over- or under-segmentation; tested on BraTS and a shifted CT set.
papers.result: Coverage met the 90% target for every class on both datasets, with narrower intervals than baselines.
papers.tools: MedSAM, conformal prediction
papers.gap: Volumes only; small calibration sets; no clinical decision link.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint; BraTS 2020 only for brain.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method produces lower and upper volume estimates for each tumour subregion from a three-headed segmentation model, then calibrates them with conformal prediction that (i) reweights calibration cases to match a shifted test distribution and (ii) widens each side of the interval according to whether that class tends to be over- or under-segmented. It keeps a per-class coverage guarantee and was evaluated on BraTS and a shifted CT benchmark. Asymmetric, class-specific uncertainty mirrors the asymmetric clinical costs in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with proof and two benchmarks (University of Victoria, preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 (multi-class: necrotic core, oedema, enhancing tumour); synthetic multi-organ CT benchmark built under covariate shift; latent-feature calibration/test sets of 66 and 73 cases for density-ratio estimation.
papers.preprocessing: Multi-modal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR); L2-normalised global-average-pooled TinyViT features; seed 42.
papers.modelDetails: MedSAM (TinyViT encoder) adapted with a TriadNet-style three-head decoder (lower, mean, upper volume) trained with Tversky losses (alpha/beta 0.3/0.7, 0.5/0.5, 0.7/0.3; thresholds 0.7/0.5/0.3); CA-WCP post-hoc wrapper combining latent density-ratio weighting, directional quantiles for lower/upper bounds and class-specific asymmetry factors from validation false-positive and false-negative rates.
papers.training: 200 epochs, Adam lr 3e-5 cosine decay, batch 2; logistic classifier for density ratio evaluated by 20-fold CV (ROC-AUC 0.78).
papers.evaluation: Per-class coverage of 90% volume intervals with Clopper-Pearson 95% CIs; interval width.
papers.baselines: Standard and weighted conformal prediction without class asymmetry.
papers.results: For every class on both benchmarks the 95% CI of observed coverage contained the nominal 90%, with narrower or more informative intervals than baselines.
papers.statistics: Clopper-Pearson intervals; theoretical guarantee of weighted-exchangeability coverage per class.

papers.title: Conformal Semantic Image Segmentation: Post-hoc Quantification of Predictive Uncertainty
papers.authors: Luca Mossina, Joseba Dalmau, Léo andéol
papers.aim: To add guaranteed pixel-level uncertainty to any trained image segmentation model.
papers.method: Conformal risk control is applied after training so each pixel gets a set of likely classes with a guaranteed error level, shown as heatmaps (PSPNet and SegFormer).
papers.result: Risk matched the targets on all datasets; very strict targets gave near-full sets, warning that the model is not good enough.
papers.tools: conformal risk control
papers.gap: Natural-image benchmarks; no medical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Marginal guarantees.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors wrap any trained segmentation model with conformal risk control so that, for each pixel, a set of plausible classes is returned with a guaranteed error level, and visualise the result as heatmaps. When the required risk is too strict for the model, sets become uninformative, which is itself a warning that the model is not good enough. The idea transfers to tumour segmentation masks.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on general segmentation benchmarks (IRT Saint Exupéry, Toulouse; CVPR workshop).
papers.datasets: Cityscapes (19 classes), ADE20K (150 classes), LoveDA (7 classes); validation data split into calibration and test, repeated shuffles.
papers.preprocessing: Pre-trained MMSegmentation models.
papers.modelDetails: Post-hoc conformal risk control for semantic segmentation producing per-pixel class sets, with binary-threshold and miscoverage losses; heatmap visualisation of conformalised predictions; PSPNet and SegFormer backbones.
papers.training: No training; pre-trained weights.
papers.evaluation: Empirical risk vs target alpha and activation ratio.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (validity check).
papers.results: Empirical risk matched targets across datasets; overly strict risk targets produced near-full sets, signalling an inadequate model.

papers.title: Anatomically-aware conformal prediction for medical image segmentation with random walks
papers.authors: Mélanie Gaillochet, Christian Desrosiers, Hervé Lombaert
papers.aim: To make conformal segmentation uncertainty form anatomically sensible regions.
papers.method: RW-CP smooths uncertainty scores with a random walk over a graph of foundation-model features before conformal calibration.
papers.result: Kept the coverage guarantee while giving much more coherent and stable prediction sets.
papers.tools: conformal prediction, conformal risk control
papers.gap: No brain-tumour-specific or clinical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Standard conformal segmentation adds scattered pixels to reach coverage. RW-CP smooths the uncertainty scores over a graph built from foundation-model features before calibration, so the guaranteed set grows as an anatomically sensible region. It improves the usefulness of guaranteed segmentation uncertainty for clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on public medical segmentation datasets (ÉTS Montréal, Polytechnique Montréal; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multi-modal public medical segmentation datasets (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Pre-trained vision foundation-model features used to build a k-nearest-neighbour graph over pixels.
papers.modelDetails: Random-Walk Conformal Prediction (RW-CP): model-agnostic conformal risk control in which non-conformity scores are diffused by a random walk on a feature graph so prediction sets are spatially coherent and anatomically plausible.
papers.training: No training of the segmenter required.
papers.evaluation: Marginal coverage/risk and segmentation quality of prediction sets; sensitivity to the calibration parameter.
papers.baselines: Standard conformal risk control for segmentation.
papers.results: Maintained marginal coverage while significantly improving the coherence and quality of prediction sets and stability with respect to the calibration parameter.

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Conformal Prediction for Catheter Placement Detection in Chest X-rays
papers.authors: Long Hui
papers.aim: To detect misplaced catheters on chest X-rays with stricter guarantees for dangerous errors.
papers.method: A multi-task model locates and classifies tubes and lines; conformal prediction uses a tighter error budget for dangerous categories than for benign ones.
papers.result: High accuracy on critical conditions with no high-risk mispredictions.
papers.tools: conformal prediction
papers.gap: Single-author preprint; no external validation or clinician study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Competition data.
papers.methodologyDetail: A multi-task model locates tubes and lines on chest X-rays and classifies their position, and conformal prediction is applied with a stricter error budget for dangerous categories than for benign ones, so the system never declares a misplaced tube confidently normal. Using different guarantees for different error types is the conformal counterpart of the asymmetric clinical costs in this study's escalation rule.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public competition dataset (independent researcher, preprint).
papers.datasets: RANZCR CLiP: >30,000 chest X-rays with 11 categories of endotracheal tube, nasogastric tube, central venous catheter and Swan-Ganz position (normal, borderline, abnormal, incompletely imaged); pixel masks and landmark annotations for a subset.
papers.preprocessing: Multi-label targets; segmentation masks and landmarks used as auxiliary supervision.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-task network for classification, segmentation and landmark detection; risk-sensitive conformal prediction giving prediction sets with stricter guarantees for clinically critical (abnormal) findings.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification performance, coverage by risk class, set size, number of high-risk mispredictions (abnormal declared confidently normal).
papers.baselines: Standard conformal prediction and the multi-task model without conformal sets.
papers.results: High accuracy for critical conditions with precise prediction sets and zero high-risk mispredictions.

papers.title: Controlling False Positives in Image Segmentation via Conformal Prediction
papers.authors: Luca Mossina, Corentin Friedrich
papers.aim: To limit false-positive pixels in image segmentation with a guarantee.
papers.method: Conformal prediction returns a smaller confidence mask inside the predicted mask, calibrated so almost no false-positive pixels remain; works with any model.
papers.result: Reached about the 90% target validity, at the cost of smaller masks.
papers.tools: conformal prediction
papers.gap: Controls false positives only; 2D polyps.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint; exchangeability assumed.
papers.methodologyDetail: When over-segmentation is harmful, the method returns a smaller 'confidence mask' inside the predicted mask, calibrated so that, for most images, almost no false-positive pixels remain. It works with any segmentation model without retraining. For surgical planning, a guaranteed-inside region is a useful complement to a guaranteed-outside region.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on a medical segmentation benchmark (IRT Saint Exupéry, preprint).
papers.datasets: Polyps dataset collection with pretrained PraNet; each run splits test data in half (250 calibration images); 10 seeds.
papers.preprocessing: None beyond pre-trained model outputs.
papers.modelDetails: Conformal procedure that shrinks predicted masks (higher sigmoid threshold or morphological erosion) to give confidence masks in which the proportion of accepted false-positive pixels stays below a tolerance with probability 1-alpha.
papers.training: No retraining.
papers.evaluation: Empirical validity, contraction ratio (retained area) and accepted true-positive fraction at 1-alpha = 0.90 and tolerances 0.1/0.01/0.001.
papers.baselines: Uncalibrated threshold at 0.5.
papers.results: Both conformal procedures achieved empirical validity close to the nominal 90% across tolerances, at the cost of shrinking masks.

papers.title: COMPASS: Robust Feature Conformal Prediction for Medical Segmentation Metrics
papers.authors: Matt Y. Cheung, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Guha Balakrishnan
papers.aim: To give tighter guaranteed intervals for measurements such as tumour volume from segmentation.
papers.method: COMPASS perturbs the network's internal features in the directions that most change the measurement and calibrates these perturbations; feature weights handle shift.
papers.result: Valid coverage with tighter intervals than black-box conformal methods, also under shift.
papers.tools: conformal prediction
papers.gap: No clinical decision evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of treating segmentation plus measurement as a black box, COMPASS perturbs the network's internal features in the directions that most change the measurement and calibrates those perturbations, giving tighter guaranteed intervals for quantities such as tumour volume. Feature-based weights restore coverage under shift. It is relevant for reporting guaranteed uncertainty on tumour measurements.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study (Rice University, preprint).
papers.datasets: Medical segmentation tasks where a downstream metric (e.g. organ or lesion size) matters; multiple public datasets.
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed.
papers.modelDetails: COMPASS: conformal prediction for segmentation-derived metrics performed in the network's feature space by perturbing intermediate features along low-dimensional directions most sensitive to the metric; importance weights from internal features handle covariate shift.
papers.training: Uses trained segmentation models.
papers.evaluation: Coverage and interval width for metric prediction intervals, including under covariate shift.
papers.baselines: Naive conformal prediction on the scalar metric and other CP variants.
papers.results: Valid marginal coverage with tighter intervals than black-box conformal methods; recovered target coverage under covariate shift with learned weights.

papers.title: Multi-pathology Chest X-ray Classification with Rejection Mechanisms
papers.authors: Yehudit Aperstein, Amit Tzahar, Alon Gottlib, Tal Verber, Ravit Shagan Damti, Alexander Apartsin
papers.aim: To let a chest X-ray classifier abstain on uncertain findings.
papers.method: The model rejects findings with high prediction entropy or wide confidence intervals, with global or per-class thresholds, tested on three large public datasets.
papers.result: Rejecting uncertain cases improved accuracy on the remaining cases on all three datasets.
papers.tools: DenseNet
papers.gap: No guaranteed error rate, no cost weighting, no clinician study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Four findings; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The classifier abstains on a chest X-ray finding when its prediction entropy or its confidence interval indicates uncertainty, with thresholds tuned on held-out data either for all classes together or per class. Across three large public datasets, rejecting a fraction of uncertain cases raised accuracy on the rest. It is a simple multi-label selective-prediction baseline.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on public chest X-ray datasets (Afeka College, HIT Holon; preprint).
papers.datasets: 122,830 chest X-rays aggregated from PadChest, NIH ChestX-ray14 and MIMIC-CXR; four labels (cardiomegaly, effusion, oedema, consolidation); 3,869 (3.15%) multi-pathology images.
papers.preprocessing: Image-level multi-label targets; separate partition for tuning rejection thresholds.
papers.modelDetails: DenseNet-121 multi-label classifier with entropy-based rejection and confidence-interval-based rejection; quantile-based calibration of thresholds globally or per class.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy/F1 vs rejection rate (coverage) per pathology.
papers.baselines: No rejection.
papers.results: Selective rejection improved the trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and coverage on all three datasets; class-specific thresholds handled imbalance.

papers.title: Uncovering Overconfident Failures in CXR Models via Augmentation-Sensitivity Risk Scoring
papers.authors: Han-Jay Shu, Wei-Ning Chiu, Shun-Ting Chang, Meng-Ping Huang, Takeshi Tohyama, Ahram Han, Po-Chih Kuo
papers.aim: To find chest X-ray cases where models are confidently wrong.
papers.method: ASRS measures how much the image representation changes under small rotations and flags unstable images as risky, without labels; tested on MIMIC-CXR.
papers.result: The most unstable cases had much lower recall (0.2-0.3 lower) even when the model was confident.
papers.tools: Augmentation-Sensitivity Risk Scoring (ASRS): label-free score from the L2 shift of RAD-DINO embeddings under rotation;
papers.gap: Only rotation perturbations; no deferral policy evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Single dataset; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: ASRS measures how much a foundation encoder's representation of an X-ray changes when the image is slightly rotated; images whose representation is unstable are flagged as risky, without needing labels. On MIMIC-CXR, the most unstable quarter of cases had markedly worse recall even when models were confident, revealing failures that softmax confidence misses. Consistency under perturbation is another signal the escalation rule could use.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method study on MIMIC-CXR (National Tsing Hua University, NTU, MIT; preprint).
papers.datasets: MIMIC-CXR-JPG frontal views with patient-level split: 30,238 train, 10,079 validation, 10,081 test patients (131,283/43,335 train/val images); tasks cardiomegaly, oedema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax.
papers.preprocessing: Rotations of +-15 and +-30 degrees applied to each image.
papers.modelDetails: Augmentation-Sensitivity Risk Scoring (ASRS): label-free score from the L2 shift of RAD-DINO embeddings under rotation; validation-derived quartiles stratify test cases into four groups; multiple classifier architectures evaluated per group.
papers.training: Classifiers trained on the training split (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUROC, recall, confidence and subgroup fairness by ASRS quartile.
papers.baselines: Confidence-based and OOD-based error detection.
papers.results: Highly sensitive cases had much lower recall (-0.2 to -0.3) despite high AUROC and confidence, exposing hidden overconfident failures.

papers.title: Towards Trustworthy AI for Glioma Diagnosis: A Task-Aware Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Gonzalo Esteban Mosquera Rojas, Sebastian R. van der Voort, Carolin M. Pirkl, Sandeep Kaushik, Marion Smits, Stefan Klein
papers.aim: To evaluate uncertainty estimation task by task in a multi-task glioma AI model.
papers.method: A network segmenting gliomas and predicting IDH, 1p/19q and grade was analysed with Monte Carlo dropout, separating aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty and testing selective prediction.
papers.result: Uncertainty behaved differently per task, and a combined trust score did not beat simple classification uncertainty.
papers.tools: U-Net, Monte Carlo dropout, selective prediction, deep ensembles
papers.gap: Single UQ family; no clinician deferral or cost analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; dataset details in appendix.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a multi-task network that segments gliomas and predicts IDH, 1p/19q and grade, the authors examined Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty task by task, separating aleatoric and epistemic parts, checking how many samples are needed, and testing whether uncertainty helps select reliable predictions. Combining tasks into one trust score did not beat simple classification uncertainty. This is the most directly relevant glioma UQ evaluation for the MRI agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective task-aware evaluation of uncertainty quantification (Erasmus MC, Amsterdam UMC, GE HealthCare; MELBA 2026).
papers.datasets: Pre-operative glioma MRI (T1w, T1wCE, T2w, FLAIR) from multi-centre public and institutional cohorts used for multi-task segmentation, IDH, 1p/19q and grade (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Pre-processing module (registration, skull stripping, normalisation; Appendix A.1).
papers.modelDetails: Multi-task encoder-decoder (U-Net-based) with segmentation as auxiliary task and fully connected classification heads; Monte Carlo dropout giving predictive, aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty; composite trust score combining tasks.
papers.training: Details in Appendix A.2; MC sample convergence assessed.
papers.evaluation: Uncertainty-error relationships per task, MC sample convergence, selective prediction (risk-coverage) for classification tasks.
papers.baselines: Classification uncertainty alone vs composite trust score; other UQ methods.
papers.results: Task-aware uncertainty behaved differently across tasks; the composite trust score did not consistently outperform classification uncertainty for selective prediction.

papers.title: AT-CXR: Uncertainty-Aware Agentic Triage for Chest X-rays
papers.authors: Xueyang Li, Mingze Jiang, Gelei Xu, Jun Xia, Mengzhao Jia, Danny Chen, Yiyu Shi
papers.aim: To build an uncertainty-aware triage agent for chest X-rays that can abstain and hand cases to a human.
papers.method: AT-CXR classifies each image, measures confidence and distance from training data, and a rule-based or LLM router decides to automate or abstain with a suggested label.
papers.result: Both routers beat vision-language models and supervised classifiers; the two routers offered different throughput-accuracy trade-offs.
papers.tools: test-time augmentation, GPU
papers.gap: Fixed heuristic thresholds without risk guarantees; small balanced dataset; one finding.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: AT-CXR is an end-to-end triage agent: each new radiograph is classified, its confidence and distance from the training distribution are computed, and a router applies a stepwise policy using extra checks such as test-time augmentation stability and expert-ensemble agreement before either issuing an automatic decision or abstaining with a suggested label for a human. Deterministic and LLM-based routers were compared on the same inputs. It is a compact precursor of this study's orchestrator for a single imaging task.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with five-fold evaluation on a public subset (University of Notre Dame, preprint).
papers.datasets: Class-balanced NIH ChestX-ray14 subset of 1,000 frontal radiographs (500 pulmonary oedema positive, 500 negative), publicly available on Kaggle.
papers.preprocessing: Rib and device suppression for a lung whiteness index; reference set for Mahalanobis statistics.
papers.modelDetails: AT-CXR agent: data ingestion via folder watcher; uncertainty check (classifier confidence and Mahalanobis distribution-fit score); guardrailed stepwise routing policy over tools (test-time augmentation stability, mixture-of-experts agreement) implemented as either a deterministic rule-based router or an LLM-decided router; outputs automated decision or abstention with suggested label, plus CAMs and lung whiteness index.
papers.training: Thresholds: confidence 0.60, OOD at 95th percentile Mahalanobis, TTA posterior SD 0.05, MoE agreement threshold; supervised classifiers with 5-fold stratified CV on one A10 GPU.
papers.evaluation: Full-coverage accuracy, AURC, selective accuracy, throughput.
papers.baselines: Zero-shot VLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, MedGemma, CheXagent, MedRAX, LLaVA-Med) and supervised classifiers (RegNetY, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-V2, RexNet).
papers.results: Both routers outperformed VLMs and supervised classifiers in full-coverage accuracy and AURC; rule-based and LLM routers gave complementary operating points (throughput vs accuracy).

papers.title: Knowing When Not to Predict: Self Supervised Learning and Abstention for Safer DR Screening
papers.authors: Muskaan Chopra, Lorenz Sparrenberg, Jan H. Terheyden, Rafet Sifa
papers.aim: To test whether self-supervised pretraining helps diabetic-retinopathy models know when not to predict.
papers.method: Fundus encoders were pretrained with self-supervised learning for different lengths and fine-tuned the same way, then calibration and abstention were compared with training from scratch.
papers.result: Self-supervised pretraining improved selective prediction, and pretraining length changed calibration and abstention quality.
papers.tools: ResNet, ViT, fine-tuning, selective prediction, self-supervised learning
papers.gap: Retinal images, not MRI; no clinician deferral study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint; public datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors pretrained fundus image encoders with self-supervised learning, saved checkpoints at different training lengths, and fine-tuned each the same way to isolate how pretraining length affects calibrated confidence and abstention in diabetic retinopathy grading. Self-supervised pretraining helped models know when not to predict, and the amount of pretraining mattered. This supports hypothesis H3, which links self-supervised pretraining to calibration.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled experimental study (University of Bonn, Fraunhofer IAIS; preprint).
papers.datasets: EyePACS (35,000 unlabelled fundus images) for SSL; APTOS-19 (3,662 images, 5 DR grades) for fine-tuning and main evaluation; Messidor (1,200) and a 7-class fundus dataset for generalisation.
papers.preprocessing: Augmentations: random crop, flip, colour jitter, Gaussian blur, light Jigsaw perturbation.
papers.modelDetails: SSL pretraining (SiCoVa non-contrastive objective and a contrastive triplet baseline) of ResNet-50 or ViT-B/16 with checkpoints at different lengths; fixed fine-tuning, calibration and confidence-based abstention.
papers.training: Fixed downstream protocol; only the SSL checkpoint varied.
papers.evaluation: Calibration, coverage, selective accuracy and selective macro-F1 at ~70% coverage.
papers.baselines: Training from scratch.
papers.results: SSL pretraining improved selective prediction over scratch training; pretraining length changed calibrated confidence and abstention quality, so it should be treated as a reliability design choice.

papers.title: OpenMIBOOD: Open Medical Imaging Benchmarks for Out-Of-Distribution Detection
papers.authors: Max Gutbrod, David Rauber, Danilo Weber Nunes, Christoph Palm
papers.aim: To provide benchmarks for detecting out-of-distribution medical images.
papers.method: OpenMIBOOD offers medical benchmarks with slight, near and far shifts and evaluates 24 post-hoc OOD detectors.
papers.result: Rankings differed from natural-image benchmarks; near-OOD detection stayed hard and feature-based methods often did best.
papers.tools: Evaluation of 24 post-hoc OOD detection methods grouped as classification-based (logits/probabilities), feature-based and hybrid.
papers.gap: Detection only; not linked to deferral or clinical cost.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Specific domains; corrigendum for two methods.
papers.methodologyDetail: OpenMIBOOD provides medical imaging benchmarks in which test data are either slightly shifted, close to but outside the training classes, or very different, and evaluates 24 post-hoc out-of-distribution detectors. The finding that natural-image rankings do not transfer means the novelty check in this study's escalation rule must be validated on medical data.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and evaluation of OOD detection in medical imaging (OTH Regensburg; CVPR 2025, with corrigendum).
papers.datasets: Three medical imaging benchmarks across domains comprising 14 datasets split into covariate-shifted in-distribution, near-OOD and far-OOD sets.
papers.preprocessing: Benchmark definitions per domain.
papers.modelDetails: Evaluation of 24 post-hoc OOD detection methods grouped as classification-based (logits/probabilities), feature-based and hybrid.
papers.training: Classifiers trained on in-distribution data.
papers.evaluation: AUROC and related metrics for near- and far-OOD detection; ranking by near-OOD AUROC.
papers.baselines: All 24 methods compared.
papers.results: Method rankings differed from natural-image benchmarks; near-OOD detection in medical images remained hard, and feature-based methods often did better than logit-based ones.

papers.title: Out-of-distribution Detection in Medical Image Analysis: A survey
papers.authors: Zesheng Hong, Yubiao Yue, Yubin Chen, Lele Cong, Huanjie Lin, Yuanmei Luo, Mini Han Wang, Weidong Wang, Jialong Xu, Xiaoqi Yang, et al.
papers.aim: To review out-of-distribution detection methods in medical image analysis.
papers.method: Survey defining types of distribution shift and grouping published OOD methods for classification and segmentation by how they use the model.
papers.result: A taxonomy of methods and open problems, including evaluation standards and subtle covariate shift.
papers.tools: temperature scaling, MC dropout, deep ensembles, survey
papers.gap: No quantitative comparison.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint survey.
papers.methodologyDetail: The survey defines distribution shift types in medical imaging and maps published OOD detection methods into a taxonomy for classification and segmentation, noting which require retraining. It is a reference for choosing the novelty detector in this study's escalation rule, where Mahalanobis-type feature distances and ensembles are the most widely used post-hoc options.
papers.studyDesign: Survey (HKUST Guangzhou and clinical partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on out-of-distribution detection in medical image classification and segmentation.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy of OOD detection: post-hoc feature processing (Mahalanobis, cosine, isolation forest, Gram matrix), learning-free UQ (MSP, entropy, temperature scaling, ODIN, MC dropout, TTA, deep ensembles), learning-based deterministic UQ (evidential learning, confidence branch), OOD-aware training (outlier exposure, reject bucket, Dirichlet prior networks), and unsupervised stand-alone detectors (autoencoders, VAEs, diffusion models).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Organises existing medical OOD methods by whether they reuse, retrain or train a separate model, for classification and segmentation, and identifies open problems including evaluation standards and subtle covariate shift.

papers.title: Contrastive Deep Encoding Enables Uncertainty-aware Machine-learning-assisted Histopathology
papers.authors: Nirhoshan Sivaroopan, Chamuditha Jayanga, Chalani Ekanayake, Hasindri Watawana, Jathurshan Pradeepkumar, Mithunjha Anandakumar, Ranga Rodrigo, Chamira U. S. Edussooriya, Dushan N. Wadduwage
papers.aim: To build label-efficient, uncertainty-aware histopathology models with contrastive self-supervised learning.
papers.method: Encoders were pretrained contrastively on large unlabelled pathology data, fine-tuned with 1-10% of labels, and an uncertainty-aware version flags uncertain patches (University of Moratuwa team).
papers.result: State-of-the-art patch classification with only 1-10% of labels; uncertainty identified unreliable predictions.
papers.tools: ResNet, MAE, fine-tuning, self-supervised learning
papers.gap: Not brain tumours; uncertainty not calibrated against clinical decisions.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Public datasets only; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team, partly based at the University of Moratuwa, pretrained histopathology encoders with contrastive self-supervised learning on large unlabelled public data, then fine-tuned with very few labels, adding an uncertainty-aware variant that flags uncertain patches for experts. The encoder also improved slide-level classification within a multiple-instance learning pipeline. It is a Sri Lankan contribution directly relevant to label-efficient, uncertainty-aware pathology.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on public histopathology datasets (University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka, and Harvard; preprint).
papers.datasets: Patch-level datasets PCAM and NCT-CRC (fine-tuning with 1-10% of labels); Camelyon-16 whole slides for weakly supervised classification.
papers.preprocessing: Large unannotated public histopathology data used for pretraining.
papers.modelDetails: SimCLRv2 self-supervised pretraining of a ResNet (chosen over MAE and SimCLRv1), fine-tuning with few labels and distillation; uncertainty-aware variant (UA-SimCLRv2) that outputs prediction uncertainty; pretrained encoder plugged into DTFD-MIL for WSIs.
papers.training: Three-stage SimCLRv2 procedure (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Patch accuracy, F1, AUC; WSI accuracy and AUC.
papers.baselines: ImageNet-initialised encoders; MIL methods (AB-MIL, DS-MIL, CLAM, TransMIL, DTFD-MIL).
papers.results: Reached state of the art for patch classification with only 1-10% of labels; uncertainty awareness helped identify unreliable predictions; encoder improved weakly supervised WSI classification.

papers.title: Selective Conformal Risk Control
papers.authors: Yunpeng Xu, Wenge Guo, Zhi Wei
papers.aim: To combine abstention with conformal risk guarantees on the cases the model keeps.
papers.method: SCRC first abstains on low-confidence inputs, then gives prediction sets with controlled risk on accepted inputs, correcting for the effect of selection.
papers.result: Reached target coverage and risk with more compact sets on accepted cases.
papers.tools: conformal risk control, conformal prediction
papers.gap: No clinical evaluation; uniform costs.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: SCRC combines abstention with conformal guarantees: the model first abstains on low-confidence inputs and then provides prediction sets with controlled risk only for the inputs it keeps, handling the fact that selection breaks the usual exchangeability assumption. This two-stage structure (decide whether to act, then guarantee what is acted on) matches the escalation rule of this study.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological and empirical study (New Jersey Institute of Technology, preprint).
papers.datasets: Two public datasets (classification tasks) used to verify coverage and risk.
papers.preprocessing: Calibration and test splits.
papers.modelDetails: Selective Conformal Risk Control: stage one selects confident samples (selective classification), stage two applies conformal risk control only to accepted samples; SCRC-T (transductive, exact finite-sample guarantee) and SCRC-I (inductive, reuses calibration thresholds, computationally cheaper).
papers.training: Uses trained classifiers.
papers.evaluation: Coverage, selective risk, prediction-set size and computation time.
papers.baselines: Standard conformal prediction/risk control without selection.
papers.results: Both variants achieved target coverage and risk with nearly identical performance; SCRC-I was computationally more efficient; prediction sets on accepted cases were more compact.

papers.title: Robust Calibration with Multi-domain Temperature Scaling
papers.authors: Yaodong Yu, Stephen Bates, Yi Ma, Michael I. Jordan
papers.aim: To calibrate models better on new, unseen domains such as a new hospital.
papers.method: MD-TS learns from several domains how the right temperature depends on the input, instead of one fixed temperature; tested on corrupted images, microscopy and federated landmark data.
papers.result: Lower calibration error than standard temperature scaling both in and out of distribution.
papers.tools: temperature scaling, ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT, DenseNet
papers.gap: Not medical imaging beyond cell microscopy; needs multiple training domains.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Standard temperature scaling uses one temperature for all data. MD-TS uses data from several domains (for example several hospitals) to learn how the right temperature depends on the input, so it calibrates better on a new, unseen domain. Tested on corrupted images, cell microscopy and federated landmark data. It is the planned calibrator for multi-site data in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological and empirical study (UC Berkeley, preprint).
papers.datasets: ImageNet-C (76 domains: 15 corruptions x 5 severities plus clean), WILDS-RxRx1 (4 validation domains as in-distribution, 14 test domains as OOD), GLDv2 federated landmarks (500 training domains; 44 evaluation domains after screening: 30 InD, 14 OOD).
papers.preprocessing: Half of in-distribution data used for calibration, half for in-distribution ECE; all OOD samples for OOD ECE.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-domain temperature scaling (MD-TS): fits per-domain temperatures and learns a regression from features to temperature, so calibration adapts to unseen domains.
papers.training: Multiple architectures (ResNet-50, EfficientNet-b1, BiT-M-R50, ViT, ResNeXt-50, DenseNet-121).
papers.evaluation: Per-domain expected calibration error on in-distribution and OOD domains.
papers.baselines: Maximum softmax probability (uncalibrated) and standard temperature scaling.
papers.results: MD-TS achieved lower ECE than standard temperature scaling on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution domains across datasets and architectures.

papers.title: Beyond Overconfidence: Foundation Models Redefine Calibration in Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Achim Hekler, Lukas Kuhn, Florian Buettner
papers.aim: To re-examine calibration of modern pretrained (foundation) models, including medical data.
papers.method: Calibration of current architectures was measured on standard and biomedical datasets with real distribution shifts, with and without post-hoc calibration.
papers.result: Modern models were underconfident rather than overconfident, and temperature scaling could make calibration worse under strong shift.
papers.tools: ConvNeXt, temperature scaling
papers.gap: Classification only; no decision-level analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors re-examined calibration with current pretrained architectures on both standard and biomedical datasets, including real-world distribution shifts. They found that the old rule 'networks are overconfident' no longer holds for modern models, which tend to be underconfident, and that temperature scaling fitted on clean data can make calibration worse under strong shift. Calibration must therefore be re-measured for the specific models and sites used.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic empirical study of calibration across model generations (Goethe University Frankfurt, DKFZ; preprint).
papers.datasets: ImageNet validation (90/10 test/calibration split), ImageNet-C (19 corruptions x 5 severities) and domain-specific biomedical imaging tasks with real distribution shifts.
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: Evaluation of inherent calibration of older CNNs and transformers versus modern pretrained hybrid models (e.g. ConvNeXt, EVA, BEiT) and of post-hoc calibration methods.
papers.training: Pretrained models fine-tuned per task.
papers.evaluation: Top-label ECE in-distribution and under synthetic and real shifts; effect of post-hoc calibration.
papers.baselines: Earlier model generations; uncalibrated outputs.
papers.results: Modern models were underconfident in-distribution (unlike the classic overconfidence) and better calibrated under shift; post-hoc calibration helped in-distribution but became less reliable and sometimes counterproductive under severe shift.

papers.title: Predictive uncertainty estimation in deep learning for lung carcinoma classification in digital pathology under real dataset shifts
papers.authors: Abdur R. Fayjie, Jutika Borah, Florencia Carbone, Jan Tack, Patrick Vandewalle
papers.aim: To test whether uncertainty estimation makes lung-cancer pathology classifiers safer under real data shifts.
papers.method: Several uncertainty methods were compared on accuracy and calibration with new carcinoma subtypes and new hospitals as test data.
papers.result: Uncertainty methods improved robustness and calibration, but performance still dropped under strong shifts.
papers.tools: MC dropout, deep ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout, ensemble
papers.gap: Lung pathology; no deferral or workload analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study asks whether uncertainty estimation makes pathology classifiers safer when test data differ from training data in realistic ways: new carcinoma subtypes and new hospitals. Several uncertainty methods were compared on accuracy and calibration across these shifts. It supports testing the Pathology Agent's uncertainty on local slides that differ from public training data.
papers.studyDesign: Comparative empirical study (KU Leuven, UZ Leuven, Gauhati University; preprint).
papers.datasets: Lung carcinoma digital pathology datasets with clinically relevant shifts: in-distribution, related diseases (carcinoma subtypes), and different centres/scanners.
papers.preprocessing: Patch-based processing of whole-slide images.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of predictive uncertainty methods (e.g. MC dropout, deep ensembles, few-shot/other UQ approaches) for lung carcinoma classification.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification performance and calibration (ECE) under each shift scenario; uncertainty-based rejection.
papers.baselines: Deterministic baseline.
papers.results: Uncertainty estimation added robustness and better calibration, but performance and calibration degraded under strong real shifts, with differences between methods.

papers.title: Benchmarking Bayesian Deep Learning on Diabetic Retinopathy Detection Tasks
papers.authors: Neil Band, Tim G. J. Rudner, Qixuan Feng, Angelos Filos, Zachary Nado, Michael W. Dusenberry, Ghassen Jerfel, Dustin Tran, Yarin Gal
papers.aim: To benchmark Bayesian uncertainty methods on diabetic retinopathy referral.
papers.method: RETINA: models refer their most uncertain cases to an expert, and accuracy on kept cases is measured at each referral rate, in-domain and on a different population.
papers.result: Ensembles were most reliable, no method was best under all shifts, and referral helped less under shift.
papers.tools: MC dropout, deep ensembles, selective prediction
papers.gap: Single disease; no human-in-the-loop measurement.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Public retina datasets only.
papers.methodologyDetail: RETINA turns diabetic retinopathy screening into a benchmark for uncertainty: models refer the most uncertain cases to an expert, and the accuracy on the cases they keep is measured at each referral rate, both on the training population and on a different population. Many Bayesian methods were reimplemented and compared fairly. The referral-curve evaluation is the same design as the risk-coverage analysis in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and systematic evaluation (Oxford, Google Research; NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks).
papers.datasets: RETINA Benchmark built on EyePACS (in-domain) and APTOS 2019 (population shift, India) high-resolution retina images graded for diabetic retinopathy.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised preprocessing and splits; tasks defined for in-domain and shifted evaluation.
papers.modelDetails: Standardised implementations of Bayesian deep learning methods: MAP (deterministic), MFVI, Radial-MFVI, function-space VI, MC dropout, Rank-1 BNNs, deep ensembles and ensembles of each.
papers.training: Optimised run scripts per method (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUC and accuracy on retained cases as a function of referral rate (selective prediction), in-domain and under population/severity shift.
papers.baselines: Deterministic MAP model.
papers.results: Ensembles of Bayesian methods were most reliable; no method was consistently best across shifts; uncertainty-based referral improved retained-case performance in-domain but less under shift.
papers.statistics: Means with standard errors over seeds.

papers.title: A Systematic Comparison of Bayesian Deep Learning Robustness in Diabetic Retinopathy Tasks
papers.authors: Angelos Filos, Sebastian Farquhar, Aidan N. Gomez, Tim G. J. Rudner, Zachary Kenton, Lewis Smith, Milad Alizadeh, Arnoud de Kroon, Yarin Gal
papers.aim: To compare Bayesian deep learning methods for diabetic retinopathy referral.
papers.method: Each method's uncertainty decided which images to refer to an expert; performance on the remaining images was plotted against referral rate, with an Indian dataset for shift.
papers.result: Ensemble MC dropout was best; methods strong on standard benchmarks did not transfer.
papers.tools: MC dropout, deep ensembles, ensemble
papers.gap: Binary task; no cost or human performance modelling.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Retina only.
papers.methodologyDetail: An early benchmark that treated diabetic retinopathy screening as a referral task: each method's uncertainty decides which images go to an expert, and performance on the remaining images is plotted against the referral rate, with a separate Indian dataset testing shift. Ensembles of MC dropout were most useful. It established the referral-curve method used later for medical deferral.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and comparison (University of Oxford).
papers.datasets: Kaggle Diabetic Retinopathy Detection (35,126 train, 53,576 test; 20% of train held out); binary sight-threatening DR (grades 2-4, ~19% positive); APTOS 2019 as a distribution-shift test set from India.
papers.preprocessing: Images cropped and resized to 512x512, channel-wise normalisation, affine augmentation (zoom +-10%, translation +-25 px, rotation).
papers.modelDetails: Bayesian deep learning baselines: MC dropout, mean-field VI, deep ensembles, ensemble MC dropout, deterministic; uncertainty used for pre-screening referral.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC and accuracy as a function of the fraction of cases referred to experts (0-50%).
papers.baselines: Deterministic and random referral.
papers.results: With no referral all methods were equal; at lower referral rates ensemble MC dropout performed best; methods that excelled on UCI benchmarks did not transfer, 'overfitting' their uncertainty.

papers.title: Confidence-Uncertainty Boundary Calibration for Bayesian Deep Learning in Medical Image Analysis
papers.authors: Hua Xu, Julián D. Arias-Londoño, Juan I. Godino-Llorente
papers.aim: To make Bayesian uncertainty a reliable signal for clinician review in medical imaging.
papers.method: A Bayesian network is trained so correct predictions are confident and errors are uncertain, followed by a two-temperature post-hoc correction; tested on three tasks.
papers.result: Better alignment between uncertainty and correctness and better calibration on all three tasks.
papers.tools: Bayesian neural network, temperature scaling
papers.gap: No deferral policy or workload evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method trains a Bayesian network so that correct predictions sit in a high-confidence, low-uncertainty region and errors fall outside it, then applies a two-temperature post-hoc correction. The goal is that uncertainty becomes a reliable flag for clinicians to review a case. Evaluated on three medical imaging tasks.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on three medical imaging tasks (Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, preprint).
papers.datasets: Pneumonia screening (chest X-ray), diabetic retinopathy detection and a third medical imaging identification task.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: Bayesian neural network with a Confidence-Uncertainty Boundary Calibration (CUBC) concept, a CUB-Loss training term that separates correct and incorrect predictions in confidence-uncertainty space, and a post-hoc Dual Temperature Scaling (DTS) strategy.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Calibration (ECE), correlation between uncertainty and correctness, ability to flag unreliable outputs, accuracy.
papers.baselines: Standard BNNs and post-hoc calibration methods.
papers.results: Improved alignment between uncertainty and correctness and better calibration across the three tasks.

papers.title: Comparative Benchmarking of Failure Detection Methods in Medical Image Segmentation: Unveiling the Role of Confidence Aggregation
papers.authors: Maximilian Zenk, David Zimmerer, Fabian Isensee, Jeremias Traub, Tobias Norajitra, Paul F. Jäger, Klaus Maier-Hein
papers.aim: To benchmark methods that detect failed medical image segmentations.
papers.method: Failure detection is evaluated with risk-coverage curves (risk = 1 - Dice), comparing many ways to turn voxel uncertainty into a case-level confidence.
papers.result: Agreement between ensemble members (pairwise Dice) was a simple, robust and best-performing confidence score.
papers.tools: ensemble, nnU-Net
papers.gap: Detection only; no clinical cost or deferral to clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Requires ensembles.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper defines segmentation failure detection as deciding whether to accept a segmentation for downstream use, evaluates it with risk-coverage curves using 1 - Dice as risk, and compares many ways of turning voxel uncertainties into one case-level confidence. The simplest strong method was agreement between ensemble members (pairwise Dice). This is adopted as a baseline confidence score for the MRI Agent in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of segmentation failure detection (DKFZ Heidelberg; MELBA/preprint).
papers.datasets: Multiple public 3D medical segmentation datasets with in-distribution and shifted test sets (details in paper; includes brain and abdominal tasks).
papers.preprocessing: Ground-truth masks used only to define risk.
papers.modelDetails: Benchmarking framework: segmentation model plus confidence scoring functions (pixel confidence aggregation such as mean entropy, pairwise Dice between ensemble members, quality-regression networks, mahalanobis-type scores); failure detection by thresholding confidence.
papers.training: nnU-Net-style segmentation models; ensembles for pairwise Dice.
papers.evaluation: Risk-coverage analysis with AURC as main metric; risk = 1 - Dice (NSD in auxiliary analysis).
papers.baselines: Single-model pixel-confidence aggregates and other failure detectors.
papers.results: Confidence aggregation strongly affected performance; pairwise Dice between ensemble predictions was a simple, robust and superior baseline for failure detection.

papers.title: Better than Average: Spatially-Aware Aggregation of Segmentation Uncertainty Improves Downstream Performance
papers.authors: Vanessa Emanuela Guarino, Claudia Winklmayr, Jannik Franzen, Josef Lorenz Rumberger, Manuel Pfeuffer, Sonja Greven, Klaus Maier-Hein, Carsten T. Lüth, Christoph Karg, Dagmar Kainmueller
papers.aim: To find better ways to summarise segmentation uncertainty than simple averaging.
papers.method: Many spatially aware uncertainty aggregators were compared with averaging for failure detection and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.result: Spatial aggregators beat averaging; the best one depended on the dataset, so combining them was more robust.
papers.tools: MC dropout, deep ensembles
papers.gap: No link to clinical decisions or calibration.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Segmentation uncertainty is usually summarised by averaging over all pixels. This study compares many alternative summaries, including ones that capture whether uncertainty is clustered or concentrated at edges, for detecting failures and out-of-distribution images. Spatial summaries worked better than the average. It informs how the MRI Agent should convert voxel uncertainty into one escalation score.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical study of uncertainty aggregation (MDC Berlin, DKFZ, Charité; preprint).
papers.datasets: Diverse segmentation datasets (biomedical and driving, including OoD variants) with U-Net 3D, U-Net, HoVer-NeXt, HRNet and DeepLabv3+ models.
papers.preprocessing: Uncertainty maps normalised to [0,1].
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of aggregation strategies that turn pixel uncertainty maps into a scalar: global average, patch-level maximum average, above-threshold and above-quantile averages, class-level and weighted class averages, and spatially aware structural measures (e.g. MOR, EDS).
papers.training: MC dropout main UQ method; replicated with MSP, deep ensembles and TTA.
papers.evaluation: Downstream OoD detection and failure detection performance.
papers.baselines: Global average.
papers.results: Spatially aware aggregators outperformed global averaging in both downstream tasks, but the best single aggregator depended on dataset; combining aggregators was more robust.

papers.title: Counterfactual Context Auditing for Glioma Segmentation Failure Detection Across MRI Datasets
papers.authors: Nguyen Linh Dan Le, Tran Dang Khoi, Nguyen Pham Hoang Le
papers.aim: To detect glioma segmentation failures on new MRI datasets.
papers.method: Feature statistics are swapped for training-like ones and large changes in the predicted tumour flag context-dependent failures, combined with ordinary uncertainty; tested on BraTS and UTSW.
papers.result: Combining context sensitivity with uncertainty detected failures better than an ensemble.
papers.tools: ensemble
papers.gap: Ranking only; no threshold or clinical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Preprint; two datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: To find glioma segmentations that are likely wrong on a new dataset, the method swaps in feature statistics typical of the training data and checks whether the predicted tumour changes a lot; a large change suggests the model is relying on site-specific context. Combined with ordinary uncertainty, this ranked failures better than an ensemble on BraTS and UTSW. It offers an extra, cheap failure signal for local data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on glioma segmentation across datasets (University of Melbourne, Vietnamese universities; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS and UT Southwestern glioma MRI datasets (cross-dataset shift).
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Counterfactual context transport (CCT): replaces a scan's feature statistics with those of training scans and measures how much the tumour mask changes; combined with prediction uncertainty to rank cases for review without retraining or extra networks.
papers.training: Uses an existing segmentation network.
papers.evaluation: Failure detection performance (ranking of poor-Dice cases) across datasets.
papers.baselines: Prediction uncertainty alone and an ensemble of separately trained networks.
papers.results: Context sensitivity gave evidence of failure that uncertainty alone missed; combining both signals gave the strongest average failure detection, better than an ensemble.

papers.title: Automatic quality control framework for more reliable integration of machine learning-based image segmentation into medical workflows
papers.authors: Elena Williams, Sebastian Niehaus, Janis Reinelt, Alberto Merola, Paul Glad Mihai, Kersten Villringer, Konstantin Thierbach, Evelyn Medawar, Daniel Lichterfeld, Ingo Roeder, et al.
papers.aim: To automatically check brain MRI segmentations before they are used clinically.
papers.method: A quality-control framework combines uncertainty and error estimates into a score or predicts Dice directly; validated on multi-site white-matter lesion data.
papers.result: Removing flagged cases raised mean Dice of accepted segmentations from 0.82 to 0.84.
papers.tools: CNN segmentation with two automatic quality-control approaches: aggregation of uncertainty and error estimates into a single score, and direct…
papers.gap: WMH, not tumours; no clinician workload measure.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Small test folds; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a framework that automatically checks each brain MRI segmentation before it is used, either by combining uncertainty and error estimates into a quality score or by predicting the Dice score directly, and validated it on multi-site white-matter lesion data. Removing flagged cases raised the average quality of accepted segmentations. It is a practical model for the quality check after the MRI Agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective framework development on public multi-site brain MRI (AICURA medical, Edinburgh, TU Dresden, Charité; preprint).
papers.datasets: 105 patients' T1 and FLAIR MRI from four public white-matter-hyperintensity / MS databases (MICCAI WMH 2017, ISBI MS 2015, MICCAI MS 2016, MS17); folds of 68 train, 16 validation, 21 test.
papers.preprocessing: Combined multi-source data to increase variation; standard preprocessing (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: CNN segmentation with two automatic quality-control approaches: aggregation of uncertainty and error estimates into a single score, and direct prediction of Dice; cases flagged as failed are excluded or sent for review.
papers.training: Cross-validation training (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Detection of failed segmentations; mean Dice on accepted cases.
papers.baselines: No QC (all cases accepted); manual evaluation.
papers.results: Both QC methods independently improved mean Dice of accepted cases from 0.82 to 0.84 by detecting failed cases.

papers.title: Assessing Reliability and Challenges of Uncertainty Estimations for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Alain Jungo, Mauricio Reyes
papers.aim: To assess how reliable common uncertainty estimates are for medical image segmentation.
papers.method: Five uncertainty methods on the same U-Net for brain tumours and skin lesions, with calibration checked for the whole dataset and per patient.
papers.result: Uncertainty looked calibrated overall but not for individual patients; ensembles were most robust.
papers.tools: U-Net, MC dropout
papers.gap: Whole-tumour only; older methods.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Two datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using the same U-Net on brain tumours and skin lesions, the study compared five common ways of estimating voxel uncertainty and checked calibration both over the whole dataset and for each patient. All methods looked well calibrated overall but not for individual patients, which is what matters clinically. This motivates subject-level calibration checks in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical evaluation of voxel-wise uncertainty (University of Bern; MICCAI 2019).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 (265 subjects: 100 train, 25 validation, 160 test; whole-tumour label) and ISIC 2017 skin lesion segmentation (2,000 train, 150 validation, 600 test).
papers.preprocessing: BraTS: per-subject z-score normalisation; ISIC: resized to 256x192 and scaled to [0,1].
papers.modelDetails: U-Net-like network (four pooling steps, dropout 0.05, batch norm) with five uncertainty measures: softmax entropy baseline, MC dropout, aleatoric uncertainty, ensembles, and auxiliary networks.
papers.training: Cross-entropy, Adam lr 1e-4, early stopping on validation Dice.
papers.evaluation: Dataset-level and subject-level calibration (ECE, uncertainty-error overlap), failure detection.
papers.baselines: Softmax entropy.
papers.results: Methods performed similarly; uncertainty was well calibrated at the dataset level but miscalibrated at the subject level, so per-patient reliability is compromised; ensembles were relatively robust.

papers.title: Information-theoretic Generalization Analysis for Expected Calibration Error
papers.authors: Futoshi Futami, Masahiro Fujisawa
papers.aim: To analyse how accurate the expected calibration error (ECE) is as a measurement.
papers.method: Information-theoretic analysis of ECE bias from binning, the best number of bins and generalisation bounds.
papers.result: Gave better bias bounds, an optimal bin count and useful generalisation bounds for ECE.
papers.tools: Analysis of estimation bias of expected calibration error under uniform-mass and uniform-width binning, optimal number of bins, and…
papers.gap: Theoretical; no medical data.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Binary/top-label settings.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper studies how accurate the expected calibration error itself is as a measurement, showing how binning choices bias it, how many bins to use, and how much ECE can be trusted on new data. It informs how calibration will be measured and reported in this study, especially with small local test sets.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical learning-theory study with experiments (Osaka University, RIKEN AIP; NeurIPS 2024).
papers.datasets: Deep learning benchmarks used to validate bounds.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of estimation bias of expected calibration error under uniform-mass and uniform-width binning, optimal number of bins, and information-theoretic generalisation bounds for ECE on unseen data.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Tightness of bounds; bias when reusing training data for recalibration.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Derived improved bias bounds, the optimal bin count, and non-vacuous generalisation bounds; showed extra bias when recalibrating on training data.

papers.title: Calibration tests in multi-class classification: A unifying framework
papers.authors: David Widmann, Fredrik Lindsten, Dave Zachariah
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019)
papers.aim: To provide proper statistical tests of whether a multi-class model is calibrated.
papers.method: A general family of calibration measures with kernel-based estimators (SKCE) that can be used as hypothesis tests, checked in simulations.
papers.result: The estimators were unbiased and gave valid calibration tests, unlike binned ECE.
papers.tools: Unifying framework of multi-class calibration measures generalising ECE, MCE and MMCE;
papers.gap: No medical application.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Kernel choice affects power.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors give a general family of calibration measures for multi-class models and kernel-based estimators that can be used as formal statistical tests of whether a model is calibrated, instead of reporting an ECE number with no notion of significance. Simulations confirmed unbiasedness and test validity. These tests could complement ECE in this study, especially for small local test sets.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and simulation study (Uppsala, Linköping; NeurIPS 2019).
papers.datasets: Synthetic datasets of 250 predictions over 10 classes from three generative models (one calibrated, two miscalibrated), 10^4 repetitions.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Unifying framework of multi-class calibration measures generalising ECE, MCE and MMCE; squared kernel calibration error (SKCE) with matrix-valued kernels and consistent, unbiased estimators that serve as statistical calibration tests with p-value approximations.
papers.training: Kernel bandwidth by median heuristic.
papers.evaluation: Bias and variance of estimators; type I and II error of calibration tests.
papers.baselines: Histogram-regression ECE with uniform and data-dependent binning.
papers.results: SKCE estimators were unbiased and gave valid hypothesis tests of calibration, unlike binned ECE, improving interpretability of calibration measurement.

papers.title: Towards Reliable WMH Segmentation under Domain Shift: An Application Study using Maximum Entropy Regularization to Improve Uncertainty Estimation
papers.authors: Franco Matzkin, Agostina Larrazabal, Diego H Milone, Jose Dolz, Enzo Ferrante
papers.aim: To improve uncertainty of white-matter lesion segmentation under scanner changes.
papers.method: Networks were trained with maximum-entropy regularisation against overconfidence and tested on data from different scanners.
papers.result: Better calibration under domain shift, and entropy predicted segmentation errors more reliably.
papers.tools: U-Net
papers.gap: WMH rather than tumours; no deferral experiment.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Two datasets; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study trains white-matter-lesion segmentation networks with a penalty that discourages overconfident outputs and tests them on a second dataset from different scanners.
