Regularised models were better calibrated after the shift and their entropy better predicted where segmentations were wrong, without needing ground truth at deployment. It is a cheap training-time option to improve calibration before local deployment.
papers.studyDesign: Application study under domain shift (CONICET Argentina, ÉTS Montréal; preprint).
papers.datasets: WMH Segmentation Challenge and 3D-MR-MS datasets (public, different scanners and sites) for in-distribution and out-of-distribution testing.
papers.preprocessing: Standard WMH preprocessing (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: U-Net segmentation with maximum-entropy regularisation schemes during training; voxel predictive entropy as uncertainty.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice, Hausdorff distance, expected calibration error, correlation of entropy-based uncertainty with segmentation error, in- and out-of-distribution.
papers.baselines: Standard U-Net training without regularisation.
papers.results: Entropy-based uncertainty anticipated segmentation errors in and out of distribution; maximum-entropy regularisation strengthened this correlation and improved calibration under domain shift.

heading: O3 - Data-efficient MRI and pathology models, fusion and federated learning

papers.title: nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation
papers.authors: Isensee F, Jaeger PF, Kohl SAA, Petersen J, Maier-Hein KH
papers.aim: To make segmentation work out-of-the-box on any new medical dataset without manual tuning.
papers.method: Rules that set preprocessing, network (2D/3D U-Net), training and post-processing automatically from dataset properties.
papers.result: Beat most specialised methods on 23 public datasets and many challenges.
papers.tools: U-Net, PyTorch, 3D CNN
papers.gap: Needs strong GPU and no uncertainty output by default.
papers.relation: Our main baseline for tumour segmentation on Sri Lankan MRI.
papers.limitations: Heavy compute, still needs good labels. Future: lighter and label-efficient versions.
papers.methodologyDetail: nnU-Net argues that the way a U-Net is configured and trained matters more than new architecture tricks, and automates all of it. Given any new dataset, it inspects voxel spacing, image size and modality, crops to the body or brain, resamples every case to the median spacing, and normalises intensities (z-score for MRI). It then sets up three candidates - a 2D U-Net, a 3D U-Net, and a 3D cascade that first segments a down-sampled image - choosing patch size, batch size and network depth to fit GPU memory. Each is trained from scratch with Dice plus cross-entropy loss, Adam at 3e-4, heavy augmentation, and a learning-rate and stopping schedule driven by loss moving averages, in five-fold cross-validation; the best configuration or ensemble is chosen automatically. On the Medical Segmentation Decathlon, including the BraTS-based brain tumour task (cross-validation Dice about 81/62/79 for the three tumour labels with the 3D U-Net), it won the challenge and its cross-validation scores held on the test set. For our PhD nnU-Net is the baseline and starting point for the MRI tumour segmentation agent, and its recipe is the default for training on small Sri Lankan datasets.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; automatic segmentation framework evaluated on the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (PDF read is the 2018 arXiv version; the 2021 Nature Methods version extends evaluation to 23 public datasets / 53 tasks).
papers.datasets: Medical Segmentation Decathlon phase 1: BrainTumour (BraTS multimodal MRI, 3 labels: oedema, non-enhancing, enhancing), Heart, Liver, Hippocampus, Prostate, Lung, Pancreas; held-out test sets on the challenge platform.
papers.preprocessing: Fully automatic: crop to non-zero region (reduces skull-stripped brain MRI size); resample all cases to the dataset's median voxel spacing (3rd-order spline for images, nearest neighbour for masks); intensity normalisation (z-score per case for MRI, global clipping and normalisation for CT); data augmentation on the fly (rotations, scaling, elastic deformation, gamma, mirroring).
papers.modelDetails: No new architecture: standard U-Net variants configured automatically from dataset properties - 2D U-Net, 3D U-Net, and a two-stage 3D U-Net Cascade (low-resolution then full-resolution) when the 3D patch cannot cover the image. Patch size, batch size (lower bound 2) and number of pooling layers chosen from image size and GPU memory. Final prediction may ensemble configurations chosen by cross-validation.
papers.training: Trained from scratch, five-fold cross-validation; loss = Dice + cross-entropy; Adam, initial learning rate 3e-4; epoch = 250 training batches; learning rate reduced by factor 5 if training-loss moving average does not improve by 5e-3 within 30 epochs; stop if validation-loss moving average does not improve by 5e-3 within 60 epochs.
papers.evaluation: Dice per foreground label in 5-fold cross-validation and on the held-out Decathlon test set (single submission).
papers.baselines: Comparison of its own configurations (2D, 3D, cascade) and with other Decathlon entries.
papers.results: Cross-validation Dice for BrainTumour labels 1/2/3: 2D U-Net 78.60 / 58.65 / 77.42; 3D U-Net 80.71 / 62.22 / 79.07. Heart 2D 91.36, 3D 92.45; Liver label 1 3D 94.11. Cross-validation results were recovered on the test set; only BrainTumour dropped on all labels, attributed to data/label shift typical of BraTS. nnU-Net ranked first in the Decathlon.
papers.statistics: Five-fold cross-validation means; single test submission.

papers.title: The RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS 2021 Benchmark on Brain Tumor Segmentation and Radiogenomic Classification
papers.authors: Baid U, Ghodasara S, Mohan S, Bilello M, Calabrese E, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To describe the BraTS 2021 dataset and tasks.
papers.method: Large multi-institution multi-parametric MRI (T1, T1Gd, T2, FLAIR) with expert labels for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour. Also MGMT prediction task.
papers.result: Around 2,000 glioma cases, the biggest public brain tumour MRI set at that time.
papers.tools: Multi-parametric MRI, standard preprocessing (skull strip, co-registration)
papers.gap: Mostly gliomas from Western centres, pre-processed and standardised.
papers.relation: Public pre-training and benchmark set before we use local data. Also shows the gap: our data is not standardised.
papers.limitations: Population and scanner bias. Future: more tumour types and regions.
papers.methodologyDetail: BraTS 2021 assembled about 2,000 pre-operative glioma MRI scans (T1, contrast T1, T2 and FLAIR) from many institutions and scanners. Every scan goes through the same public pipeline: conversion to NIfTI (which removes patient identifiers), registration to the SRI24 brain template, resampling to 1 mm voxels and deep-learning skull stripping. Tumour sub-regions were first drawn automatically by fusing earlier winning algorithms, then corrected by trained annotators and approved by expert neuroradiologists, giving labels for enhancing tumour, necrotic core and oedema. A second task gives MGMT promoter methylation status from laboratory testing of the resected tissue. Data are split into training (with labels), validation (labels hidden) and a hidden test set; segmentation is scored with Dice and 95% Hausdorff distance on enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour. For our PhD this defines the public development dataset, the preprocessing pipeline to apply to Sri Lankan scans so models transfer, and the standard metrics for the segmentation agent.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge / benchmark description paper (RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS 2021): dataset creation, annotation protocol and evaluation framework for two tasks.
papers.datasets: About 2,000 multi-institutional glioma cases (up from 660 in earlier BraTS) with pre-operative mpMRI: native T1, post-contrast T1 (T1Gd), T2, T2-FLAIR, from different scanners and protocols. Task 1: tumour sub-region segmentation (enhancing tumour, tumour core, whole tumour). Task 2: prediction of MGMT promoter methylation status (from laboratory assessment of surgical specimens). Split into training (labels given), validation (no labels) and hidden test sets.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS pipeline (public in CaPTk and the FeTS tool): DICOM to NIfTI (removes PHI), co-registration to SRI24 anatomical template, resampling to 1 mm^3 isotropic, deep-learning skull stripping (shape-prior, sequence-agnostic). Task 1 volumes pre-segmented by STAPLE fusion of earlier top BraTS algorithms, then manually refined by annotators and approved by expert neuroradiologists.
papers.modelDetails: Not a model paper. Defines labels: GD-enhancing tumour, peritumoural oedema/invaded tissue, necrotic tumour core; evaluated regions ET, TC (ET + necrosis), WT (TC + oedema).
papers.training: Rules: participants may not use extra public/private data or pre-trained models for the ranked submission (allowed only for separate publications).
papers.evaluation: Task 1: Dice similarity coefficient and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance per region, plus sensitivity/specificity; ranking across cases. Task 2: MGMT classification evaluated on Kaggle (AUC). Platforms: Synapse (Task 1) and Kaggle (Task 2); $60,000 prizes.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (benchmark definition).
papers.results: Not applicable for model results; provides the largest public annotated glioma mpMRI dataset (~2,000 cases) and a standard pipeline and metrics.
papers.statistics: Ranking scheme with case-wise ranks across metrics (described in challenge documentation).
papers.availability: Data: https://www.synapse.org/brats (registration); preprocessing in CaPTk / FeTS tool.

papers.title: Swin UNETR: Swin Transformers for Semantic Segmentation of Brain Tumors in MRI Images
papers.authors: Hatamizadeh A, Nath V, Tang Y, Yang D, Roth HR, Xu D
papers.aim: To use a Swin transformer encoder for 3D brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: Swin transformer encoder with shifted windows, CNN decoder, skip connections. Trained on BraTS 2021.
papers.result: Among the top methods in BraTS 2021 validation.
papers.tools: Swin Transformer, MONAI, PyTorch
papers.gap: Transformers usually need lots of data.
papers.relation: Candidate model for our MRI agent, compared with nnU-Net.
papers.limitations: Heavy model, small data risk. Future: pretraining.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors adapt the Swin Transformer to 3D brain MRI segmentation. The four MRI sequences are split into small 3D patches, and a hierarchical transformer computes self-attention inside shifted local windows at four scales; these features are passed through skip connections to a convolutional decoder that outputs enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour maps. Training uses BraTS 2021's 1,251 cases in five-fold cross-validation with 128-cube random crops, flips and intensity augmentation, soft Dice loss, learning rate 8e-4, on eight V100 GPUs in MONAI. On identical folds it slightly beat nnU-Net, SegResNet and TransBTS (average Dice 0.913 vs 0.908 for nnU-Net). For our PhD Swin UNETR is the main transformer alternative to nnU-Net for the segmentation agent, especially when combined with self-supervised pre-training (O3-P04) for small local datasets.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper evaluated by five-fold cross-validation on BraTS 2021 and on the BraTS 2021 challenge validation/test sets.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2021 training set (1,251 multi-parametric MRI cases: T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR) for five-fold cross-validation; BraTS 2021 validation and test leaderboards.
papers.preprocessing: BraTS-preprocessed volumes; intensities normalised to zero mean, unit SD over non-zero voxels; random 128x128x128 patches; random mirror flips (p = 0.5 per axis); random intensity scaling/shifting.
papers.modelDetails: Swin UNETR: 3D Swin Transformer encoder (shifted-window self-attention, hierarchical features at 4 resolutions, patch size 2, window size 7) connected by skip connections to a CNN decoder (U-Net style). Input: 4 MRI channels; output: ET, TC, WT sigmoid maps. Configurations, parameters and FLOPs in Table 1.
papers.training: PyTorch + MONAI on a DGX-1 with 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs; soft Dice loss; learning rate 0.0008 (AdamW, cosine schedule); five-fold cross-validation; ensemble of fold models for submission.
papers.evaluation: Dice per region (ET, WT, TC) and 95% Hausdorff distance; comparison with nnU-Net, SegResNet and TransBTS under the same folds.
papers.baselines: nnU-Net, SegResNet, TransBTS.
papers.results: Five-fold mean Dice (ET / WT / TC / average): Swin UNETR 0.891 / 0.933 / 0.917 / 0.913; nnU-Net 0.883 / 0.927 / 0.913 / 0.908; SegResNet 0.883 / 0.927 / 0.913 / 0.907; TransBTS 0.868 / 0.911 / 0.898 / 0.891. Swin UNETR ranked among the top teams in the BraTS 2021 validation phase.
papers.statistics: Per-fold and average Dice; no formal significance tests.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Pre-Training of Swin Transformers for 3D Medical Image Analysis
papers.authors: Tang Y, Yang D, Li W, Roth HR, Landman B, Xu D, Nath V, Hatamizadeh A
papers.aim: To pretrain 3D models on unlabelled scans so less labelled data is needed later.
papers.method: Self-supervised tasks: masked volume inpainting, rotation prediction and contrastive coding, on about 5,000 unlabelled CT scans.
papers.result: State-of-the-art results on BTCV and Medical Segmentation Decathlon after fine-tuning.
papers.tools: Swin UNETR, self-supervised learning, MONAI
papers.gap: Pretrained on CT, transfer to brain MRI not shown well.
papers.relation: Our labelled Sri Lankan data will be small. Self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled local MRI is a key option.
papers.limitations: Big compute for pretraining. Future: pretraining on MRI.
papers.methodologyDetail: Because labelled 3D medical data are scarce, the authors pre-train a 3D Swin Transformer encoder on 5,050 unlabelled CT scans using three self-supervised tasks at once: fill in randomly masked 3D regions (30% dropped), predict how a sub-volume was rotated, and pull together embeddings of two augmented views of the same sub-volume while pushing apart others. Pre-training runs 450K iterations with AdamW (lr 4e-4, warm-up cosine schedule, batch 4 per GPU on 96-cube patches). The pre-trained encoder is then joined to a convolutional decoder and fine-tuned with five-fold cross-validation on BTCV abdominal organs and on all ten Medical Segmentation Decathlon tasks, with fold ensembles for the final result. It topped both public leaderboards, and ablations show pre-training helps most with little labelled data. For our PhD this is the template for data-efficient learning: pre-train on unlabelled Sri Lankan MRI (and public scans) with these proxy tasks, then fine-tune the segmentation agent on the few labelled local cases.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper: large-scale self-supervised pre-training on unlabelled CT, fine-tuned and evaluated on public segmentation benchmarks.
papers.datasets: Pre-training: 5,050 unlabelled CT volumes from public datasets (multiple body regions). Fine-tuning: BTCV multi-organ abdominal CT (30 labelled scans, 13 organs) and Medical Segmentation Decathlon (10 tasks, CT and MRI, including brain tumour).
papers.preprocessing: Dataset-specific preprocessing in supplementary material; 96x96x96 patches for pre-training.
papers.modelDetails: Swin UNETR encoder (3D Swin Transformer, hierarchical shifted windows, 4 resolutions) pre-trained with three proxy tasks: masked volume inpainting (30% of regions dropped), 3D image rotation prediction (0/90/180/270 degrees) and 3D contrastive coding (embedding size 512). After pre-training, a CNN decoder is attached and the network fine-tuned for segmentation.
papers.training: Pre-training: AdamW, warm-up cosine scheduler 500 iterations, batch 4 per GPU, 96^3 patches, initial learning rate 4e-4, momentum 0.9, decay 1e-5, 450K iterations; PyTorch + MONAI. Fine-tuning: five-fold cross-validation, best model per fold, ensemble of folds for final predictions.
papers.evaluation: Dice and Normalised Surface Distance (NSD / surface Dice) on BTCV and MSD public leaderboards; ablations on pre-training tasks and data size.
papers.baselines: nnU-Net, UNETR, TransBTS, other leaderboard entries; Swin UNETR without pre-training.
papers.results: State-of-the-art on the BTCV leaderboard (best average Dice among submissions) and first place on the MSD public test leaderboard overall; pre-training improved performance, especially with fewer labelled training cases (exact per-task values in Tables 1-2).

papers.title: Segment Anything in Medical Images (MedSAM)
papers.authors: Ma J, He Y, Li F, Han L, You C, Wang B
papers.aim: To build one promptable segmentation model for many medical image types.
papers.method: Fine-tuned Segment Anything on over 1.5 million medical image-mask pairs across 10 modalities. User gives a bounding box.
papers.result: Better than SAM and comparable or better than specialist models on many internal and external tests.
papers.tools: SAM, ViT, box prompts
papers.gap: 2D slices, needs a box prompt, weaker on very small or unclear edges.
papers.relation: Clinician can draw a box and correct the result. Good for human-in-the-loop correction and fast labelling of local data.
papers.limitations: Not 3D native. Future: 3D and text prompts.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors build a general medical segmentation model by fine-tuning Meta's Segment Anything Model on more than 1.5 million image-mask pairs from ten modalities. Data are split by scan, video or slide to avoid leakage, images are resized to 1024x1024, and each training example is a bounding box around the target with its mask. Training uses AdamW (lr 1e-4) for 150 epochs on 20 A100 GPUs without augmentation. MedSAM is compared with the original SAM and with 20 specialist U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models on 86 internal and 60 external tasks, using Dice and surface distance. It beats SAM everywhere and matches or exceeds specialists, including on unseen modalities. For our PhD MedSAM is a candidate for the anatomical reconstruction and surgical-planning agent: a clinician or the detection agent draws a box around a tumour or structure at risk, and MedSAM produces the outline, which helps with structures not labelled in BraTS.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development (fine-tuning SAM on a very large medical dataset) with internal and external validation across many tasks.
papers.datasets: 1,570,263 medical image-mask pairs covering 10 modalities (CT, MRI, chest X-ray, dermoscopy, endoscopy, ultrasound, mammography, OCT, pathology, and more), over 30 cancer types and many protocols; 86 internal validation tasks and 60 external validation tasks (including brain tumour MRI).
papers.preprocessing: Random 80/10/10 split into training, tuning and validation at the 3D scan / video level (no leakage across slices or frames); whole-slide images split by slide then tiled into 1024x1024 patches; images resized to 1024x1024; bounding-box prompts derived from masks.
papers.modelDetails: MedSAM = Segment Anything Model (ViT-B image encoder, prompt encoder, mask decoder) fine-tuned for medical images with bounding-box prompts; the user (or another agent) gives a box around the target and MedSAM outputs the mask.
papers.training: AdamW, learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 0.01, global batch 160, no data augmentation, 150 epochs on 20 A100 (80 GB) GPUs; last checkpoint used. Comparison specialist models: 20 modality-specific U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and Normalised Surface Distance (NSD) per task, median and IQR; ranking across 86 internal and 60 external tasks; qualitative examples (liver, brain, breast cancer, polyps).
papers.baselines: Original SAM; specialist U-Net and DeepLabV3+ trained per modality.
papers.results: MedSAM ranked first on most internal tasks and outperformed SAM across tasks, on par with or better than specialist models; e.g. nasopharynx cancer median DSC 87.8% (IQR 85.0-91.4%), +52.3 points over SAM, +15.5 over U-Net, +22.7 over DeepLabV3+; up to 10% better on unseen modalities (abdomen T1 in/out-phase).
papers.statistics: Median and IQR of DSC/NSD; rank frequency analysis; significance tests reported in the paper.

papers.title: Attention-based Deep Multiple Instance Learning
papers.authors: Ilse M, Tomczak JM, Welling M
papers.aim: To learn from bag-level labels only (e.g. one label per slide) and still find important instances.
papers.method: Attention pooling over instance features, trained end-to-end.
papers.result: Matched or beat other MIL methods and gives attention maps showing important patches (tested on histopathology data).
papers.tools: CNN, attention pooling
papers.gap: Assumes instances are independent.
papers.relation: Biopsy slides will have only slide-level diagnosis. This is the basic method for our pathology agent.
papers.limitations: Small datasets in paper. Future: larger WSI.
papers.methodologyDetail: In pathology a whole slide often has one label while only a few regions show the disease. The authors treat each image as a bag of patches and learn a network that embeds every patch, then combines them with a learned attention-weighted average, so patches that matter get high weights. The bag embedding goes to a classifier trained only with bag labels. They test on standard MIL benchmarks, on synthetic bags of MNIST digits, and on breast and colon histology where each image is split into small patches around nuclei. Attention pooling gave the best colon cancer results (accuracy 0.904, AUC 0.968) and its weights highlighted the epithelial patches that define the label. For our PhD attention-based MIL is the core building block for the biopsy-slide agent: it learns from slide-level diagnoses (which hospitals have) rather than pixel annotations, and its attention map shows the pathologist which regions drove the AI's decision.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with experiments on classical multiple-instance learning (MIL) benchmarks, MNIST-bags and two histopathology datasets.
papers.datasets: Classical MIL: MUSK1, MUSK2, FOX, TIGER, ELEPHANT. MNIST-bags: bags of random numbers of 28x28 MNIST digits (positive if any '9'). Histopathology: Breast Cancer (UCSB) and Colon Cancer (H&E images; 27x27 patches centred on marked nuclei; positive if epithelial cells present).
papers.preprocessing: Histology images split into 27x27 (colon) or 32x32 patches as instances; augmentation with rotations, flips and colour jitter (as described in the paper).
papers.modelDetails: Bag-level MIL with a neural network: instance embeddings from a CNN, combined by attention-based pooling z = sum_k a_k h_k, where weights a_k come from a small network (tanh, or gated tanh x sigmoid). The attention weights show which instances (patches) drive the bag label. Compared with instance-level max/mean pooling and embedding-level max/mean pooling.
papers.training: Adam optimiser; experiments repeated 5 times; settings per dataset in the appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy (classical MIL); accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for histopathology (mean +/- SEM over 5 runs); attention heatmaps vs ground-truth positive patches.
papers.baselines: mi-SVM, MI-SVM, MI-Kernel, EM-DD, mi-Graph, miVLAD, miFV; instance+max/mean and embedding+max/mean pooling networks.
papers.results: Colon Cancer: Attention accuracy 0.904 +/- 0.011, AUC 0.968 +/- 0.009; Gated-Attention accuracy 0.898, AUC 0.968; best pooling baseline embedding+mean accuracy 0.860, AUC 0.940; instance+max 0.842 / 0.914. Competitive with best methods on classical MIL datasets; attention heatmaps highlighted epithelial patches.

papers.title: Data-efficient and weakly supervised computational pathology on whole-slide images (CLAM)
papers.authors: Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Chen TY, Chen RJ, Barbieri M, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To classify whole slides using only slide labels and small datasets.
papers.method: Attention MIL with clustering constraint on top of frozen pretrained features. Tested on renal cancer subtyping, lung cancer subtyping and lymph node metastasis.
papers.result: High AUC with limited labels, worked on independent test sets and even on smartphone microscopy images. Gives interpretable heatmaps.
papers.tools: ResNet-50 features, attention MIL, PyTorch, OpenSlide
papers.gap: Not tested on brain tumours. Feature extractor from ImageNet.
papers.relation: Strong baseline for our pathology agent on small Sri Lankan biopsy sets.
papers.limitations: Scanner/stain differences. Future: better features.
papers.methodologyDetail: CLAM classifies whole-slide images using only the slide's diagnosis, with no hand-drawn regions. Each slide is segmented into tissue, cut into 256-pixel patches, and every patch is turned once into a 1,024-number feature vector by an ImageNet ResNet50. An attention network then scores how important each patch is for each class and combines patches into a slide representation for the final prediction; an extra clustering loss teaches the model to separate highly attended (diagnostic) patches from weakly attended ones, which makes learning more data-efficient. Trained with 10-fold cross-validation on TCGA kidney and lung and Camelyon lymph-node slides, it reached AUCs of 0.95-0.99, kept good performance with fewer training slides, transferred from resections to biopsies, and even worked on photos taken through a microscope with a smartphone (AUC 0.87-0.92). Attention heatmaps show which areas drove the decision. For our PhD CLAM is the baseline for the biopsy-slide agent: it fits small Sri Lankan slide collections with only diagnosis labels, its heatmaps support pathologist review, and the smartphone result is relevant where slide scanners are scarce.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with public datasets and independent test cohorts (biopsies, smartphone microscopy images).
papers.datasets: TCGA-Kidney (3-class RCC subtyping: papillary, chromophobe, clear cell); TCGA + CPTAC Lung (NSCLC: adenocarcinoma vs squamous); Camelyon16 + Camelyon17 (breast cancer lymph-node metastasis); independent in-house test cohorts including biopsy WSIs and cellphone-captured microscopy fields of view (lung and kidney CPI datasets).
papers.preprocessing: Tissue segmentation of each WSI; 256x256 patches extracted from tissue regions (20x for kidney/lung, 40x for Camelyon); each patch encoded once by an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 (truncated after the 3rd residual block, adaptive mean pooling) into a 1,024-dimensional feature vector.
papers.modelDetails: CLAM (Clustering-constrained Attention MIL): attention network ranks every patch for each class and attention-pools patch features into a slide representation (multi-branch, one attention branch per class); instance-level clustering on strongly vs weakly attended patches adds pseudo-label supervision to refine the feature space; attention scores produce interpretable heatmaps.
papers.training: Slide-level labels only; 10-fold Monte Carlo cross-validation; features pre-extracted so thousands of WSIs train in hours; tests with systematically reduced training label fractions to show data efficiency.
papers.evaluation: Macro-averaged one-vs-rest AUC (mean over folds) on test sets; independent cohort AUC; performance vs fraction of training data; attention heatmaps vs pathologist annotations.
papers.baselines: Standard MIL (max pooling), attention MIL (Ilse et al.), other weakly supervised WSI methods.
papers.results: Test AUC: RCC 3-class 0.991; NSCLC subtyping 0.956; Camelyon metastasis 0.953 (40x). Smartphone microscopy: lung average AUC 0.873 (best 0.899), kidney 0.921 (best 0.958). Strong performance retained with reduced training labels; models trained on resections applied directly to biopsies.
papers.statistics: Mean test AUC across 10 folds with confidence intervals in figures.

papers.title: Towards a general-purpose foundation model for computational pathology (UNI)
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Ding T, Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Jaume G, et al., Mahmood F
papers.aim: To pretrain one strong pathology feature model useful for many tasks.
papers.method: Self-supervised (DINOv2) training on over 100 million tissue patches from about 100,000 slides, tested on 34 tasks.
papers.result: Better than earlier pathology encoders on most tasks, including rare cancer classification and few-shot learning.
papers.tools: ViT-Large, DINOv2, self-supervised learning
papers.gap: Trained on US hospital data. Licence and compute limits.
papers.relation: Feature extractor for our pathology agent so we need fewer local labels.
papers.limitations: Bias to source data, big model. Future: multimodal.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors pre-train a large Vision Transformer on more than 100 million H&E tissue patches from about 100,000 slides covering 20 tissue types, using the DINOv2 self-supervised method, so no labels are needed. The resulting encoder, UNI, is then frozen and used to turn patches into features for 33 downstream tasks, from region classification and segmentation to whole-slide diagnosis with attention-based MIL, and compared with ImageNet and earlier pathology encoders, including in few-shot settings. On brain tumour slides from the EBRAINS atlas and TCGA it reached 85.6% balanced accuracy for IDH1 mutation and 88.3% for 12-class tumour typing, beating the next best encoder, and it generally needs fewer labels. For our PhD UNI (or a similar foundation encoder) is the feature extractor for the pathology agent, so that a small number of labelled Sri Lankan neuropathology slides can train an accurate CLAM/ABMIL head.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development (self-supervised pre-training) with evaluation on 33-34 clinical computational pathology tasks.
papers.datasets: Pre-training: Mass-100K - over 100 million tissue patches from 100,426 diagnostic H&E WSIs across 20 major tissue types (MGH, Brigham and Women's Hospital, GTEx). Evaluation: ROI- and slide-level tasks including brain tumour tasks from the EBRAINS Digital Tumor Atlas and TCGA-GBMLGG (glioma IDH1 mutation, 5-class histomolecular subtyping, 12-class and 30-class brain tumour subtyping).
papers.preprocessing: Tissue patches extracted from WSIs at multiple magnifications for pre-training; downstream: patch features extracted with the frozen encoder, then slide-level ABMIL or linear probing.
papers.modelDetails: UNI: Vision Transformer Large (ViT-L) pre-trained with DINOv2 self-supervised learning (student-teacher distillation + masked image modelling). Used as a frozen feature extractor for ROI classification, segmentation, retrieval, and slide-level weakly/semi-supervised learning (attention-based MIL).
papers.training: DINOv2 pre-training on Mass-100K (details in Online Methods); downstream linear probes, KNN and ABMIL trained on task data with few-shot experiments.
papers.evaluation: Balanced accuracy, AUC, weighted F1 across 33 tasks; few-shot label efficiency; comparisons with ResNet-50 (ImageNet), CTransPath and REMEDIS.
papers.baselines: ImageNet ResNet-50, CTransPath, REMEDIS (other pathology encoders).
papers.results: Brain tumour tasks (balanced accuracy): IDH1 mutation 85.6%, 5-class histomolecular subtyping 56.2%, 12-class subtyping 88.3%, 30-class subtyping 67.5%, outperforming the next best model (CTransPath or REMEDIS) (e.g. +2.0%, p = 0.076, on IDH1). UNI outperformed baselines on most of the 33 tasks and showed strong few-shot (label-efficient) performance and resolution-agnostic behaviour.
papers.statistics: Bootstrapped confidence intervals and p-values for comparisons.
papers.availability: Model: https://github.com/mahmoodlab/UNI (Hugging Face weights, research licence)

papers.title: Pathomic Fusion: An Integrated Framework for Fusing Histopathology and Genomic Features for Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Lu MY, Wang J, Williamson DFK, Rodig SJ, Lindeman NI, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To combine histology images and molecular data for glioma grading and survival.
papers.method: CNN and graph network features from histology fused with genomic features using gated attention and Kronecker product.
papers.result: Fusion did better than single-source models and the WHO 2016 grading on TCGA glioma and kidney cancer.
papers.tools: CNN, GCN, SNN, Kronecker fusion
papers.gap: Assumes all data sources are present for every patient.
papers.relation: Our combined diagnosis agent fuses imaging, pathology and lab markers. We need it to work when markers are missing.
papers.limitations: TCGA data only. Future: handle missing modalities.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathomic Fusion combines what a pathologist sees with molecular data. For 769 TCGA glioma patients it takes stain-normalised H&E regions, builds three representations - CNN image features, a graph of segmented nuclei processed by a graph convolutional network, and a network over 320 genomic features (copy number, IDH mutation, top RNA-Seq genes) - and fuses them: a gating attention step decides how much each modality contributes, then a Kronecker product captures interactions between all pairs (or triplets) of features. The fused vector predicts survival (Cox loss) and WHO grade, trained with 15-fold cross-validation and compared with Cox models on grade/subtype and single-modality networks. The tri-modal model reached c-Index 0.826 versus 0.777 for grade plus molecular subtype and 0.792 for histology alone, and produced 'digital grades' that stratified survival like WHO molecular classes. For our PhD this is the design reference for the marker-fusion agent: combine slide features with whatever markers are available, with gating so missing or weak modalities count less.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multimodal method study on TCGA glioma and renal cancer cohorts with 15-fold cross-validation.
papers.datasets: TCGA-GBMLGG (astrocytomas and glioblastomas): 1,505 H&E ROIs (1024x1024) from 769 patients with 320 genomic features (79 CNV, 1 mutation status, 240 RNA-Seq genes; ~40% missing RNA-Seq); outcomes: survival and WHO grade (II/III/IV). TCGA-KIRC (clear cell renal cell carcinoma): 417 patients, 3 x 512x512 40x ROIs each (1,251 images) with 357 genomic features.
papers.preprocessing: Sparse stain normalisation of ROIs to a standard H&E image; cell graph construction from nuclei segmentation for the GCN branch; genomic features normalised.
papers.modelDetails: Three unimodal networks: histology CNN (VGG19 features), cell-graph GCN (graph convolution on nuclei graphs), genomic self-normalising network (SNN). Fusion: gating-based attention controls each modality's expressiveness, then Kronecker product models pairwise (or three-way) feature interactions; output used for survival (Cox loss) and grade classification. Integrated gradients give modality attribution.
papers.training: 15-fold cross-validation (480 models in ablations); unimodal networks pre-trained then fused; details in appendix.
papers.evaluation: Concordance index (c-Index) for survival; AUC, average precision, micro F1 and Grade IV F1 for grading; Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank test for digital grades (33/66/100 percentile for glioma).
papers.baselines: Cox models on age+gender, grade, molecular subtype; histology CNN; histology GCN; genomic SNN; SCNN and GSCNN (Mobadersany et al.).
papers.results: Glioma c-Index: Cox (grade + molecular subtype) 0.777; histology CNN 0.792; genomic SNN 0.808; GSCNN 0.781; Pathomic Fusion GCN x SNN 0.812, CNN x SNN 0.820, CNN x GCN x SNN 0.826 +/- 0.009 (all p < 0.05). CCRCC: Cox (grade) 0.675, histology CNN 0.671, genomic SNN 0.684, Pathomic Fusion higher (Table II). Digital grades stratified survival similar to WHO molecular subtypes and separated intermediate vs high risk better than histology alone.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- SD over 15 folds; p < 0.05; log-rank tests.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data (FedAvg)
papers.authors: McMahan HB, Moore E, Ramage D, Hampson S, Aguera y Arcas B
papers.aim: To train a shared model without collecting raw data in one place.
papers.method: Federated Averaging: each client trains locally for some steps, server averages the weights.
papers.result: Needed far fewer communication rounds than synchronised SGD, and worked with non-IID data in their tests.
papers.tools: CNN, LSTM, MNIST, Shakespeare
papers.gap: Performance drops with strong data differences between clients.
papers.relation: The basic federation method we start with across hospitals.
papers.limitations: No privacy guarantee alone. Future: heterogeneity handling.
papers.methodologyDetail: Federated averaging trains one model across many devices or institutions without moving their data. In each round the server sends the current model to a random fraction of clients; each client trains it for a few epochs on its own data with small batches, and the server averages the returned models, weighting each by how much data the client has. The authors compare this with sending one gradient per round (FedSGD) on MNIST split across 100 clients (including a harsh split where each client sees only two digits), CIFAR-10, and Shakespeare and social-network text where each user is a client. More local computation per round (E = 5-20 epochs, batch 10) reduced communication rounds by up to 35x on MNIST and 95x on Shakespeare, even with non-IID data. For our PhD FedAvg is the starting algorithm for training the MRI and pathology agents across Sri Lankan hospitals without sharing patient data, with the number of local epochs and batch size as the key settings.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper introducing federated averaging, with experiments on image and language tasks partitioned across simulated clients.
papers.datasets: MNIST (100 clients; IID and pathological non-IID partitions - each client gets 2 digit classes), CIFAR-10, Shakespeare text (one client per speaking role, naturally non-IID), large-scale social network posts for next-word prediction.
papers.preprocessing: Data partitioned across clients IID or non-IID; unbalanced client sizes in language tasks.
papers.modelDetails: FederatedAveraging (FedAvg): each round, a fraction C of clients is selected; each client runs E local epochs of SGD with minibatch size B on its own data starting from the global model; the server averages client models weighted by number of samples n_k / n. FedSGD (E = 1, B = infinity) is the baseline. Models: 2-layer MLP (2NN) and CNN for MNIST, CNN for CIFAR, LSTM for Shakespeare and next-word prediction.
papers.training: Grid over C (client fraction), E (local epochs) and B (local batch); expected local updates per round u = nE/(KB); learning rates tuned per setting.
papers.evaluation: Number of communication rounds needed to reach a target test accuracy (e.g. 99% MNIST CNN, 54% Shakespeare LSTM); speed-up vs FedSGD.
papers.baselines: FedSGD (large-batch synchronous SGD across clients).
papers.results: MNIST CNN to 99%: FedSGD 626 rounds (IID) / 483 (non-IID); FedAvg E = 20, B = 10 needed 18 rounds (34.8x faster) IID and 173 (2.8x) non-IID; E = 5, B = 10: 20 / 229 rounds. Shakespeare LSTM to 54%: FedSGD 2,488 / 3,906 rounds; FedAvg E = 5, B = 10: 192 (13x) / 41 (95.3x). FedAvg was robust to unbalanced and non-IID data and cut communication by 10-100x.
papers.availability: Algorithm widely implemented (e.g. Flower, NVFlare, OpenFL).

papers.title: Federated Optimization in Heterogeneous Networks (FedProx)
papers.authors: Li T, Sahu AK, Zaheer M, Sanjabi M, Talwalkar A, Smith V
papers.aim: To make federated training stable when clients have very different data and compute.
papers.method: Adds a proximal term so local models do not drift too far from the global model, and allows partial work from clients.
papers.result: More stable convergence and better accuracy than FedAvg in heterogeneous settings (around 22% average absolute gain in very heterogeneous settings).
papers.tools: Federated optimisation, LEAF benchmarks
papers.gap: Extra hyper-parameter to tune.
papers.relation: Our case is a few hospitals with small and very different cohorts. FedProx is a must-try baseline.
papers.limitations: Not medical data. Future: personalisation.
papers.methodologyDetail: FedAvg assumes every client does the same amount of local work and that client data are similar; in practice some clients are slow and data differ, which makes training unstable. FedProx keeps FedAvg's structure but adds a proximal penalty that stops each client's model drifting too far from the current global model, and it accepts whatever partial work slow clients return instead of discarding them. The authors prove convergence under heterogeneity and test on synthetic data with tunable differences between devices, on MNIST spread over 1,000 devices that each hold only two digits, and on FEMNIST, Shakespeare and Sent140, simulating up to 90% stragglers. FedProx trains more stably and reaches higher accuracy than FedAvg in heterogeneous settings (about 22 points higher on average with many stragglers). For our PhD, with a few Sri Lankan hospitals of unequal size, compute and scanner mix, FedProx is the standard alternative to FedAvg to compare in federated training of the agents.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with convergence theory and experiments on synthetic and real federated benchmarks with statistical and systems heterogeneity.
papers.datasets: Synthetic federated data with controlled heterogeneity (Synthetic(alpha, beta)); MNIST across 1,000 devices (each with 2 digits, power-law sizes) with multinomial logistic regression; FEMNIST (62-class Federated Extended MNIST); Shakespeare next-character prediction; Sent140 sentiment (tweets per user).
papers.preprocessing: Non-IID partitions per device; systems heterogeneity simulated by giving devices different amounts of local work (stragglers doing fewer epochs).
papers.modelDetails: FedProx = FedAvg plus a proximal term (mu/2) ||w - w_t||^2 in each client's local objective, which keeps local models close to the global model and allows partial (inexact) local updates from stragglers to be aggregated rather than dropped. mu tuned from a small set (e.g. 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1).
papers.training: Local SGD with E local epochs; fraction of devices per round; 0%, 50% or 90% stragglers; settings in Appendix C; code public.
papers.evaluation: Training loss and test accuracy vs communication rounds; stability under increasing heterogeneity and stragglers.
papers.baselines: FedAvg (dropping stragglers); FedProx with mu = 0.
papers.results: Under high systems heterogeneity (90% stragglers) FedProx improved absolute test accuracy by about 22% on average over FedAvg across realistic datasets, and converged more stably as statistical heterogeneity increased (curves in figures).
papers.statistics: Not reported beyond curves over repeated runs.

papers.title: FedBN: Federated Learning on Non-IID Features via Local Batch Normalization
papers.authors: Li X, Jiang M, Zhang X, Kamp M, Dou Q
papers.aim: To handle feature shift between clients, like different scanners.
papers.method: Keep batch normalisation layers local at each client and only average the other weights.
papers.result: Better than FedAvg and FedProx on feature-shift benchmarks, including a medical imaging one.
papers.tools: CNN, batch normalisation, federated learning
papers.gap: Only for models with BN, and a new site needs some local data.
papers.relation: Scanner and protocol differences between Sri Lankan hospitals are exactly this feature shift.
papers.limitations: Small number of clients tested. Future: other normalisation types.
papers.methodologyDetail: When hospitals use different scanners, the same anatomy looks different in each site's images - a 'feature shift'. FedBN handles this with one change to FedAvg: batch-normalisation layers stay local to each client, so each site normalises features with its own statistics, while all other weights are shared and averaged. The authors prove it converges faster than FedAvg under feature shift, and test on digit datasets from different sources, Office-Caltech and DomainNet image domains, and real fMRI data from four ABIDE institutions, each treated as a client, over five trials. FedBN beat FedAvg, FedProx and training alone on most clients (e.g. DSLR 83.1% vs 66.9% FedAvg; NYU ABIDE 65.6% vs 62.7%). For our PhD FedBN is a simple, strong choice for federated MRI training across Sri Lankan hospitals whose scanners and protocols differ, and it lets each site keep site-specific normalisation.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with theory (convergence under feature shift) and experiments on benchmark and real medical multi-site data.
papers.datasets: Digits-type benchmark (MNIST, SVHN, USPS, SynthDigits, MNIST-M as clients); Office-Caltech 10 (Amazon, Caltech, DSLR, WebCam); DomainNet (Clipart, Infograph, Painting, Quickdraw, Real, Sketch); ABIDE I autism fMRI from medical institutions (NYU, USM, UM, UCLA) as clients.
papers.preprocessing: Each client = one domain or institution (feature-shift non-IID: same labels, different image appearance/scanner); 5-trial runs.
papers.modelDetails: FedBN: like FedAvg but batch-normalisation layers are kept local - each client keeps its own BN statistics and parameters, which are not averaged; all other layers are aggregated. Handles feature shift such as different scanners or equipment.
papers.training: Local epochs per round as in FedAvg; same architecture across methods (AlexNet-style CNN for images; MLP/CNN for ABIDE); 5 trials.
papers.evaluation: Test accuracy per client (mean and SD over 5 trials); convergence speed; effect of number of clients and local epochs.
papers.baselines: SingleSet (each client trains alone), FedAvg, FedProx.
papers.results: Office-Caltech accuracy (A / C / D / W): SingleSet 54.9 / 40.2 / 78.7 / 86.4; FedAvg 54.1 / 44.8 / 66.9 / 85.1; FedProx 54.2 / 44.5 / 65.0 / 84.4; FedBN 63.0 / 45.3 / 83.1 / 90.5. DomainNet: FedBN best on most domains (e.g. Clipart 51.2 vs 48.8 FedAvg). ABIDE: FedBN best at NYU (65.6 vs 62.7 FedAvg) and competitive at other sites.

papers.title: Federated learning in medicine: facilitating multi-institutional collaborations without sharing patient data
papers.authors: Sheller MJ, Edwards B, Reina GA, Martin J, Pati S, Kotrotsou A, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To check if federated learning can match central training for brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: BraTS data split by institution, compared federated learning with institutional incremental and cyclic training, and with data-sharing.
papers.result: Federated model reached about 99% of the quality of the centrally trained model, better than the other collaborative methods.
papers.tools: U-Net, BraTS, federated averaging
papers.gap: Simulated federation on public data, not real hospitals.
papers.relation: Direct proof that FL works for brain tumour MRI. Our job is to show it with a few small real Sri Lankan sites.
papers.limitations: Simulated sites. Future: real deployment.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors simulate a federation of 10 hospitals by splitting BraTS glioma MRI by the institution each scan came from, then train the same 3D U-Net for whole-tumour segmentation in several ways: each hospital alone, all data pooled centrally, federated learning where every hospital trains locally and updates are averaged each round, and simpler schemes that pass the model from hospital to hospital once or in cycles. They test on held-out BraTS data, on two institutions outside the federation (WashU and MD Anderson), and with each hospital held out in turn. Federated learning reached Dice 0.858 versus 0.863 for pooled data (99% of its quality) and far above the single-hospital average of 0.732, and it generalised to outside institutions almost as well as pooling; passing models sequentially was worse. For our PhD this is the key evidence that federating a few Sri Lankan hospitals can approach centralised performance without sharing patient scans, and it shows how to evaluate: local validation, held-out sites and leave-one-site-out.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-institution simulation study of federated learning for brain tumour segmentation (BraTS data split by originating institution), with comparison to centralised training and other collaborative approaches.
papers.datasets: BraTS glioma mpMRI split into the 10 originating institutions (Original Institution group); external out-of-federation test data from other institutions (e.g. WashU, MD Anderson Cancer Center) and a held-out BraTS test set (BTest); leave-one-institution-out (LOO) evaluation.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing (co-registration, 1 mm resampling, skull stripping); each institution's data kept as a separate client.
papers.modelDetails: 3D U-Net style segmentation network (whole tumour); collaborative schemes compared: centralised data sharing (CDS), federated learning (FedAvg-type, all institutions train each round), institutional incremental learning (IIL, model passed institution to institution once) and cyclic IIL (CIIL, repeated cycles).
papers.training: Same network and hyper-parameters across schemes; multiple experimental runs; details in supplementary information.
papers.evaluation: Dice on local validation sets, held-out BTest, out-of-federation institutions (WashU, MDACC), global validation, and LOO test.
papers.baselines: Single-institution models, CDS, IIL, CIIL ('best local' and 'random local' model selection).
papers.results: FL reached 99% of centralised model quality. Test Dice (BTest / WashU / MDACC / global val / LOO): average single institution 0.732 / 0.666 / 0.705 / 0.733 / -; CDS 0.863 / 0.782 / 0.828 / 0.862 / 0.84; FL 0.858 / 0.771 / 0.820 / 0.857 / 0.835; CIIL best-local 0.855 / 0.775 / 0.82 / 0.853 / 0.831; IIL 0.833 / 0.751 / 0.781 / 0.825 / 0.785. On local validation sets, CDS was 3.17% and FL 2.63% better than single-institution models.
papers.availability: Implementation in the Intel OpenFL / FeTS ecosystem; BraTS data public.

papers.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
papers.authors: Pati S, Baid U, Edwards B, Sheller M, Wang SH, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To run a real worldwide federated study for glioblastoma boundary detection.
papers.method: 71 sites on 6 continents trained a segmentation model together with FL, data never left the site.
papers.result: Big improvement over the model trained on public data for both surgically targetable tumour and whole tumour boundaries.
papers.tools: 3D U-Net, OpenFL, federated learning
papers.gap: Large sites with good IT. Little on what happens with a handful of small sites.
papers.relation: Biggest real FL proof in brain tumours. Our gap is small low-resource sites, which they did not study.
papers.limitations: Heterogeneity across sites not fully solved. Future: smaller sites, more tumour types.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is the largest real federated learning study in medical imaging. Seventy-one hospitals on six continents each preprocessed their own glioblastoma MRI with the open FeTS tool, created reference labels for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour, and kept all images on site. Training started from a 'public initial model' built on 231 BraTS cases, and each federated round every site trained a 3D residual U-Net (30 base filters, Adam 5e-5, mirrored generalised Dice loss) on its data and sent only weight updates to an aggregation server running in a secure enclave, which averaged them. After 73 rounds the consensus model was tested on each site's local validation split and on 332 centrally held out-of-sample cases: it improved tumour-core segmentation by 33% and whole-tumour by 23% over the public model. For our PhD this is the main evidence and practical blueprint (tooling, preprocessing, starting from a public model, secure aggregation, local and central validation) for federated training across Sri Lankan hospitals, and it is one of the base papers.
papers.studyDesign: Real-world global federated learning study across 71 institutions on 6 continents (FeTS initiative), with local validation and centralised out-of-sample evaluation.
papers.datasets: 25,256 MRI scans (>5 TB) of 6,314 glioblastoma patients from 71 sites (T1, T1Gd, T2, FLAIR); public initial model trained on 231 cases from 16 sites (BraTS); centralised out-of-sample set of 332 cases; each site also kept a local validation split.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS-style preprocessing at each site via the FeTS tool (DICOM to NIfTI, co-registration to SRI24, 1 mm resampling, skull stripping); sites created reference labels by refining automatic pre-segmentations.
papers.modelDetails: 3D U-Net with residual connections (3D-ResUNet), 30 base filters; sigmoid output with 3 channels (enhancing tumour, tumour core, whole tumour); loss: generalised Dice on the absolute complement of each sub-compartment ('mirrored' DSC loss). Aggregation server with FedAvg-type averaging; aggregator run in trusted execution environments for confidentiality.
papers.training: Adam, learning rate 5e-5; initialised from the public initial model; 73 federated rounds (no meaningful change after round 42); implemented with OpenFL / FeTS platform.
papers.evaluation: Dice per sub-compartment (ET, TC, WT) on collaborators' local validation data and on the 332-case centralised out-of-sample set; comparison of final consensus model vs public initial model; run-time in clinical computing environments.
papers.baselines: Public initial model (trained on 231 public cases only); prior FL vs centralised learning comparisons.
papers.results: Final consensus model improved over the public initial model by 33% for the surgically targetable tumour (tumour core) and 23% for the whole tumour extent on out-of-sample data; improvements also seen on local validation data at all sites (distributions in violin plots).
papers.statistics: Distributions of Dice across cases and sites (median, mean, IQR); comparisons reported in figures.
papers.availability: FeTS tool and OpenFL: https://github.com/FETS-AI/Front-End; consensus model released for research.

papers.title: Towards fair decentralized benchmarking of healthcare AI algorithms with the Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge
papers.authors: Zenk M, Baid U, Pati S, et al.
papers.aim: To benchmark federated aggregation methods and the real-world robustness of brain tumour segmentation algorithms across many international sites, through the FeTS challenge (2021-2022).
papers.method: Task 1: simulated federated learning on a multicentric BraTS-derived dataset partitioned by institution; teams innovate on weight aggregation and client selection under a time budget. Task 2: segmentation algorithms (no FL requirement) are evaluated in a decentralised way on data held at 32 institutions worldwide, including sites unseen in training.
papers.result: Adaptive weight aggregation and selective client sampling improved both segmentation performance and efficiency (no trade-off). In Task 2, algorithms generalised well on average (median Dice mostly > 0.9 per institution) but worst-case performance exposed site-specific failure modes, both at seen and unseen institutions.
papers.tools: OpenFL / FeTS platform, MedPerf-style federated evaluation, 3D U-Net variants, nnU-Net-based submissions.
papers.gap: Glioma only; Task 1 FL is simulated; failure analysis per site is descriptive.
papers.relation: Benchmarks federated aggregation and generalisation of brain-tumour segmentation across real hospitals, the core setting for federated training across Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.limitations: Participation-dependent; evaluation infrastructure complex; some evaluations could not be completed at all sites.
papers.methodologyDetail: The FeTS challenge had two parts. In Task 1 the organisers split a large BraTS-derived glioma dataset by originating institution and ran federated learning simulations with a fixed 3D U-Net and limited training time; teams competed by designing how client weights are aggregated each round and which hospitals train in each round. In Task 2 teams submitted segmentation models in containers, which were sent to 32 institutions on several continents and evaluated on their local data without the data ever leaving the sites, including institutions whose data had not been used for training. Results showed that sampling a subset of clients and adapting aggregation weights improved both accuracy and efficiency, and that while top algorithms achieved median Dice above 0.9 at most sites, certain hospitals and cases had much worse results. For our PhD this supports evaluating agents at every Sri Lankan site in a federated way and reporting worst-case site performance, not just averages.
papers.studyDesign: International challenge with simulated FL (Task 1) and decentralised multi-site evaluation (Task 2).
papers.datasets: Multi-institutional glioma mpMRI derived from BraTS with institution labels for partitioning (Task 1); test data distributed across 32 institutions on several continents (Task 2), including institutions not represented in training.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing via the FeTS tool at every site.
papers.modelDetails: Task 1: fixed 3D U-Net; participants change aggregation (e.g. adaptive / similarity-weighted averaging) and collaborator selection per round. Task 2: participants submit containerised segmentation models (mostly nnU-Net or ensembles) for federated evaluation.
papers.training: Task 1 under a limited simulated federated training time; Task 2 centralised training on BraTS training data.
papers.evaluation: Dice and HD95 for ET, TC, WT; convergence/efficiency score (Task 1); per-institution mean and worst-case Dice (Task 2); ranking schemes.
papers.baselines: FedAvg baseline aggregation; earlier challenge iterations.
papers.results: Task 1: teams using selective client sampling and adaptive aggregation consistently improved performance and training efficiency. Task 2: median Dice > 0.9 at most institutions, but some institutions and outlier cases had markedly lower performance (heatmap per site and model).
papers.statistics: Ranking with bootstrapping / statistical comparisons described in methods.

papers.title: The MICCAI Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) Challenge 2024: Efficient and Robust Aggregation Methods
papers.authors: Linardos A, Pati S, Baid U, et al.
papers.aim: To evaluate new federated weight-aggregation methods for robust and communication-efficient glioma segmentation in a standardised FL setup.
papers.method: Six teams' aggregation methods were run in the same simulated FL setup on a multi-institutional BraTS-derived dataset and ranked by a cumulative score combining Dice, HD95 and a convergence (communication-efficiency) score.
papers.result: A PID-controller-based aggregation method won: mean Dice 0.733 (ET), 0.761 (TC), 0.751 (WT), HD95 33.922 / 33.623 / 32.309 mm, and best convergence score 0.764, surpassing top methods from earlier FeTS editions.
papers.tools: FeTS challenge code (OpenFL-based), 3D U-Net, PID-controller aggregation.
papers.gap: Simulated FL; absolute Dice lower than centralised models; glioma only.
papers.relation: Compares efficient and robust federated aggregation strategies for glioma segmentation, guiding the choice of aggregation for a small hospital network.
papers.limitations: Six teams only; fixed network; simulation rather than real deployment.
papers.methodologyDetail: The 2024 FeTS challenge isolates one design choice in federated learning: how the server combines client updates. Using a fixed 3D U-Net and BraTS glioma data split into institutional clients (1,251 training, 219 validation and 570 hidden test cases), six teams submitted aggregation methods that were all run in the same simulated federation and ranked on Dice and 95% Hausdorff distance for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour, plus how quickly training converged. A method that treats aggregation like a control problem, using a PID controller to adjust weights based on how client updates evolve, gave the best accuracy and fastest convergence. For our PhD, where only a few hospitals with uneven data will participate, such adaptive aggregation is a candidate to compare with FedAvg, FedProx and FedBN.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge (benchmark) report, MICCAI 2024.
papers.datasets: BraTS-derived multi-institutional glioma mpMRI: 1,251 training cases, 219 validation cases, 570 hidden test cases; labels ET, TC, WT; data partitioned by institution for FL.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing (registration, 1 mm resampling, skull stripping).
papers.modelDetails: Fixed segmentation network (3D U-Net) trained in a standardised FL simulation; teams designed the aggregation rule. Winning method uses a PID controller (proportional-integral-derivative) to adapt aggregation weights from the history of client updates, stabilising training.
papers.training: Standardised FL simulation with limited rounds/time; same splits for all teams.
papers.evaluation: Dice and HD95 per region on the hidden test set; convergence score for communication efficiency; cumulative ranking.
papers.baselines: FedAvg and previous FeTS top performers.
papers.results: Winner (PID-based): Dice ET 0.733, TC 0.761, WT 0.751; HD95 33.922 / 33.623 / 32.309 mm; convergence score 0.764 (best).
papers.statistics: Ranking via cumulative scoring across metrics.

papers.title: Federated brain tumor segmentation: An extensive benchmark
papers.authors: Manthe M, Duffner S, Lartizien C
papers.aim: To benchmark global, personalised and clustered federated learning algorithms for brain tumour segmentation on the FeTS 2022 dataset.
papers.method: Implements federated methods from three classes - global (one final model, e.g. FedAvg, FedProx, FedNova, FedAdam), personalised (one model per institution, e.g. FedBN, local fine-tuning, Ditto) and hybrid/clustered (one model per cluster of institutions) - and compares them on the naturally partitioned FeTS 2022 data, plus IID and limited-data partitions.
papers.result: Standard FedAvg already performed very well; some methods in each class gave slight improvements and could reduce bias of the final model towards the dominant data distribution in the federation. Behaviour differed under IID and limited-data partitions.
papers.tools: 3D U-Net (nnU-Net-style), PyTorch, FeTS 2022 dataset; code: https://github.com/MatthisManthe/Benchmark_FeTS2022
papers.gap: Simulated federation; one dataset; small gains over FedAvg.
papers.relation: Systematically benchmarks global, personalised and hybrid federated methods for brain-tumour segmentation on heterogeneous partitions.
papers.limitations: FeTS 2022 partition dominated by a few large institutions; simulation only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors take the FeTS 2022 glioma dataset, where scans are already split by the hospital they came from (very unequal sizes), and train the same 3D U-Net with a wide range of federated algorithms: global methods that produce one shared model, personalised methods that give each hospital its own adapted model, and clustered methods that group similar hospitals. They also re-split the pooled data evenly (IID) and into small pieces (limited data) to see how algorithms behave in other situations, and compare everything with pooled centralised training. FedAvg already came close to pooled training; some personalised and clustered methods added small gains and reduced the tendency of a federated model to fit mainly the largest hospital. For our PhD this means FedAvg is the first baseline, and personalised or clustered variants should be tried when one Sri Lankan hospital dominates the data.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study with simulated federations.
papers.datasets: FeTS 2022 (BraTS-derived) glioma mpMRI partitioned by institution (natural, highly unbalanced partition), plus artificial IID partition and a limited-data partition.
papers.preprocessing: BraTS preprocessing; 3D patches; standard augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Same 3D U-Net segmentation backbone for all algorithms; global methods produce one model, personalised methods adapt per institution (local BN, fine-tuning, regularised personal models), clustered methods group institutions and train one model per group.
papers.training: Fixed number of federated rounds and local epochs per method; hyper-parameters tuned per method (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice per tumour region per institution and averaged; comparison with centralised training; analysis of bias toward the largest institution.
papers.baselines: Centralised (pooled) training; local training; FedAvg.
papers.results: FedAvg close to centralised performance; best methods in each class gave small Dice gains and more balanced performance across institutions (detailed tables in paper).
papers.statistics: Statistical comparisons across institutions reported in the paper.

papers.title: Federated Modality-Specific Encoders and Multimodal Anchors for Personalized Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Dai Q, Wei D, Liu H, et al.
papers.aim: To do federated brain tumour segmentation when some hospitals only have a subset of MRI sequences, while giving each hospital a personalised model.
papers.method: FedMEMA: one exclusive encoder per MRI modality shared across clients; a server with full-modal data trains a fusion decoder that combines all modality encoders and extracts multimodal 'anchors'; clients with missing modalities calibrate their features toward these global anchors using scaled dot-product cross-attention, with personalised decoders per client.
papers.result: On BraTS 2020 simulating clients with only FLAIR, T1c, T1 or T2, FedMEMA outperformed recent multimodal and personalised FL methods in mean Dice for clients and server; ablations confirmed the value of anchors and cross-attention calibration (Table 1, p < 0.05 comparisons).
papers.tools: 3D segmentation networks with modality-specific encoders, cross-attention calibration, BraTS 2020, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Simulated missing modalities; assumes one server with full-modal data.
papers.relation: Handles hospitals that acquire different MRI sequence sets in federated brain-tumour segmentation, a realistic heterogeneity in low-resource sites.
papers.limitations: Requires a full-modality server; evaluated on one benchmark.
papers.methodologyDetail: In real federations, some hospitals only acquire one or two MRI sequences. FedMEMA gives each sequence its own encoder, and every hospital trains and shares only the encoders for the sequences it has. A central server that holds complete four-sequence data trains a fusion decoder that combines all encoders, which also improves them, and summarises the fused features into a few 'anchors' per tumour class. These anchors are sent to hospitals with missing sequences, which use cross-attention to pull their incomplete features towards the full-modal anchors, then decode with their own personalised decoder. Tested on BraTS 2020 with clients holding only FLAIR, T1c, T1 or T2, it beat current multimodal and personalised federated methods. For our PhD this is relevant if some Sri Lankan sites have incomplete MRI protocols: the federation can still help them, using the referral centre with complete scans as the server.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with simulated federated experiments on a public benchmark.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 multimodal glioma MRI (FLAIR, T1c, T1, T2); clients simulated each holding a single modality, server holding full-modal data.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing; per-client modality subsets.
papers.modelDetails: Modality-specific encoders (shared via FL); server fusion decoder D_M fuses encoder features and is used to backpropagate into encoders; N_k multimodal anchors per class extracted by clustering fused features at scale level l; clients compute calibrated features via cross-attention to anchors and add them to decoder features; personalised client decoders.
papers.training: Federated rounds with encoder aggregation; ablations on N_k (anchors per class, best 3) and feature level l (best 4, the bottleneck).
papers.evaluation: Mean Dice (%) per client modality (FLAIR, T1c, T1, T2), their average, and server performance; significance tests (p < 0.05).
papers.baselines: Recent multimodal FL and personalised FL methods (e.g. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, personalised FL variants, multimodal missing-modality methods).
papers.results: FedMEMA achieved the best average client and server Dice among compared methods; best settings N_k = 3 anchors and level l = 4 (values in Table 1/2).

papers.title: A review on brain tumor segmentation based on deep learning methods with federated learning techniques
papers.authors: Ahamed MF, Hossain MM, Nahiduzzaman M, et al.
papers.aim: To review deep learning methods for brain tumour segmentation and the federated learning techniques that can train them across institutions while protecting privacy.
papers.method: Narrative literature review of more than 100 papers from IEEE, Springer, Elsevier, MDPI, Wiley, major conferences (MICCAI, ISBI, IPMI, MIDL, CVPR, ECCV, ICCV), BraTS challenge entries and arXiv; summary tables of datasets, architectures, FL training strategies and limitations; discussion of open problems and a client-based FL training strategy.
papers.result: Summarises public datasets (BraTS, TCGA-GBM and others), CNN/U-Net/transformer segmentation families and FL approaches (e.g., U-Net variants with FedAvg); identifies open issues - data heterogeneity across sites, class imbalance, missing modalities, communication cost, privacy attacks and limited external validation.
papers.tools: Literature synthesis and comparison tables.
papers.gap: Non-systematic review; few quantitative comparisons under identical conditions; little on low-resource sites.
papers.relation: Surveys deep-learning and federated approaches specifically for brain-tumour segmentation, framing the method space for O3.
papers.limitations: Breadth over depth; quality of included studies not formally assessed.
papers.methodologyDetail: This review surveys more than 100 studies on automatic brain tumour segmentation with deep learning and on federated learning, which lets hospitals train a shared model without exchanging scans. It lists the public datasets used (mainly BraTS), groups segmentation networks from classic CNNs and U-Nets to attention and transformer models, and tabulates federated approaches such as U-Net models trained with FedAvg together with their limitations. It ends with unsolved problems - different scanners and protocols across hospitals, imbalanced tumour classes, missing MRI sequences, communication costs and privacy risks - and a suggested client-based federated training strategy. For our PhD it is a broad map of the O3 design space and a checklist of problems our federated segmentation agent must address across Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review.
papers.datasets: More than 100 papers; datasets discussed include BraTS editions, TCGA-GBM/LGG and other public brain MRI sets.
papers.preprocessing: Review of common MRI preprocessing (skull stripping, registration, normalisation, bias correction) in included studies.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (surveyed CNN, U-Net, attention and transformer segmentation models; FL algorithms such as FedAvg and variants).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Comparison of reported Dice and other metrics across studies.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Taxonomy of methods and FL strategies; list of open challenges and proposed client-based federated training approach.

papers.title: HarmoFL: Harmonizing Local and Global Drifts in Federated Learning on Heterogeneous Medical Images
papers.authors: Jiang M, Wang Z, Dou Q
papers.aim: To reduce both local (client) and global (server) drift in federated learning when medical images differ across sites because of scanners or protocols.
papers.method: HarmoFL: (1) amplitude normalisation - each client transforms images to the frequency domain and normalises the amplitude spectrum to mimic a unified imaging setting, harmonising features across clients; (2) client weight perturbation that guides each local model to a flat optimum, so aggregating several flat local optima gives a better-converged global model, with no extra communication.
papers.result: Prostate MRI segmentation average Dice 94.28% vs 91.44% (FedAvg); histology nuclei segmentation 74.42% vs 67.49% (FedAvg); also best breast cancer histology classification accuracy on Camelyon17 across 5 hospitals; faster convergence.
papers.tools: U-Net (segmentation), DenseNet121 (Camelyon17 classification), Fourier transform amplitude normalisation, PyTorch; code on GitHub.
papers.gap: Only intensity/appearance shift addressed; 2D tasks.
papers.relation: Addresses scanner/site feature shift in federated medical imaging, relevant to heterogeneous MRI across Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.limitations: Assumes amplitude carries most of the site style; not tested on 3D brain MRI.
papers.methodologyDetail: In multi-site medical imaging, each hospital's scanner gives images a different 'style', which makes local models drift apart and the averaged global model drift too. HarmoFL tackles both. Locally, each hospital converts its images to the frequency domain and normalises the amplitude spectrum (which carries most of the scanner style) while keeping the phase (structure), so all clients train on harmonised-looking data. During local training a small weight perturbation pushes each client's model towards a flat minimum, so that averaging them on the server lands in a good region. The authors test on Camelyon17 histology from five hospitals with DenseNet121, histology nuclei segmentation from six sources and prostate MRI from six sites with U-Net, against FedAvg, FedProx, FedNova, FedAdam, FedBN and MOON. HarmoFL gave the best averages (prostate Dice 94.3 vs 91.4 FedAvg; nuclei 74.4 vs 67.5) and converged faster. For our PhD it is a candidate for federated training across Sri Lankan sites with different MRI scanners and slide stains.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with simulated federated experiments on three public multi-site medical datasets.
papers.datasets: Camelyon17 breast cancer histology (450,000 patches from 5 hospitals with different stains; each hospital a client; normal vs tumour); histology nuclei segmentation (6 data sources as clients A-F); prostate T2 MRI segmentation (6 sites as clients A-F).
papers.preprocessing: Each client normalises the amplitude spectrum of its images (Fourier transform, keep phase, normalise amplitude) before training.
papers.modelDetails: Local training with amplitude-normalised images and weight perturbation towards flat minima (similar in spirit to sharpness-aware minimisation but without extra communication); server averages client weights (FedAvg-style).
papers.training: Camelyon17: DenseNet121, cross-entropy, SGD lr 1e-3, 100 local epochs total with different communication frequencies; segmentation: U-Net with Dice loss; settings in paper.
papers.evaluation: Per-client and average Dice (segmentation) and accuracy (classification) with SD over runs; convergence curves vs communication rounds; local epochs ablation.
papers.baselines: FedAvg, FedProx, FedNova, FedAdam, FedBN, MOON.
papers.results: Histology nuclei Dice average: FedAvg 67.49, FedProx 67.49, FedNova 67.55, HarmoFL 74.42 (client F 69.20 vs 49.69 FedAvg). Prostate MRI Dice average: FedAvg 91.44, FedProx 91.08, HarmoFL 94.28. Camelyon17: HarmoFL best average accuracy; MOON dropped on client E.

papers.title: FedDG: Federated Domain Generalization on Medical Image Segmentation via Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space
papers.authors: Liu Q, Chen C, Qin J, Dou Q, Heng PA
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.aim: To learn a federated segmentation model from several hospitals that generalises directly to completely unseen hospitals outside the federation.
papers.method: Episodic Learning in Continuous Frequency Space (ELCFS): clients share only amplitude spectra (image style, privacy-preserving) and interpolate their own images' amplitudes with other clients' amplitudes to simulate other domains; boundary-oriented episodic meta-learning (meta-train on own data, meta-test on frequency-transformed data) with a boundary-aware contrastive loss.
papers.result: Prostate MRI (6 sites, leave-one-site-out): average Dice 87.39% vs about 85.6-86.3% for FedAvg and other domain-generalisation methods, HD 10.88 vs 11.5-12.4. Fundus optic disc/cup (4 centres): best overall Dice and HD on unseen sites.
papers.tools: U-Net-style segmentation network, Fourier amplitude interpolation, meta-learning, PyTorch.
papers.gap: 2D tasks; amplitude sharing may leak some site information; not brain tumour.
papers.relation: Federated domain generalisation lets a model trained on some hospitals generalise to unseen sites, important for new Sri Lankan centres.
papers.limitations: Assumes style captured by amplitude spectrum; leave-one-site-out simulation.
papers.methodologyDetail: Federated models still perform worse on hospitals that were not part of training. FedDG lets each hospital learn what other hospitals' images look like without sharing patient images: each client shares only the amplitude spectrum of its images (which carries scanner style, not anatomy). During local training, a client mixes the amplitude of its own images with amplitudes from other clients, generating realistic versions of its images in other sites' styles, and uses episodic meta-learning - train on original images, then check that the update also works on the restyled images - plus a loss that sharpens boundaries. Models are averaged across clients as in FedAvg. In leave-one-site-out tests on prostate MRI from six sites and fundus images from four centres, it gave the best average Dice and boundary distance on the unseen sites. For our PhD this is the method family to try when the trained agents must work at a new Sri Lankan hospital that did not contribute training data.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; leave-one-domain-out evaluation on two multi-site medical segmentation tasks.
papers.datasets: Retinal fundus images from 4 clinical centres (public datasets) for optic disc and cup segmentation; prostate T2-weighted MRI from 6 data sources (public datasets) as sites A-F.
papers.preprocessing: Fundus: centre-crop 800x800 disc region and resize to 384x384. Prostate: slices from T2 MRI, normalised; each site used once as the unseen test domain.
papers.modelDetails: Each client keeps raw images local but shares its amplitude spectrum bank; local training augments images by interpolating amplitude with other clients' amplitudes (continuous frequency space). Episodic learning: inner update on original data, meta-test on interpolated data, meta-objective optimises original parameters; boundary-oriented contrastive loss on boundary vs background features.
papers.training: Federated averaging of meta-learned client models; settings in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice and Hausdorff distance on each unseen site and their average.
papers.baselines: FedAvg, JiGen, BigAug, Epi-FCR, RSC (domain generalisation methods adapted to federated setting).
papers.results: Prostate unseen-site Dice A-F: 90.19 / 87.17 / 85.26 / 88.23 / 83.02 / 90.47, average 87.39 (JiGen 86.26, BigAug 85.99, Epi-FCR 86.17, RSC 85.80, FedAvg about 85.6); average HD 10.88. Fundus: ELCFS Dice e.g. 95.37 / 87.52 / 93.37 / 94.50 (disc) with best averages.
