papers.title: Medical SAM adapter: Adapting segment anything model for medical image segmentation
papers.authors: Junde Wu, Ziyue Wang, Mingxuan Hong et al.
papers.aim: To adapt the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to medical images efficiently, including 3D scans, without full fine-tuning.
papers.method: Medical SAM Adapter (Med-SA): small adapter modules inserted into SAM; Space-Depth Transpose (SD-Trans) to process 3D volumes with the 2D model, and Hyper-Prompting Adapter (HyP-Adpt) for prompt-conditioned adaptation; evaluated on 17 segmentation tasks across modalities.
papers.result: Med-SA outperformed state-of-the-art medical segmentation methods (e.g., TransUNet, UNETR, Swin-UNETR, diffusion-based models) on the 17 tasks, including brain tumour, abdominal organs (BTCV), optic disc/cup, thyroid nodule and melanoma, while updating only about 2% of SAM's parameters.
papers.tools: SAM ViT backbone, adapter layers, PyTorch.
papers.gap: Still needs prompts and labelled fine-tuning data; compute of SAM backbone.
papers.relation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning option for the segmentation agent on small Sri Lankan datasets (update a small adapter instead of the whole model).
papers.limitations: Comparisons mostly on public benchmarks.
papers.methodologyDetail: SAM is a strong general segmentation model but performs poorly on medical images. Rather than retraining all of it, Med-SA freezes SAM and adds small 'adapter' layers that learn medical knowledge, changing only about 2% of the parameters. A special module lets the 2D model work on 3D scans by treating depth as an extra dimension, and another lets the adapters change depending on the user's prompt. Across 17 tasks - including brain tumour MRI, abdominal CT organs and skin lesions - it beat well-known medical segmentation networks. For our PhD it is a data- and compute-efficient way to fine-tune a foundation segmentation model on the small Sri Lankan dataset.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with multi-dataset evaluation.
papers.datasets: 17 medical segmentation tasks across CT, MRI, ultrasound, fundus and dermoscopy (e.g., BTCV multi-organ CT, BraTS brain tumour, REFUGE optic disc/cup, thyroid nodule ultrasound, ISIC melanoma).
papers.preprocessing: Dataset-specific resizing; 3D volumes handled through SD-Trans.
papers.modelDetails: Frozen SAM image encoder with lightweight adapters; SD-Trans for depth/space attention; HyP-Adpt generating adapter weights from prompt embeddings.
papers.training: Only adapters trained (about 2% of parameters).
papers.evaluation: Dice, IoU and HD95 per task versus task-specific SOTA and SAM variants.
papers.baselines: TransUNet, UNETR, Swin-UNETR, nnU-Net, TransBTS, diffusion-based segmenters, original SAM and MedSAM.
papers.results: Best or comparable average Dice across tasks with far fewer trainable parameters.

papers.title: Segment anything model for medical image analysis: An experimental study
papers.authors: Maciej A. Mazurowski, Haoyu Dong, Hanxue Gu et al.
papers.aim: To measure how well the Segment Anything Model (SAM) segments medical images out of the box with different prompts.
papers.method: Extensive evaluation of SAM on 19 medical imaging datasets across modalities and anatomies with point and box prompts (single and iterative), compared with interactive segmentation methods RITM, SimpleClick and FocalClick.
papers.result: Single-prompt performance varied widely, from IoU 0.1135 (spine MRI) to 0.8650 (hip X-ray); better for well-circumscribed objects and poorer for others such as brain tumours; box prompts much better than point prompts; SAM beat the other methods with a single point, but with iterative multiple points the others overtook SAM.
papers.tools: SAM (ViT-H/L/B), RITM, SimpleClick, FocalClick.
papers.gap: Zero-shot only; no medical fine-tuning.
papers.relation: Shows zero-shot SAM is unreliable for brain tumours, so the segmentation agent needs medical adaptation (MedSAM, Med-SA) and box prompts from a detector or clinician.
papers.limitations: 2D slices; mostly public datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors tested SAM, a general-purpose 'segment anything' model, on 19 medical imaging datasets without retraining, giving it either clicks or boxes as hints. Quality depended heavily on the task - from very poor on spine MRI (IoU 0.11) to good on hip X-rays (IoU 0.87) - and it struggled on less clear-cut targets like brain tumours. Boxes worked much better than single clicks, and while SAM beat other interactive tools with one click, those tools caught up and passed it when several clicks were given. For our PhD it shows a general foundation model cannot be used as-is for brain tumours; it needs medical adaptation and good box prompts.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental benchmark study.
papers.datasets: 19 public medical imaging datasets (MRI, CT, X-ray, ultrasound, others) including brain tumour MRI, spine MRI and hip X-ray.
papers.preprocessing: Prompt generation from ground-truth masks (central points, boxes, iterative error-region points).
papers.modelDetails: SAM foundation model variants used without fine-tuning.
papers.training: None (zero-shot).
papers.evaluation: IoU per dataset and prompt mode; iterative prompting curves.
papers.baselines: RITM, SimpleClick, FocalClick.
papers.results: IoU range 0.1135-0.8650 with single prompts; box > point; SAM best with one point, others better with many points.

papers.title: A weakly supervised deep learning-based method for glioma subtype classification using WSI and mpMRIs
papers.authors: Hsu WW, Guo JM, Pei L, Chiang LA, Li YF, Hsiao JC, Colen R, Liu P
papers.aim: To classify glioma subtype from both pathology slides and MRI using only case-level labels.
papers.method: Weakly supervised learning on slide patches plus tumour-region MRI features, with the two predictions combined.
papers.result: Third place in the CPM-RadPath 2020 challenge, showing radiology-pathology fusion works with weak labels.
papers.tools: ensemble
papers.gap: No uncertainty or missing-modality handling; pre-2021 subtypes.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Challenge data only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method classifies glioma subtype from both pathology slides and MRI when only a case-level label is available: patches from the slide are learned with weak supervision, MRI tumour-region features add radiological evidence, and predictions are combined. Its placing in an international challenge shows feasibility of radiology-pathology fusion with weak labels, the setting expected in the registry.
papers.studyDesign: Method development in a public challenge (National Taiwan University of Science and Technology and US partners; Scientific Reports 2022).
papers.datasets: CPM-RadPath 2020 challenge: paired whole-slide images and multi-parametric MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) with case-level glioma subtype labels (astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma).
papers.preprocessing: WSI tiling and patch selection; MRI preprocessing as in BraTS; only case-level labels available.
papers.modelDetails: Weakly supervised framework: CNN on WSI patches with case-level label propagation and an MRI branch using tumour-region features; ensemble/fusion of pathology and radiology predictions.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Balanced accuracy, F1 and kappa on validation and challenge test phase.
papers.baselines: Other CPM-RadPath challenge entries.
papers.results: Third place in the CPM-RadPath 2020 testing phase; competitive performance from weak labels and multimodal fusion.

papers.title: A multicenter proof-of-concept study on deep learning-based intraoperative discrimination of primary central nervous system lymphoma
papers.authors: Zhang X, Zhao Z, Wang R, Chen H, Zheng X, Liu L, Lan L, Li P, Wu S, Cao Q, et al.
papers.aim: To tell brain lymphoma from glioma on frozen sections during surgery, where the answer changes the operation.
papers.method: LGNet, an ensemble of five networks, trained on one centre's frozen-section slides, validated on two external centres, compared with pathologists and combined with their judgement.
papers.result: External AUROC 0.965-0.993, better than several pathologists; combining AI and pathologists improved results further.
papers.tools: ensemble, ResNet
papers.gap: No explicit uncertainty-based deferral; binary task.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; Chinese centres.
papers.methodologyDetail: LGNet classifies frozen-section slides taken during brain surgery as lymphoma or glioma, which changes the operation (lymphoma is usually not resected). An ensemble of five networks was trained on one centre's slides, validated on two external centres and a proof-of-concept set, compared with pathologists, and combined with pathologists' judgements. It is a strong example of ensemble-based intra-operative pathology support with human-machine fusion.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre retrospective development and validation with a proof-of-concept study (Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center and partners; ethics SL-B2022-613-01, consent waived).
papers.datasets: H&E frozen-section WSIs (2014-2021): internal dataset from 432 patients, external dataset 1 from 300 patients, external dataset 2 from 386 patients, and a 68-patient proof-of-concept set; PCNSL vs glioma and vs other non-PCNSL lesions.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs tessellated into non-overlapping 512x512 tiles at 10x; two random 224x224 crops per tile; tile probabilities averaged to slide level.
papers.modelDetails: LGNet: five-fold ensemble of ResNet-50 classifiers averaging probabilities; heatmaps for interpretation; human-machine fusion combining model and pathologist diagnoses.
papers.training: K-fold training on the internal dataset (details in supplement).
papers.evaluation: AUROC, sensitivity, specificity on external cohorts; comparison with pathologists of varying expertise; fusion performance.
papers.baselines: Pathologists (junior to senior).
papers.results: External AUROC 0.965 and 0.972 for PCNSL vs glioma and 0.981 and 0.993 for PCNSL vs non-PCNSL; outperformed several pathologists; human-machine fusion improved performance further.

papers.title: Deep Neural Network Analysis of Pathology Images With Integrated Molecular Data for Enhanced Glioma Classification and Grading
papers.authors: Pei L, Jones KA, Shboul ZA, Chen JY, Iftekharuddin KM
papers.aim: To improve glioma classification and grading by combining pathology images with molecular data.
papers.method: A representative high-cellularity region is chosen per slide, colour-normalised, cellularity measured by nuclei segmentation, and networks trained with and without molecular markers.
papers.result: Adding molecular data improved classification and grading.
papers.tools: ResNet, U-Net
papers.gap: Single ROI per slide; WHO 2016 labels; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: TCGA only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors select one representative high-cellularity region from each glioma slide using super-pixel segmentation, normalise its colour, measure cellularity with a nuclei-segmentation network, and train networks to classify glioma type and grade with and without molecular markers. Adding molecular information improved results, foreshadowing the integrated WHO classification.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method development on TCGA (Old Dominion University, University of Iowa, UC San Diego).
papers.datasets: 549 TCGA glioma WSIs with molecular data (IDH, ATRX, 1p/19q, MGMT): 201 LGG grade II, 229 LGG grade III, 119 HGG grade IV; one 1000x1000 ROI per WSI; MoNuSeg (30 images, ~22,000 nuclei) for nuclei segmentation training.
papers.preprocessing: ROI selection by over-segmentation into super-pixels on the thumbnail and choosing low-intensity (high cellularity) regions; colour normalisation to a reference; nuclei segmentation with U-Net to compute cellularity.
papers.modelDetails: Deep neural networks on pathology ROIs combined with cellularity features and molecular data for WHO 2016 glioma type and grade classification and molecular subtype prediction.
papers.training: 5-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy for type, grade and molecular subtype.
papers.baselines: Image-only models.
papers.results: Integrating molecular data with pathology improved classification and grading; molecular subtype was partly predictable from images and cellularity.

papers.title: Prognostic risk stratification of gliomas using deep learning in digital pathology images
papers.authors: Chunduru P, Phillips JJ, Molinaro AM
papers.aim: To predict glioma survival risk directly from pathology slides.
papers.method: A residual network learns a risk score from slides, combined with IDH status and age by recursive partitioning into prognostic groups.
papers.result: Four distinct survival groups, with median survival from about 1 to over 14 years.
papers.tools: Kaplan-Meier
papers.gap: Prognosis rather than diagnosis; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective cohorts.
papers.methodologyDetail: A residual network learns survival risk directly from glioma slides, and its risk score is combined with IDH status and age through recursive partitioning to form clinically distinct prognostic groups. It shows that slides carry prognostic information beyond molecular markers, relevant to the Follow-up Agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective prognostic modelling study (UCSF).
papers.datasets: Glioma H&E whole-slide images with survival and molecular data (TCGA and/or UCSF cohorts; details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: WSI tiling and quality filtering.
papers.modelDetails: Survival deep learning (SDL): residual CNN combined with a survival model to predict patient risk from H&E WSIs; recursive partitioning analysis (RPA) combining SDL risk score with IDH status and age.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Concordance and risk stratification of overall survival.
papers.baselines: Clinical and molecular prognostic factors.
papers.results: Four distinct survival risk groups defined by SDL risk score, IDH status and age, with median OS ranging from about 1 to over 14 years.

papers.title: Classification of Diffuse Glioma Subtype from Clinical-Grade Pathological Images Using Deep Transfer Learning
papers.authors: Im S, Hyeon J, Rha E, Lee J, Choi HJ, Jung Y, Kim TJ
papers.aim: To classify diffuse glioma subtype from routine clinical-grade slide scans.
papers.method: Slides were split into patches, each classified by a transfer-learned ResNet, and patch votes combined into a slide decision.
papers.result: Balanced accuracy 0.87 for oligodendroglioma vs other diffuse gliomas.
papers.tools: transfer learning, ResNet
papers.gap: Strong class imbalance; no uncertainty; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Small ODG group; WHO 2016 labels.
papers.methodologyDetail: Slides scanned in routine clinical practice were split into patches, each classified by a transfer-learned ResNet, and the patch votes were combined into a slide-level decision on oligodendroglioma versus other diffuse glioma and on grade. It shows that clinical-grade, non-research scans can support subtype classification, relevant to local Sri Lankan slides.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre study (Catholic University of Korea, KAIST; IRB SC18RNSI0005).
papers.datasets: H&E WSIs of 468 gliomas (2017-2019) scanned during routine 1p/19q FISH testing; 369 with full molecular profiles: 38 IDH-mutant 1p/19q co-deleted oligodendrogliomas vs 331 non-ODG; all 468 used for grade II-III vs IV.
papers.preprocessing: Slides with folds, pen marks or bubbles removed; patches extracted from each WSI.
papers.modelDetails: ResNet50V2 deep transfer learning on patches with majority voting to give slide labels; separate binary models for subtype and grade.
papers.training: ImageNet-pretrained transfer learning (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Balanced accuracy and related metrics.
papers.baselines: Not reported.
papers.results: Balanced accuracy 0.8727 for oligodendroglioma vs other diffuse glioma with majority voting.

papers.title: Segmentation and Classification in Digital Pathology for Glioma Research: Challenges and Deep Learning Approaches
papers.authors: Kurc T, Bakas S, Ren X, Bagari A, Momeni A, Huang Y, Zhang L, Kumar A, Thibault M, Qi Q, et al.
papers.aim: To describe brain-tumour pathology challenges and the best deep learning methods for them.
papers.method: Summary of CPM challenges for nuclei segmentation and case classification using slides plus MRI, explaining the top pipelines.
papers.result: Top classification accuracies were 0.75-0.90; the best method combined radiology and pathology.
papers.tools: Nucleus instance segmentation method and three classification methods, including the top method combining an MRI classifier and a WSI classifier.
papers.gap: Small challenge datasets; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Older WHO categories.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper describes CPM challenges for brain-tumour pathology: segmenting nuclei and classifying cases using pathology slides together with MRI. It explains the top methods, including the pipeline that preprocesses MRI, segments the tumour, extracts features and fuses MRI and slide predictions. It is an early demonstration that radiology-pathology fusion helps glioma classification.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge summary and methods paper (Stony Brook, UPenn and others; MICCAI CPM challenges).
papers.datasets: Computational Precision Medicine challenge data: brain tumour digital pathology tiles for nucleus segmentation and paired WSI plus multi-parametric MRI for glioma classification (LGG/GBM, astrocytoma/oligodendroglioma).
papers.preprocessing: MRI: skull stripping, co-registration to T1c, resampling to 1 mm isotropic, tumour segmentation; WSI tiling.
papers.modelDetails: Nucleus instance segmentation method and three classification methods, including the top method combining an MRI classifier and a WSI classifier.
papers.training: Details per method.
papers.evaluation: Dice-type metrics for nuclei; classification accuracy.
papers.baselines: Challenge participants.
papers.results: Classification methods achieved accuracies of 0.75, 0.80 and 0.90; the best combined radiology and pathology predictions.

papers.title: Predicting the recurrence and overall survival of patients with glioma based on histopathological images using deep learning
papers.authors: Luo C, Yang J, Liu Z, Jing D
papers.aim: To predict glioma recurrence and survival from biopsy slides.
papers.method: Patch features from a pre-trained network are combined into a patient risk score that splits patients into high- and low-risk groups.
papers.result: The score separated patients into groups with significantly different recurrence and survival.
papers.tools: Kaplan-Meier, Cox regression, ResNet
papers.gap: Single centre; no external validation reported; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using representative biopsy slides, the model extracts features from small patches with a pre-trained network, aggregates them into a patient risk score and splits patients at the median into high- and low-risk groups for recurrence and survival. It adds to evidence that routine slides carry prognostic information for follow-up planning.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective prognostic study (Xiangya Hospital, China).
papers.datasets: Glioma patients with representative H&E biopsy slides and follow-up for disease-free and overall survival (single institution; details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Slides split into non-overlapping 180x180 patches; patch features extracted by a pre-trained ResNet.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning survival model aggregating patch-level features to patient-level hazard scores for recurrence and overall survival.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: C-index, risk-group separation (median hazard 0.083 for DFS, -0.177 for OS).
papers.baselines: Clinical factors.
papers.results: Hazard scores stratified patients into low- and high-risk groups with significant differences in DFS and OS.

papers.title: Weakly supervised deep learning-based classification for histopathology of gliomas: a single center experience
papers.authors: Zuo M, Xing X, Zheng L, Wang H, Yuan Y, Chen S, Yu T, Zhang S, Yang Y, Mao Q, et al.
papers.aim: To classify gliomas from pathology slides with only slide-level labels, aligned with WHO 2021.
papers.method: Attention-based ResNet trained with slide labels on local and TCGA slides, ten-fold cross-validation, with heatmaps.
papers.result: High AUCs for glioma grades and types; IDH status predicted in TCGA with AUC 0.95.
papers.tools: ResNet, OpenSlide, Python
papers.gap: No external test of the local model; no uncertainty estimates.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; cross-validation only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Slides from a Chinese hospital and TCGA were tiled, colour-normalised and classified by an attention-based ResNet trained with slide-level labels, using ten-fold cross-validation, with heatmaps to show which regions drove each prediction. It demonstrates WHO 2021-aligned weakly supervised glioma pathology with local and public data, similar to the Pathology Agent design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre study with public data (West China Hospital, Sichuan University; ethics No. 2021.1319, written consent).
papers.datasets: 472 H&E WSIs from 226 patients at West China Hospital (scanned on Hamamatsu NanoZoomer-SQ) and 1,604 WSIs from 880 TCGA patients; five subtypes (astrocytoma, anaplastic astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, anaplastic oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma); TCGA diagnoses revised to WHO 2021.
papers.preprocessing: OpenSlide loading, DeepZoom patch tiling at 10x, Reinhard colour normalisation; damaged or blurry regions excluded; diagnoses confirmed by two senior pathologists.
papers.modelDetails: Weakly supervised ResNet-50 with an attention mechanism for slide-level classification; heatmap visualisation.
papers.training: Ten-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: AUC for grade and subtype distinctions and IDH inference.
papers.baselines: Not reported.
papers.results: High AUCs for distinguishing grades of astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma; IDH status inferred in TCGA with AUC 0.9488.
papers.availability: TCGA public; hospital data on reasonable request.

papers.title: Brain Tumor/Mass Classification Framework Using Magnetic-Resonance-Imaging-Based Isolated and Developed Transfer Deep-Learning Model
papers.authors: Alanazi MF, Ali MU, Hussain SJ, Zafar A, Mohatram M, Irfan M, AlRuwaili R, Alruwaili M, Ali NH, Albarrak AM
papers.aim: To detect and classify brain tumours from 2D MRI with a small CNN and transfer learning.
papers.method: Small CNNs trained from scratch on public 2D MRI slices; the best was transferred to other datasets for detection and three-class typing.
papers.result: 96.9% accuracy on an unseen 2D dataset, though curated 2D data do not reflect clinical 3D MRI.
papers.tools: Isolated CNNs built from scratch (19, 22, 25 layers) for 2-, 3- and 4-class tasks;
papers.gap: 2D slices from web datasets; possible patient overlap; no uncertainty or external clinical test.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Curated public images only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained small CNNs from scratch on public 2D brain MRI slices and then transferred the best one to other datasets for tumour detection and three-class tumour typing. Results were high on curated 2D Kaggle-type data. Such datasets are useful for quick baselines but do not reflect 3D clinical MRI, so their accuracy should not be expected locally.
papers.studyDesign: Model development on public MRI datasets (Jouf University and partners, Saudi Arabia).
papers.datasets: Dataset I: 3,000 Kaggle MRI images (tumour/no tumour); Dataset II: 2,870 Kaggle images (glioma 826, meningioma 822, no tumour 395, pituitary 827); Dataset III: 3,064 slices from 233 patients (Figshare, Chinese hospitals: glioma 1,426, meningioma 708, pituitary 930).
papers.preprocessing: Extreme-point cropping, erosion and dilation for noise removal, resizing to 227x227, scaling.
papers.modelDetails: Isolated CNNs built from scratch (19, 22, 25 layers) for 2-, 3- and 4-class tasks; best CNN reused as a transfer-learning model on another dataset.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on held-out and unseen datasets.
papers.baselines: Isolated CNNs and pretrained networks.
papers.results: Transfer-learned model reached 96.89% accuracy on an unseen brain MRI dataset.

papers.title: Deep Transfer Learning Approaches in Performance Analysis of Brain Tumor Classification Using MRI Images
papers.authors: Srinivas C, K S NP, Zakariah M, Alothaibi YA, Shaukat K, Partibane B, Awal H
papers.aim: To compare transfer learning networks for brain tumour detection on a small MRI set.
papers.method: Several ImageNet-pretrained networks were fine-tuned on a very small public set of 2D brain MRI images and compared.
papers.result: VGG-16 did best; ResNet-50 was unstable with many false negatives (11 of 31).
papers.tools: transfer learning, VGG, ResNet, Inception, fine-tuning
papers.gap: Very small JPEG dataset; no patient-level split, no uncertainty, no external test.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Not clinically representative.
papers.methodologyDetail: Several ImageNet-pretrained networks were fine-tuned on a very small public set of 2D brain MRI images to detect tumours, and their accuracy and errors compared. It illustrates transfer learning on scarce data but also how unstable such small-sample results are; false negatives are particularly concerning clinically.
papers.studyDesign: Model comparison on a small public dataset (India, Saudi Arabia, Australia, Ghana authors; Journal of Healthcare Engineering 2022).
papers.datasets: Kaggle brain MRI set of about 256 JPEG images labelled tumour yes/no (158 and 98 images); split into training, validation and test.
papers.preprocessing: Resizing to 256x256, intensity normalisation (z-score), cropping.
papers.modelDetails: Transfer learning with ImageNet-pretrained CNNs (VGG-16, ResNet-50, Inception-v3 and others) with frozen convolutional layers and new classification heads.
papers.training: Fine-tuning details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, confusion matrices, training/validation curves.
papers.baselines: Comparison among pretrained architectures.
papers.results: VGG-16 performed best; ResNet-50 showed unstable validation accuracy and many false negatives (11 of 31).

papers.title: Multiconvolutional Transfer Learning for 3D Brain Tumor Magnetic Resonance Images
papers.authors: Sangeetha SKB, Muthukumaran V, Deeba K, Rajadurai H, Maheshwari V, Dalu GT
papers.aim: To use transfer learning from 3D autoencoders for brain tumour classification with very few patients.
papers.method: A 3D autoencoder is pretrained by reconstruction and its features transferred to a 45-patient classification task with leave-one-out validation.
papers.result: About 94% accuracy, 1.5% better than CNN baselines, but specificity was only about 73%.
papers.tools: transfer learning, autoencoder
papers.gap: Very small cohort; low specificity; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Single public dataset.
papers.methodologyDetail: An autoencoder is pretrained to reconstruct 3D medical images and its features are transferred to a small tumour-classification task with 45 patients, evaluated with repeated leave-one-out cross-validation. Pretraining beat random initialisation. It is a small example of self-supervised feature learning for scarce 3D data, though specificity remained low.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public 3D MRI dataset (SRM, VIT and other Indian institutions; Computational Intelligence and Neuroscience 2022).
papers.datasets: REMBRANDT-derived 3D brain MRI from 45 patients (T2-weighted fat-saturated coronal images), patients aged 18-45.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic augmentations (32 per sample, 764-image training sets).
papers.modelDetails: Multi-convolutional transfer learning (MCTL): a convolutional autoencoder learns features from different 3D medical imaging datasets, then transferred to tumour/healthy classification.
papers.training: Grid search over hyperparameters; leave-one-out cross-validation repeated 15 times.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity.
papers.baselines: SVM, KNN, naive Bayes, DNN, CNN.
papers.results: Best average validation accuracy about 94% (specificity about 73%); MCTL improved accuracy by about 1.5% over CNN baselines.

papers.title: Nationwide federated learning for histopathology: secure deployment across Germany behind firewalls
papers.authors: Babendererde N, Lemke N, Stieber J, Fuchs M, Weng Z, Eich ML, Lingscheidt T, Mairinger F, Büttner R, Tolkach Y, et al.
papers.aim: To deploy federated learning for pathology across real German hospitals behind firewalls.
papers.method: TheODen ran in three university hospitals, with clients connecting out through a secure reverse proxy; federated segmentation models were trained for breast and colorectal pathology.
papers.result: Dice 0.76 and 0.75, close to central training, despite firewalls and data differences.
papers.tools: federated learning
papers.gap: Segmentation of non-brain tissue; no calibration analysis after aggregation.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Three sites; public datasets partitioned to sites.
papers.methodologyDetail: TheODen was deployed on real hospital infrastructure in three German university hospitals behind their firewalls, with clients connecting outward through a secure reverse proxy so no hospital had to open network ports. Federated segmentation models for breast and colorectal pathology reached performance near central training. It addresses the practical IT barriers that federated learning will face in Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Real-world nationwide federated deployment across three German university hospitals (Cologne, Essen, Leipzig) with a new open-source framework (TU Darmstadt and partners; npj Digital Medicine 2026).

papers.modelDetails: TheODen: federated training framework requiring no open client-side ports, using a secure reverse-proxy architecture; abstract-server and control-server modes; pluggable aggregation methods, datasets and models; segmentation networks trained federatedly.
papers.training: Federated configurations and hardware per site described in methods.
papers.evaluation: Global average Dice on test sets; comparison with centralised and local training; robustness to heterogeneity and network constraints.
papers.baselines: Centralised training and single-site (local) training.
papers.results: Global average Dice 0.764 (BCSS) and 0.754 (SemiCOL) despite heterogeneity and firewall constraints, close to centralised performance.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Histopathology Image Classification: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Touhami M, Ahmad Fauzi MF, Ur Rehman Z, Mansor S
papers.aim: To review federated learning for histopathology image classification.
papers.method: Systematic review of studies from 2020 to 2025, tabulating datasets, methods, strengths and weaknesses.

papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: No protocol registration.

papers.studyDesign: PRISMA systematic review (Multimedia University, KPJ Healthcare University, Malaysia); no registered protocol.
papers.datasets: Studies (2020-2025) applying federated learning to histopathology image classification (e.g. LC25000, TCGA CRC-DX, BreakHis, HAM10000, TCGA, MC-CRC datasets).

papers.evaluation: Narrative and tabular synthesis of performance, advantages and limitations.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: FL achieves performance comparable to centralised learning in many studies, but issues include IID assumptions, non-IID performance drops, communication and encryption costs, and lack of large-scale validation; recommends standardised evaluation, efficient communication and real deployments.

papers.title: Federated learning and differential privacy for medical image analysis
papers.authors: Adnan M, Kalra S, Cresswell JC, Taylor GW, Tizhoosh HR
papers.aim: To test federated learning with differential privacy for pathology slide classification.
papers.method: Slides are summarised into patch mosaics, encoded and classified with attention MIL; simulated hospitals train with differential privacy and the server averages models, varying site number, size and difference.
papers.result: Private federated training came close to central training; small and very different sites reduced performance.
papers.tools: DP-SGD, FedAvg, federated learning, DenseNet, differential privacy
papers.gap: Simulated federation; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Public TCGA only.
papers.methodologyDetail: WSIs are summarised into a representative mosaic of patches, encoded with a pretrained network, and classified with attention-based multiple-instance learning. Each simulated hospital trains locally with differential privacy and the server averages models. The study varies the number of hospitals, their data size and how different their data are, and checks external validity. It supports the feasibility of private federated pathology for WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Simulation case study of differentially private federated learning on public histopathology data (University of Waterloo, Vector Institute, Layer 6; Scientific Reports 2022).
papers.datasets: TCGA whole-slide images (lung cancer subtype tasks) distributed across simulated hospitals with IID and non-IID splits and varying client numbers and dataset sizes; external validation on a different source domain.
papers.preprocessing: Mosaic patch selection per WSI: tissue thresholding, clustering of patches, random 10% per cluster; 1000x1000 patches at 20x (0.5 mpp); DenseNet features.
papers.modelDetails: Attention-based multiple-instance learning (MEM model) trained locally with DP-SGD for quantitative privacy bounds and aggregated by FedAvg.
papers.training: DP-SGD with varying privacy budgets; FedAvg rounds (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy/AUC vs centralised training; effect of privacy budget, number of clients, IID vs non-IID; external validation.
papers.baselines: Centralised (non-private) training.
papers.results: Differentially private federated training achieved performance close to centralised training with strong privacy guarantees; non-IID data and small sites reduced performance.

papers.title: IDH Mutation Assessment in Gliomas from Anatomical MRI Using Deep Learning: A Comparative Analysis of Centralized and Federated Learning Frameworks
papers.authors: Bas A, Ozturk-Isik E
papers.aim: To compare central and federated training for predicting IDH mutation from routine MRI.
papers.method: IDH was predicted from MRI slices with different ways of highlighting the tumour while keeping context, trained centrally and federated across simulated sites.
papers.result: Keeping surrounding context improved results; federation protected privacy with some loss of accuracy.
papers.tools: federated learning, U-Net, ANTs
papers.gap: Simulated federation; 2D slices; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Single-source data.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a public glioma dataset with expert segmentations, the authors predict IDH mutation from routine MRI slices, comparing ways of emphasising the tumour while keeping surrounding context, and compare central training with federated training across simulated sites. Keeping context helped, and federation cost some accuracy. It quantifies the federation trade-off for a brain-tumour molecular task relevant to H5.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective comparison of centralised and federated learning (Bogazici University, Istanbul; Diagnostics 2026).
papers.datasets: UCSF-PDGM: 501 pre-operative diffuse gliomas (103 IDH-mutant, 398 wild-type), 3T GE MRI (T1c IR-SPGR, 3D T2 FSE, FLAIR) with expert-corrected multi-compartment segmentations.
papers.preprocessing: Resampling to 1 mm isotropic, nonlinear co-registration with ANTs, deep-learning skull stripping; tumour ROI from combined compartments; Naive Soft Filtering (non-tumour weight 0.3) or Gradient-Based Soft Filtering; axial slices with FLAIR, T1c, T2 mapped to RGB channels.
papers.modelDetails: 2D CNN classifiers for IDH status trained centrally or with federated learning across simulated clients.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity for IDH prediction; centralised vs federated.
papers.baselines: Centralised learning; hard tumour masking.
papers.results: Context-preserving soft filtering substantially improved performance across training schemes; federated learning was a privacy-preserving alternative but with some performance cost relative to centralised training.

papers.title: Byzantine robust federated learning for heterogeneous brain MRI using multisignal gradient fingerprinting and adaptive trust aggregation
papers.authors: Karami M, Kebriaei H, Ghassemi F, Azadegan H
papers.aim: To protect federated brain MRI training from faulty or malicious hospital updates.
papers.method: Each update is described by several plausibility signals, trust weights are learned for aggregation, and a batch-norm-aware optimiser handles site differences; tested under attacks.
papers.result: Detected scaling attacks with F1 above 0.98 while keeping accuracy, also with very different sites.
papers.tools: federated learning, VAE, FedAvg
papers.gap: Classification, not tumour segmentation; adaptive parts not fully exercised in clinical runs.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Simulated clients; short clinical runs.
papers.methodologyDetail: The framework protects federated training on brain MRI from malicious or corrupted hospital updates by describing each update with several signals of plausibility and contribution, learning trust weights for aggregation, and combining this with a batch-normalisation-aware optimiser suited to heterogeneous sites. It was tested on benchmark data and a clinical brain MRI cohort under strengthened attacks. Robust aggregation is a safeguard for a federation in which sites may have faulty data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with benchmark and clinical MRI validation (Sharif University of Technology and partners; Scientific Reports 2026).
papers.datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, an Alzheimer's MRI dataset (proof of concept) and the OASIS clinical brain-MRI cohort (clinical validation); simulated clients with IID, Dirichlet and label-skew (70%, 90%) partitions.
papers.preprocessing: Partitioned into clients; attacks injected (30-40% malicious clients: scaling, sign flip, Gaussian noise, label flip).
papers.modelDetails: Trust-aware federated learning: each client update gets a six-dimensional fingerprint (VAE reconstruction error, cosine similarity to server reference, peer similarity, gradient norm, sign consistency, Monte Carlo Shapley contribution); a dual-attention module and reinforcement-learning controller map fingerprints to trust weights within FedBN-P (FedBN with proximal regularisation).
papers.training: Multiple seeds with mean, SD and 95% CIs; 8-round clinical runs used warm-started VAE/RL modules.
papers.evaluation: Detection F1 for malicious clients, accuracy under attacks and heterogeneity, scalability.
papers.baselines: Widely used Byzantine-robust defences (e.g. Krum, trimmed mean, median, FLTrust) and FedAvg.
papers.results: Detection F1 above 0.98 for gradient-scaling attacks while preserving accuracy under magnitude-preserving attacks where explicit detection was limited; robust under non-IID splits.
papers.statistics: Means, SDs and 95% CIs; statistical comparisons with baselines.

papers.title: Federated learning for lesion segmentation in multiple sclerosis: a real-world multi-center feasibility study
papers.authors: Hindawi S, Szubstarski B, Boernert E, Tackenberg B, Wuerfel J
papers.aim: To test federated MS lesion segmentation across three real hospitals.
papers.method: nnU-Net trained federatedly with an open-source imaging platform and a governance layer that kept each hospital in control; different round settings compared.
papers.result: Competitive segmentation; 50 rounds of one local epoch worked best, and results varied by site.
papers.tools: nnU-Net, FedAvg, federated learning
papers.gap: No calibration or uncertainty analysis; MS lesions rather than tumours.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Three sites; industry-led.
papers.methodologyDetail: Three hospitals trained one MS lesion segmentation model together using nnU-Net, an open-source imaging platform for local execution and a governance layer that kept each institution in control of what ran on its data. Fifty rounds of one local epoch each worked best, as more local training destabilised FedAvg. It is a practical template for deploying nnU-Net federatedly in hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Real-world multi-centre feasibility study of federated learning (Roche with three hospital sites; Frontiers in Neurology 2025).
papers.datasets: 512 MRI cases from three sites for MS lesion segmentation, without sharing raw data.
papers.preprocessing: Local preprocessing and nnU-Net configuration at each site.
papers.modelDetails: Self-configuring nnU-Net trained with FedAvg in a client-server architecture built on Kaapana (open-source imaging platform) with Apheris enterprise governance for secure, governed execution.
papers.training: 50 federated rounds, one local epoch per round (more local epochs caused abrupt degradation).
papers.evaluation: Dice and lesion-level metrics per site vs local models.
papers.baselines: Locally trained models.
papers.results: Federated model achieved competitive segmentation; performance varied across sites due to heterogeneity; most loss reduction in first 10-15 rounds.

papers.title: Magnetic resonance imaging-based deep learning for predicting subtypes of glioma
papers.authors: Yang Z, Zhang P, Ding Y, Deng L, Zhang T, Liu Y
papers.aim: To predict WHO 2021 glioma molecular subtypes from routine MRI.
papers.method: Deep learning models trained on four public glioma MRI datasets using each sequence alone and all together, tested on the hospital's own patients.
papers.result: The model using all four sequences gave the best AUCs on the local test set.
papers.tools: Python
papers.gap: Small local test set; no uncertainty; imaging-only molecular prediction remains imperfect.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors pooled four public glioma MRI datasets for training and validation and tested on their own hospital's patients, predicting the three main WHO 2021 molecular groups from routine sequences. Using all four sequences worked best. Training on public data and testing on a local cohort mirrors the planned strategy for the MRI Agent in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-dataset study with an independent local test set (Hefei and Xuzhou hospitals, China; ethics XYFY2022-KL476-01).
papers.datasets: 811 adult gliomas: TCGA-LGG (86), TCGA-GBM (88), UCSF-PDGM (382), Erasmus Glioma Database (191) for training/validation, and 64 local patients (2019-2022) as independent test; IDH-wildtype 490, IDH-mutant 1p/19q intact 105, IDH-mutant co-deleted 216.
papers.preprocessing: Inclusion required T1w, T1c, T2w and FLAIR and clear molecular status; poor-quality scans excluded after consensus of two physicians; ROI delineation.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning models built on five input categories (each sequence and all sequences combined) for three-class WHO 2021 molecular subtype prediction.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, precision, recall, F1 per subtype on validation and independent test.
papers.baselines: Single-sequence models.
papers.results: The all-sequence model gave the best AUCs for the three subtypes on the independent test set (exact values in paper).
papers.statistics: Chi-square, Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni; ROC analysis in Python.

papers.title: Deep-learning and conventional radiomics to predict IDH genotyping status based on magnetic resonance imaging data in adult diffuse glioma
papers.authors: Zhang H, Fan X, Zhang J, Wei Z, Feng W, Hu Y, Ni J, Yao F, Zhou G, Wan C, et al.
papers.aim: To compare deep learning and radiomics for predicting IDH status from multi-vendor MRI.
papers.method: Deep features and thousands of radiomics features from about 500 gliomas, with models evaluated by nested cross-validation.
papers.result: Deep features beat radiomics (AUC 0.915 vs 0.830); combining both was most stable.
papers.tools: radiomics, PyTorch
papers.gap: No external test; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; IDH only.
papers.methodologyDetail: From multi-vendor MRI of nearly 500 gliomas, the authors extracted both deep features and thousands of handcrafted radiomics features and built models to predict IDH mutation, evaluated by nested cross-validation. Deep features were better and combining them improved stability. It shows the heterogeneity typical of real data and a careful validation design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective study combining public and local data (Nanjing Medical University; Frontiers in Oncology 2023).
papers.datasets: 486 adult diffuse gliomas from TCGA-GBM, TCGA-LGG and the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (2015-2020) with known IDH status and four MRI sequences from 1.5T/3T Philips, GE and Siemens scanners.
papers.preprocessing: Heterogeneous protocols; sequences of 11 consecutive slices with stride 2 (12 samples per patient per modality); 6,736 conventional radiomics features.
papers.modelDetails: Deep-learning signatures and conventional radiomics features combined as predictors in machine-learning models for IDH status.
papers.training: PyTorch, sklearn, PyCaret; SiLU activations, BCE loss, batch 32, lr 1e-6; nested 10-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy and relative standard deviation of AUC across folds and subgroups.
papers.baselines: Conventional radiomics alone.
papers.results: DL signatures outperformed radiomics (AUC 0.915 +/- 0.054 vs 0.830; accuracy 0.835), and combined models were most stable.

papers.title: Clinical application of machine-based deep learning in patients with radiologically presumed adult-type diffuse glioma grades 2 or 3
papers.authors: Gómez Vecchio T, Neimantaite A, Thurin E, Furtner J, Solheim O, Pallud J, Berger M, Widhalm G, Bartek J, Häggström I, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether deep learning adds value for IDH prediction in presumed lower-grade gliomas in practice.
papers.method: A deep learning IDH predictor was compared with a simple clinical model in a large international cohort and tested on an unseen external set.
papers.result: Deep learning was not clearly better than the simple clinical model, a caution for imaging-only molecular prediction.
papers.tools: logistic regression
papers.gap: WHO 2016 classification; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; heterogeneous cohorts.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a large international cohort of presumed lower-grade gliomas, the authors compared a deep learning IDH predictor with a simple clinical model and tested both on an unseen external dataset. Deep learning did not clearly add value in this clinically realistic setting. This is an important negative result supporting cautious use of imaging-only molecular prediction and a fair comparison with simple baselines.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre study with external validation (University of Gothenburg and neurosurgical departments in Sweden, Norway, France, Austria and the USA; Neuro-Oncology Advances 2024).
papers.datasets: 1,576 screened; 469 adults with WHO 2016 diffuse glioma grade 2-3 included (modelling cohort from six departments plus Erasmus Glioma Database as unseen external cohort); 75% IDH-mutant, 37% 1p/19q co-deleted.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions for other diagnoses (570), missing molecular data (181) and missing sequences after processing (356); routine pre-operative MRI.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning model for IDH mutation from routine MRI compared with a clinical multivariable model (age, sex, imaging features) and combined models.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, clinical usefulness (e.g. high-specificity operating points) on the external cohort.
papers.baselines: Clinical model based on age and simple imaging features.
papers.results: In radiologically presumed lower-grade glioma, deep learning was not clearly superior to conventional clinical models for IDH prediction; cohorts differed in sex distribution and IDH wild-type rate (30.9% vs 12.9%).

papers.title: Federated radiomics analysis of preoperative MRI across institutions: toward integrated glioma segmentation and molecular subtyping
papers.authors: Ren R, Zhu A, Li Y, Liu H, Huang G, Gu J, Ni J, Miao Z
papers.aim: To segment gliomas and predict molecular markers with one federated model across institutions.
papers.method: Each public glioma dataset acts as a site; a federated multi-task model segments the tumour and predicts several markers, tested on an external cohort.
papers.result: Good segmentation and marker prediction on an external set of 466 patients.
papers.tools: radiomics
papers.gap: Simulated institutions; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.

papers.methodologyDetail: The study treats each public glioma dataset as a separate institution and trains a single federated model that both segments the tumour region and predicts several molecular markers, then tests it on an external cohort. It demonstrates federated multi-task learning for integrated glioma analysis.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective federated multi-task study with external validation (Jiangnan University and partners; Frontiers in Radiology 2025).

papers.training: Federated training across dataset-sites (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice for segmentation; AUC for molecular predictions on external validation.
papers.baselines: Locally trained and centralised models.
papers.results: Good segmentation and molecular-prediction performance on the external dataset of 466 patients.

papers.title: The University of Texas Southwestern Glioma Dataset - MRI, Molecular Markers and Segmentations
papers.authors: Reddy DD, Saadat N, Holcomb JM, Wagner BC, Truong NC, Bowerman J, Hatanpaa KJ, Patel TR, Pinho MC, Yu F, et al.

papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.

papers.datasets: UTSW glioma cohort: pre-operative multi-parametric MRI with molecular markers (e.g. IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT) and tumour segmentations.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised preprocessing (registration, skull stripping) and segmentation curation described in the paper.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (dataset release with technical validation).
papers.training: Not applicable.

papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Provides a public benchmark linking MRI features with tumour genetics and segmentations.

papers.title: Lightweight self supervised learning framework for domain generalization in histopathology
papers.authors: Shafique A, Dy A, Qin X, Alshamlan N, Androutsos D, Done SJ, Khademi A
papers.aim: To build a lightweight pathology model that stays robust when the slide scanner changes.
papers.method: HistoLite trains small autoencoders with contrastive learning; the same slides scanned on two scanners measure pure scanner shift.
papers.result: Smallest drop under scanner shift with far less compute than foundation models, though large models were more accurate in some settings.
papers.tools: autoencoder, self-supervised learning, UNI
papers.gap: Breast tissue; no uncertainty output.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Single evaluation cohort.
papers.methodologyDetail: HistoLite trains small autoencoders with contrastive learning on public breast slides to learn features that do not change with the scanner. A carefully designed test scanned the same slides on two scanners and registered them, so the change in features and in classification could be attributed purely to scanner shift. HistoLite was more robust to that shift than much larger foundation models. A lightweight approach suits hospitals with limited GPUs.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmarking against foundation models (Toronto Metropolitan University and partners; Scientific Reports 2025).
papers.datasets: Training: 2,761 public breast cancer WSIs (CAMELYON16, CAMELYON17, HEROHE, TCGA-BRCA). Evaluation: 111 FFPE breast cancer slides from OICR scanned on Aperio AT2 and Sakura VisionTek (222 WSIs), with 9,904 aligned 512x512 patches (2,959 tumour, 1,993 non-tumour per scanner) from pathologist-annotated HPFs.
papers.preprocessing: VisionTek upsampled and affinely registered to Aperio; patches extracted at identical coordinates across scanners at 0.5 mpp.
papers.modelDetails: HistoLite: lightweight dual-stream autoencoder contrastive self-supervised framework (41M parameters; encoder 7.6M per stream) learning domain-invariant features.
papers.training: Self-supervised training with augmentations (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Zero-shot representation shift across scanners; downstream tumour vs non-tumour patch classification.
papers.baselines: Histopathology foundation models (KimiaNet, PathDino, HIPT, iBOT-Path, Hibou-B, UNI, Virchow, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath).
papers.results: HistoLite had low representation shift between scanners and the lowest performance drop under scanner shift, with far less compute than foundation models, though large FMs had higher absolute accuracy in some settings.

papers.title: Generalizable biomarker prediction from cancer pathology slides with self-supervised deep learning: A retrospective multi-centric study
papers.authors: Niehues JM, Quirke P, West NP, Grabsch HI, van Treeck M, Schirris Y, Veldhuizen GP, Hutchins GGA, Richman SD, Foersch S, et al.
papers.aim: To find which pipeline predicts genetic biomarkers from cancer slides best on new hospitals.
papers.method: Six pipelines were compared, trained on one colorectal trial cohort and validated on a large independent cohort.
papers.result: Self-supervised features with attention MIL generalised best (MSI AUROC 0.94, BRAF 0.82); some mutations were not predictable.
papers.tools: Comparison of six deep learning approaches: ImageNet-pretrained tile-level (INPT) vs self-supervised encoders (Ciga, Wang) with attention-based…
papers.gap: Colorectal, not brain; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors systematically compared six pipelines for predicting genetic biomarkers from colorectal cancer slides, training on one trial cohort and validating on a large independent cohort. Self-supervised feature extractors combined with attention-based multiple-instance learning generalised best, while some mutations were not predictable. It supports the chosen pathology pipeline (self-supervised encoder + attention MIL) for WP4.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-centric study with large external validation (Dresden, Leeds, Heidelberg and others; Cell Reports Medicine 2023).
papers.datasets: Colorectal cancer H&E slides from two large multi-centric studies (QUASAR trial for training and DACHS for external validation; thousands of patients) with MSI, BRAF, KRAS, NRAS and PIK3CA status.
papers.preprocessing: Tiling, colour normalisation; features from self-supervised encoders.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of six deep learning approaches: ImageNet-pretrained tile-level (INPT) vs self-supervised encoders (Ciga, Wang) with attention-based multiple-instance learning; multi-input models.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUROC for each biomarker, internal and external.
papers.baselines: INPT approach and other architectures.
papers.results: Self-supervised attention MIL (Wang encoder) performed best: AUROC 0.94 (MSI), 0.82 (BRAF), 0.67 (KRAS), 0.52 (NRAS), 0.57 (PIK3CA); MSI and BRAF predictable, others below clinical grade; multi-input models generalised better for BRAF.

papers.title: Self-supervised attention-based deep learning for pan-cancer mutation prediction from histopathology
papers.authors: Saldanha OL, Loeffler CML, Niehues JM, van Treeck M, Seraphin TP, Hewitt KJ, Cifci D, Veldhuizen GP, Ramesh S, Pearson AT, et al.

papers.evaluation: AUROC per gene, internal and external.

papers.title: Cluster-based histopathology phenotype representation learning by self-supervised multi-class-token hierarchical ViT

papers.title: A clinical benchmark of public self-supervised pathology foundation models
papers.authors: Campanella G, Chen S, Singh M, Verma R, Muehlstedt S, Zeng J, Stock A, Croken M, Veremis B, Elmas A, et al.

papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of benchmarks built from public research collections, this study uses real clinical slides to test publicly released pathology foundation models under the same downstream protocol, and examines what in their training explains performance. It provides guidance on which encoder to use as the frozen feature extractor for the Pathology Agent and shows the value of testing on local data.
papers.studyDesign: Clinical benchmark of public pathology foundation models (Mount Sinai, MSKCC and partners; Nature Communications 2025).
papers.datasets: Clinical slide datasets from routine practice across several institutions and cancer types, curated for diagnostic and biomarker tasks and released for benchmarking.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised tiling and feature extraction for each foundation model.
papers.modelDetails: Systematic evaluation of public self-supervised pathology foundation models (e.g. UNI, Virchow, Prov-GigaPath, CTransPath, Phikon and others) with a common slide-level aggregator.
papers.training: Downstream aggregator training per task with consistent protocol.
papers.evaluation: AUC across clinical tasks; analysis of pretraining data size, model size and training recipe.
papers.baselines: All foundation models compared with each other and ImageNet baselines.
papers.results: Foundation models improved over ImageNet features but no single model dominated all tasks; insights on best practices for training and selecting pretrained models; benchmark released.
papers.availability: Datasets and code released for community evaluation.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning for 3D Medical Image Analysis using 3D SimCLR and Monte Carlo Dropout
papers.authors: Yamen Ali, Aiham Taleb, Marina M. -C. Höhne, Christoph Lippert
papers.aim: To use 3D self-supervised learning and Monte Carlo dropout for tumour segmentation with few labels.
papers.method: 3D SimCLR pretraining on volumes, fine-tuning for brain and pancreatic tumour segmentation, and MC dropout at prediction.
papers.result: Pretraining improved Dice with fewer labels, and MC dropout improved results further.
papers.tools: SimCLR, Monte Carlo dropout, fine-tuning, MC dropout, self-supervised learning
papers.gap: Small workshop study; uncertainty used for accuracy, not calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Public benchmark data.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors extend contrastive self-supervised learning to 3D volumes by contrasting augmented versions of the same 3D patch against other patches, then fine-tune the encoder for brain-tumour and pancreatic tumour segmentation with limited labels, and add Monte Carlo dropout at prediction time. Pretraining reduced label needs and MC dropout helped further. It directly supports H3 (self-supervised pretraining on local MRI).
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation (TU Berlin, Hasso Plattner Institute; ML4H 2021).
papers.datasets: Brain tumour segmentation from 3D MRI (BraTS) and pancreas tumour segmentation from 3D CT (Medical Segmentation Decathlon); unlabelled scans for pretraining, limited labels for fine-tuning.
papers.preprocessing: Each 3D scan split into equally sized non-overlapping 3D patches; two random composite augmentations per patch (3D rotation, colour distortion, Gaussian noise/blur, Sobel filtering, identity).
papers.modelDetails: 3D SimCLR: 3D-CNN encoder with non-linear projection head trained with NT-Xent contrastive loss; encoder fine-tuned for segmentation; Monte Carlo dropout at inference.
papers.training: Pretraining then fine-tuning with varying fractions of labelled data (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice on test data with different amounts of labels; effect of MC dropout.
papers.baselines: Training from scratch; 2D SimCLR or other SSL baselines.
papers.results: 3D SimCLR pretraining improved data efficiency and segmentation Dice, and MC dropout at inference further improved results on both tasks.

papers.title: CONSULT: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning for Few-shot Tumor Detection
papers.authors: Sin Chee Chin, Xuan Zhang, Lee Yeong Khang, Wenming Yang
papers.aim: To detect brain tumours when only a few normal scans are available.
papers.method: CONSULT adapts a feature extractor by contrasting normal brain MRI with synthetic tumour-like defects, then flags anomalies against a memory of normal features.
papers.result: Better than state-of-the-art anomaly detectors in very few-shot settings.
papers.tools: self-supervised learning
papers.gap: 2D slices; detection only; synthetic anomalies may not reflect real tumours.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Single public dataset; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: With only a handful of normal brain scans, CONSULT adapts a feature extractor to brain MRI by contrasting normal images with synthetic tumour-like defects, then detects tumours as anomalies relative to a memory of normal features. It is an approach for detecting unusual cases when labelled tumours are scarce, which can complement the out-of-distribution check in the escalation rule.
papers.studyDesign: Method development for few-shot anomaly detection (Tsinghua University, ViTrox; preprint).
papers.datasets: Public brain MRI dataset; training on 2-8 healthy images only (K2-K8 shots), all tumour images used for validation; images resized to 256x256.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic tumour-like anomalies generated with Bezier curves; elastic distortion and translation for normal images.
papers.modelDetails: CONSULT: stage 1 fine-tunes a pretrained feature extractor with attention modules on brain MRI using contrastive learning with a new Tritanh loss on synthetic anomalies; stage 2 replaces PatchCore's feature extractor with the fine-tuned one for anomaly detection.
papers.training: Stage 1: 50 epochs, Adam lr 1e-4; stage 2: coreset ratio 10%, k=9 nearest neighbours.
papers.evaluation: Image-level AUROC for tumour detection with 2-8 shots.
papers.baselines: f-AnoGAN, GANomaly, PaDIM, EfficientAD, PatchCore.
papers.results: Outperformed state-of-the-art anomaly detectors in extreme few-shot settings, improving with more shots.

papers.title: BraTS-PEDs: Results of the Multi-Consortium International Pediatric Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2023
papers.authors: Anahita Fathi Kazerooni, Nastaran Khalili, Xinyang Liu, Debanjan Haldar, Zhifan Jiang, Anna Zapaishchykova, Julija Pavaine, Lubdha M. Shah, Blaise V. Jones, Nakul Sheth, et al.
papers.aim: To set up and report the first large paediatric brain tumour segmentation challenge.
papers.method: BraTS-PEDs collected expert-labelled routine paediatric MRI from many institutions and summarised the competing methods.
papers.result: 18 teams took part; the best methods were ensembles of nnU-Net, Swin UNETR and related networks.
papers.tools: nnU-Net, UNETR, Auto3DSeg, SegResNet, MedNeXt
papers.gap: Segmentation only; no uncertainty ranking.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: High-grade paediatric glioma only.
papers.methodologyDetail: BraTS-PEDs created the first large multi-consortium benchmark for paediatric brain-tumour segmentation, with expert labels on routine-care MRI from many institutions, and summarised the methods of competing teams. Winning approaches were ensembles of nnU-Net, Swin UNETR and related networks. It provides a public set for checking the MRI Agent on paediatric cases, which the registry will include.
papers.studyDesign: International segmentation challenge and results paper (CBTN, DIPG/DMG Registry, CONNECT and many institutions; MELBA 2024).
papers.datasets: Multi-consortium paediatric high-grade glioma MRI (astrocytoma, DMG/DIPG) with pre- and post-contrast T1, T2 and FLAIR from treatment-naive sessions; heterogeneous protocols and scanners.
papers.preprocessing: Quality control by experienced researchers; exclusion of low-quality scans and infants under one month; standard BraTS preprocessing; expert-refined labels.
papers.modelDetails: Challenge design: participants' methods included ensembles of nnU-Net and Swin UNETR, Auto3DSeg, self-supervised nnU-Net, STU-Net, SegResNet+MedNeXt ensembles, and others.
papers.training: Per team; unlimited validation on the Synapse platform.
papers.evaluation: Lesion-wise Dice and Hausdorff distance on held-out test data; cumulative rank across subjects.
papers.baselines: Participating teams ranked against each other.
papers.results: 18 teams submitted 159 validation entries; nine completed testing; top methods were ensembles of established architectures; the challenge fostered clinician-AI collaboration and data sharing.

papers.title: Imbalance-Aware Self-Supervised Learning for 3D Radiomic Representations
papers.authors: Hongwei Li, Fei-Fei Xue, Krishna Chaitanya, Shengda Luo, Ivan Ezhov, Benedikt Wiestler, Jianguo Zhang, Bjoern Menze
papers.aim: To learn 3D tumour representations without labels while handling class and centre imbalance.
papers.method: A memory-efficient Siamese network compares augmented views of each scan, with batches rebalanced using unsupervised clusters; then glioma grade is classified.
papers.result: Better than handcrafted radiomics and other baselines on both tasks.
papers.tools: radiomics
papers.gap: Single sequence; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Small downstream sets.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method learns 3D tumour representations without labels by comparing two augmented views of each scan in a memory-efficient Siamese network, and handles imbalance between classes and centres by re-weighting or rebalancing training batches based on unsupervised clusters. The representations then classify glioma grade better than handcrafted radiomics. Local registry data will also be imbalanced by site and tumour type.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (TUM, Zurich, ETH, SUSTech; MICCAI 2021 workshop/preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS (326 patients, FLAIR only, imbalanced grade labels and centres) and NSCLC-radiomics lung CT (420 patients, stage I/II/III ratio 2:1:6).
papers.preprocessing: Tumour-centred 96x96x96 bounding boxes for BraTS; 224x224x224 lung boxes resized to 112^3 for CT; intensities rescaled to [0,255].
papers.modelDetails: 3DSiam: 3D Siamese self-supervised network trained with extensive augmentation (affine, appearance, contrast, noise); RE/SE module clusters features with k-means and uses sample re-weighting or sample selection to counter data imbalance.
papers.training: Details in supplement.
papers.evaluation: Downstream classification of high vs low grade glioma and lung cancer stage using learned representations.
papers.baselines: Classical radiomics and supervised/self-supervised baselines without imbalance handling.
papers.results: Imbalance-aware self-supervised representations outperformed radiomics and other baselines on both tasks.

papers.title: Residual Vision Transformer (ResViT) Based Self-Supervised Learning Model for Brain Tumor Classification
papers.authors: Meryem Altin Karagoz, O. Ufuk Nalbantoglu, Geoffrey C. Fox
papers.aim: To improve brain tumour classification with a self-supervised residual vision transformer.
papers.method: ResViT is pretrained without labels on brain MRI and fine-tuned on several public 2D datasets.
papers.result: Highest accuracy among compared models (90.6% BraTS, 98.5% Figshare, 98.5% Kaggle), on curated 2D data.
papers.tools: Vision Transformer, fine-tuning, self-supervised learning, Transformer, ViT, ResNet
papers.gap: 2D curated datasets; no external clinical test; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: A hybrid residual-transformer network is first pretrained without labels on brain MRI and then fine-tuned to classify tumour types on several public 2D datasets, giving strong accuracy. It supports self-supervised pretraining for limited MRI data, though on curated 2D datasets.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public brain MRI datasets (preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS (T1 sequence), Figshare brain tumour dataset (3,064 slices, three tumour types) and a Kaggle brain MRI dataset.
papers.preprocessing: 2D slices with standard resizing and normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Residual Vision Transformer (ResViT) self-supervised pretraining (e.g. masked/generative pretext) followed by fine-tuning for brain tumour classification.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy on each dataset.
papers.baselines: CNNs and ViTs without SSL pretraining.
papers.results: Highest accuracies among compared models: 90.56% on BraTS T1, 98.53% on Figshare, 98.47% on the Kaggle dataset.

papers.title: A self-supervised framework for learning whole slide representations
papers.authors: Xinhai Hou, Cheng Jiang, Akhil Kondepudi, Yiwei Lyu, Asadur Chowdury, Honglak Lee, Todd C. Hollon
papers.aim: To learn whole-slide pathology representations without labels.
papers.method: SPT treats a slide as a sequence of patch tokens and trains a transformer to give consistent representations for different views of the same slide.
papers.result: Beat weakly supervised methods for diagnosis, subtyping and mutation prediction, including glioma molecular groups.
papers.tools: Transformer, self-supervised learning, fine-tuning
papers.gap: No uncertainty or calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; compute-heavy.
papers.methodologyDetail: SPT learns whole-slide representations without labels by treating each slide as a sequence of patch tokens and training a transformer to produce consistent representations across different transformed views of the same slide. On brain-tumour benchmarks from optical and H&E imaging and on standard TCGA tasks, it beat weakly supervised aggregators. Slide-level self-supervision is useful when diagnosis labels are few.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmarking (University of Michigan; IRB HUM00083059 for SRH data).
papers.datasets: Five benchmarks: SRH CNS tumour benchmark (six CNS tumour types plus normal brain; 2,035 training and 925 evaluation WSIs, pathologist-labelled); H&E diffuse glioma molecular classification from TCGA and Digital Brain Tumour Atlas (2,309 training, 341 TCGA evaluation slides, three WHO molecular subgroups); TCGA BRCA, NSCLC and RCC.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs partitioned into non-overlapping patches; frozen pre-trained patch encoder produces tokens with coordinates.
papers.modelDetails: Slide Pre-trained Transformers (SPT): a transformer whole-slide encoder trained with self-supervision using view-generation strategies from language and vision (splitting, cropping, masking, dropping patches) on patch tokens; compatible with existing SSL objectives.
papers.training: Patch encoder frozen; large mini-batch training of slide encoder (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Slide-level classification accuracy/AUC with linear probes and fine-tuning for diagnosis, subtyping and mutation prediction.
papers.baselines: ABMIL and other MIL aggregators; slide-level SSL baselines.
papers.results: SPT significantly outperformed baselines for histopathologic diagnosis, cancer subtyping and genetic mutation prediction, including glioma molecular groups and SRH CNS tumours.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.authors: Richard J. Chen, Rahul G. Krishnan
papers.aim: To test whether self-supervised Vision Transformers learn meaningful tissue concepts in pathology.
papers.method: Several self-supervised encoders were trained on pathology patches and compared with ImageNet features at different amounts of training data.
papers.result: DINO-trained ViTs learned interpretable, data-efficient tissue features and were more robust without stain normalisation.
papers.tools: ResNet, SimCLR, DINO, ViT, transfer learning
papers.gap: No brain tumours; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Workshop study.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained several self-supervised encoders on pathology patches and compared them with ImageNet features on slide- and patch-level tasks with varying amounts of training data. DINO-trained Vision Transformers learned meaningful tissue concepts and worked well with less data. This underlies later pathology foundation models used as frozen encoders.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical comparison of self-supervised pretraining in pathology (Harvard Medical School, University of Toronto; workshop preprint).
