papers.datasets: TCGA BRCA (IDC vs ILC subtyping, 10-fold CV with 25-100% of training data) and CRC-100K patch-level tissue phenotyping with and without Macenko normalisation, plus other patch tasks.
papers.preprocessing: Macenko stain normalisation in some experiments.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of ImageNet transfer (ResNet-50), SimCLR (ResNet-50) and DINO (ViT) self-supervised encoders pretrained on histopathology; KNN on embeddings for patch tasks; weakly supervised slide classification.
papers.training: Self-supervised pretraining on TCGA patches (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUC for slide subtyping and patch phenotyping; attention visualisation.
papers.baselines: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50.
papers.results: ImageNet features were a strong baseline (BRCA AUC 0.884 vs SimCLR 0.879, DINO 0.886); DINO ViTs learned data-efficient, interpretable features capturing distinct tissue concepts, and were more robust without stain normalisation.

papers.title: DeepSMILE: Contrastive self-supervised pre-training benefits MSI and HRD classification directly from H&E whole-slide images in colorectal and breast cancer
papers.authors: Yoni Schirris, Efstratios Gavves, Iris Nederlof, Hugo Mark Horlings, Jonas Teuwen
papers.aim: To predict MSI and HRD from slides with fewer labels using contrastive self-supervised pretraining.
papers.method: DeepSMILE pretrains a tile encoder without labels and aggregates tiles with a MIL model that accounts for tumour variation.
papers.result: Matched the supervised baseline with only 40% of labels and improved AUROC.
papers.tools: SimCLR, self-supervised learning, multiple instance learning
papers.gap: Colorectal and breast; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: TCGA only.
papers.methodologyDetail: DeepSMILE pretrains a tile encoder on cancer tissue without labels and aggregates tiles with a multiple-instance model that accounts for variation across the tumour, predicting genomic labels such as MSI and HRD from slides. With self-supervision it matched the supervised baseline using 40% of the labels. It reinforces that domain-specific self-supervised encoders reduce labelling needs.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on TCGA (Netherlands Cancer Institute, University of Amsterdam, Radboud; Medical Image Analysis 2022).
papers.datasets: TCGA-CRCk: 192,314 colour-normalised tumour tiles from 360 patients (train 260 incl. 39 MSI; test 100 incl. 26 MSI), 5-fold patient-level splits; TCGA-BC breast cancer WSIs with HRD scores (median and tertile binarisation).
papers.preprocessing: Tiles from tumour annotations; colour normalisation; HRD labels binarised at median (mHRD) or by tertiles (tHRD).
papers.modelDetails: DeepSMILE: SimCLR contrastive self-supervised pretraining of a tile feature extractor on cancer tissue, plus variability-aware deep multiple-instance learning (modelling tumour heterogeneity) for slide-level MSI and HRD prediction.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUROC for MSI and HRD with varying amounts of labelled data.
papers.baselines: ImageNet-pretrained features and standard MIL; two-stage tile-supervised methods.
papers.results: Reached baseline performance using only 40% of labelled data on both datasets and improved overall AUROC.

papers.title: Anomaly Detection-Inspired Few-Shot Medical Image Segmentation Through Self-Supervision With Supervoxels
papers.authors: Stine Hansen, Srishti Gautam, Robert Jenssen, Michael Kampffmeyer
papers.aim: To segment new structures from one labelled example.
papers.method: ADNet models only the target and treats everything else as anomaly, learning the threshold, trained with supervoxels as automatic pseudo-labels.
papers.result: Better than earlier few-shot segmentation methods without needing training annotations.
papers.tools: PyTorch, ResNet
papers.gap: Cardiac and abdominal organs; no tumours; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: 2D slices within 3D volumes.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of modelling both organ and background, ADNet models only the target structure from one labelled example and treats everything unlike it as anomalous, learning the threshold; training uses supervoxels as automatically generated pseudo-labels. It allows segmentation of new structures from very few annotations, relevant to delineating structures at risk for surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public 3D segmentation datasets (UiT The Arctic University of Norway; Medical Image Analysis 2022).
papers.datasets: MS-CMRSeg bSSFP (35 cardiac MRI scans) and CHAOS abdominal MRI (20 scans) and related public sets for few-shot organ segmentation.
papers.preprocessing: Supervoxels generated offline per volume for self-supervision.
papers.modelDetails: ADNet: anomaly-detection-inspired prototypical few-shot segmentation using only a foreground prototype, anomaly scores for query features and a learned threshold; supervoxel-based self-supervision for training without labels.
papers.training: PyTorch, ResNet-101 encoder pretrained on MS-COCO with 1x1 conv to 256 channels; SGD momentum 0.9, lr 1e-3 decaying 0.98 per 1k epochs, weight decay 5e-4, 50k iterations; foreground/background weights 1.0/0.1; 1.8 h on an RTX 2080Ti.
papers.evaluation: Dice in few-shot settings.
papers.baselines: SSL-ALPNet and other prototypical few-shot methods.
papers.results: Outperformed previous few-shot segmentation methods without needing annotations for training, especially for heterogeneous backgrounds.

papers.title: Towards Foundation Models and Few-Shot Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Volumetric Organ Segmentation
papers.authors: Julio Silva-Rodríguez, Jose Dolz, Ismail Ben Ayed
papers.aim: To adapt large segmentation foundation models to new structures with few labelled scans and little compute.
papers.method: A realistic hospital scenario comparing lightweight (parameter-efficient) adaptation methods with full fine-tuning.
papers.result: Small adapters beat full fine-tuning when labels were scarce, at much lower compute.
papers.tools: fine-tuning, ViT, LoRA
papers.gap: CT organs; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint version.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper defines a realistic hospital scenario in which a large pretrained segmentation model must be adapted to a new structure using only a few labelled scans and little compute, and compares lightweight adaptation methods. Small adapters beat full fine-tuning when labels are scarce. This is directly applicable to adapting brain segmentation models to local Sri Lankan scans.
papers.studyDesign: Method and benchmark development (ÉTS Montréal, CR-CHUM; preprint/Medical Image Analysis).
papers.datasets: Foundation model pretrained on 2,042 CT volumes from nine public datasets (BTCV, CHAOS, LiTS, KiTS, AbdomenCT-1K, AMOS, MSD, AbdomenCT-12organ, CT-ORG) with 29 partially labelled structures; adaptation to new tasks with K = 1, 5 or 10 labelled volumes.
papers.preprocessing: Standard CT preprocessing (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: Few-Shot Efficient Fine-Tuning (FSEFT) scenario: supervised volumetric segmentation foundation model (CNN/ViT encoder, CNN decoder) adapted with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, BitFit, AdaptFormer) or black-box adapters (linear probing and a new Spatial Adapter).
papers.training: Few-shot adaptation with limited compute (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice on downstream organ/tumour tasks with 1-10 labelled volumes.
papers.baselines: Full fine-tuning and training from scratch.
papers.results: Parameter-efficient and spatial black-box adapters outperformed full fine-tuning in data-scarce settings at much lower compute.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Guided Mutual Consistency Learning for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Yichi Zhang, Rushi Jiao, Qingcheng Liao, Dongyang Li, Jicong Zhang
papers.aim: To use unlabelled scans for medical image segmentation by learning only from confident predictions.
papers.method: Semi-supervised training enforces consistency over time and between masks and distance maps, guided by uncertainty; tested including glioma data.
papers.result: Better than state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods with few labels.
papers.tools: Uncertainty-guided mutual consistency: a network jointly predicts segmentation and signed distance maps;
papers.gap: Whole tumour from FLAIR only; uncertainty used internally, not reported for decisions.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Public datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: With only part of the scans labelled, the model learns from unlabelled scans by enforcing that its predictions are consistent over time and between two related outputs (masks and distance maps), but only where it is confident. On a glioma dataset it improved segmentation over other semi-supervised methods. It is a way to use the registry's many unlabelled scans.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public datasets (Beihang University; preprint/Medical Image Analysis).
papers.datasets: Left Atrium MRI (100 scans: 80 train with 16 labelled/64 unlabelled, 20 test) and multi-institutional pre-operative glioma MRI (335 patients; T2-FLAIR whole tumour; 250 train, 25 validation, 60 test) with labelled fractions of training data.
papers.preprocessing: Resampling to 1 mm isotropic; z-score normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Uncertainty-guided mutual consistency: a network jointly predicts segmentation and signed distance maps; intra-task consistency with self-ensembled predictions and cross-task consistency between tasks, using only relatively certain predictions (estimated uncertainty) for consistency learning on unlabelled data.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice, Jaccard, 95HD, ASD.
papers.baselines: Supervised baseline and semi-supervised methods (mean teacher, UA-MT, SASSNet, DTC and others).
papers.results: Outperformed state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods on both datasets, including glioma whole-tumour segmentation with few labels.

papers.title: M-GenSeg: Domain Adaptation For Target Modality Tumor Segmentation With Annotation-Efficient Supervision
papers.authors: Malo Alefsen de Boisredon d'Assier, Eugene Vorontsov, Samuel Kadoury
papers.aim: To segment tumours in a new MRI sequence that has no labels.
papers.method: M-GenSeg learns to translate between sequences and between healthy and tumour images, so source-sequence labels transfer to the target.
papers.result: Consistent Dice gains over domain-adaptation baselines with limited source labels.
papers.tools: PyTorch
papers.gap: Simulated modality shift within BraTS; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Generative training complexity.
papers.methodologyDetail: When the MRI sequence available at a new hospital differs from the one the model was trained on, M-GenSeg learns to translate between sequences and between healthy and tumour-containing images, so labels from the source sequence transfer to the target. It worked with limited source labels. This addresses sequence mismatch expected in Sri Lankan routine MRI.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public brain tumour dataset (Polytechnique Montréal, CR-CHUM, Paige; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS-derived brain tumour MRI with four modalities treated as unpaired source and target domains, plus healthy images; varying fractions of pixel-level source annotations.
papers.preprocessing: Same on-the-fly augmentation as GenSeg.
papers.modelDetails: M-GenSeg: semi-supervised generative model with shared latent representations performing healthy-diseased translation (tumour disentangling and synthetic tumour generation) and cross-modality translation, so source-modality pixel labels enable segmentation in an unannotated target modality; attention gates in skip connections.
papers.training: PyTorch on one A100; batch 15, AMSGrad (beta1 0.5, beta2 0.999), lr 1e-4, 300 epochs, best validation Dice checkpoint; three seeds; loss weights given in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice on the unannotated target modality.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art domain-adaptive segmentation methods.
papers.results: Consistent Dice improvements over domain-adaptive baselines on the target modality with limited source annotations.
papers.statistics: Mean and SD over three runs.

papers.title: Addressing data annotation scarcity in Brain Tumor Segmentation on 3D MRI scan Using a Semi-Supervised Teacher-Student Framework
papers.authors: Jiaming Liu, Cheng Ding, Daoqiang Zhang
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours with few labelled 3D scans using a teacher-student approach.
papers.method: A teacher labels unlabelled scans with uncertainty; the student learns from the most confident pseudo-labels first and adds harder ones gradually.
papers.result: Dice rose from 0.39 to 0.87 as labels increased, and the student beat the teacher on some subregions.
papers.tools: U-Net
papers.gap: Single dataset; uncertainty calibration not assessed.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: A teacher network trained on labelled scans labels unlabelled scans and estimates its uncertainty; a student then learns from the most confident pseudo-labelled scans first, adding less confident ones gradually and ignoring uncertain regions. This confidence-driven curriculum improved tumour subregion segmentation with limited annotation, a direct strategy for the registry where most scans will be unlabelled.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS 2021 (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2021 multi-institutional multi-parametric glioma MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) with labelled fractions from 10% to 100%.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Semi-supervised teacher-student framework: a U-Net teacher (Dice + cross-entropy) produces probabilistic pseudo-labels and per-pixel uncertainty by stochastic inference; unlabelled scans ranked by image-level confidence and added in stages (progressive curriculum); student learns from high-confidence regions and unlearns low-confidence ones; agreement-based pseudo-label refinement.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice per subregion; confidence and error analyses.
papers.baselines: Teacher model and supervised training at each label fraction.
papers.results: Validation DSC rose from 0.393 (10% labels) to 0.872 (100%); teacher 0.922; student surpassed teacher on subregions (NCR/NET 0.797, oedema 0.980) and recovered enhancing tumour (0.620) where the teacher failed.

papers.title: Generalizable Brain Tumor Segmentation with Self-Training and Tumor-Aware Deformations
papers.authors: Henrique Zan Grande, Jeovane Honorio Alves, Rayson Laroca, Andre Gustavo Hochuli
papers.aim: To make brain tumour segmentation generalise across tumour types using unlabelled scans.
papers.method: A teacher labels unlabelled scans, only confident pseudo-labels are kept, and the student trains with a new tumour-aware deformation augmentation.
papers.result: Whole-tumour Dice 0.88 and tumour-core 0.82; self-training and augmentation each helped.
papers.tools: nnU-Net
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty output; challenge data.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; validation on hidden challenge set.
papers.methodologyDetail: The approach trains a strong teacher, uses it to label unlabelled scans, keeps only its most confident pseudo-labels, and trains a student with a new augmentation that deforms the tumour locally without distorting the rest of the brain, aiming to generalise across tumour types. Ablations isolate each component's effect. It is a practical recipe for using unlabelled local scans with nnU-Net.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge method paper (PUCPR Brazil, University of Luxembourg; BraTS 2026 GoAT task, accepted to MICCAI 2026 BraTS cluster).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2026 Generalizability Across Tumors (GoAT) data: heterogeneous brain tumour types and populations with labelled and unlabelled training cases; hidden validation via challenge platform.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing; tumour-aware deformable augmentation locally deforms lesions while preserving surrounding anatomy.
papers.modelDetails: Self-training: teacher nnU-Net v2 3D full-resolution with large residual encoder, group normalisation, axial attention in decoder and Hausdorff loss term; pseudo-labels for unlabelled cases, top-k most confident merged with labelled data; unmodified large-residual-encoder nnU-Net student trained with tumour-aware deformation augmentation.
papers.training: All hyperparameters, code and weights publicly released.
papers.evaluation: Dice, NSD and HD95 per region on challenge validation.
papers.baselines: Student trained on labelled data only; augmentation-only and self-training-only ablations.
papers.results: Submitted configuration Dice/NSD 0.881/0.473 whole tumour and 0.817/0.490 tumour core (other regions in paper); self-training and augmentation each helped, best combined.

papers.title: Cross-Modality Brain Tumor Segmentation via Bidirectional Global-to-Local Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
papers.authors: Kelei He, Wen Ji, Tao Zhou, Zhuoyuan Li, Jing Huo, Xin Zhang, Yang Gao, Dinggang Shen, Bing Zhang, Junfeng Zhang
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours in an unlabelled MRI sequence using a labelled one.
papers.method: BiGL translates images both ways between sequences and enforces consistent segmentations and features on real and synthetic images.
papers.result: Beat several state-of-the-art unsupervised domain-adaptation methods.
papers.tools: GAN, PyTorch
papers.gap: Simulated modality shift; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: BraTS only.
papers.methodologyDetail: To segment tumours in an MRI sequence that has no labels, BiGL translates images between the labelled and unlabelled sequences in both directions and enforces consistent segmentations and features across real and synthetic images. It improved cross-sequence segmentation over other unsupervised adaptation methods, relevant when local protocols differ from training data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS 2019 (Nanjing University and partners; preprint/IEEE journal).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2019 multi-modal glioma MRI with manual labels for three regions; modalities treated as source (e.g. T1, labelled) and target (e.g. T2, unlabelled) domains.
papers.preprocessing: Unpaired images per domain.
papers.modelDetails: Bidirectional Global-to-Local (BiGL) unsupervised domain adaptation: bidirectional image-to-image translator (pix2pix-like GAN) creates synthetic images in both directions; four weight-shared segmentation networks segment real and synthetic images; a global-to-local adaptor with feature, segmentation and attention consistency reduces domain shift.
papers.training: PyTorch on four V100 GPUs; synthesis module trained first then fixed; lr 5e-3 with polynomial decay (power 0.75), 150 epochs; discriminator lr 5e-5; consistency weights 0.001/0.1/0.1/0.1.
papers.evaluation: Dice and Hausdorff distance on target modality.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation methods.
papers.results: Outperformed several state-of-the-art UDA methods on cross-modality brain tumour segmentation.

papers.title: On the Role of MRI Sequences in Cross-Dataset Generalization for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Henrique Zan Grande, João G. Pitol, Lucas B. Schuck, Rafael V. Serenato, Rayson Laroca, Andre Gustavo Hochuli
papers.aim: To find which MRI sequences help a brain tumour model work on another dataset.
papers.method: Separate models per sequence, results by tumour size, and the gain from a few labelled target cases were measured.
papers.result: FLAIR transferred best (Dice over 75%), multi-sequence training helped more, and a few local labels gave fast gains.
papers.tools: fine-tuning
papers.gap: Binary 2D segmentation; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Two datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study isolates how each MRI sequence affects how well a segmentation model trained on one dataset works on another, by training separate models per sequence, stratifying by tumour size, and measuring the benefit of a few labelled target cases. FLAIR transferred best and small amounts of local labels helped quickly. This guides which sequences to prioritise when local scans are incomplete and how many local labels are needed.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled cross-dataset evaluation (PUCPR, Brazil; SIBGRAPI 2026).
papers.datasets: Two well-known public brain tumour MRI datasets used as source and target for binary tumour vs non-tumour segmentation, stratified by tumour size.
papers.preprocessing: Each sequence (T1n, T1c, T2w, T2f/FLAIR) processed and trained independently; 2D slices.
papers.modelDetails: 2D ResUNet trained per sequence and with multiple sequences; fine-tuning with limited labelled target-domain data.
papers.training: Standardised pipeline (details and code public).
papers.evaluation: Dice across datasets by sequence and tumour size; performance vs amount of target-domain labels.
papers.baselines: Each sequence compared; no adaptation vs limited adaptation.
papers.results: FLAIR achieved the best cross-dataset performance (Dice >75%) across most tumour sizes; multi-sequence training improved further; even limited target-domain adaptation gave rapid gains.

papers.title: MedMAP: Promoting Incomplete Multi-modal Brain Tumor Segmentation with Alignment
papers.authors: Tianyi Liu, Zhaorui Tan, Muyin Chen, Xi Yang, Haochuan Jiang, Kaizhu Huang
papers.aim: To segment brain tumours when some MRI sequences are missing.
papers.method: MedMAP aligns each sequence's features to a common reference distribution during training, added to three missing-modality methods.
papers.result: Improved all methods on BraTS, e.g. mmFormer +7.7 Dice points.
papers.tools: knowledge distillation
papers.gap: Simulated missing modalities; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: BraTS only.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedMAP makes the features from each MRI sequence follow a common reference distribution during training, so a model can work when some sequences are missing. Added to three existing missing-modality methods, it improved Dice on BraTS, especially for mmFormer. It helps the MRI Agent handle incomplete routine protocols.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS (Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Duke Kunshan; preprint, IEEE TMI submission).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 (split as in Proto-KD) and BraTS 2020 (three-fold cross-validation) with simulated missing MRI modalities.
papers.preprocessing: All modality subsets evaluated.
papers.modelDetails: MedMAP: a training paradigm that aligns latent features of each modality to a defined distribution anchor (best single modality or an adaptive mixture) in place of a pretrained model, inserted into existing missing-modality backbones (PMKL knowledge distillation, mmFormer shared latent space, ACN domain adaptation).
papers.training: Each backbone retrained with its released settings (batch sizes adjusted: mmFormer 1, PMKL 4) on one RTX 3090Ti.
papers.evaluation: Average Dice across missing-modality combinations.
papers.baselines: Same backbones without MedMAP.
papers.results: MedMAP improved all backbones, e.g. BraTS2018 mmFormer +7.67 to 78.29% and PMKL +3.68 to 69.12%; BraTS2020 mmFormer +6.76.
papers.statistics: Descriptive with proof of alignment properties.

papers.title: Rethink Domain Generalization in Heterogeneous Sequence MRI Segmentation
papers.authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Linkai Peng, Wanying Dou, Cuiling Sun, Halil Ertugrul Aktas, Andrea M. Bejar, Elif Keles, Gorkem Durak, Ulas Bagci
papers.aim: To show that MRI sequence differences hurt segmentation more than hospital differences.
papers.method: A new six-centre pancreas MRI dataset; a semi-supervised pretraining method based on sequence-independent anatomy.
papers.result: Sequence shift was a bigger problem than centre shift; the method raised Dice from about 44% to 70% on new centres.
papers.tools: Analysis of cross-centre vs cross-sequence shift;
papers.gap: Pancreas, not brain; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a new six-centre pancreas MRI dataset, the authors show that differences between MRI sequences cause larger performance drops than differences between hospitals, and that small samples can create apparent shifts. A semi-supervised pretraining approach based on anatomy that does not change with sequence greatly improved cross-sequence segmentation. The finding that sequence differences dominate is relevant to heterogeneous brain MRI protocols.
papers.studyDesign: Dataset creation and domain-generalisation benchmark with a new method (Northwestern University; preprint).
papers.datasets: PancreasDG: 563 3D MRI scans from six institutions with venous-phase and out-of-phase sequences; pixel-accurate pancreas masks from a double-blind two-pass protocol.
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed in extract.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of cross-centre vs cross-sequence shift; semi-supervised pretraining approach exploiting anatomical invariances for cross-sequence generalisation.
papers.training: Trained only on venous-phase data for cross-sequence tests (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice on unseen centres and sequences.
papers.baselines: Domain generalisation methods, SAM-based large segmentation models, pretraining baselines.
papers.results: Cross-sequence shift posed fundamentally different challenges than cross-centre shift; limited sampling variance can be mistaken for shift; proposed method raised Dice from 43.55% to 70.39% and from 35.62% to 66.61% on two independent test centres.
papers.availability: Dataset, code and models to be released.

papers.title: Causality-inspired Single-source Domain Generalization for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Cheng Ouyang, Chen Chen, Surui Li, Zeju Li, Chen Qin, Wenjia Bai, Daniel Rueckert
papers.aim: To make segmentation robust to unseen scanners when training on one source only.
papers.method: Augmentations generate many synthetic appearances with random shallow networks while keeping anatomy fixed, and break false background links.
papers.result: Consistently better across cross-modality, cross-sequence and cross-centre tests.
papers.tools: data augmentation
papers.gap: Not tumour-specific; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: 2D experiments.
papers.methodologyDetail: When a model can only be trained on data from one source, these augmentations expose it to many synthetic appearances generated by random shallow networks while keeping anatomy fixed, and break accidental links between background and target appearance. This made segmentation more robust to unseen scanners, sequences and modalities. It is an easy-to-add training step for the MRI Agent before local deployment.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (Imperial College London, Oxford; IEEE TMI).
papers.datasets: Three cross-domain settings: abdominal CT to T2-SPIR MRI (liver, kidneys, spleen), cardiac bSSFP to LGE MRI, and prostate MRI across six centres.
papers.preprocessing: 2D slices; standard normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Causality-inspired single-source domain generalisation: Global Intensity Non-linear augmentation (GIN) with randomly weighted shallow networks to vary appearance while preserving shape, and Interventional Pseudo-correlation Augmentation (IPA) blending GIN-augmented images spatially to break spurious correlations between objects.
papers.training: Standard segmentation training with these augmentations added.
papers.evaluation: Dice on unseen target domains.
papers.baselines: Other single-source domain generalisation and augmentation methods.
papers.results: Consistently outperformed competing methods across cross-modality, cross-sequence and cross-centre settings.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Medical Image Classification: A Comprehensive Benchmark
papers.authors: Zhekai Zhou, Guibo Luo, Mingzhi Chen, Zhenyu Weng, Yuesheng Zhu
papers.aim: To benchmark federated learning algorithms for medical image classification.
papers.method: Many FL algorithms were compared under the same conditions on medical datasets, measuring accuracy and system costs.
papers.result: No algorithm was best everywhere, so FedAvg remains a reasonable default.
papers.tools: FedAvg, FedProx, federated learning
papers.gap: Classification only; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Simulated clients.
papers.methodologyDetail: The benchmark evaluates many federated learning algorithms under the same conditions on medical classification datasets, measuring accuracy and system costs. The main finding is that algorithm rankings vary by dataset and none wins everywhere, so plain FedAvg remains a reasonable default with targeted alternatives tested locally, as planned in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of federated learning algorithms on medical image classification (Peking University Shenzhen; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multiple medical imaging classification datasets (e.g. COVIDx chest X-ray, HAM10K dermoscopy, retina DR, BreakHis pathology and others) partitioned across clients with IID and non-IID settings.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised partitioning and preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Fair comparison of traditional FL optimisers (FedAvg, FedProx, FedNova, SCAFFOLD, FedDyn and others), personalised FL (FedBN, Ditto, FedKD) and one-shot FL; proposed method combining denoising diffusion generative models with label-smoothing augmentation.
papers.training: Common training configuration across algorithms.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, communication cost and computational efficiency across architectures.
papers.baselines: All listed algorithms.
papers.results: Medical datasets posed substantial challenges; no single algorithm consistently performed best; the generative augmentation method improved robustness and efficiency.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Medical Image Analysis: A Survey
papers.authors: Hao Guan, Pew-Thian Yap, Andrea Bozoki, Mingxia Liu
papers.aim: To survey federated learning for medical image analysis.
papers.method: Survey organising methods by where they act in the system and by organ, with an empirical comparison.
papers.result: Data differences between sites strongly affect performance; privacy attacks, communication and evaluation remain open problems.
papers.tools: federated learning, survey
papers.gap: Survey; limited calibration discussion.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Up to 2023.
papers.methodologyDetail: A broad survey organising federated learning research in medical imaging by where in the system each technique acts and listing applications by organ, with an empirical comparison of representative methods. It provides background and terminology for WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Survey with an experimental study (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; Pattern Recognition 2024).
papers.datasets: Literature on federated learning in medical image analysis 2017-2023 grouped by organ (brain, chest, lung, etc.), with tasks and datasets catalogued (e.g. BraTS, ABIDE, ADNI, RSNA, CheXpert).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy of FL methods (client-end, server-end and communication techniques) and an empirical evaluation of typical FL methods.
papers.training: Not applicable for review; experiments use standard settings.
papers.evaluation: Empirical comparison metrics on representative tasks.
papers.baselines: Typical FL algorithms.
papers.results: Summarises progress, challenges (heterogeneity, privacy attacks, communication, evaluation) and directions; empirical results show heterogeneity strongly affects performance.

papers.title: In-depth Analysis of Privacy Threats in Federated Learning for Medical Data
papers.authors: Badhan Chandra Das, M. Hadi Amini, Yanzhao Wu
papers.aim: To analyse privacy attacks on federated learning with medical images.
papers.method: A framework to attack and defend federated training, showing image reconstruction from shared gradients, including brain MRI.
papers.result: Private images could be reconstructed under default settings, and common defences either failed or cost accuracy.
papers.tools: federated learning, ResNet, U-Net, differential privacy, secure aggregation
papers.gap: Classification models; small-batch attack settings.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a framework to attack and defend federated learning on medical images, showing that, without protection, an adversary can reconstruct brain MRI and other images from the gradients hospitals share. Common defences involve trade-offs between privacy and accuracy. This is why WP5 includes differential privacy and secure aggregation options and audit of what leaves each site.
papers.studyDesign: Framework development and empirical privacy-risk analysis (Florida International University and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: Public medical image datasets: melanoma skin cancer images, COVID-19 X-rays and brain tumour MRI scans.
papers.preprocessing: Standard image preprocessing per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: MedPFL framework for analysing privacy risk in federated learning: gradient-inversion attacks (DLG, iDLG, GradInv, CPL) against LeNet, ResNet and U-Net, and defences (gradient perturbation, gradient compression, differential privacy, secure multi-party computation).
papers.training: FL training with shared gradients (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Attack success rate, SSIM and MSE of reconstructed images; model accuracy under defences.
papers.baselines: Undefended federated training.
papers.results: Adversaries could accurately reconstruct private medical images from shared gradients under default FL settings; prevalent defences did not always protect adequately or reduced accuracy.

papers.title: Future-Proofing Medical Imaging with Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning and Uncertainty Quantification: A Review
papers.authors: Nikolas Koutsoubis, Asim Waqas, Yasin Yilmaz, Ravi P. Ramachandran, Matthew Schabath, Ghulam Rasool
papers.aim: To review privacy-preserving federated learning together with uncertainty quantification in medical imaging.
papers.method: Review of FL, its privacy weaknesses and defences, and uncertainty estimation under federation.
papers.result: Site differences make uncertainty estimation in FL especially hard; trustworthy private FL with uncertainty is needed.
papers.tools: differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation, conformal prediction, federated learning
papers.gap: No empirical comparison.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review brings together federated learning, its privacy weaknesses and defences, and uncertainty quantification under federation, arguing that site heterogeneity makes uncertainty estimation in FL especially hard. It directly frames the gap this study addresses about calibration after federated aggregation.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Moffitt Cancer Center, University of South Florida, Rowan University; preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on federated learning, privacy-preserving FL and uncertainty quantification in FL for medical imaging.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Review of FL algorithms, privacy-preserving techniques (differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation) and UQ methods adapted to FL (ensembles, Bayesian FL, conformal prediction).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Identifies gaps: non-IID heterogeneity, gradient leakage, and the difficulty of UQ in FL because site data differ; calls for privacy-preserving FL with trustworthy uncertainty.

papers.title: Multi-Institutional Deep Learning Modeling Without Sharing Patient Data: A Feasibility Study on Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Micah J Sheller, G Anthony Reina, Brandon Edwards, Jason Martin, Spyridon Bakas
papers.aim: To show brain tumour segmentation can be trained across institutions without sharing patient data.
papers.method: BraTS was split by institution; federated training was compared with pooled data and with sequential institution-by-institution training.
papers.result: Federated Dice 0.852, nearly equal to pooled data and better than sequential training.
papers.tools: U-Net, federated learning
papers.gap: Simulated federation; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Older architecture; BraTS only.
papers.methodologyDetail: This was the first demonstration that brain-tumour segmentation models can be trained across institutions without moving patient data. By partitioning BraTS by source institution, the authors showed federated training reached nearly the same Dice as pooling the data, whereas sequential institution-by-institution training lost performance. It is the starting point for federated brain-tumour work.
papers.studyDesign: Simulated federated learning feasibility study on BraTS (Intel and University of Pennsylvania; MICCAI BrainLes 2018).
papers.datasets: BraTS multimodal brain tumour MRI partitioned by original institution into simulated federations of 4 to 32 institutions.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net segmentation trained with federated learning (weighted averaging of institutional updates by data fraction), compared with cyclic institutional incremental learning (CIIL), institutional incremental learning (IIL) and centralised data sharing.
papers.training: Adam lr 0.0005, loss = negative log Dice with Laplace smoothing 1; epochs per round studied.
papers.evaluation: Whole-tumour Dice on validation; percentage of data-sharing performance.
papers.baselines: Centralised data sharing, CIIL, IIL.
papers.results: Federated Dice 0.852, close to data-sharing performance and to expert inter-rater agreement (0.85 +/- 0.08), and better than incremental approaches as institutions increased.

papers.title: FedFMS: Exploring Federated Foundation Models for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Yuxi Liu, Guibo Luo, Yuesheng Zhu
papers.aim: To test training a large segmentation foundation model (SAM) with federated learning.
papers.method: FedFMS compares full federated SAM with an adapter-only version (FedMSA) against central training.
papers.result: Federated SAM matched central training, and adapters cut communication and training cost.
papers.tools: SAM, ViT, FedAvg, federated learning
papers.gap: No brain-tumour focus; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study asks whether a large segmentation foundation model can be trained federatedly and shows that full federated SAM matches centralised training, while training only small adapters cuts communication substantially. Adapter-based federation suits hospitals with slow connections.
papers.studyDesign: Exploratory study of federated foundation models for segmentation (Peking University Shenzhen; preprint).
papers.datasets: Diverse public medical segmentation datasets partitioned across clients (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing for SAM inputs.
papers.modelDetails: FedFMS: Federated SAM (FedSAM, full model with ViT-B/16 or ViT-L/16 encoder and lightweight decoder) and FedMSA (Medical SAM Adapter, training only adapters and decoder for communication and compute efficiency), with multi-class segmentation head.
papers.training: Federated rounds with FedAvg (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice vs centralised training; communication and training cost; effect of pretraining.
papers.baselines: Centralised SAM training.
papers.results: Federated foundation models performed comparably to centralised training; FedMSA reduced communication and training cost while keeping performance; pretraining enriched prior knowledge.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Federated Learning in Medical Imaging
papers.authors: Vishwa S Parekh, Shuhao Lai, Vladimir Braverman, Jeff Leal, Steven Rowe, Jay J Pillai, Michael A Jacobs
papers.aim: To test federated learning when sites hold different imaging modalities or tasks.
papers.method: One U-Net trained with CT at one site and PET at another for kidney localisation, plus other multi-task settings.
papers.result: Encouraging results, e.g. 0.79 overlap for organ localisation across PET and CT sites.
papers.tools: U-Net, FedAvg, federated learning
papers.gap: Small cohorts; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Workshop-scale.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study tests whether federated learning still helps when participating sites hold different imaging modalities or tasks, by training one U-Net with CT at one node and PET at another for kidney localisation, plus other multi-task settings. Cross-domain federation gave reasonable results. It is relevant because Sri Lankan hospitals may hold different sequences or data types.
papers.studyDesign: Exploratory multi-domain, multi-task federated learning study (Johns Hopkins University; MIDL 2022 submission, IRB-approved retrospective clinical data).
papers.datasets: Experiment 1: 50 patients with whole-body 18F-DCFPyL PET/CT (35 train, 15 test) for kidney localisation, CT at one node and PET at another; further experiments with multi-task settings (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Split of modalities across nodes.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net (five encoder, one bridge, five decoder blocks; batch norm, ReLU) trained with FedAvg across nodes holding different modalities and tasks; one local epoch per communication round.
papers.training: Batch size 4, sigmoid output, binary cross-entropy, Adam.
papers.evaluation: Overlap similarity (Dice) for organ localisation and segmentation.
papers.baselines: Locally trained models.
papers.results: Encouraging cross-domain results, e.g. overlap similarity of 0.79 for organ localisation across PET and CT nodes.

papers.title: FedSODA: Federated Cross-assessment and Dynamic Aggregation for Histopathology Segmentation
papers.authors: Yuan Zhang, Yaolei Qi, Xiaoming Qi, Lotfi Senhadji, Yongyue Wei, Feng Chen, Guanyu Yang
papers.aim: To improve federated pathology segmentation across very different datasets.
papers.method: FedSODA scores each site's contribution with synthetic data, aggregates layers differently, and uses a loss that balances large and small structures.
papers.result: Beat FL baselines on a seven-dataset multi-site pathology benchmark.
papers.tools: FedSODA: synthetic-driven cross-assessment operation (Gaussian synthetic information with a memory bank uploaded to the server to evaluate clients)…
papers.gap: Non-brain tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: FedSODA tackles very different pathology datasets acting as sites by evaluating each client's contribution with synthetic data and by aggregating different network layers differently, plus a loss that stops large structures dominating small cells. It improved federated segmentation across seven datasets. Layer-wise aggregation is one option for heterogeneous sites in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public histopathology segmentation datasets (Southeast University and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: Seven datasets as clients: CoNSeP, CPM-17, CRAG, CryoNuSeg, GlaS, Kumar and others (nuclei and tissue segmentation across organs).
papers.preprocessing: Standard patching per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: FedSODA: synthetic-driven cross-assessment operation (Gaussian synthetic information with a memory bank uploaded to the server to evaluate clients) with a segmentation consistency loss, and dynamic stratified-layer aggregation that adaptively combines shallow and deep layers.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice/AJI-type segmentation metrics across clients.
papers.baselines: FedAvg, FedProx and other FL methods.
papers.results: Outperformed FL baselines on the largest multi-site histopathology segmentation benchmark assembled from seven datasets.

papers.title: FedDropoutAvg: Generalizable federated learning for histopathology image classification
papers.authors: Gozde N. Gunesli, Mohsin Bilal, Shan E Ahmed Raza, Nasir M. Rajpoot
papers.aim: To make federated pathology models generalise to unseen centres.
papers.method: FedDropoutAvg randomly drops sites and parameters during averaging as regularisation, using real TCGA centres as sites.
papers.result: Better than FedAvg and FedProx, especially on unseen centres.
papers.tools: federated learning, FedAvg, FedProx
papers.gap: No calibration or uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective TCGA.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using real centre boundaries in TCGA as federation sites, the authors add randomness to which sites contribute each round and which parameters are averaged, which acts as regularisation. Tested on held-out data from training centres and on completely unseen centres, it generalised better than FedAvg and FedProx. It is a simple aggregation option for small, heterogeneous federations.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and multi-site evaluation on real centre partitions (University of Warwick; preprint).
papers.datasets: TCGA CRC-DX: 599 diagnostic WSIs from 591 colorectal cancer patients from 36 centres; centres with <5 patients excluded; ~1.2 million tiles from 21 centres used for testing, including independent centres not in training; tumour tiles selected by a ResNet18 tumour classifier (99% accuracy).
papers.preprocessing: Otsu tissue thresholding; 512x512 tiles at 20x; tumour vs non-tumour filtering.
papers.modelDetails: FedDropoutAvg: federated training with randomness in client selection and random dropout of parameters during federated averaging to improve generalisation; classifier for slide-derived tile labels (e.g. MSI-type task).
papers.training: 3-fold experiments (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Mean F1 and AUROC on held-out test sets of training centres and on independent centres.
papers.baselines: Centralised model, FedAvg, FedProx.
papers.results: FedDropoutAvg outperformed other FL approaches and came closer to centralised training, especially on independent unseen centres.
papers.statistics: Mean and SD across folds and centres.

papers.title: Benchmarking Differentially Private Residual Networks for Medical Imagery
papers.authors: Sahib Singh, Harshvardhan Sikka, Sasikanth Kotti, Andrew Trask
papers.aim: To measure the accuracy cost of differential privacy for medical image classifiers.
papers.method: Residual networks were trained with Local DP and with DP-SGD over a range of privacy budgets.
papers.result: Stronger privacy lowered accuracy, and the two DP methods behaved differently.
papers.tools: differential privacy, DP-SGD
papers.gap: Simple 2D tasks; no federated or calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained medical image classifiers with two forms of differential privacy across a range of privacy budgets and measured the cost to accuracy, discussing what the guarantees mean in practice. It provides reference points for choosing a privacy budget in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of differential privacy for medical imaging (OpenMined, Harvard, Oxford and others; preprint).
papers.datasets: Chest X-ray pneumonia dataset (~5,800 images) and APTOS 2019 diabetic retinopathy dataset (~3,600 training fundus images, grades 0-4).
papers.preprocessing: Standard image preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Residual networks trained with Local Differential Privacy and with DP-SGD at varying epsilon values.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy versus privacy budget epsilon; practical usefulness of guarantees.
papers.baselines: Non-private training.
papers.results: Showed the accuracy-privacy trade-off: stronger privacy (smaller epsilon) reduced accuracy, with DP-SGD and Local-DP behaving differently.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving in Medical Image Analysis: A Review of Methods and Applications
papers.authors: Yanming Zhu, Xuefei Yin, Alan Wee-Chung Liew, Hui Tian
papers.aim: To review privacy-preserving methods for medical image analysis.
papers.method: Review grouping techniques by the practical privacy problem they solve, including new cryptographic methods.
papers.result: Maps methods to privacy problems and highlights their trade-offs.
papers.tools: differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, federated learning
papers.gap: No empirical comparison.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review organises privacy-preserving techniques in medical imaging according to the practical problems they solve rather than by technology, and discusses newer cryptographic approaches. It is background for designing the registry's de-identification and federated privacy protections.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Griffith University, Australia; preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on privacy-preserving medical image analysis across diagnosis, pathology and telemedicine.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Review organised by privacy challenge: encryption, differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, federated learning, image obfuscation/deformation, and emerging methods such as zero-knowledge proofs and secure multi-party computation.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Maps techniques to concrete privacy problems and highlights trade-offs and emerging directions.

papers.title: Vision Through the Veil: Differential Privacy in Federated Learning for Medical Image Classification
papers.authors: Kishore Babu Nampalle, Pradeep Singh, Uppala Vivek Narayan, Balasubramanian Raman
papers.aim: To add differential privacy to federated medical image classification without losing too much accuracy.
papers.method: Each site adds calibrated noise to its update, with noise adapted across training rounds.
papers.result: Accuracy dropped less than with naive noise while giving meaningful privacy.
papers.tools: federated learning, differential privacy
papers.gap: Classification on dermatoscopy; no calibration of predictions.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Simulated clients; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Each simulated hospital adds calibrated noise to its model update before sending it, with the amount of noise adapted over training rounds, so that privacy is formally protected. Accuracy fell less than with naive noise. It gives a concrete differentially private federated design for WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (IIT Roorkee; preprint).
papers.datasets: HAM10000 dermatoscopic images (10,015: 8,902 benign, 1,113 malignant) and other medical image classification data distributed across simulated clients.
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing and partitioning.
papers.modelDetails: Differentially private federated learning: Laplace noise added to each client's model update with a noise calibration mechanism and adaptive privacy budget allocation across rounds; formal privacy-utility analysis.
papers.training: Details in Algorithm 1.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy across privacy budgets.
papers.baselines: Non-private federated learning.
papers.results: Confirmed an accuracy-privacy trade-off, but strategic noise calibration and budget allocation preserved accuracy while giving meaningful privacy.

papers.title: Multiple Instance Learning for Digital Pathology: A Review on the State-of-the-Art, Limitations & Future Potential
papers.authors: Michael Gadermayr, Maximilian Tschuchnig
papers.aim: To review multiple instance learning for digital pathology.
papers.method: Review explaining how MIL learns from slide labels and surveying the main method families.
papers.result: MIL works because slide labels are routinely available; interpretability, data efficiency and validation remain challenges.
papers.tools: Transformer, multiple instance learning
papers.gap: No quantitative comparison.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Fast-moving field.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review explains how multiple instance learning lets models learn from slide-level labels, surveys the main families of MIL methods and discusses open problems. It provides the conceptual basis for the slide-level Pathology Agent.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Salzburg University of Applied Sciences; Computerized Medical Imaging and Graphics).
papers.datasets: Literature on deep multiple instance learning in digital pathology.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Overview of MIL concepts (instance vs embedding level, pooling operators, attention-based MIL, transformer MIL, graph MIL, multi-scale, self-supervised features) and their use for WSI classification and segmentation.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: MIL is effective because slide labels are routinely available while patch labels are not; remaining challenges include interpretability, data efficiency, multi-scale context, label noise and validation.

papers.title: CAMIL: Context-Aware Multiple Instance Learning for Cancer Detection and Subtyping in Whole Slide Images
papers.authors: Olga Fourkioti, Matt De Vries, Chen Jin, Daniel C. Alexander, Chris Bakal
papers.venue: The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2024
papers.aim: To improve slide classification by letting each tile's importance depend on its neighbours.
papers.method: CAMIL adjusts attention using surrounding tiles so isolated noisy tiles are down-weighted.
papers.result: Better subtyping and metastasis detection (AUC above 0.95) and better tumour localisation.
papers.tools: Transformer, multiple instance learning
papers.gap: No brain tumours; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Public benchmarks.
papers.methodologyDetail: CAMIL mimics how pathologists look at a region and its surroundings: each tile's importance is adjusted according to its neighbours, so isolated high-attention tiles likely to be noise are down-weighted. It improved slide classification and tumour localisation over standard attention MIL. Context-aware attention may help with heterogeneous gliomas.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public WSI benchmarks (Institute of Cancer Research and UCL; ICLR 2024).
papers.datasets: TCGA-NSCLC (subtyping), CAMELYON16 and CAMELYON17 (lymph-node metastasis detection).
papers.preprocessing: Automatic tissue segmentation and tiling into 256x256 tiles.
papers.modelDetails: CAMIL: tile feature extraction followed by a Nystromformer-based global transformer and neighbour-constrained attention that recalibrates each tile's attention by its neighbourhood, then attention pooling for slide classification.
papers.training: Details in appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and AUC; localisation of tumour regions.
papers.baselines: CLAM-SB, CLAM-MB, TransMIL, DTFD-MIL, GTP, DSMIL.
papers.results: Outperformed baselines on subtyping and metastasis detection (reported AUCs above 0.95 on the benchmarks) and improved localisation by using tile context.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Computational Pathology on Gigapixel Whole Slide Images
papers.authors: Ming Y. Lu, Dehan Kong, Jana Lipkova, Richard J. Chen, Rajendra Singh, Drew F. K. Williamson, Tiffany Y. Chen, Faisal Mahmood
papers.aim: To train slide-level pathology models across institutions without sharing slides.
papers.method: Attention-based MIL on gigapixel slides combined with federated learning and differential privacy, for diagnosis and survival.
papers.result: Close to central training and better than single-site models while keeping privacy.
papers.tools: multiple instance learning, CLAM, differential privacy, federated learning
papers.gap: No calibration; non-brain cancers.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Simulated institutional partitions.
papers.methodologyDetail: This early study combined attention-based multiple instance learning on gigapixel slides with federated learning and differential privacy, showing that institutions can jointly train slide-level diagnostic and survival models from slide labels only without sharing slides. It is the template for federated pathology in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on multi-institutional WSIs (Brigham and Women's / Harvard, Northwell; Medical Image Analysis).
papers.datasets: Thousands of H&E WSIs with slide-level labels for two diagnostic problems (e.g. breast and renal cell carcinoma subtyping) and survival prediction, partitioned across institutions as federated clients.
papers.preprocessing: Tissue segmentation and patching; frozen feature extraction.
papers.modelDetails: Weakly supervised attention-based multiple instance learning (CLAM-style) trained with federated averaging across institutions, with differential privacy via randomised noise added to model updates; weakly supervised survival prediction framework.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification AUC and accuracy; C-index for survival; comparison with centralised and single-institution training.
papers.baselines: Centralised training and individual-site models.
papers.results: Federated models reached accuracy close to centralised training and better than single-site models while preserving differential privacy; survival stratification effective in federated setting.

papers.title: Glioma Classification Using Multimodal Radiology and Histology Data
papers.authors: Azam Hamidinekoo, Tomasz Pieciak, Maryam Afzali, Otar Akanyeti, Yinyin Yuan
papers.aim: To classify glioma subtype by combining MRI and pathology.
papers.method: One network for MRI and one for slides from the same patients, with predictions combined.
papers.result: F1 0.886 and balanced accuracy 0.86 on challenge validation.
papers.tools: DenseNet, ensemble
papers.gap: Assumes both modalities present; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Small challenge dataset.
papers.methodologyDetail: The pipeline trains one network on MRI and another on pathology slides for the same patients and combines their predictions to classify glioma subtype. The fused model reached high agreement with the reference labels in the challenge. It is an early demonstration of the radiology-pathology fusion planned in WP4.
papers.studyDesign: Method development in the CPM-RadPath challenge (Institute of Cancer Research and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: CPM-RadPath 2020: paired multi-institutional mp-MRI (T1w, T2w, Gd-T1w, FLAIR; co-registered, 1 mm, skull-stripped) and one H&E WSI per patient; labels A (IDH-mutant astrocytoma), O (oligodendroglioma) and G (glioblastoma/IDH-wildtype); 221 training (133 G, 54 O, 34 A), 35 validation, 73 test.
papers.preprocessing: Challenge preprocessing for MRI; WSI patching at varying magnifications.
papers.modelDetails: Separate DenseNet-based classifiers for radiology and histology, combined in an ensemble/fusion pipeline for three-class glioma classification.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: F1, Cohen's kappa, balanced accuracy.
papers.baselines: Single-modality models.
papers.results: F1 0.886, kappa 0.811, balanced accuracy 0.860 on validation.

papers.title: Glioma subtype classification from histopathological images using in-domain and out-of-domain transfer learning: An experimental study
papers.authors: Vladimir Despotovic, Sang-Yoon Kim, Ann-Christin Hau, Aliaksandra Kakoichankava, Gilbert Georg Klamminger, Felix Bruno Kleine Borgmann, Katrin B. M. Frauenknecht, Michel Mittelbronn, Petr V. Nazarov
papers.aim: To classify glioma subtypes from slides in a small national cohort using transfer learning.
papers.method: ImageNet and pathology-pretrained networks compared on a WHO 2021-labelled cohort, then trained models labelled unannotated regions for retraining.
papers.result: Pathology-pretrained networks and weak-label retraining both improved performance.
papers.tools: semi-supervised learning
papers.gap: Very small cohort; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Single centre.
papers.methodologyDetail: With a small national glioma cohort annotated by a neuropathologist under WHO 2021, the authors compared ImageNet and histopathology-pretrained networks and then used the trained models to label unannotated regions and retrain, gaining performance. A small-country cohort with expert annotation is comparable to the situation in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental comparison study with an in-house cohort (Luxembourg Institute of Health, National Center of Pathology Luxembourg, Frankfurt; ethics CNER REC-LRNO-20110708).
papers.datasets: 75 H&E WSIs from 28 adult-type diffuse glioma cases (2017-2021) scanned on Philips IntelliSite at 0.25 um/px; WHO CNS5 classes: IDH-mutant 1p/19q co-deleted oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, plus normal brain; region annotations by a neuropathologist.
papers.preprocessing: FFPE processing; pseudonymised region-annotated images; patch extraction from annotated regions.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of transfer-learning strategies (out-of-domain ImageNet vs in-domain histopathology pretraining) and architectures for patch-level glioma subtype classification; semi-supervised step in which fine-tuned models label unannotated regions and models are retrained on ground-truth plus weak labels.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Patch and slide-level accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1.
papers.baselines: Different architectures and pretraining sources.
papers.results: In-domain pretraining and the semi-supervised weak-label retraining improved performance over standard transfer learning.

papers.title: Multi-Beholder: Biomarker Prediction for Low-Grade Glioma with Multiple Instance Learning and One-Class Classification
papers.authors: Zijie Fang, Yihan Liu, Yifeng Wang, Xiangyang Zhang, Yang Chen, Changjing Cai, Yiyang Lin, Ying Han, Zhi Wang, Shan Zeng, et al.
papers.aim: To predict molecular markers of low-grade glioma from routine slides.
papers.method: Multi-Beholder combines MIL with one-class classification to pseudo-label confident patches and adapts at test time.
papers.result: Better than MIL baselines across biomarkers, with interpretable tissue patterns.
papers.tools: multiple instance learning
papers.gap: No calibration or deferral when marker prediction is uncertain.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Multi-Beholder predicts several molecular markers of low-grade glioma directly from routine slides. It adds one-class classification to multiple instance learning so that confident patches get pseudo-labels, improving learning from slide-level labels, and adapts predictions at test time. It is relevant to estimating markers when molecular tests are unavailable, though such estimates must stay advisory.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on two LGG cohorts (Central South University and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: Two low-grade glioma cohorts with diverse races and scanners, H&E WSIs and five biomarkers (e.g. 1p/19q N = 831 with 39% positive; ATRX N = 828 with 34% positive; IDH, TERT, others).
papers.preprocessing: WSIs cut into non-overlapping patches.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-Beholder: attention-based MIL with one-class classification (OCSVM) to pseudo-label confident instances in negative and positive bags, instance feature refinement, and test-time adaptation (T3A) of the final prediction.
papers.training: Hyperparameters (number of confident instances, noisy-instance ratio, OCSVM nu) listed in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy, F1 with 95% CIs per biomarker.
papers.baselines: ABMIL, CLAM-SB and other MIL methods.
papers.results: Outperformed MIL baselines across biomarkers (e.g. ABMIL 1p/19q AUC 0.830 vs higher for Multi-Beholder) and gave interpretable histomorphology.

papers.title: Benchmarking Pathology Foundation Models: Adaptation Strategies and Scenarios
papers.authors: Jeaung Lee, Jeewoo Lim, Keunho Byeon, Jin Tae Kwak
papers.aim: To find the best way to adapt pathology foundation models to new hospitals and few labels.
papers.method: Adaptation strategies were benchmarked across datasets from different hospitals and scanners and in few-shot settings.
papers.result: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning worked best; with very few labels, few-shot test-time methods helped most.
papers.tools: fine-tuning
papers.gap: No brain tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Patch-level tasks.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors tested how best to adapt pathology foundation models to new datasets from different hospitals and scanners, and how they behave when only a few labelled examples exist. Lightweight adaptation worked best in most cases. This informs how the Pathology Agent's encoder will be adapted to local slides.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of pathology foundation models (Korea University; preprint).
papers.datasets: 14 public pathology datasets across breast (PCam, BACH, BRACS), colorectal (Kather19, Kather16, CRC-TP, KBSMC Colon I/II, DigestPath, Chaoyang), prostate (PANDA, AGGC22, UBC), gastric (KBSMC Gastric) and lung/colorectal (LC25000), with different scanners, magnifications and pixel sizes.
papers.preprocessing: Native patch sizes and resolutions per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: Four pathology-specific foundation models evaluated in two scenarios: consistency assessment with five fine-tuning methods (including parameter-efficient fine-tuning) and flexibility assessment with five few-shot learning methods.
papers.training: Standardised fine-tuning and few-shot protocols.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy/F1 across datasets and scenarios.
papers.baselines: Full fine-tuning, linear probing and other adaptation methods.
papers.results: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning was efficient and effective across datasets; in data-limited settings, foundation models benefited most from few-shot methods that modify only test-time behaviour.

papers.title: Domain-Specific Foundation Model Improves AI-Based Analysis of Neuropathology
papers.authors: Ruchika Verma, Shrishtee Kandoi, Robina Afzal, Shengjia Chen, Jannes Jegminat, Michael W. Karlovich, Melissa Umphlett, Timothy E. Richardson, Kevin Clare, Quazi Hossain, et al.
papers.aim: To build a pathology foundation model specialised for brain tissue.
papers.method: NeuroFM was pretrained on hundreds of thousands of slides rich in brain tissue and compared with general pathology models.
papers.result: Brain-specific pretraining beat general models on neuropathology tasks.
papers.tools: NeuroFM: domain-specific self-supervised foundation model for neuropathology, compared with general pathology foundation models on neuropathology tasks.
papers.gap: Mostly neurodegenerative tasks; tumour tasks less emphasised; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; model availability may be restricted.
papers.methodologyDetail: NeuroFM is pretrained on hundreds of thousands of slides, enriched with brain tissue from neurodegenerative and neuro-oncological sources, and benchmarked against general pathology foundation models. Brain-specific pretraining helped. It is a candidate encoder for brain-tumour slides in the Pathology Agent, alongside general models.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development and benchmarking (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and collaborators; preprint).
papers.datasets: Pretraining corpus of 585,657 H&E and Luxol fast blue-H&E WSIs; neuropathology data 23,144 slides (~800 million tiles) from Mount Sinai autopsy, diagnostic and brain bank services, PSP/CBD, Boston University CTE and Columbia Essential Tremor collections, plus 200 million tiles from general pathology.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised to 20x (0.5 um/px).
papers.modelDetails: NeuroFM: domain-specific self-supervised foundation model for neuropathology, compared with general pathology foundation models on neuropathology tasks.
papers.training: Monte Carlo cross-validation with 20 random 80/20 splits, two runs each; majority-class subsampling for slide classification.
papers.evaluation: Slide- and tile-level classification and regression metrics on neuropathology benchmarks.
papers.baselines: General-purpose pathology foundation models (e.g. UNI, Virchow, Prov-GigaPath).
papers.results: The neuropathology-specific model captured brain-tissue features better and outperformed general models on neuropathology tasks.

papers.title: RandStainNA: Learning Stain-Agnostic Features from Histology Slides by Bridging Stain Augmentation and Normalization
papers.authors: Yiqing Shen, Yulin Luo, Dinggang Shen, Jing Ke
papers.aim: To make pathology models robust to different stain colours across centres.
papers.method: RandStainNA samples realistic stain styles from the training distribution and applies them as augmentation.
papers.result: Better generalisation to other centres than either normalisation or augmentation alone.
papers.tools: ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT
papers.gap: Colorectal tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Patch-level tasks.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of normalising all slides to one template or randomly distorting colours, RandStainNA samples realistic stain styles from the distribution seen in training data and applies them as augmentation. Models trained this way generalised better to slides from other centres. It is a simple preprocessing option for local slides stained differently from public data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ShanghaiTech; MICCAI 2022).
papers.datasets: NCT-CRC-HE-100K-NONORM (100,000 patches, 80/20 train/validation, background class removed) and CRC-VAL-HE-7K (7,180 patches) for external testing of 8-class classification; MoNuSeg for nuclei segmentation.
papers.preprocessing: Images converted to LAB colour space; stain style characterised by mean and SD of each channel.
papers.modelDetails: RandStainNA: random stain normalisation and augmentation that samples a virtual template from estimated stain-style distributions, bridging normalisation and augmentation; tested on ResNet-18/50, MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-B0, ViT-Tiny and Swin-Tiny.
papers.training: Standard training per backbone (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Top-1 accuracy (classification); Dice and IoU (segmentation) on external data.
papers.baselines: Stain normalisation alone and stain augmentation alone.
papers.results: Consistently improved generalisation over both normalisation and augmentation across architectures.

papers.title: Do Histopathological Foundation Models Eliminate Batch Effects? A Comparative Study
papers.authors: Jonah Kömen, Hannah Marienwald, Jonas Dippel, Julius Hense
papers.aim: To test whether pathology foundation models remove differences between hospitals.
papers.method: Foundation-model features were analysed for how well they reveal the source hospital, with and without stain normalisation.
papers.result: Strong hospital signatures remained in the features and dominated them, so local validation is still needed.
papers.tools: Analysis of embeddings from several histopathological foundation models for site-specific signatures (batch effects): site prediction from features…
papers.gap: No mitigation method proposed.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Two datasets.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study checks whether pathology foundation models remove differences between hospitals and finds they do not: the site a slide came from can be predicted from its features, and site differences dominate. This means local validation and site-aware calibration remain necessary even with foundation encoders.
papers.studyDesign: Comparative empirical study (TU Berlin, BIFOLD, Aignostics; preprint).
papers.datasets: TCGA-LUSC-5: up to 50 patients from each of five tissue source sites; CAMELYON16: 400 sentinel lymph node slides from two Dutch hospitals with tumour annotations.
papers.preprocessing: 256x256 patches at 20x, Otsu background removal, minimum patch SD of 8; patches labelled by site and tumour status.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of embeddings from several histopathological foundation models for site-specific signatures (batch effects): site prediction from features, feature-space distances, principal components, and effect of stain normalisation.
papers.training: Linear and other probes on frozen features.
