papers.methodologyDetail: Two experienced oncologists contoured the same prostate CT scans manually and later with AI-proposed contours they could edit; all contours were compared with a consensus reference and the treatment plans were recalculated on each set. AI support reduced variability but clinicians tended to keep AI contours with few changes, showing automation bias. The paper argues for structured quality assurance and human oversight, which supports the PhD's review-and-escalate design for surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective clinical validation study in radiation oncology (Iran Mehr Hospital, Birjand University of Medical Sciences, Iran), two phases separated by 2 months.
papers.datasets: Non-contrast planning CT scans of 17 randomly selected patients with localised early-stage prostate cancer (GE LightSpeed 16, 120 kVp, 512×512, 0.82-0.97 mm in-plane, 3-5 mm slices); two radiation oncologists with over 10 years' experience.
papers.preprocessing: Patients without prostatectomy, rectal spacer or femoral implants; each oncologist contoured each case twice at least 2 weeks apart; consensus reference contour (Cref) as benchmark.
papers.modelDetails: Three workflows: manual contouring (Cman), unedited commercial AI contours, and AI contours adjusted by oncologists (CAI,adj) for CTV, rectum, bladder and femoral heads in a 3D PCRT TPS.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial tool).
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient and HD95 for intra- and inter-observer variability; dosimetric impact by recalculating and replanning on each contour set.
papers.baselines: Manual contouring from scratch.
papers.results: AI-adjusted contours improved agreement: CTV DSC 0.86 to 0.90 (p = 0.044) and HD95 6.3 to 2.6 mm for oncologist 1; 0.83 to 0.92 (p < 0.001) for oncologist 2; evidence of automation bias when clinicians accepted AI contours with minimal edits.
papers.statistics: Paired statistical tests (p-values) on geometric and dosimetric metrics.

papers.title: Explainability in context: calibrating appropriate trust and reliance in artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Davis SE, Salwei ME
papers.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
papers.aim: To argue that clinicians need context about AI reliability, not only feature explanations, to trust AI appropriately.
papers.method: Perspective proposing layered information on model reliability for the local setting, patient subgroup and individual case, including uncertainty.
papers.result: Contextual explanation helps clinicians calibrate trust and avoid both over- and under-reliance.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: Framework not yet empirically evaluated.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Conceptual only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors argue that explaining why a model made a prediction is not enough; clinicians also need to know how reliable the model is in their setting, for the patient's subgroup, and for this particular case, including uncertainty. They propose layered contextual information built into decision support workflows. This directly supports the PhD's design of showing calibrated uncertainty and site-level performance at the point of escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Perspective / conceptual paper (Vanderbilt University Medical Center, USA) in JAMIA.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (conceptual framework drawing on literature).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Context-based explainable AI framework with four levels of contextualisation (model, setting, subpopulation and patient), including historical and in-the-moment performance, algorithmic fairness and prediction uncertainty.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable; illustrative workflow integration proposed.
papers.baselines: Conventional feature-attribution XAI.
papers.results: Argues that explanation of context, rather than only of features, helps clinicians calibrate appropriate trust and reliance, avoiding both automation bias and under-reliance, without adding cognitive burden.

papers.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
papers.authors: Frazer HML, Peña-Solorzano CA, Kwok CF, Elliott MS, Chen Y, Wang C, BRAIx Team, Lippey JF, Hopper JL, Brotchie P, et al.
papers.aim: To compare ways of adding AI to population breast screening, including human-AI interaction.
papers.method: Real screening decisions were used to simulate five AI pathways and how readers might defer to the AI.
papers.result: Using AI as a second reader or high-confidence filter raised sensitivity by about 2%, and cut human reads by 48-81%.
papers.tools: BRAIx AI reader producing a cancer score;
papers.gap: Simulation, not prospective deployment; automation bias modelled not observed.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single programme; retrospective.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using real decisions from a population screening programme, the team simulated how five different ways of inserting an AI reader would change cancer detection, recalls and radiologist workload. They also modelled how readers might defer to the AI. Using the AI only for high-confidence cases and passing uncertain ones to humans saved most work while improving accuracy, which is close to the confidence-based escalation logic of the PhD's Objective 2.
papers.studyDesign: Large retrospective simulation study of AI-integrated screening pathways (BRAIx project, BreastScreen Victoria, Australia); ethics approved by St Vincent's Hospital Melbourne HREC.
papers.datasets: ADMANI datasets: population screening mammograms (four standard 2D views per client) from women attending BreastScreen Victoria 2016-2019, with recorded decisions of two independent readers plus arbitration.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified image and non-image data linked by unique identifier; retrospective reader decisions used to simulate pathways.
papers.modelDetails: BRAIx AI reader producing a cancer score; five simulated pathways including AI as second reader, AI as high-confidence filter (band-pass), and AI replacing readers; human-AI interaction modelled to study automation bias.
papers.training: AI reader trained and validated on held-out ADMANI data (details in the paper).
papers.evaluation: Sensitivity, specificity, number of assessments and human reads for each pathway compared with the current two-reader-plus-arbitration programme; simulated automation-bias scenarios.
papers.baselines: Current BreastScreen double reading with arbitration; individual radiologists.
papers.results: AI as second reader or high-confidence filter improved sensitivity by 1.9-2.5% and specificity by up to 0.6%, cut assessments by 4.6-10.9% and human reads by 48-80.7%; automation bias degraded performance in multi-reader settings but improved it for single readers.
papers.statistics: Bootstrap confidence intervals for pathway metrics.
papers.availability: Data under licence; code details in paper.

papers.title: Will You Tell Them When They Are Wrong? Automation Bias and Artificial Intelligence in Medicine
papers.authors: Bittencourt MS
papers.aim: To explain automation bias and complacency in medical AI and why clinicians must notice when an AI tool is wrong.
papers.method: Editorial discussion with cardiology examples (ECG pre-reading, imaging measurements, prescribing alerts) linked to EU AI Act rules on human oversight.
papers.result: Argues that AI must be evaluated on how clinicians interact with it and whether they spot its errors, not only on sensitivity, specificity and AUC.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No empirical data.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Opinion piece.
papers.methodologyDetail: This editorial explains how over-reliance on automated tools shows up as automation bias (trusting the tool over one's own judgement) and complacency (reduced vigilance), using ECG software as an example. It calls for studies that test human-tool interaction in real use and links this to legal requirements for human oversight. It supports the PhD's choice to evaluate escalation quality and over-reliance, not only model accuracy.
papers.studyDesign: Editorial (University of Pittsburgh, USA) in Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia.
papers.datasets: Not applicable.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual discussion distinguishing automation bias from automation complacency, with cardiology examples (ECG pre-reading, imaging measurements, prescribing alerts) and the EU AI Act requirement for human oversight.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Argues that evaluation of decision support must go beyond sensitivity, specificity and AUC to measure how clinicians interact with tools and whether they recognise when the tool is wrong.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Trust in Healthcare: Focus on Clinicians
papers.authors: Asan O, Bayrak AE, Choudhury A
papers.aim: To explain what shapes clinicians' trust in healthcare AI.
papers.method: Conceptual review defining AI and automation, trust as coping with uncertainty, and factors behind trust and distrust.
papers.result: Trust depends on performance, transparency, bias, users and regulation, and should be calibrated, not maximised.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No empirical testing of the factors.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Viewpoint; focuses on clinicians only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors define AI versus automation, explain trust as a way of coping with uncertainty, and review what makes clinicians trust or distrust AI tools. They argue that the aim is appropriate (calibrated) trust, with design attention to transparency, bias and human factors. This provides the theoretical basis for the trust measures used in the PhD's clinical evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Viewpoint paper (Stevens Institute of Technology, USA) in JMIR.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (conceptual synthesis of literature on trust and automation).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual analysis of clinician-AI trust, drawing on the Fitts list of human versus machine strengths, human factors and trust-in-automation theory; discusses fairness, transparency, robustness and FDA policy.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Identifies factors shaping clinician trust in AI (system performance, transparency, bias, user characteristics, regulation) and argues that trust must be calibrated, not maximised, with key challenges for AI developers.

papers.title: How physicians embrace AI: insights from technology acceptance and trust theories
papers.authors: Cicin FN, Çetin Gürkan G
papers.aim: To find what drives physicians to adopt AI, using technology acceptance and trust theories.
papers.method: Questionnaire of physicians in Turkey analysed with structural equation modelling.
papers.result: Trust was the main pathway from attitudes and perceived control to intention to use AI.
papers.tools: Likert, survey
papers.gap: Intention, not actual use; single country.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Self-report; cross-sectional.
papers.methodologyDetail: Physicians across Turkey completed a questionnaire measuring their attitudes, perceived social pressure, perceived ability to use AI, trust in AI and intention to use it. Structural equation modelling showed that trust is the main pathway through which the other factors lead to intention to adopt. This supports including validated trust and acceptance questionnaires in the PhD's clinician evaluation (WP7).
papers.studyDesign: Cross-sectional survey with structural equation modelling (Istinye University, Turkey), integrating the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Technology Acceptance Model and trust theory.
papers.datasets: 414 physicians from 38 cities in Turkey.
papers.preprocessing: Validated Likert-scale questionnaire; reliability and validity checks (measurement model).
papers.modelDetails: Research model with direct and mediating hypotheses: attitude, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control influencing trust in AI and behavioural intention to use AI.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Measurement model (reliability, convergent and discriminant validity) and structural model path coefficients; mediation analysis.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Trust fully mediated the effect of perceived behavioural control (p < 0.001) and other constructs on intention; subjective norms and perceived behavioural control had weaker direct effects (p < 0.05 and p = 0.07).
papers.statistics: Structural equation modelling with mediation tests.

papers.title: Trust of Artificial Intelligence-Augmented Point-of-Care Ultrasound Among Pediatric Emergency Physicians
papers.authors: Lin-Martore M, Kornblith A, Firnberg M, Haque A, O'Brien B
papers.venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians Open
papers.aim: To understand what makes paediatric emergency physicians trust AI in bedside ultrasound.
papers.method: Framework-guided interviews analysed with template analysis.
papers.result: Five groups of trust factors (technology, context, user, social, organisation) and the tasks where AI could help were identified.
papers.tools: semi-structured interviews
papers.gap: Hypothetical AI; single institution.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small sample; academic physicians only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Paediatric emergency physicians were interviewed about how they would decide whether to trust AI built into bedside ultrasound, using an established trust framework to structure questions. Template analysis grouped their views into five types of trust factors and listed the tasks where AI could help. The framework-guided interview design is a model for the PhD's clinician interviews in WP7.
papers.studyDesign: Qualitative interview study with interpretivist approach and template analysis (University of California, San Francisco, USA), November 2023 to April 2024.
papers.datasets: 14 academic paediatric emergency medicine physicians (1-34 years' experience) using POCUS across three urban paediatric EDs.
papers.preprocessing: Purposive recruitment for a range of POCUS experience; verbal consent; 30-45 minute semi-structured interviews recorded and transcribed.
papers.modelDetails: Interview guide sensitised by Yang's framework of user trust in AI (technological, contextual, user, social and organisational factors).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Template analysis of transcripts to identify themes on factors influencing trust in AI-augmented POCUS.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Five factor themes shaped trust: technological (accuracy, transparency), contextual, user, social and organisational; perceived benefits included image acquisition guidance, landmark identification, interpretation, measurements and reduced mental load.

papers.title: Facilitating Trust Calibration in Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnostic Decision Support Systems for Determining Physicians' Diagnostic Accuracy: Quasi-Experimental Study
papers.authors: Sakamoto T, Harada Y, Shimizu T
papers.aim: To test whether telling physicians how reliable an AI is improves their diagnostic accuracy.
papers.method: Quasi-experiment: physicians diagnosed 20 cases with AI differential lists, one group also given AI reliability information.
papers.result: No significant improvement in accuracy, possibly due to the small study and weak calibration method.
papers.tools: logistic regression
papers.gap: Calibration information not case-specific; underpowered.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Formative, small sample; vignette cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: Physicians diagnosed twenty written cases with help from AI-generated differential lists; one group was additionally told how reliable the AI tends to be so they could calibrate their trust. Accuracy did not differ significantly between groups, which the authors link to the small study and weak calibration method. The study shows that simply telling users about AI reliability is not enough, supporting the PhD's case-level calibrated confidence and escalation instead of global reliability statements.
papers.studyDesign: Quasi-experimental study at Dokkyo Medical University, Japan (August-September 2023); ethics approved, written consent.
papers.datasets: 20 clinical cases built from medical histories recorded by the AI Monshin automated history-taking system; physicians allocated 1:1 to intervention and control groups.
papers.preprocessing: Cases include AI-generated top-10 differential diagnoses with known correctness.
papers.modelDetails: Trust-calibration intervention informing physicians of the actual reliability of the AI differential list so they could adjust their reliance; AI Monshin (used in over 1,400 facilities) converts patient tablet input into medical history and differentials.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Physicians' diagnostic accuracy with and without the trust-calibration intervention; reliance on correct and incorrect AI suggestions.
papers.baselines: Control group using AI differentials without calibration information.
papers.results: No significant improvement in diagnostic accuracy from the trust-calibration intervention; authors attribute this to small sample size and suboptimal calibration methods in this formative study.
papers.statistics: Group comparison of accuracy with statistical testing.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and clinical decision support: clinicians' perspectives on trust, trustworthiness, and liability
papers.authors: Jones C, Thornton J, Wyatt JC
papers.aim: To clarify what clinicians mean by trusting AI decision support, including liability.
papers.method: Philosophical analysis separating trust (an attitude) from trustworthiness (a property to be shown), linked to clinicians' concerns.
papers.result: Trustworthiness must be demonstrated, not assumed, and liability worries are part of clinicians' trust judgements.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No new empirical data; UK legal focus.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Conceptual and jurisdiction-specific.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors examine what clinicians mean when they talk about trusting AI decision support, using a philosophical framework that separates trust (an attitude) from trustworthiness (a property to be shown). They link clinicians' worries about accuracy and legal responsibility to this distinction. This helps the PhD frame escalation and audit trails as ways of making the system demonstrably trustworthy and of clarifying accountability.
papers.studyDesign: Socio-legal conceptual analysis (Swansea University, Nottingham Trent University, University of Southampton, UK) in Medical Law Review.
papers.datasets: Not applicable; analysis of published empirical studies of clinicians' perspectives on AI and CDSS.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Application of Onora O'Neill's conceptualisation of trust and trustworthiness to clinicians' reported concerns about AI-based CDSS (accuracy of advice and legal liability).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Clarifies who or what is being trusted (system, developer, institution, regulator); shows stakeholders often talk at cross purposes; liability concerns are part of clinicians' trust judgements; trustworthiness should be demonstrated, not assumed.

papers.title: Clinical experience and perception of risk affect the acceptance and trust of using AI in medicine
papers.authors: Schulz PJ, Kee KM, Lwin MO, Goh WW, Chia KY, Cheung MFK, Lam TYT, Sung JJY
papers.aim: To find how clinical experience and risk perception affect gastroenterologists' acceptance of AI.
papers.method: Validated questionnaire across Asia-Pacific for three colonoscopy AI tasks, analysed by experience and risk perception.
papers.result: Seniors who saw low risk accepted AI most; acceptance fell as AI tasks became more autonomous.
papers.tools: TAM, survey
papers.gap: Intentions only; scenarios hypothetical.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Self-report survey; response bias.
papers.methodologyDetail: Gastroenterologists across the Asia-Pacific region answered a validated questionnaire about trust and acceptance of AI for three colonoscopy tasks of increasing complexity. Analysis of covariance compared groups defined by experience and perceived risk. Experience and risk perception together shaped acceptance, and acceptance dropped for more autonomous tasks, which supports keeping humans in charge of higher-risk decisions such as surgical planning in the PhD.
papers.studyDesign: Cross-sectional online survey (Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, with Asia-Pacific partners); IRB approved (IRB-2022-756).
papers.datasets: 319 gastroenterologists and GI surgeons trained in colonoscopy from ten Asia-Pacific countries/regions.
papers.preprocessing: Validated questionnaire items adapted from Theory of Planned Behaviour, TAM, expectancy-value framework and prior trust and risk-tolerance scales; reliability checked (e.g. McDonald's ω = 0.91).
papers.modelDetails: Three AI scenarios of increasing sophistication (polyp detection, polyp characterisation, polypectomy with complication management); participants grouped by clinical experience and risk perception.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Acceptance and trust per scenario; four groups (experience × risk perception) compared.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Senior clinicians with low risk perception were highly accepting of AI, whereas seniors with high risk perception were substantially less accepting; acceptance fell as AI tasks became more sophisticated.
papers.statistics: ANCOVA comparing groups with covariates; reliability statistics.

papers.title: How Explainable Artificial Intelligence Can Increase or Decrease Clinicians' Trust in AI Applications in Health Care: Systematic Review
papers.authors: Rosenbacke R, Melhus Å, McKee M, Stuckler D
papers.aim: To review whether explainable AI increases clinicians' trust.
papers.method: Systematic review of ten empirical studies where clinicians received AI explanations and trust was measured.
papers.result: Explanations raised trust in about half the studies but sometimes lowered it, and could increase acceptance of wrong advice.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: Few studies; need validated cognitive and affective trust measures and strategies for appropriate trust.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Only two databases; heterogeneous studies.
papers.methodologyDetail: Two reviewers searched two databases for empirical studies in which practising clinicians were given AI explanations and their trust was measured, ending with ten studies. The synthesis shows that explanations can increase, decrease or not change trust, and may increase acceptance of wrong advice. This warns the PhD that explanations alone do not calibrate trust and supports pairing them with calibrated uncertainty and escalation, with careful measurement of trust.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA (Copenhagen Business School, Uppsala University, LSHTM, Bocconi University).
papers.datasets: PubMed (373) and Web of Science (713) records searched 23 March 2023; 778 after de-duplication; 48 full texts; 10 empirical studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Broad search on XAI and health care without restricting trust terms; inclusion required trust as outcome, XAI as intervention, ML model, empirical design and practising clinicians; dual-reviewer screening.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of how explanation types (feature importance, example-based, counterfactual, etc.) affect clinicians' cognitive and affective trust.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Classification of findings into trust increased, decreased or unchanged; assessment of trust measurement approaches.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: XAI increased trust in about half the studies but sometimes reduced it or had no effect; explanations could raise acceptance of AI advice without helping clinicians detect incorrect recommendations (over-reliance risk); trust measurement was inconsistent.

papers.title: Clinicians' Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence: Focus on Workload, Risk, Trust, Clinical Decision Making, and Clinical Integration
papers.authors: Shamszare H, Choudhury A
papers.aim: To study clinicians' views on AI workload, risk, trust and decision making.
papers.method: Survey of US healthcare workers analysed with structural equation modelling.
papers.result: Trust was the key route to acceptance, and perceived risk lowered trust.
papers.tools: survey, Likert
papers.gap: Mostly nurses and limited AI experience; intention only.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Self-selected online sample; cross-sectional.
papers.methodologyDetail: Healthcare workers in the US completed a questionnaire on AI workload, risk, trust and decision making, and the relationships were tested with structural equation modelling after checking reliability and validity. Trust emerged as the key route to acceptance, while perceived risk lowered trust. These validated constructs inform the workload and trust measures planned for the PhD's clinician evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Cross-sectional online survey with partial least squares structural equation modelling (West Virginia University, USA).
papers.datasets: 265 complete responses from US healthcare professionals (35% registered nurses, 11% nurse practitioners, 8% physicians, 6% residents, others); 17% had used AI.
papers.preprocessing: Validated Likert-scale items; convergent and discriminant validity, factor loadings > 0.50, VIF < 5, composite reliability > 0.70, AVE > 0.50.
papers.modelDetails: Structural model linking perceived workload, perceived risk and trust in AI to perceived effect on clinical decision making and intention to integrate AI into practice.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: PLS-SEM path coefficients and explained variance.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Trust in AI positively influenced perceptions of AI's role in decision making and integration; perceived risk reduced trust; AI should be perceived as supportive rather than intrusive, reducing workload.

papers.title: Recent Outcomes and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning in Neurosurgery
papers.authors: Awuah WA, Adebusoye FT, Wellington J, David L, Salam A, Weng Yee AL, Lansiaux E, Yarlagadda R, Garg T, Abdul-Rahman T, et al.
papers.aim: To review recent outcomes and challenges of AI in neurosurgery.
papers.method: Narrative review of AI use across neurosurgical care, from imaging and grading to surgery and outcome prediction.
papers.result: AI has improved diagnosis, planning and outcome prediction, but data, generalisability, transparency and regulation remain problems.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No systematic method or quality appraisal; few prospective validations cited.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Narrative review; broad scope.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors review how AI, machine learning and deep learning are being used at each stage of neurosurgical care, from imaging diagnosis and tumour grading to intraoperative guidance and outcome prediction. They also summarise barriers such as limited data, poor generalisability and lack of transparency. The review gives the clinical context for the PhD's surgical-planning demonstrator and its emphasis on human oversight.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (international author group led from Sumy State University) in World Neurosurgery: X.
papers.datasets: Not applicable; published studies of AI, ML and DL across pre-, intra- and postoperative neurosurgery.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis covering applications in neuro-oncology (glioma grading and segmentation), spine (MESCC), epilepsy (seizure onset zone), vascular neurosurgery (aneurysms, ICH, LVO), surgical planning, VR training and outcome prediction.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative summary of reported outcomes and challenges.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI has improved diagnosis, prognosis, surgical planning and complication reduction in neurosurgery, but faces challenges of data quality, generalisability, interpretability, ethics, regulation and integration into workflows.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Surgical Planning for Neurosurgery: Artificial Intelligent Approaches to the Cranium
papers.authors: Dundar TT, Yurtsever I, Pehlivanoglu MK, Yildiz U, Eker A, Demir MA, Mutluer AS, Tektaş R, Kazan MS, Kitis S, et al.
papers.aim: To use machine learning to plan safe paths to brain lesions.
papers.method: Neurosurgeons labelled brain voxels by risk using MRI and tractography, and a Q-learning agent found straight and curved trajectories, compared with expert paths.
papers.result: Feasible trajectories consistent with expert choices, a proof of concept for AI cranial planning.
papers.tools: Two-stage architecture to find linear and non-linear access paths to cranial targets: path candidates computed on labelled voxel maps, and model-free…
papers.gap: Small proof of concept; no uncertainty estimate; not clinically validated.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective single-centre; manual labelling.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using patients' MRI and diffusion tractography, neurosurgeons labelled brain voxels by risk, and a reinforcement learning agent (Q-learning) learned to find safe straight and curved paths to lesions. Results were compared with the paths experts would choose. It is an early example of AI-assisted neurosurgical trajectory planning relevant to the PhD's surgical-planning proof of concept, where the surgeon must remain the final decision maker.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective imaging study with algorithm development (Bezmiâlem Vakif University and Kocaeli University, Turkey); ethics approved, consent waived.
papers.datasets: Retrospective brain MRI including DTI tractography of patients with intracranial lesions (1.5 T Siemens Magnetom Avanto).
papers.preprocessing: T1W, T2W, FLAIR (5 mm), DTI (30 directions, b = 1,000 s/mm²) and 3D MPRAGE with and without gadolinium; tractography on Syngo.via; voxels labelled for eloquent structures and optimal paths by neurosurgeons in consensus.
papers.modelDetails: Two-stage architecture to find linear and non-linear access paths to cranial targets: path candidates computed on labelled voxel maps, and model-free Q-learning reinforcement learning run on labelled voxel values to learn optimal trajectories avoiding critical structures.
papers.training: Q-learning with reward based on voxel labels (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Comparison of algorithm-generated trajectories with neurosurgeon-defined optimal paths.
papers.baselines: Expert manual trajectory planning.
papers.results: Q-learning produced feasible linear and non-linear trajectories consistent with expert-defined optimal paths, showing proof of concept for ML-based cranial surgical planning.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurosurgery: A State-of-the-Art Review from Past to Future
papers.authors: Tangsrivimol JA, Schonfeld E, Zhang M, Veeravagu A, Smith TR, Härtl R, Lawton MT, El-Sherbini AH, Prevedello DM, Glicksberg BS, et al.
papers.aim: To review machine learning in neurosurgery from past to future.
papers.method: Review of highly cited studies in neuro-oncology, spine, epilepsy and vascular neurosurgery, explaining algorithm types.
papers.result: ML is effective for tumour identification and outcome prediction but needs better validation and integration.
papers.tools: SVM
papers.gap: No systematic search or bias assessment.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Selection by citation count may bias towards older work.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors selected highly cited studies and summarised how machine learning has been used in neuro-oncology, spine, epilepsy and vascular neurosurgery, explaining the main algorithm types for clinicians. They conclude that ML shows strong promise but needs better validation and integration. It provides background for the neurosurgical use case of the PhD, especially tumour identification and surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: State-of-the-art narrative review (Chulabhorn Royal Academy, Ohio State, Stanford, Harvard and others) in Diagnostics.
papers.datasets: Highly cited seminal papers identified through PubMed and Google Scholar across tumour, spine, epilepsy and vascular neurosurgery.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative summary of ML/DL methods (ANN, CNN, RNN, SVM, random forests) and their neurosurgical applications, with a primer for clinicians and future outlook.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative summary of reported performance.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: ML is effective in tumour identification, surgical outcome prediction, seizure outcome prediction and aneurysm prediction; challenges include data, validation, interpretability and integration.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurosurgery: a Systematic Review Using Topic Modeling. Part I: Major Research Areas
papers.authors: Danilov GV, Shifrin MA, Kotik KV, Ishankulov TA, Orlov YN, Kulikov AS, Potapov AA
papers.aim: To map the main research areas of AI in neurosurgery using topic modelling.
papers.method: 327 PubMed articles (1996-2019) were grouped by LDA and ARTM topic models and themes named by experts.
papers.result: Identified main areas such as neuro-oncology imaging, outcome prediction, spine, epilepsy and vascular surgery, with fast-growing output.
papers.tools: topic modelling, LDA, ARTM, NLP, PRISMA
papers.gap: Topic modelling shows themes but not quality or results.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Abstract-level analysis; part I only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Rather than reading every paper by hand, the team applied two topic-modelling algorithms to the abstracts of AI-in-neurosurgery publications to discover the main research themes, which experts then named and interpreted. This mapped where AI work in neurosurgery is concentrated. The NLP-assisted review technique is a useful method idea for keeping the PhD's large literature bank organised.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review with AI topic modelling (N.N. Burdenko National Medical Research Center for Neurosurgery and Keldysh Institute, Russia), PRISMA-guided.
papers.datasets: Publications on AI/ML in neurosurgery retrieved from bibliographic databases (abstracts analysed as a text corpus).
papers.preprocessing: Text preprocessing of abstracts (tokenisation, lemmatisation, stop-word removal) for NLP.
papers.modelDetails: Topic modelling with Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Additive Regularization of Topic Models (ARTM) to identify major research areas objectively, followed by expert interpretation of topics.
papers.training: Topic number and regularisation chosen by coherence and expert review.
papers.evaluation: Keywords specific to each topic; distribution and growth of publications across topics.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Identified major AI research areas in neurosurgery (e.g. neuro-oncology imaging, outcome prediction, spine, epilepsy, vascular, neuro-intensive care) with their characteristic keywords; publication volume rising rapidly.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence innovations in neurosurgical oncology: a narrative review
papers.authors: Baker CR, Pease M, Sexton DP, Abumoussa A, Chambless LB
papers.aim: To review AI innovations in brain and spinal tumour surgery.
papers.method: Narrative review, organised along the patient pathway from diagnosis to surgery and training.
papers.result: AI helps at every stage, but generalisability, bias and data security remain; federated learning is proposed.
papers.tools: federated learning
papers.gap: No systematic appraisal; few prospective trials.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Narrative review.
papers.methodologyDetail: With help from a research librarian, the authors gathered key studies on AI in brain and spinal tumour surgery and described them in the order a patient experiences care, from diagnosis and planning to surgery and training. They point to federated learning and shared data consortia as solutions to bias and privacy problems. This closely matches the PhD's neuro-oncology focus, surgical-planning use case and federated design.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Vanderbilt, Indiana, Duke and UNC neurosurgery, USA) in Journal of Neuro-Oncology.
papers.datasets: Key articles on AI, ML, computer vision, NLP and AR/VR for neurosurgical care of brain and spinal tumours, found through a librarian-assisted literature search.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis organised along the patient pathway: pre-operative diagnosis and prognostication, automated tumour segmentation and extent-of-resection prediction for planning, intra-operative rapid histopathological classification, post-operative video analysis and simulation for training.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI is improving CNS tumour care at each stage; concerns remain about generalisability, bias and data security; federated learning and data consortia are proposed as the route to safer, stronger AI.

papers.title: The future of artificial intelligence in neurosurgery: A narrative review
papers.authors: Iqbal J, Jahangir K, Mashkoor Y, Sultana N, Mehmood D, Ashraf M, Iqbal A, Hafeez MH
papers.aim: To review the future of AI in neurosurgery.
papers.method: Narrative review under diagnosis, outcomes and treatment, with obstacles and future directions.
papers.result: AI should assist rather than replace neurosurgeons; data quality, ethics and acceptance are key challenges.
papers.tools: Narrative summary of AI use in neurosurgery grouped into diagnostic, outcome-prediction and treatment models, plus challenges and future directions.
papers.gap: Unsystematic; no quality assessment.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Narrative; limited depth.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed published work on AI in neurosurgery and summarised it under diagnosis, outcomes and treatment, then discussed obstacles and the future. Their conclusion that AI should support, not replace, the neurosurgeon fits the PhD's human-in-the-loop position, though the review adds little methodological detail.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative literature review (authors from Pakistan, India and UK) in Surgical Neurology International.
papers.datasets: Online literature on AI and ML in neurosurgery.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative summary of AI use in neurosurgery grouped into diagnostic, outcome-prediction and treatment models, plus challenges and future directions.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Main research areas are diagnosis, outcome prediction and treatment planning; challenges include data quality, ethics, interpretability and clinical acceptance; AI should assist rather than replace neurosurgeons.

papers.title: Neurosurgical Management of Cerebrospinal Tumors in the Era of Artificial Intelligence : A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Agadi K, Dominari A, Tebha SS, Mohammadi A, Zahid S
papers.aim: To map AI use in the surgical management of brain and spinal tumours.
papers.method: Scoping review of seven databases; 110 studies mapped by type of application.
papers.result: AI covers diagnosis, grading, segmentation, planning, intraoperative use and prognosis; more clinically useful and affordable work is needed.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: No quality appraisal; search ended 2021.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: English only; heterogeneous evidence.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched seven databases for studies applying AI to the surgical management of brain and spinal cord tumours, screened them in two stages and mapped 110 studies by type of application. Because the studies were so varied, they did not grade quality. The map shows where AI is used along the neuro-oncology pathway, giving background for the PhD's choice of MRI segmentation, pathology classification and planning tasks.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework (Larkin Health System, USA, with partners in Greece and Pakistan); PRISMA 2020 flow diagram.
papers.datasets: PubMed, Ovid, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, EMBASE and Scopus searched 10 January to 10 April 2021; 1,521 records, 361 unique relevant, 110 studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Two-stage screening (title/abstract, then full text) by all authors in Excel; English-language human studies on AI in neurosurgical management of brain and spinal tumours; grey literature, preprints, systematic reviews and animal studies excluded.
papers.modelDetails: Data extraction and thematic classification of AI applications (diagnosis, tumour classification, segmentation, surgical planning, intra-operative guidance, outcome prediction).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive mapping in tables.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI applications span diagnosis, grading, segmentation, planning, intra-operative tissue identification and prognosis; further research is needed on clinically essential and economically feasible applications.
papers.statistics: None (no formal quality assessment due to heterogeneity).

papers.title: Knowledge, interest and perspectives on Artificial Intelligence in Neurosurgery. A global survey
papers.authors: Boaro A, Mezzalira E, Siddi F, Bagattini C, Gabrovsky N, Marchesini N, Broekman M, Sala F, EANS ETIN Task Force
papers.aim: To survey neurosurgeons' knowledge of and attitudes to AI worldwide.
papers.method: Piloted 24-item online survey testing knowledge of AI terms and attitudes.
papers.result: Knowledge was limited but attitudes were very positive; neurosurgeons asked for AI training and guidelines.
papers.tools: survey
papers.gap: Few respondents from low- and middle-income countries.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Self-selected sample; European bias.
papers.methodologyDetail: Neurosurgeons worldwide answered a piloted 24-item online survey testing what they actually know about basic AI terms and how they feel about using AI. Most were keen on AI but had limited understanding of it. This highlights the need for clear explanations and training when the PhD introduces its escalation system to Sri Lankan neurosurgeons.
papers.studyDesign: Cross-sectional global online survey (University of Verona, Leiden University and EANS ETIN Task Force), reported per CHERRIES.
papers.datasets: 248 complete responses from neurosurgeons and trainees in 61 countries (69% Europe; 62% post-residency; 68% academic hospitals).
papers.preprocessing: 24-item questionnaire built from a targeted literature review and expert consensus, piloted with a small sample for clarity.
papers.modelDetails: Three sections: demographics and work setting; perceived and actual knowledge of basic AI concepts (machine learning, deep learning, big data) and interest in AI research; attitudes and perspectives on AI integration.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive statistics of knowledge, interest and attitudes; comparison of perceived versus actual knowledge.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Knowledge of basic AI concepts was limited, but interest and attitude toward AI implementation were strongly positive; respondents called for systematic AI training and guidelines.
papers.statistics: Descriptive and inferential comparisons between subgroups.

papers.title: Publicly Available Datasets for Artificial Intelligence in Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Chan B, Kim B, Schonfeld E, Nageeb G, Pant A, Sjoholm A, Medikonda R, Hani U, Veeravagu A
papers.aim: To catalogue public datasets for AI in neurosurgery.
papers.method: Systematic PubMed review of newly released, accessible neurosurgical datasets, with quality of their baseline models assessed.
papers.result: 86 datasets, mostly neuro-oncology imaging; baseline models were poorly validated, and some populations and subspecialties are missing.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: PubMed only; underrepresentation of LMIC data.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single database; English only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Two reviewers searched PubMed for studies that released new neurosurgical datasets which others can access, and catalogued 86 of them by disease, imaging type, size and access. They also judged the quality of the baseline models shipped with the data. The review helps the PhD choose public datasets (for example brain tumour MRI) for early baselines and confirms the lack of data from South Asian populations, supporting the national registry.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA (Stanford Neurosurgical AI and ML Laboratory, USA).
papers.datasets: PubMed search on 8 February 2025 (publications from 2016) returning 267 articles; 86 studies releasing novel public or access-on-application neurosurgical datasets included.
papers.preprocessing: Dual independent screening; inclusion: novel primary data, publicly available or applicable, human neurosurgically relevant data; exclusion: sample < 100, non-novel or restricted data, non-English, non-primary designs.
papers.modelDetails: Data extraction and categorisation of datasets by anatomy, pathology, modality, size, access route and any baseline models provided.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive mapping of dataset characteristics and quality of provided baseline models (external validation, reproducibility, evaluation metrics).
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 86 public datasets catalogued, dominated by neuro-oncology imaging; baseline models from these datasets are limited by poor external validation, lack of reproducibility and reliance on suboptimal evaluation metrics; gaps in several neurosurgical subspecialties and populations.

papers.title: Randomized Controlled Trials of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: Systematic Review
papers.authors: Lam TYT, Cheung MFK, Munro YL, Lim KM, Shung D, Sung JJY
papers.aim: To review randomised controlled trials of AI in clinical practice.
papers.method: Systematic review of five databases; 39 RCTs checked for endpoints and risk of bias.
papers.result: Most trials were positive but small, single-centre and rarely measured patient outcomes.
papers.tools: PRISMA, reader study
papers.gap: Few multicentre trials or patient-outcome end points.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Search ended 2021; heterogeneous trials.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched five databases for every randomised trial that tested an AI tool in patient care, ending with 39 trials, and checked their end points and risk of bias. Most trials reported benefits but were small and single-centre, with few hard patient outcomes. This shows the PhD that rigorous prospective evaluation is still rare and that a well-designed reader study is a realistic step before any trial.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials of AI tools across all specialties (Chinese University of Hong Kong, Nanyang Technological University, Yale); PRISMA 2020, PROSPERO CRD42021286539.
papers.datasets: CINAHL, Cochrane Central, Embase, MEDLINE and PubMed from inception to 14 July 2021: 11,839 records, 6,823 screened, 147 full texts, 39 RCTs included (34 plus 4 hand-searched).
papers.preprocessing: Dual independent screening with senior-author arbitration; conference abstracts and preprints included.
papers.modelDetails: Data extraction on specialty, AI tool, setting, sample size, design and primary end points; assessment of clinical relevance of end points and risk of bias.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Proportion of trials with positive primary end points and clinically relevant outcomes; risk of bias.
papers.baselines: Standard care in each trial.
papers.results: Growing evidence supports AI tools in clinical practice, mostly in gastroenterology (e.g. polyp detection), with most trials positive on primary end points; small sample sizes and single-centre designs limited generalisability, and few trials measured patient outcomes.

papers.title: Randomized Clinical Trials of Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Why, When, and How?
papers.authors: Park SH, Choi JI, Fournier L, Vasey B
papers.aim: To explain why, when and how randomised clinical trials of medical AI should be run.
papers.method: Methodological guidance that summarises the AI-specific items of SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI for trial protocols and reports.
papers.result: Randomised trials are the best way to show AI improves patient outcomes, after adequate validation; trials must describe the human-AI interaction and plan error analysis.
papers.tools: SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI, reader study
papers.gap: Guidance only; no new trial data.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Commentary.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors explain that the real test of a clinical AI system is whether patient outcomes improve when it is used, best shown by a randomised trial, and list what an AI trial protocol and report must describe, such as algorithm version, input data checks, how clinicians see and act on outputs, and how errors will be analysed. This checklist guides how the PhD should report its reader study and any later trial of the escalation system.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological editorial / guidance article (Asan Medical Center, Catholic University of Korea, Université Paris Cité, University of Oxford) in Korean Journal of Radiology.
papers.datasets: Not applicable.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Explains why, when and how to run RCTs of clinical AI, summarising AI-specific reporting items from SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI (participant- and input-data-level eligibility, AI version, handling of poor-quality input, human-AI interaction, how outputs feed decisions, analysis of performance errors and harms, user recruitment and training).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: RCTs are the ideal design to show that AI improves clinical outcomes compared with no AI, but should follow adequate preclinical validation; trial design must describe the human-AI interaction and plan error analysis.

papers.title: A randomized controlled trial of artificial intelligence-based analytics for clinical deterioration
papers.authors: Keim-Malpass J, Ratcliffe SJ, Clark MT, Krahn KN, Monfredi OJ, Hamil S, Yousefvand G, Jones MK, Nelson A, Moorman LP, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether showing an AI deterioration risk score to hospital staff improves patient outcomes.
papers.method: Cluster RCT: rooms randomly showed or hid the AI display, covering over 10,000 admissions.
papers.result: No clear improvement; a passive display without a required action did not change outcomes.
papers.tools: CONSORT-AI
papers.gap: Passive display without linked actions; contamination from pragmatic bed allocation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; cardiology ward only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Hospital rooms were randomly assigned, and periodically re-assigned, to show or not show an AI display of each patient's deterioration risk, and outcomes for over ten thousand admissions were compared with appropriate models for clustering. The passive display, with no required action, did not clearly reduce deterioration, partly because staff moved sicker patients into display beds. The lesson for the PhD is that AI output must be tied to a defined action, such as an explicit escalation pathway.
papers.studyDesign: Pragmatic cluster-randomised controlled trial (University of Virginia, USA; NCT04359641), January 2021 to October 2022, reported per CONSORT-AI; IRB waiver of consent; DSMB oversight.
papers.datasets: 10,422 inpatient visits on an 85-bed acute cardiology and cardiac surgery ward; 11 clusters defined by room number.
papers.preprocessing: Clusters re-randomised every 2 months with a Latin square design within strata; intention-to-treat.
papers.modelDetails: CoMET passive display of AI-based predictive analytics (continuous risk trajectories of deterioration from monitoring and EHR data) with implementation and education plan; no mandated response.
papers.training: Pre-existing validated predictive models.
papers.evaluation: Primary: hours free of clinical deterioration (death, emergent ICU transfer, intubation, cardiac arrest, emergent surgery); 21-day mortality.
papers.baselines: Usual medical care without display.
papers.results: No clear improvement in event-free hours overall; patients with large spikes in risk score had more events, and the pragmatic design allowed sicker patients to be moved towards displayed beds, complicating interpretation.
papers.statistics: GEE with zero-inflated negative binomial model for event-free hours; Cox proportional hazards for time to first event, accounting for clustering and repeat admissions.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted colonoscopy: A prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial of polyp detection
papers.authors: Xu L, He X, Zhou J, Zhang J, Mao X, Ye G, Chen Q, Xu F, Sang J, Wang J, et al.
papers.aim: To test AI-assisted colonoscopy for polyp detection in a multicentre RCT.
papers.method: Patients at six hospitals were randomised to colonoscopy with or without real-time AI.
papers.result: Overall detection did not rise significantly (38.8% vs 36.2%), but more small and flat polyps were found, varying by centre.
papers.tools: logistic regression, randomised controlled trial
papers.gap: No adenoma or cancer outcomes; centre variability unexplained.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Unblinded; regional Chinese centres.
papers.methodologyDetail: Patients at six hospitals were randomly allocated to colonoscopy with or without a real-time AI polyp detector, and detection rates were compared. AI did not significantly raise the overall polyp detection rate but helped find small, flat and additional polyps, with benefit varying by centre and operator. This shows that AI value depends on the setting and user, which the PhD's multi-site evaluation must account for.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective multicentre randomised controlled trial at six centres in Zhejiang, China (ChiCTR1800015607).
papers.datasets: 2,352 patients undergoing colonoscopy included in final analysis.
papers.preprocessing: Eligible patients randomly assigned to conventional colonoscopy or AI-assisted colonoscopy.
papers.modelDetails: Newly developed real-time deep learning system for colonoscopic polyp detection overlaid on the endoscopy video.
papers.training: Developed previously by the team (details referenced).
papers.evaluation: Primary: polyp detection rate (PDR); secondary: polyps per positive patient, polyps per colonoscopy, non-first polyps per colonoscopy (PPC-Plus); subgroup by centre, endoscopist and patient factors.
papers.baselines: Conventional colonoscopy.
papers.results: PDR not significantly higher with AI (38.8% vs 36.2%, p = 0.183); PPC-Plus higher (0.5 vs 0.4, p < 0.05); more diminutive (76.0% vs 68.8%) and flat polyps (5.9% vs 3.3%) detected; effects varied between centres; in regression AI independently increased PDR, especially for certain endoscopist and patient subgroups.

papers.title: A responsible AI framework for infection surveillance in low-resource settings: ethics, opportunities and threats for LMICs (EOT-LMICs)
papers.authors: Alzyood M
papers.aim: To propose a responsible AI framework for infection surveillance in low- and middle-income countries.
papers.method: Commentary combining literature on AI, digital health and surveillance into a framework: ethics as preconditions, then opportunities weighed against threats.
papers.result: A structured pathway for context-appropriate, human-centred AI in LMICs, highlighting data governance, local validation and model drift.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: Framework not empirically tested.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Commentary; single author.
papers.methodologyDetail: The author combined literature on AI, digital health and infection surveillance in low-resource settings into a framework that first checks ethical preconditions, then weighs opportunities against threats such as model drift and fragile infrastructure. Although focused on infection surveillance, the framework applies to deploying the PhD's system in Sri Lanka, an LMIC, and supports its attention to data governance, local validation and drift monitoring.
papers.studyDesign: Short communication / conceptual framework (Oxford Brookes University, UK) in International Health.
papers.datasets: Not applicable; synthesis of literature on AI adoption, digital health implementation and infection surveillance in resource-limited settings.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: EOT-LMICs framework: ethical foundations (equity, data governance, contextual validity) as preconditions; opportunities (workforce augmentation, standardised surveillance, outbreak detection); threats (misclassification, infrastructure fragility, model drift, regulatory gaps); aligned with the 4Ps model (precision, partnership, practice, people).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Provides policymakers and practitioners with a structured pathway for context-appropriate, human-centred AI implementation in LMICs.

papers.title: Effectiveness of AI-Based Tools in Detecting Diabetic Retinopathy in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Performance and Implementation Feasibility
papers.authors: Onyeze N, Sartawi S, Nayyer Z
papers.aim: To review AI diabetic retinopathy screening in low- and middle-income countries.
papers.method: Systematic review of six databases; six LMIC studies with accuracy or implementation data.
papers.result: High accuracy (e.g. 94.7% in Thailand) and better referral uptake with instant AI results, but infrastructure challenges remain.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: Only six studies; few RCTs or cost analyses.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: English only; small evidence base.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched six databases for studies of AI diabetic retinopathy screening carried out in low- and middle-income countries and found six with usable accuracy or implementation data. They summarised both how accurate the tools were and how well they worked in practice, including a randomised trial showing better referral uptake. This LMIC evidence supports the PhD's argument that AI can help fill specialist gaps in Sri Lanka if implementation is planned carefully.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review of diagnostic performance and implementation feasibility (Ninewells Hospital, Dundee, UK), PRISMA; studies January 2015 to June 2025 from six databases.
papers.datasets: 109 records, 86 screened, 58 full texts, 6 studies included from LMICs (World Bank FY25 classification), e.g. Thailand (nine primary care sites), Rwanda RCT (n = 275), Brazil portable-camera pilot (n = 1,046), India.
papers.preprocessing: Inclusion: AI/ML/DL on retinal images for DR detection in LMICs with quantitative accuracy or implementation outcomes; English peer-reviewed or high-quality preprints.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC) and implementation outcomes (referral uptake, cost, workload, feasibility) of AI DR screening tools.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Tabulated accuracy and implementation outcomes; quality appraisal.
papers.baselines: Human graders / retina specialists.
papers.results: High accuracy (e.g. Thai DL system for vision-threatening DR: accuracy 94.7%, sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 95.4%); immediate AI feedback raised referral uptake in Rwanda (51.5% vs 39.6%, p = 0.048); handheld embedded AI feasible in rural Brazil; early evidence of lower costs and workload, but infrastructure and integration challenges.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted chest X-ray for tuberculosis case finding in low- and middle-income countries: implementation experiences and impact
papers.authors: Vijayan S, Nair AM, Dominic N, Chiramal JA, Pawar S, Goswami L
papers.aim: To summarise experience with AI chest X-ray reading for tuberculosis case finding in LMICs.
papers.method: Review by industry authors of deployment models and reported effects.
papers.result: AI improved case detection and turnaround time and supported decentralised care (possible conflict of interest).
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No systematic method; vendor perspective.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Conflict of interest; narrative.
papers.methodologyDetail: Authors from an AI company summarised how AI reading of chest X-rays has been used to find tuberculosis cases in low- and middle-income countries, describing deployment models and their reported effects on case detection and speed. It shows that AI can extend scarce radiology capacity in LMICs, relevant to Sri Lanka's limited neuroradiology workforce, though the industry authorship is a potential conflict of interest.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review of implementation experiences (Qure.ai Technologies, India and USA) in BJR|Open.
papers.datasets: Published studies and programme reports on AI-assisted chest X-ray for TB case finding in LMICs.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of AI CXR deployment models (triage before molecular testing, active case finding, mobile vans, integrated multi-disease pathways).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative summary of reported case-detection, accuracy, turnaround time and cost outcomes.
papers.baselines: Human radiologist reading or symptom screening.
papers.results: AI CXR improved case detection, diagnostic accuracy and turnaround time in high-burden settings, identified subclinical TB, and enabled integrated workflows for multiple chest diseases and decentralised care.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Human-Artificial Intelligence Collaboration in Cephalometric Landmark Detection
papers.authors: Le VNT, Kang J, Oh IS, Kim JG, Yang YM, Lee DW
papers.aim: To test whether AI helps less experienced clinicians locate cephalometric landmarks.
papers.method: A model trained on over 1,000 cephalograms; beginners marked 41 landmarks alone and then with AI suggestions.
papers.result: AI error was 1.87 mm on average, and beginners were more accurate with AI help.
papers.tools: SPSS
papers.gap: Only beginners tested; no uncertainty on landmarks.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; paediatric only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a deep learning model on over a thousand children's cephalograms to locate 41 landmarks, then had less experienced clinicians mark the same landmarks on test images alone and again with the AI suggestions, comparing errors at several distance thresholds. Collaboration made beginners more accurate. It is evidence that human-AI teamwork helps less experienced users most, relevant to supporting junior clinicians in the PhD's setting.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and human-AI collaboration study (Jeonbuk National University, South Korea); IRB approved (CUH2019-05-057).
papers.datasets: 1,293 lateral cephalograms of children and adolescents aged 6-18 years (2008-2018) from the hospital PACS; 1,193 for training and 100 for testing; 41 landmarks.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified JPG images (550×550 to 4066×4345 pixels); random training/test split; expert landmark annotation.
papers.modelDetails: DACFL deep learning model for cephalometric landmark detection; beginner clinicians detected landmarks alone and with AI-suggested positions (beginner-AI collaboration).
papers.training: Details in paper (CNN trained on 1,193 images).
papers.evaluation: Mean radial error (MRE) and successful detection rate (SDR) within 2, 2.5, 3 and 4 mm thresholds per landmark, for AI alone, beginners alone and beginner-AI collaboration.
papers.baselines: Beginners alone; AI alone.
papers.results: AI MRE 1.87 ± 2.04 mm (sella lowest at 0.76 mm, glabella highest at 5.18 mm); beginner-AI collaboration improved SDR over beginners alone for many landmarks.
papers.statistics: t-tests comparing SDR between beginner-only and beginner-AI groups (SPSS, PRISM), p < 0.05.

papers.title: A scoping review of human-AI collaboration patterns and task divisions in healthcare applications
papers.authors: You Y, Li X
papers.aim: To classify how humans and AI share work in healthcare.
papers.method: Scoping review of 85 studies comparing human-AI teams with either alone, classified by where AI enters the workflow and how tasks are divided.
papers.result: Higher-risk tasks keep more human control, and evaluation is moving beyond accuracy to efficiency and user experience.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: Few studies on dynamic or uncertainty-based task allocation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: English only; heterogeneous designs.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors screened the literature for studies comparing humans working with AI against either alone, included 85, and classified how the AI was inserted into the workflow (before the human's decision, after it, or as a filter) and how tasks were divided. Higher-risk tasks kept more human control. This taxonomy helps the PhD position its confidence-based escalation as a risk-aware division of labour and supports multidimensional evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR (npj Digital Medicine).
papers.datasets: 85 journal papers (2016-July 2025) comparing human-AI collaboration with AI-only or human-only benchmarks in healthcare.
papers.preprocessing: Screening with explicit inclusion criteria (human-AI collaboration, healthcare application, benchmark comparison, English); VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence analysis of titles and abstracts.
papers.modelDetails: Classification of collaboration patterns (e.g. AI-prior aid, AI-late aid / second opinion, AI triage and filtering, task division), task allocation mechanisms and evaluation metrics.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive mapping of patterns versus task risk and automation level; evaluation metrics used.
papers.baselines: AI-only and human-only benchmarks in included studies.
papers.results: Collaboration patterns relate to task risk and automation level, with clear division of labour; evaluation is shifting from single accuracy metrics to multidimensional outcomes including efficiency and user experience.

papers.title: A Dataset for Understanding Radiologist-Artificial Intelligence Collaboration
papers.authors: Moehring A, Kutwal M, Huang R, Banerjee O, Jacobi A, Eber C, Mendoza D, Chung M, Dayan E, Gupta Y, et al.
papers.aim: To release a dataset for studying how radiologists use AI advice.
papers.method: Hundreds of radiologists read chest X-rays online while AI predictions and clinical history were randomly shown or hidden.
papers.result: The largest public dataset of radiologist-AI collaboration, with detailed reader data.
papers.tools: reader study
papers.gap: Remote experimental setting; single modality.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Historical cases; incentive variation across designs.
papers.methodologyDetail: Hundreds of radiologists read historical chest X-rays through an online interface while the researchers randomly varied whether they saw AI predictions and clinical history, collecting probability judgements for over a hundred findings. The resulting dataset lets others study when and how humans benefit from AI advice. Its randomised information-condition design is a useful template for the PhD's reader study comparing reads with and without calibrated AI and escalation cues.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental data descriptor (MIT, Harvard, Stanford and partners) in Scientific Data; MIT COUHES exempt protocol E-2953.
papers.datasets: Collab-CXR: 227 professional radiologists (mean 22 years' experience; 17% US-based; recruited including via a Vietnamese healthcare system) assessing subsets of 324 historical chest X-ray cases.
papers.preprocessing: Remote custom interface mimicking clinical reading with training, consent and practice cases; randomised information conditions; monetary accuracy incentives for a random subset in designs 1 and 3.
papers.modelDetails: Three experimental designs varying AI assistance (CheXpert-type AI probabilities) and clinical history availability; probabilistic assessments for 104 thoracic pathologies in a hierarchical reporting structure.
papers.training: Not applicable (existing AI model).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, speed and confidence under each condition; within- and between-subject comparisons enabled.
papers.baselines: Radiologists alone; AI alone.
papers.results: Largest known dataset comparing human-AI collaboration with AI or humans alone in radiology, with rich metadata on radiologist characteristics and decisions, released for research on how radiologists incorporate AI.

papers.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Healthcare: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Strong J, Rogers H, Sun E, Todsen AL, Ede J, Lumley C, Yeung N, Higham H, Noble JA
papers.aim: To review empirical studies of clinicians working with AI.
papers.method: Registered scoping review; 140 studies charted from over 17,000 records.
papers.result: Team benefits were common but depended on task fit, workflow, training and calibrated trust; patient outcomes and accountability were rarely measured.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: Few studies with patient outcomes or empirical governance evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Scoping review; no quality appraisal.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a registered protocol, the team screened over seventeen thousand records and charted 140 empirical studies of clinicians working with AI. They found that benefits are common but depend on fit with the task and workflow, training and calibrated trust, and that effects on patients and accountability are seldom measured. This directly supports the PhD's plan to evaluate workflow, trust calibration and accountability alongside accuracy.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR (University of Oxford), protocol registered on OSF.
papers.datasets: MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane and Google Scholar, January 2015 to October 2025: 17,463 records, 269 full texts, 140 empirical studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Predefined eligibility; dual screening; data charting; five registered research questions consolidated into three (effectiveness in task context, determinants of collaboration, ethics and governance).
papers.modelDetails: Charting and thematic synthesis of human-AI collaboration studies by task context (diagnostic interpretation, screening and triage, therapeutic decisions, administration).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: How effectiveness was defined and measured; success factors; ethics and governance evaluation.
papers.baselines: Human-only and AI-only comparators in included studies.
papers.results: Evidence concentrated on diagnostic interpretation; effectiveness usually measured with short-term task metrics rather than patient or system outcomes; most studies reported team benefits that depended on task fit, workflow integration, training and calibrated trust; ethics and accountability discussed but rarely evaluated empirically.

papers.title: A quantitative study of pathologists' perceptions towards artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic system
papers.authors: Ye Z, Lu Q, Wang J, Jiang Y, Xue P
papers.aim: To study pathologists' views on AI-assisted diagnosis in China.
papers.method: Piloted online questionnaire with regression to find factors linked to willingness to use AI.
papers.result: Most were supportive but wanted more accurate systems; knowledge and perceived usefulness predicted willingness.
papers.tools: survey, Likert, logistic regression, SPSS
papers.gap: Intentions rather than observed use; cervical-cytology network focus.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Snowball sampling; self-report.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathologists across China completed a piloted online questionnaire about what they know about AI diagnostic aids, how they feel about them and whether they intend to use them, and regression identified the factors linked to willingness. Most were supportive but wanted more accurate systems. This informs how the PhD should engage Sri Lankan pathologists for the pathology arm and its trust measures.
papers.studyDesign: Online nationwide cross-sectional KAP survey of pathologists in China (Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College), August 2024; IRB approved, written consent.
papers.datasets: 235 questionnaires, 224 valid (95.3%) from pathologists at over 120 hospitals in 27 provinces; 73.2% female; mean age 40.3; 37.9% had used an AI-assisted diagnostic system (AIADS).
papers.preprocessing: Recruitment through a national multicentre cervical cancer cohort network plus snowball sampling; questionnaire piloted (n = 30) and expert-reviewed; one response per IP; mandatory fields; quality-control question.
papers.modelDetails: Questionnaire on knowledge, attitudes and behavioural intention/practice toward AIADS, with demographic and influencing-factor sections.
