papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Scale scores for knowledge, attitudes and intention; factors associated with willingness to use AIADS.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Most pathologists supported clinical use of AIADS but wanted better diagnostic performance; knowledge, prior use and perceived usefulness were associated with willingness to use; training and trust-building recommended.
papers.statistics: t-tests/ANOVA, chi-square tests, logistic regression of behavioural intention (SPSS 29.0, α = 0.05).

papers.title: Impact of a deep learning assistant on the histopathologic classification of liver cancer
papers.authors: Kiani A, Uyumazturk B, Rajpurkar P, Wang A, Gao R, Jones E, Yu Y, Langlotz CP, Ball RL, Montine TJ, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether a deep learning assistant improves pathologists' liver cancer classification.
papers.method: Eleven pathologists classified 80 slides with and without the AI tool in randomised order with a washout.
papers.result: No overall gain: accuracy rose when the AI was right and fell significantly when it was wrong.
papers.tools: logistic regression, reader study
papers.gap: No uncertainty display to warn of likely-wrong predictions.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Binary task; small number of pathologists.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a deep learning classifier on TCGA liver cancer slides and put it into a web tool, then had eleven pathologists classify eighty slides with and without the tool in randomised order separated by a washout. Overall accuracy did not change, because correct AI advice helped and wrong advice harmed. This is a key motivation for the PhD's escalation design: uncertain predictions should be flagged rather than shown as confident advice.
papers.studyDesign: Diagnostic assistant development and randomised crossover reader study (Stanford University, USA).
papers.datasets: Training from 70 TCGA H&E WSI (35 HCC from LIHC, 35 cholangiocarcinoma from CHOL): 25,000 patches of 512×512 px (128×128 µm); validation 26 WSI; independent Stanford test set of 80 WSI; 11 pathologists of varying expertise.
papers.preprocessing: Tumour regions patched; random split at slide level (20,000 training patches from 20 WSI, 2,400 tuning from 24 WSI, 2,600 validation from 26 WSI) with 50:50 class balance.
papers.modelDetails: CNN patch classifier in a web-based assistant showing predicted probabilities and class activation maps for HCC versus cholangiocarcinoma.
papers.training: Patch-level training with tuning set for model selection (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Model accuracy on validation and test sets; pathologist accuracy with and without assistance in randomised order (assisted first or unassisted first) with a 2-week washout; effect stratified by correctness of model prediction.
papers.baselines: Unassisted pathologists.
papers.results: Model accuracy 0.885 (validation) and 0.842 (test); assistance did not change mean pathologist accuracy (p = 0.184, OR 1.281) but significantly improved accuracy when the model was correct (OR 4.289) and significantly reduced it when the model was wrong.
papers.statistics: Mixed-effects logistic regression with odds ratios.
papers.availability: Code and model details in paper/supplement.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted cancer diagnosis improves the efficiency of pathologists in prostatic biopsies
papers.authors: Eloy C, Marques A, Pinto J, Pinheiro J, Campelos S, Curado M, Vale J, Polónia A
papers.aim: To test whether AI improves pathologists' efficiency with prostate biopsies.
papers.method: Four pathologists diagnosed the same biopsies without and later with AI; accuracy, agreement and extra tests compared.
papers.result: Accuracy was similar (95.0% vs 93.8%), but AI cut immunostains by about 20% and second opinions.
papers.tools: SPSS, reader study
papers.gap: Small reader and case numbers; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Sequential design without randomised order.
papers.methodologyDetail: Four pathologists diagnosed the same prostate biopsies first without and later with an AI tool, and their accuracy, agreement and use of extra tests were compared. Accuracy stayed similar but pathologists needed fewer immunostains and second opinions, saving time and cost. This shows that efficiency and resource use, not only accuracy, are important outcomes for the PhD's pathology evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Two-phase retrospective reader study (IPATIMUP and University of Porto, Portugal).
papers.datasets: 105 prostate core needle biopsy slides from 41 men (median age 69): 66 benign, 39 acinar adenocarcinoma (GrG1-5); 4 pathologists.
papers.preprocessing: Digitised whole-slide images; ground truth established by reference diagnosis; phase 1 unaided, phase 2 assisted after interval.
papers.modelDetails: Paige Prostate clinical-grade AI tool for detecting, grading and quantifying prostate cancer on WSI.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial tool).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, intra- and interobserver concordance, ASAP reporting rate, number of IHC requests and second opinions, reading time.
papers.baselines: Unaided pathologists (phase 1).
papers.results: Accuracy 95.00% unaided and 93.81% assisted, intraobserver concordance 98.81%; with AI, ASAP reported about 30% less, IHC requests about 20% fewer and fewer second opinions; discordances mainly between ASAP and small well-differentiated cancer foci.
papers.statistics: Chi-square and McNemar tests; Kruskal-Wallis; simple and quadratic weighted kappa with Landis-Koch interpretation (SPSS 27).

papers.title: Artificial intelligence assistance significantly improves Gleason grading of prostate biopsies by pathologists
papers.authors: Bulten W, Balkenhol M, Belinga JA, Brilhante A, Çakır A, Egevad L, Eklund M, Farré X, Geronatsiou K, Molinié V, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether AI assistance improves pathologists' Gleason grading.
papers.method: A pathologist panel graded biopsies without and later with AI pattern predictions, against expert consensus.
papers.result: AI-assisted pathologists beat both unaided pathologists and the AI alone, with biggest gains for less experienced readers.
papers.tools: Deep learning Gleason grading system showing grade-group prediction and overlaid Gleason pattern maps as assistance.
papers.gap: No uncertainty-based routing; retrospective reads only.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Enriched test set; single-source slides.
papers.methodologyDetail: A panel of pathologists graded a set of prostate biopsies without help and later with an AI showing predicted Gleason patterns, and both reads were scored against an expert consensus. With AI support, the human-AI team graded better than either pathologists alone or the AI alone, and variation fell. This is strong evidence for the PhD's premise that human-AI teams with clear AI output can beat either alone, especially in difficult grading tasks.
papers.studyDesign: International observer study with crossover reads (Radboud University Medical Center, Netherlands, with ISUP expert panel); ethics waiver IRB 2016-2275.
papers.datasets: System trained on 5,759 H&E biopsies from 1,243 patients (Radboud 2012-2017, scanned at 20×, 0.24 µm/pixel); 550 independent test biopsies; observer panel of 14 pathologists from 16 invited (board-certified and residents), multiple countries.
papers.preprocessing: Consensus reference standard from three uropathology experts with majority-vote rules; anonymised slides; reads with and without AI separated by washout.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning Gleason grading system showing grade-group prediction and overlaid Gleason pattern maps as assistance.
papers.training: Previously developed system (semi-automatic labelling and CNN segmentation, details in earlier study).
papers.evaluation: Quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa against reference (median kappa at group level); sensitivity/specificity for cancer detection; comparison with stand-alone AI.
papers.baselines: Unassisted pathologists; stand-alone AI.
papers.results: AI-assisted pathologists outperformed both unassisted pathologists and the stand-alone AI at group level; kappa improved significantly with assistance, with the largest gains for less experienced pathologists.
papers.statistics: Shapiro-Wilk test; Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired kappa differences.
papers.availability: Test data available via grand-challenge (details in paper).

papers.title: How can artificial intelligence models assist PD-L1 expression scoring in breast cancer: results of multi-institutional ring studies
papers.authors: Wang X, Wang L, Bu H, Zhang N, Yue M, Jia Z, Cai L, He J, Wang Y, Xu X, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether AI improves pathologists' PD-L1 scoring in breast cancer across institutions.
papers.method: A model quantifying PD-L1-positive cells; 31 pathologists from 10 hospitals scored 109 images in three rounds, the last with AI.
papers.result: AI help raised agreement and accuracy for pathologists at every experience level (model accuracy 0.963).
papers.tools: Deep learning AI-assisted PD-L1 immune-cell (IC) scoring model segmenting tumour area and PD-L1-positive immune cells to compute IC percentage and categories.
papers.gap: Single antibody clone and single source of slides.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Image patches rather than whole slides.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team built a deep learning model that quantifies PD-L1-positive immune cells in breast cancer images, then ran three rounds in which 31 pathologists from 10 hospitals scored the same 109 images, the last round with AI help. Agreement and accuracy rose with assistance at every experience level. The multi-institutional ring-study design is a useful template for the PhD's multi-site reader evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Model development and three-round multi-institutional ring study (Fourth Hospital of Hebei Medical University with Tencent AI Lab and other hospitals, China).
papers.datasets: 100 invasive breast cancer resection blocks (January-June 2019) stained with PD-L1 SP142; 4,246 patches cut from tumour regions, 2,395 after exclusions; 109 test images; 31 pathologists from 10 hospitals.
papers.preprocessing: 4 µm sections, Ventana BenchMark staining, scanned at ×40 (Unic); tumour, necrosis, in situ and normal areas annotated per Roche SP142 guide; non-overlapping 3290×3290 patches resized to 2160×2160 (~×20).
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning AI-assisted PD-L1 immune-cell (IC) scoring model segmenting tumour area and PD-L1-positive immune cells to compute IC percentage and categories.
papers.training: Supervised training on annotated patches (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Model 2- and 4-category accuracy, AUC and weighted F1; pathologist concordance (ICC, kappa), accuracy against gold standard and acceptance of AI results across ring studies RS1-RS2 (guideline) and RS3 (AI-assisted).
papers.baselines: Guideline-based visual scoring in RS1 and RS2.
papers.results: Model 2-category accuracy 0.963 (105/109), AUC 0.888, weighted F1 0.962; AI assistance raised inter-pathologist concordance and accuracy for pathologists at all experience levels.
papers.statistics: Intraclass correlation coefficients, kappa and accuracy comparisons across rounds.

papers.title: Assessing the influence of two deep-learning assistance modes on pathologists in cancer identification
papers.authors: Chuang WY, Yu WH, Liu YJ, Huang CC, Lee KF, Hwang CC, Chang LC, Ueng SH, Yeh CJ, Chuang HC, et al.
papers.aim: To compare two ways of showing AI help to pathologists identifying cancer.
papers.method: Ten pathologists classified nasopharyngeal biopsies with no AI, a whole-slide heatmap, or AI-selected high-power fields.
papers.result: Showing selected fields kept accuracy high and limited the effect of false-positive AI predictions.
papers.tools: ResNeXt-based nasopharyngeal carcinoma detector (trained on 726 independent cases, patch AUC 0.99) presented either as a whole-slide cancer…
papers.gap: Binary task; no calibrated uncertainty display tested.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small case set; one centre group.
papers.methodologyDetail: Ten pathologists classified nasopharyngeal biopsies with no AI, with a full-slide AI heatmap, or with AI-selected high-power fields, and their speed, accuracy and perceived difficulty were modelled with mixed-effects statistics. Showing selected fields kept accuracy high and limited the pull of false-positive predictions. This shows that how AI output is presented changes automation bias, which matters for the PhD's escalation interface design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-reader study comparing two AI assistance modes (Chang Gung Memorial Hospital and aetherAI, Taiwan); IRB 202000956B0.
papers.datasets: 70 nasopharyngeal biopsies (35 carcinoma, 35 benign) from three hospital branches, one H&E slide each, scanned at 40× (NanoZoomer S360); 60 cases used in the experiment; 10 board-certified pathologists.
papers.preprocessing: Diagnoses confirmed by two senior pathologists excluded from reading; three review modes prepared for each case.
papers.modelDetails: ResNeXt-based nasopharyngeal carcinoma detector (trained on 726 independent cases, patch AUC 0.99) presented either as a whole-slide cancer probability heatmap (AI-heatmap) or as AI-selected high-power fields (AI-HPF).
papers.training: Pre-trained model from earlier study.
papers.evaluation: Review time, diagnostic accuracy and subjective difficulty in unassisted, AI-heatmap and AI-HPF modes; influence of false-positive AI predictions.
papers.baselines: Unassisted review.
papers.results: AI-HPF mode kept high diagnostic accuracy and was robust to false-positive AI predictions, while assistance modes affected review time and perceived difficulty differently.
papers.statistics: Generalised linear mixed-effect models with readers and cases as random effects; ANOVA model comparison; TukeyHSD or simple main effects.

papers.title: Computer-assisted mitotic count using a deep learning-based algorithm improves interobserver reproducibility and accuracy
papers.authors: Bertram CA, Aubreville M, Donovan TA, Bartel A, Wilm F, Marzahl C, Assenmacher CA, Becker K, Bennett M, Corner S, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether AI-assisted mitotic counting improves pathologists' reproducibility and accuracy.
papers.method: Pathologists counted mitoses alone, with an AI hotspot, and with hotspot plus AI-marked mitoses with confidence, against an immunostain reference.
papers.result: More AI assistance gave better agreement and accuracy; full help with confidence overlays was best.
papers.tools: reader study
papers.gap: Sequential non-randomised order; veterinary tumour type.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Possible learning effect across stages.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathologists counted mitoses on the same tumour slides three times: alone, with an AI-chosen hotspot, and with the hotspot plus AI-marked candidate mitoses and their confidence scores, compared with an immunostain-based ground truth. Agreement and accuracy rose with more assistance. Showing confidence values alongside detections is directly relevant to the PhD's plan to present calibrated confidence to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Multi-centre, three-stage reader study with increasing computer assistance (University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna, FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg and international partners).
papers.datasets: WSIs of 50 canine cutaneous mast cell tumours; 23 of 26 pathologists from 11 laboratories completed (96% board-certified diplomates).
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth by destaining H&E sections, re-staining with phosphohistone H3 IHC and registering both images at cellular level; at least 3 days between stages.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning mitotic-figure detector over the whole slide; stage 1 no assistance, stage 2 algorithm-selected mitotic hotspot ROI, stage 3 ROI plus overlay of detected mitotic figures and lookalikes with algorithmic confidence values.
papers.training: Algorithm trained previously on annotated canine tumour datasets.
papers.evaluation: Mitotic count reproducibility (ICC) between pathologists; accuracy of mitotic figure detection (sensitivity, precision, F1) and MC against pHH3-assisted ground truth.
papers.baselines: Unassisted pathologists (stage 1).
papers.results: Computer assistance improved interobserver reproducibility of the mitotic count and accuracy of mitotic figure detection versus unassisted counting; full assistance with confidence overlays gave the largest improvement.
papers.statistics: Intraclass correlation and accuracy comparisons across stages.
papers.availability: Datasets and algorithm referenced from earlier open datasets.

papers.title: Assessing the impact of deep-learning assistance on the histopathological diagnosis of serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) in fallopian tubes
papers.authors: Bogaerts JM, Steenbeek MP, Bokhorst JM, van Bommel MH, Abete L, Addante F, Brinkhuis M, Chrzan A, Cordier F, Devouassoux-Shisheboran M, et al.
papers.venue: The Journal of Pathology. Clinical Research
papers.aim: To test AI assistance for diagnosing early serous carcinoma in fallopian tubes.
papers.method: International pathologists and residents diagnosed slides with and without an AI highlighting suspicious areas, against an expert panel.
papers.result: AI improved accuracy and reduced reading time.
papers.tools: reader study
papers.gap: Enriched case mix; no uncertainty communication.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; prevalence higher than practice.
papers.methodologyDetail: A diverse international group of pathologists and residents diagnosed fallopian tube slides for early serous carcinoma with and without an AI model that highlights suspicious areas, against an expert-panel reference standard. AI support improved accuracy and saved time. It shows the value of measuring both accuracy and efficiency in a held-out, multi-source case set, as planned for the PhD reader study.
papers.studyDesign: International multi-reader crossover study (Radboud University Medical Center, Netherlands, with AI-STIC Study Group); ethics 2019-5879 and partner approvals.
papers.datasets: 100 fallopian tube slides (21 STIC, 9 STIL, 70 controls) from Radboudumc, PALGA, Johns Hopkins, CWZ and Rijnstate, held out from model training; diverse group of pathologists and residents.
papers.preprocessing: Reference standard from an international panel of 15 gynaecological pathologists; one slide per specimen; reads with and without AI separated by washout.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning STIC detection model producing heatmaps/region highlights of suspicious epithelium.
papers.training: Model developed in earlier study.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, inter-observer agreement and reading time with versus without AI support.
papers.baselines: Unassisted reading.
papers.results: AI support significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and reduced reading time for STIC across pathologists and residents.
papers.statistics: Mixed-effects or paired statistical comparisons; kappa agreement.

papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Patient Safety Outcomes: Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: Choudhury A, Asan O
papers.aim: To review how AI affects patient safety outcomes.
papers.method: Systematic review of 53 studies over ten years that measured safety outcomes, not only accuracy.
papers.result: Promising effects, but no common benchmark and inconsistent reporting.
papers.tools: NLP, PRISMA
papers.gap: Lack of standardised safety benchmarks and reporting.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Three databases; up to 2019.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases for ten years of studies that measured how AI actually changed patient safety outcomes, not just model accuracy, and analysed 53 such studies. They found promising effects but no common benchmark and inconsistent reporting. This supports the PhD's emphasis on measuring safety outcomes such as missed escalations and on transparent, standard reporting.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review following PRISMA, protocol registered on OSF 15 September 2019 (Stevens Institute of Technology, USA).
papers.datasets: PubMed, PubMed Central and Web of Science, English, January 2009 to August 2019; 53 quantitative studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Librarian-assisted MeSH-based Boolean search; studies reporting only AI performance without patient safety outcomes excluded.
papers.modelDetails: Synthesis of quantitative studies using ML or NLP applications that reported positive, negative or intermediate changes in clinical-level patient safety outcomes (e.g. adverse drug events, falls, pressure ulcers, sepsis, clinical deterioration).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Categorisation by safety outcome, AI type and data source; assessment of reporting standards.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI applications showed potential to improve safety outcomes, but there was no standardised benchmark and AI reporting was heterogeneous, limiting comparison and evidence of real clinical impact.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence related safety issues associated with FDA medical device reports
papers.authors: Handley JL, Krevat SA, Fong A, Ratwani RM
papers.aim: To find safety issues of AI devices in FDA adverse-event reports.
papers.method: AI-enabled FDA devices were matched to adverse-event reports and each report was reviewed.
papers.result: 25% of reports were possibly AI-related and 35% lacked enough detail to judge, so AI incident reporting is inadequate.
papers.tools: Human-factors content review classifying each report as potentially AI/ML-related, not related, or insufficient information.
papers.gap: Report data too sparse for causal attribution.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Reliance on voluntary and mandatory reports; name-matching may miss events.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team matched the FDA's list of AI-enabled devices to the national device adverse-event database and read each report to judge whether AI could have contributed. A quarter could have, but a third did not contain enough detail to tell. This shows the need for better AI incident logging, supporting the PhD's audit trail and post-deployment monitoring design.
papers.studyDesign: Brief communication: retrospective analysis of FDA MAUDE adverse event reports (MedStar Health National Center for Human Factors in Healthcare, USA).
papers.datasets: 429 MAUDE reports matched to FDA-listed AI/ML-enabled medical devices up to 18 October 2023.
papers.preprocessing: Device brand, generic and manufacturer names matched to MAUDE via the openFDA Elasticsearch API (exact or partial match); reports reviewed manually.
papers.modelDetails: Human-factors content review classifying each report as potentially AI/ML-related, not related, or insufficient information.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Proportion of reports with possible AI/ML contribution to safety events.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 108 of 429 reports (25.2%) were potentially AI/ML related and 148 (34.5%) lacked enough information to judge an AI/ML contribution; current reporting is insufficient for AI safety surveillance.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: transforming patient safety with intelligent systems-A systematic review
papers.authors: De Micco F, Di Palma G, Ferorelli D, De Benedictis A, Tomassini L, Tambone V, Cingolani M, Scendoni R
papers.aim: To review how AI can improve patient safety.
papers.method: Systematic review of three databases, grouped by type of harm addressed.
papers.result: AI can predict and prevent adverse events, but implementation and standardisation problems remain.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: Few implementation studies; heterogeneous outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Three databases; no meta-analysis.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases for studies in which AI was actually tested to prevent adverse events, screened them with set criteria, and grouped the evidence by the kind of harm addressed. AI looks promising for risk prediction and prevention, but implementation and standardisation remain problems. It frames the PhD's escalation system as a clinical risk-management tool whose safety benefit must be demonstrated.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA-DTA guidance (Università Campus Bio-Medico di Roma and University of Macerata, Italy).
papers.datasets: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science searched February 2024: 662 records, 489 after de-duplication, 68 initially included and further screened (16 excluded at full review).
papers.preprocessing: Search string combining risk management/clinical governance, patient safety/quality and AI/ML/DL terms; Rayyan for screening; five inclusion criteria (AI system, healthcare, clinical risk management, active experimentation results, prevention of adverse events).
papers.modelDetails: Synthesis of AI applications in clinical risk management grouped by adverse event type (e.g. medication errors, falls, infections, diagnostic errors, surgical complications).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative and descriptive synthesis of reported effectiveness in preventing adverse events.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI shows potential to predict and prevent adverse events and support risk management, but socio-technical issues, implementation barriers and lack of standardisation persist.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Patient Safety and Surgical Education in Neurosurgery
papers.authors: Sugiyama T, Sugimori H, Tang M, Fujimura M
papers.aim: To review AI for patient safety and surgical training in neurosurgery.
papers.method: Review of AI, especially computer vision on surgical video, for skill assessment and safety.
papers.result: AI could reduce preventable errors (about 25% of adverse events), but data, bias and explainability limit use.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No systematic method; few prospective validations.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Narrative; authors' own work emphasised.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors review how AI, especially computer vision on surgical video, can improve neurosurgical safety and training, for example by assessing microsurgical skill and analysing operations. They note that preventable technical errors are common in neurosurgery and that data and transparency problems limit adoption. It supports the patient-safety motivation and surgical-planning use case of the PhD.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Hokkaido University, Japan) in JMA Journal.
papers.datasets: Recent studies on AI in neurosurgery related to patient safety and surgical education.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of ML, deep learning and computer vision applications: diagnosis and outcome prediction, intra-operative video analysis, instrument tracking, microsurgical skill assessment and surgical education.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI can reduce errors and costs, broaden access and improve safety and training in neurosurgery, where about 25% of adverse events are attributed to preventable technical errors; practical use remains limited by data volume and diversity, quality, algorithmic bias, explainability, ethics and regulation.

papers.title: Evaluation of a Deep Learning and XAI based Facial Phenotyping Tool for Genetic Syndromes: A Clinical User Study
papers.authors: Sümer Ö, Huber T, Duong D, Ledgister Hanchard SE, Conati C, André E, Solomon BD, Waikel RL
papers.aim: To test whether explanations help geneticists use a facial phenotyping AI.
papers.method: Geneticists diagnosed syndromes from photos, then revised answers after seeing AI probabilities alone or with saliency explanations.
papers.result: Explanations did not raise accuracy overall but made users more critical when the AI was wrong.
papers.tools: ResNet
papers.gap: Small sample; no calibrated uncertainty shown.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; public images may differ from clinical photos.
papers.methodologyDetail: Medical geneticists diagnosed syndromes from face photos, then revised their answers after seeing either AI probabilities alone or probabilities with saliency-based explanations. Explanations did not raise overall accuracy but made users more critical when the AI was wrong. This supports the PhD's view that explanations help users question AI but need to be paired with calibrated confidence to improve accuracy.
papers.studyDesign: Clinical user study with randomised AI-only versus XAI groups (University of Augsburg, TH Ingolstadt, NHGRI/NIH, UBC); medRxiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Publicly available facial images of individuals with 22q11.2 deletion, Angelman, Kabuki, Noonan and Williams syndromes plus unaffected controls; medical geneticists as participants.
papers.preprocessing: Image selection from prior work; participants first diagnosed unaided, then saw AI output (pre/post design).
papers.modelDetails: ResNet-50 CNN classifying face images into five syndromes or unaffected, with probabilities; XAI group additionally saw DeepLIFT saliency maps and region relevance scores.
papers.training: CNN trained as in earlier work (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Prediction improvement after AI or XAI support, stratified by whether the AI was correct; user perceptions.
papers.baselines: AI-only output (probabilities without explanation); unaided performance.
papers.results: Mean improvement 0.031 ± 0.129 for XAI vs 0.056 ± 0.11 for AI-only (not significantly different); when AI was correct AI-only improved more (0.190 vs 0.146); XAI prompted users to critically evaluate images when the AI was wrong.
papers.statistics: Group comparisons of prediction improvement with significance testing.

papers.title: Reducing the workload of medical diagnosis through artificial intelligence: A narrative review
papers.authors: Jeong J, Kim S, Pan L, Hwang D, Kim D, Choi J, Kwon Y, Yi P, Jeong J, Yoo SJ
papers.aim: To review how AI reduces diagnostic workload.
papers.method: Narrative review of 51 PubMed studies from five years, grouped by how AI saves effort.
papers.result: AI cut diagnosis time substantially (e.g. 22-99% in radiology), though standards and ethics remain issues.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: Mostly retrospective, heterogeneous efficiency measures.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single database; narrative synthesis.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched PubMed for five years of studies measuring how AI changes diagnostic time or workload and sorted 51 studies into four types according to how AI saves effort. Most reported large time savings, especially when AI pre-screens or highlights findings. This evidence supports the PhD's workload hypothesis and the use of time and workload measures in its evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review with structured PubMed search (Korean authors) in Medicine.
papers.datasets: PubMed search January 2019 to February 2024 with terms for AI, efficiency/workload and patient/clinical: 2,587 articles, 51 reviewed.
papers.preprocessing: Screening for studies quantifying diagnostic efficiency changes.
papers.modelDetails: Classification of studies into four categories (A-D) by efficiency mechanism: supporting material for clinicians' decisions, AI triage or pre-screening, AI replacing a reading step, and reduction of data volume/workload.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Reported percentage reductions in diagnosis time or workload, by specialty (radiology, pathology, gastroenterology, haematology, others).
papers.baselines: Conventional unaided workflows in included studies.
papers.results: AI reduced diagnosis time substantially across specialties (e.g. 22-99% reductions in radiology; 39.6% workload reduction in DBT screening), though standardisation of applications and ethical concerns remain challenges.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as triage in breast screening: simulated impact on workload and detection
papers.authors: Riccardi MT, Nurchis MC, Savoia C, Gigli S, Marotta D, Di Lullo F, Damiani G, Pettinicchio V
papers.venue: The European Journal of Public Health
papers.aim: To simulate AI triage in breast screening and its effect on workload and missed cancers.
papers.method: A year of real screening data; low-AI-score exams sent to one reader instead of two.
papers.result: Workload fell only about 5%, and up to one extra cancer could be missed, mostly microcalcifications.
papers.tools: Lunit INSIGHT MMG AI score used as triage: below-threshold exams single-read, others double-read.
papers.gap: Simulation only; threshold not optimised.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Abstract; single programme, single year.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a year of real screening data, the authors simulated sending mammograms with low AI scores to a single reader instead of two and counted the reading saved and the cancers that might be missed. Workload fell only modestly and some cancers with microcalcifications scored low. This shows that a triage threshold must be set with care and checked for systematic blind spots, which is central to the PhD's escalation threshold design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective simulation study (conference abstract) in a population-based screening programme (Local Health Unit Roma 2 and Università Cattolica, Italy), funded by the Italian Ministry of Health.
papers.datasets: 38,075 screening mammograms from the 2025 cohort of the largest Italian Local Health Unit.
papers.preprocessing: AI scores compared with a predefined threshold (2.9); exams below threshold assigned to simulated single reading.
papers.modelDetails: Lunit INSIGHT MMG AI score used as triage: below-threshold exams single-read, others double-read.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI).
papers.evaluation: Workload reduction and potentially missed cancers versus standard double reading; characteristics of AI-missed cancers.
papers.baselines: Standard double reading.
papers.results: 4,542 exams (11.9%) below threshold; 96% of these were negative at double reading, 201 recalled with 18 cancers; up to one extra cancer could be missed; workload reduction about 5% of annual reading volume; AI-missed cancers mainly microcalcifications (61%), distortions (22%).

papers.title: Can we reduce the workload of mammographic screening by automatic identification of normal exams with artificial intelligence? A feasibility study
papers.authors: Rodriguez-Ruiz A, Lång K, Gubern-Merida A, Teuwen J, Broeders M, Gennaro G, Clauser P, Helbich TH, Chevalier M, Mertelmeier T, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether AI can safely remove normal mammograms from human reading.
papers.method: AI scores for exams from nine reader studies; every cut-off for excluding low-risk exams was tested.
papers.result: A low cut-off cut workload by 17% while excluding only 1% of true-positive exams.
papers.tools: Transpara 1.4.0 deep learning CNN AI system assigning a 1-10 cancer-likelihood score;
papers.gap: Enriched data; not prospective screening.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Older AI version; simulated reading.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using exams and radiologist reads from nine earlier reader studies, the team scored each mammogram with an AI and tested every possible cut-off for removing low-risk exams from human reading. A low cut-off cut workload by about a sixth while losing very few cancers. This threshold-sweep method is a direct template for choosing the PhD's escalation threshold by trading workload against missed cases.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre feasibility study (Radboud University Medical Center and international partners) in European Radiology.
papers.datasets: 2,652 digital mammography exams (653 cancers, 768 benign, 1,233 normal) from nine previous MRMC ROC studies, with 28,296 interpretations by 101 radiologists (USA and Europe); four vendors, seven countries.
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth from histopathology and/or at least one year follow-up; enriched datasets; anonymised data with ethics waivers.
papers.modelDetails: Transpara 1.4.0 deep learning CNN AI system assigning a 1-10 cancer-likelihood score; thresholds 1-9 tested to exclude low-score exams from radiologist reading.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI).
papers.evaluation: Workload reduction and proportion of excluded true-positive exams at each threshold; effect of pre-selection on radiologists' simulated performance (AUC).
papers.baselines: All exams read by radiologists.
papers.results: 72.5% of cancers scored 10 and 95.1% scored 5-10; threshold of 2 gave 17% workload reduction excluding only 1% of true-positive exams; pre-selection did not change radiologists' performance; higher thresholds traded more workload savings for more missed cancers.

papers.title: Diagnostic capabilities of artificial intelligence as an additional reader in a breast cancer screening program
papers.authors: Seker ME, Koyluoglu YO, Ozaydin AN, Gurdal SO, Ozcinar B, Cabioglu N, Ozmen V, Aribal E
papers.aim: To evaluate AI as an additional reader in a breast screening programme.
papers.method: AI scored screening and prior mammograms; a threshold was chosen from the ROC curve and an AI triage workflow simulated.
papers.result: AUC 0.90; AI flagged some cancers a round earlier and could cut reading workload by about 70%.
papers.tools: R
papers.gap: Retrospective simulation; single institution.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small cancer numbers; Youden threshold not clinically tuned.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team scored screening mammograms and the earlier mammograms of women later diagnosed with cancer using an AI system, chose a threshold from the ROC curve, and simulated a workflow in which AI triages exams. AI could have flagged some cancers a round earlier and greatly reduced reading workload in the hybrid scenario. This supports using a data-driven threshold for routing cases between AI and humans, as in the PhD's escalation design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective observational single-institution study of AI as an additional reader in a population screening programme (Acibadem and partner universities, Istanbul, Turkey).
papers.datasets: Screening mammograms from a Turkish breast screening programme: 4,893 negative exams and exams of 105 cancer patients, plus 138 prior mammograms of these patients.
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth from histopathology; analysis of current and prior screening rounds; subgroup factors (density, tumour size, mass/calcification type, stage, molecular subtype).
papers.modelDetails: Commercial AI software assigning risk scores 1-100; Youden-index threshold for cancer identification; simulated hybrid triage workflow.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI).
papers.evaluation: ROC AUC, sensitivity, specificity at threshold, detection of cancers on prior (earlier) mammograms, workload and accuracy in hybrid triage scenario.
papers.baselines: Radiologist screening reads.
papers.results: AUC 89.6% (95% CI 86.1-93.2); threshold score 30.44 gave sensitivity 72.38% and specificity 92.86%; AI flagged 35 prior mammograms of 24 cancer patients (earlier detection); hybrid triage scenario showed potential 69.5% workload reduction and 30.5% accuracy increase.
papers.statistics: ROC analysis, Youden's index, Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality tests and group comparisons in R 4.1.0.

papers.title: Current practical experience with artificial intelligence in clinical radiology: a survey of the European Society of Radiology
papers.authors: European Society of Radiology (ESR)
papers.aim: To survey European radiologists' real experience with clinical AI tools.
papers.method: European Society of Radiology survey on integration, reliability and time savings of certified AI.
papers.result: Most users found AI reliable, but few saw workload savings and only 13% planned to buy AI.
papers.tools: survey
papers.gap: Low response rate; self-reported experience.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Selection bias towards interested radiologists.
papers.methodologyDetail: European radiologists were asked about their real clinical experience with certified AI tools, including how well they integrate, how reliable they seem and whether they save time. Most users found results reliable, but workload savings were rare and few planned to buy AI. This tempers expectations and shows the PhD should measure real workload effects rather than assume them.
papers.studyDesign: Online survey of European Society of Radiology members by the ESR eHealth and Informatics Subcommittee.
papers.datasets: 690 radiologist respondents from 44 countries (response rate 2.5%); 276 with practical clinical AI experience from 229 institutions in 32 countries (52% academic, 37% regional hospitals, 11% private practice).
papers.preprocessing: Brief questionnaire stating answers should reflect clinical routine, not research use.
papers.modelDetails: Questions on certified AI algorithms used, integration difficulties, use cases (diagnostic interpretation, post-processing, prioritisation), confidence in performance, quality control, communication to patients and reports, and workload effect.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive frequencies of responses.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Main uses were diagnostic interpretation, post-processing and prioritisation; integration problems reported by 17.8%; 75.7% of diagnostic users found results generally reliable; few reported workload reduction; only 13.3% of all respondents intended to acquire AI tools.

papers.title: Constrained-Spherical Deconvolution Tractography in the Evaluation of the Corticospinal Tract in Glioma Surgery
papers.authors: Sheng Z, Yu J, Chen Z, Sun Y, Bu X, Wang M, Sarica C, Hernesniemi J, Nelson BJ, Zemmar A, et al.
papers.aim: To compare tractography methods for showing the motor tract in glioma surgery.
papers.method: In 12 glioma patients the motor tract was reconstructed with an advanced probabilistic (CSD) and a standard tensor method, and tract injury related to motor outcome.
papers.result: The advanced method showed a more complete tract; overlap of the resection with the tract was linked to permanent deficits.
papers.tools: Two tractography approaches for the corticospinal tract: constrained spherical deconvolution probabilistic (CSD-Prob) versus tensor-based…
papers.gap: Very small sample; no validation with stimulation mapping.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; selection excluded brain shift cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: In twelve glioma patients, the team reconstructed the motor pathway with an advanced probabilistic method and a standard tensor method, compared how each showed the tract around the tumour, and related tract injury after surgery to motor outcome. The advanced method gave a more complete tract, which matters for planning safe resections. This supports using advanced tractography inputs in the PhD's surgical-planning demonstrator.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective methodological imaging study (Henan Provincial People's Hospital, China, with Toronto and ETH Zurich partners); ethics approved, consent obtained.
papers.datasets: 12 of 53 glioma patients operated January 2017 to January 2019 (4 WHO grade II, 8 GBM; mean age 50) with tumours in or near motor areas and mild or no motor deficit; 3T Siemens MRI pre- and postoperatively (within 2 days).
papers.preprocessing: Exclusion of significant brain shift or oedema; co-registration of pre- and postoperative T1-gadolinium and diffusion images; extent of resection (GTR > 90%) and permanent motor deficit (MRC scale at ~2 months) recorded.
papers.modelDetails: Two tractography approaches for the corticospinal tract: constrained spherical deconvolution probabilistic (CSD-Prob) versus tensor-based deterministic (Tens-DET); diffusion metrics (FA, MD, RD) along ipsilesional and contralesional CST.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: CST reconstruction pattern and displacement; overlap of resection cavity with CST; diffusion metric differences; relation to postoperative motor outcome.
papers.baselines: Tensor-based deterministic tractography.
papers.results: CST identified in all patients by both methods; CSD-Prob showed the anatomically expected fan-shaped tract while Tens-DET showed a narrow straight path missing lateral fibres; ipsilesional CST had lower FA (p = 0.006) and higher MD (p = 0.0004) and RD (p = 0.005); cavity-CST overlap related to permanent deficits.

papers.title: Tractography for Subcortical Resection of Gliomas Is Highly Accurate for Motor and Language Function: ioMRI-Based Elastic Fusion Disproves the Severity of Brain Shift
papers.authors: Ille S, Schwendner M, Zhang W, Schroeder A, Meyer B, Krieg SM
papers.aim: To check how accurate tractography is for resecting gliomas near motor and language pathways.
papers.method: Function-based tractography; after resection, cavity-to-tract distance was measured before and after brain-shift correction with intraoperative MRI and related to new deficits.
papers.result: Corrected tractography was highly accurate, and brain shift mattered less than often assumed.
papers.tools: Comparison of distances between resection cavity and preoperative tractography with and without IBEF correction, correlated with new motor and…
papers.gap: Single centre; specialised nTMS and ioMRI equipment not widely available.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Heterogeneous tumours; short follow-up.
papers.methodologyDetail: For glioma patients near motor or language pathways, the team mapped function with magnetic stimulation, built tractography from it, and after resection measured how close the cavity came to the tracts, both before and after correcting for brain shift with intraoperative MRI, relating this to new deficits. Corrected tractography predicted function well. This informs the PhD's surgical-planning proof of concept and the need to account for brain shift.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective cohort study (Technical University of Munich, Germany); ethics 336/17 and 192/18, written consent.
papers.datasets: 78 cases of eloquent gliomas with preoperative nTMS-based fibre tracking and intraoperative MRI: 46 motor tracking, 32 left-hemispheric language tracking (12 awake surgeries).
papers.preprocessing: nTMS used to seed function-based DTI fibre tracking; resection with neuronavigation and continuous MEP monitoring; ioMRI after resection; ioMRI-based elastic fusion (IBEF) to correct preoperative tracts for brain shift.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of distances between resection cavity and preoperative tractography with and without IBEF correction, correlated with new motor and language deficits.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Distance from cavity to tracts; postoperative functional status at different time points; accuracy of tractography for predicting deficits.
papers.baselines: Uncorrected preoperative tractography.
papers.results: Preoperative tractography corrected by IBEF was highly accurate for subcortical resections; brain shift had less effect on tract accuracy than often assumed for such resections.
papers.statistics: Statistical correlation of distance with functional outcome.

papers.title: The Relevant Role of Navigated Tractography in Speech Eloquent Area Glioma Surgery: Single Center Experience
papers.authors: Salvati LF, De Marco R, Palmieri G, Minardi M, Massara A, Pesaresi A, Cagetti B, Melcarne A, Garbossa D
papers.aim: To describe navigated tractography in surgery for gliomas near language areas.
papers.method: Eighteen patients had language pathways mapped by tractography and loaded into navigation; language tested before and after surgery.
papers.result: Supported maximal safe resection and identified zones at high risk of permanent language damage.
papers.tools: Navigated DTI tractography of language tracts (arcuate, SLF, IFOF, uncinate, etc.) integrated into neuronavigation for resection planning.
papers.gap: Small uncontrolled series.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; short follow-up.
papers.methodologyDetail: Eighteen patients with gliomas near language areas had language pathways mapped with tractography and loaded into the navigation system, and their language was tested before surgery, a week after and at three months. The series describes resection extent, outcomes and anatomical zones where damage tends to be permanent. It supports the surgical-planning use case of the PhD, where AI would add to such tractography-based planning.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective observational single-centre study (Department of Neurosurgery, Turin, Italy) over about one year to August 2020; written consent.
papers.datasets: 18 adults (11 women, 7 men; median age 52) with left gliomas near presumed language areas: 13 high-grade, 5 low-grade; 6 awake surgeries.
papers.preprocessing: 3T Philips Ingenia MRI (T1, T2, 3D FLAIR, subtraction); manual tumour segmentation and volumes in Brainlab iPlan; extent of resection from subtraction or FLAIR; language assessed with Italian Aachen Aphasia Test before, within 7 days and at 3 months (4-level aphasia score).
papers.modelDetails: Navigated DTI tractography of language tracts (arcuate, SLF, IFOF, uncinate, etc.) integrated into neuronavigation for resection planning.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Extent of resection (gross total, subtotal, partial), postoperative and 3-month aphasia scores, relation of tumour location and tract involvement to language outcome.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (no control group).
papers.results: Gross total resection in 9 patients, subtotal in 6, partial in 3; areas at high risk of permanent language damage identified (e.g. temporoparietal junction and related regions); navigated tractography supported maximal safe resection.

papers.title: Significance of navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation and tractography to preserve motor function in patients undergoing surgery for motor eloquent gliomas
papers.authors: Eibl T, Schrey M, Liebert A, Ritter L, Lange R, Steiner HH, Schebesch KM
papers.aim: To assess magnetic stimulation and tractography for preserving motor function in glioma surgery.
papers.method: Retrospective review of patients mapped with nTMS and tractography; resection-to-tract distance on postoperative MRI related to motor outcome.
papers.result: A larger distance from the motor tract was linked to preserved motor function.
papers.tools: SPSS
papers.gap: Retrospective; no intraoperative stimulation in all cases.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; selected cohort.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed glioma patients whose motor areas and pathways were mapped before surgery with magnetic stimulation and tractography, then measured how close the resection came to the motor tract on postoperative MRI and related this to motor outcome. Keeping a larger distance was linked to preserved function. Such distance-based risk measures are candidate inputs and evaluation endpoints for the PhD's surgical-planning demonstrator.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective cohort study (Paracelsus Medical University Nuremberg, Germany), April 2016 to June 2021; IRB-2020-022 and IRB-2022-012, consent waived.
papers.datasets: Adults with WHO grade 2-4 motor-eloquent gliomas with preoperative nTMS motor mapping and DTI, and pre- and postoperative MRI.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions: lesion-to-tract distance > 20 mm, postoperative subcortical ischaemia, in-hospital death; 5-ALA fluorescence-guided microsurgery with nTMS data in neuronavigation.
papers.modelDetails: nTMS motor mapping and nTMS-based tractography of the corticospinal tract; measurement of cavity-to-tract distance (CTD) and lesion-to-tract distance on MRI.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Association of postoperative motor status with CTD, extent of resection and nTMS-derived risk factors; positive and negative predictive values.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Distances between resection cavity and CST were larger in patients with stable postoperative motor function; extent of resection and distance-related nTMS measures were associated with motor outcomes.
papers.statistics: Fisher exact and Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests with Cramer's V; Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests; PPV/NPV (SPSS 27).

papers.title: Preoperative tractography algorithm for safe resection of tumors located in the descending motor pathways zone
papers.authors: Ordonez-Rubiano EG, Johnson JM, Abdalá-Vargas N, Zorro OF, Marin-Munoz JH, Álvarez-Tobián R, Forlizzi V, Rangel CC, Luzzi S, Campero A, et al.
papers.aim: To use preoperative tractography to plan safe resection of tumours near the motor pathways.
papers.method: Retrospective review: motor tracts traced before surgery were classed as reduced, displaced, infiltrated or disrupted and used to plan resection.
papers.result: Motor function was kept or improved in most patients (median KPS 78 before, 80 after).
papers.tools: Preoperative tractography algorithm classifying the relation of descending motor pathways to tumour as volume reduction, displacement (preserved FA)…
papers.gap: Small uncontrolled series; no intraoperative mapping comparison.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; heterogeneous tumours.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed glioma patients whose motor pathways were traced before surgery and classified each tract as reduced, displaced, infiltrated or disrupted, using this to plan the resection. Most patients kept or improved motor function. The structured classification of tract involvement is the type of planning information an AI surgical-planning tool in the PhD could support or automate.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective review of a prospectively acquired database at two academic institutions (Hospital de San José, Bogotá, Colombia, with MD Anderson and international co-authors), January 2013 to May 2020; ethics approved.
papers.datasets: 25 glioma patients with DTI fibre tracking and neuronavigation; 19 resections with preoperative tracking of descending motor pathways (12 male; age 19-81, mean 44.5; 10 HGG, 9 LGG).
papers.preprocessing: Tumour location confirmed by neuroradiologist and neurosurgeon; fibre tracking by a dedicated neuroradiologist; extent of resection from ABC/2 volumes (GTR 100%, STR ≥ 90%, partial < 90%).
papers.modelDetails: Preoperative tractography algorithm classifying the relation of descending motor pathways to tumour as volume reduction, displacement (preserved FA), infiltration (reduced FA) or disruption, to guide surgical approach.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Karnofsky Performance Score and motor function before and after surgery; extent of resection.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Descending motor pathways identified bilaterally in all patients; median KPS 78 preoperatively and 80 postoperatively; motor function unchanged or improved in most patients.

papers.title: Emerging paradigms in connectome-guided neurosurgery for central nervous system tumors: a narrative review of structural and functional connectomics
papers.authors: Patel T, Yousuf Ibrahim H, Abbas M, Amir Ali M, Sohrab S, Nawaz K, Zehra SF, Patel BD, Anand N
papers.aim: To review connectome-guided brain tumour surgery.
papers.method: Narrative review of three databases on structural and functional brain-network mapping in tumour surgery and the role of AI.
papers.result: Surgery is shifting from removing lesions to protecting networks; tractography errors, cost and lack of standards are limits.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: Narrative; limited clinical outcome evidence.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: No quality assessment.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases and summarised how mapping brain networks, both structural wiring and functional activity, is changing brain tumour surgery from removing a lesion to protecting networks, and how AI may help. They also list technical limitations. This review frames future extensions of the PhD's surgical-planning component and shows where uncertainty in tractography must be communicated.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review with structured search and dual screening (authors from USA, Pakistan and India) in Annals of Medicine & Surgery.
papers.datasets: PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar, January 2000 to May 2025, using connectome, neurosurgery, CNS tumour, brain mapping, tractography, fMRI and AI terms.
papers.preprocessing: Two independent reviewers with third-reviewer arbitration; English peer-reviewed studies, trials, meta-analyses and reviews included; abstracts, editorials and animal studies excluded.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of structural (DTI/tractography) and functional (fMRI, MEG, EEG) connectomics for preoperative planning, intraoperative guidance, connectome-based predictive modelling and AI integration.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Connectome-guided neurosurgery shifts from lesion-centric to network-centric surgery, supporting function preservation; limitations include tractography errors, fMRI neurovascular uncoupling, cost and lack of standardisation.

papers.title: Tracking the Corticospinal Tract in Patients With High-Grade Glioma: Clinical Evaluation of Multi-Level Fiber Tracking and Comparison to Conventional Deterministic Approaches
papers.authors: Zhylka A, Sollmann N, Kofler F, Radwan A, De Luca A, Gempt J, Wiestler B, Menze B, Krieg SM, Zimmer C, et al.
papers.aim: To compare advanced and standard fibre tracking of the motor tract in high-grade glioma.
papers.method: In 40 patients the corticospinal tract was reconstructed with standard DTI and two advanced methods (MLFT, CSD) and compared.
papers.result: Advanced methods gave more complete tracts and detected tumour contact more often; DTI missed lateral fibres.
papers.tools: Three corticospinal tract reconstruction methods: DTI-based deterministic tractography, constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD)-based tractography…
papers.gap: No intraoperative stimulation ground truth.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; single centre.
papers.methodologyDetail: In forty high-grade glioma patients, the motor tract was reconstructed with a standard tensor method and two advanced methods, and the results were compared visually and by overlap. The advanced methods captured more of the tract, including parts close to the tumour that the standard method missed. This highlights method-dependent uncertainty in tract maps that the PhD's surgical-planning tool should communicate to surgeons.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective clinical evaluation study (Eindhoven University of Technology, Technical University of Munich, KU Leuven, UMC Utrecht); IRB approved, consent waived.
papers.datasets: 40 adults with high-grade glioma in suspected motor-eloquent locations (mean age 62.6; 17 female) with preoperative 3T MRI including diffusion imaging, identified from PACS February 2019 to February 2020.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusion of implant or motion artefacts and prior brain surgery; diffusion preprocessing and registration to anatomical scans.
papers.modelDetails: Three corticospinal tract reconstruction methods: DTI-based deterministic tractography, constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD)-based tractography, and multi-level fibre tracking (MLFT) designed to disentangle crossing and tumour-affected fibres.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative assessment of CST anatomy and tumour contact; quantitative overlap and volume comparison between methods; plausibility of reconstructions.
papers.baselines: Conventional DTI-based deterministic tractography.
papers.results: All methods traced the CST through internal capsule and cerebral crus; MLFT and CSD reconstructed more complete, fan-shaped tracts and almost fully included DTI-derived bundles, while DTI often missed lateral projections; tumour contact detected more often with advanced methods.
papers.statistics: Statistical comparison of overlap and volumes between methods.

papers.title: Standardized evaluation of the extent of resection in glioblastoma with automated early post-operative segmentation
papers.authors: Luque L, Skogen K, MacIntosh BJ, Emblem KE, Larsson C, Bouget D, Helland RH, Reinertsen I, Solheim O, Schellhorn T, et al.
papers.aim: To automatically assess extent of glioblastoma resection on early postoperative MRI.
papers.method: A U-Net segmented residual enhancing tumour on MRI within three days of surgery, tested on internal and external data against experts.
papers.result: Classified extent of resection reliably, comparable to expert raters.
papers.tools: U-Net, Kaplan-Meier
papers.gap: Enhancing tumour only; early postoperative blood products remain challenging.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; Norwegian centres only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a U-Net to outline remaining enhancing tumour on MRI scans taken within three days of glioblastoma surgery and tested whether it could judge if resection was complete, on internal and external hospital data. Its judgements matched experts reliably. Automated postoperative assessment like this could provide objective outcome measures for the PhD's surgical-planning evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and external validation study (Oslo University Hospital and St. Olavs/SINTEF Trondheim, Norway).
papers.datasets: Internal cohort of 616 glioblastoma patients operated 2003-2020 with early postoperative MRI (within 72 h: T1w, T1wc, T2w, FLAIR); labelled train/validation subset of 122 exams (87 with 3D sequences, 2016-2020); external dataset of 248 patients from another national institution.
papers.preprocessing: Expert manual segmentation of residual contrast-enhancing tumour; co-registration of sequences; scans differ by manufacturer, field strength and 2D/3D acquisition.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net-based deep learning model segmenting residual contrast-enhancing tumour on early postoperative MRI to classify extent of resection (gross total vs residual).
papers.training: Cross-validation on labelled internal subset (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Segmentation Dice and volume agreement; EOR classification accuracy, sensitivity and specificity versus expert ratings on internal and external data.
papers.baselines: Expert radiologist assessment.
papers.results: Model reliably classified EOR of glioblastoma on early postoperative MRI in both internal and external datasets, comparable to expert raters, supporting standardised EOR evaluation.
papers.availability: Model shared via Raidionics-related tools (details in paper).

papers.title: The effect of editing clinical contours on deep-learning segmentation accuracy of the gross tumor volume in glioblastoma
papers.authors: Hochreuter KM, Ren J, Nijkamp J, Korreman SS, Lukacova S, Kallehauge JF, Trip AK
papers.venue: Physics and Imaging in Radiation Oncology
papers.aim: To test whether cleaning clinical tumour contours improves deep learning segmentation for glioblastoma radiotherapy.
papers.method: Two models were trained: one on original multi-oncologist contours and one on contours corrected by one expert, and compared on matched test sets.
papers.result: Edited, consistent labels gave significantly better models, although volume changes were small.
papers.tools: nnU-Net, R
papers.gap: Single editor; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Edited labels may encode one observer's bias.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained two tumour-contouring models for glioblastoma radiotherapy, one on the original clinical outlines drawn by several oncologists and one on outlines carefully corrected by a single expert, then compared them on matched test sets. Cleaner, consistent labels gave significantly better models. This underlines the PhD's plan for careful clinician annotation protocols when building the Sri Lankan dataset.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre deep learning study (Danish Centre for Particle Therapy, Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark); approved by the Danish Patient Safety Authority and Danish Neuro-Oncology Registry.
papers.datasets: 406 eligible glioblastoma patients treated with postoperative radiotherapy 2012-2019 identified through DNOR; 292 with complete planning MRI and CT; 259 used (207 training/validation, 52 test).
papers.preprocessing: T1, T1C and FLAIR rigidly registered to planning CT (mutual information, skull ROI); clinical GTVs delineated by at least five oncologists were edited by a single observer using all imaging (tightening, excluding subdural haematoma, including enhancement and cavity).
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning segmentation models trained on clinical GTVs versus single-observer edited GTVs, using T1C/T1/FLAIR/CT inputs; robustness by extent of resection (complete, partial, biopsy).
papers.training: Details in paper (nnU-Net-type training on 207 cases).
papers.evaluation: Surface DSC at 1 mm tolerance, DSC, mean surface distance and HD95; head-to-head comparison of models on clinical and edited test sets; subgroup analysis by EOR.
papers.baselines: Model trained on unedited clinical GTVs.
papers.results: Editing changed GTV volumes slightly (median 0.85 cc; 65% decreased) but significantly improved DL performance with a relevant effect size; performance robust across extent of resection.
papers.statistics: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in R, significance level 0.01.

papers.title: DeepEOR: automated perioperative volumetric assessment of variable grade gliomas using deep learning
papers.authors: Zanier O, Da Mutten R, Vieli M, Regli L, Serra C, Staartjes VE
papers.aim: To measure glioma volumes and extent of resection automatically before and after surgery.
papers.method: DeepEOR: U-Net ensembles trained on BraTS and local Zurich scans segment tumour components and compute extent of resection.
papers.result: Preoperative segmentation was good, but resection category was correct in only 44% of cases, so not ready for clinical use.
papers.tools: ensemble, U-Net
papers.gap: Small postoperative training set; student labels.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Not clinically usable yet.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained U-Net ensembles on public BraTS and local Zurich scans to outline glioma components before and after surgery and calculate how much tumour was removed. Preoperative segmentation was good, but postoperative segmentation was hard and resection category was correct in fewer than half of cases. This shows that postoperative assessment is a difficult, uncertain task where the PhD's escalation to human review is essential.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective model development and validation study (University Hospital Zurich, Switzerland); Cantonal Ethics Committee Zürich BASEC 2021-01147.
papers.datasets: Preoperative: 1,053 MRI scans from BraTS 2021 training set and Zurich (87 pre-op), holdout 285; postoperative: 72 training and 45 validation scans from BraTS 2015 and Zurich (92 post-op); LGG and HGG.
papers.preprocessing: Zurich images hand-labelled by medical students after expert teaching; segmentation of enhancing tumour (ET), non-enhancing tumour (NET) and whole tumour (WT).
papers.modelDetails: DeepEOR: ensembles of U-Nets for pre- and postoperative segmentation to compute extent of resection and residual tumour volume automatically.
papers.training: Ensemble U-Net training (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice and volumetric agreement for ET, NET, WT; accuracy of EOR category against ground truth.
papers.baselines: Manual segmentation.
papers.results: Preoperative segmentation performed well, but postoperative segmentation was weaker and the algorithm determined correct EOR in only 44.1% of cases; not yet suitable for clinical use.

papers.title: Augmented and virtual reality usage in awake craniotomy: a systematic review
papers.authors: Mofatteh M, Mashayekhi MS, Arfaie S, Chen Y, Mirza AB, Fares J, Bandyopadhyay S, Henich E, Liao X, Bernstein M
papers.aim: To review augmented and virtual reality use in awake brain surgery.
papers.method: Systematic review of three databases; six small original studies.
papers.result: AR and VR can be used safely to support intraoperative mapping, but evidence is limited.
papers.tools: PRISMA
papers.gap: Very small evidence base; no comparative outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Only six studies from two countries.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases for original studies using augmented or virtual reality during awake brain surgery and found six small studies. They describe the devices used and the functions tested, concluding that these tools are safe and can extend intraoperative mapping. It is background for how planning outputs from the PhD's system might eventually be displayed to surgeons.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA (international authors; senior author University of Toronto).
papers.datasets: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 20 May 2022; 6 studies included (4 France, 2 Germany) with 118 patients in total (cohorts 3 to 55; ages 14-81).
papers.preprocessing: Boolean search combining AR/VR/mixed reality terms with awake craniotomy terms; title/abstract and full-text screening; reference-list checking by three authors; English original human studies only.
papers.modelDetails: Data extraction on AR/VR type, hardware and software (e.g. Oculus DK1/DK2, Samsung Gear VR), user (patient or staff), timing (pre-, intra-, postoperative) and mapped function (visual field, optic radiation, language, social cognition).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative synthesis of feasibility, safety and outcomes.
papers.baselines: Conventional awake mapping tasks.
papers.results: AR and VR can be safely incorporated during awake craniotomy to supplement, augment or replace conventional testing, e.g. VR for visual field and social cognition mapping and AR for navigation; evidence is limited to small studies.

papers.title: Augmented reality for intracranial meningioma resection: a mini-review
papers.authors: Gómez Amarillo DF, Ordóñez-Rubiano EG, Ramírez-Sanabria AD, Figueredo LF, Vargas-Osorio MP, Ramon JF, Mejia JA, Hakim F
papers.aim: To review augmented reality for meningioma surgery.
papers.method: Mini-review of AR overlays of preoperative 3D models onto the surgeon's view, with workflow, benefits and limits.
papers.result: AR improves understanding of anatomy, but registration error, brain shift and cost are limits.
papers.tools: Narrative review of AR workflows: preoperative 3D reconstruction of tumour, vessels and venous sinuses, registration to the patient, and overlay into…
papers.gap: No systematic method or outcome comparisons.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Mini-review; mostly case series.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors review how augmented reality overlays 3D models built from preoperative imaging onto the surgeon's view during meningioma surgery, describing the workflow and its benefits and limits. It shows a route for presenting planning outputs, such as AI segmentations from the PhD's system, directly in the operative field, while noting accuracy problems such as brain shift.
papers.studyDesign: Mini-review (Fundación Santa Fe de Bogotá and partners, Colombia) in Frontiers in Neurology.
papers.datasets: Published literature on augmented reality in intracranial meningioma surgery.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative review of AR workflows: preoperative 3D reconstruction of tumour, vessels and venous sinuses, registration to the patient, and overlay into the operating microscope or head-mounted display for planning and intraoperative guidance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Conventional neuronavigation.
papers.results: Integrating preoperative 3D reconstructions into the microsurgical field with AR improves spatial understanding of anatomy for meningioma resection; limitations include registration error, brain shift and cost.

papers.title: Cerebral Anatomy Detection and Surgical Planning in Patients with Anterior Skull Base Meningiomas Using a Virtual Reality Technique
papers.authors: Zawy Alsofy S, Nakamura M, Suleiman A, Sakellaropoulou I, Welzel Saravia H, Shalamberidze D, Salma A, Stroop R
papers.aim: To test whether virtual reality changes surgical planning for skull base meningiomas.
papers.method: Neurosurgeons planned cases from standard scans and, four weeks later, from 3D VR in a different order.
papers.result: VR significantly changed detection of key structures (p = 0.002), head positioning and surgical approach.
papers.tools: Raters reviewed conventional 2D and screen-3D CT/MRI, then four weeks later reconstructed 3D virtual reality (3D-VR) images of the same patients in a…
papers.gap: Decisions not linked to patient outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; small number of raters.
papers.methodologyDetail: Experienced neurosurgeons planned meningioma operations first from standard scans and, four weeks later, from 3D virtual reality reconstructions of the same patients presented in a different order. VR changed which structures they identified and how they would position the patient and approach the tumour. The within-rater design with washout is a model for testing whether the PhD's planning outputs change surgical decisions.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective within-surgeon comparison study (Witten/Herdecke University and partners, Germany); ethics Ref-Nr. 201/2018.
papers.datasets: Adults with anterior skull base meningiomas operated 2016-2019 with thin-slice CT/CTA and MRI/MRA; experienced board-certified neurosurgeons (not the operating surgeons) as raters.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions for multimorbidity, other pathologies, prior craniotomy, recurrent or multiple meningiomas; clinical data withheld from raters; 3D-VR reconstructions built from CT/MRI.
