papers.modelDetails: Raters reviewed conventional 2D and screen-3D CT/MRI, then four weeks later reconstructed 3D virtual reality (3D-VR) images of the same patients in a different order, completing the same questionnaire on anatomical structures, head positioning and surgical approach.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Detection of tumour-related anatomical structures; recommended positioning and approach; comparison between modalities.
papers.baselines: Conventional 2D and screen-3D imaging.
papers.results: 3D-VR significantly influenced detection of tumour-related anatomical structures (p = 0.002) and recommended head positioning and surgical approach.
papers.statistics: Paired statistical tests comparing questionnaire responses across modalities.

papers.title: Intraoperative Imaging and Optical Visualization Techniques for Brain Tumor Resection: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Bin-Alamer O, Abou-Al-Shaar H, Gersey ZC, Huq S, Kallos JA, McCarthy DJ, Head JR, Andrews E, Zhang X, Hadjipanayis CG
papers.aim: To review intraoperative imaging and visualisation tools for brain tumour resection.
papers.method: Narrative review of microscopes, fluorescence, intraoperative MRI, ultrasound and molecular imaging.
papers.result: Each tool improves precision but has usage and learning challenges; AI and multimodal imaging are future directions.
papers.tools: Not applicable (no software or model used)
papers.gap: No systematic evidence grading.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Narrative review.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors describe the main tools that help surgeons see brain tumours during surgery, from microscopes and fluorescence to intraoperative MRI and molecular imaging, with their pros and cons. They expect AI to help interpret these data. This gives the PhD context on intraoperative information that a future version of the planning assistant could use.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (University of Pittsburgh Medical Center Center for Image-Guided Neurosurgery, USA) in Cancers.
papers.datasets: Literature on intraoperative imaging and optical visualisation for brain tumour resection.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative review of operating microscope, exoscope, Raman spectroscopy, confocal microscopy, fluorescence-guided surgery (5-ALA, fluorescein, ICG), intraoperative ultrasound, MRI and CT.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative comparison of benefits, limitations and evidence.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Each modality improves precision and safety of resection but faces challenges in usage, interpretation and learning curve; future directions include AI, integrated multimodal imaging and VR.

papers.title: Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice Among Chinese Physicians: Nationwide Cross-Sectional Survey Using Extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology and Explainable Machine Learning
papers.authors: Shi X, Tian Z, Guo Q, Qiao B, Wang X
papers.aim: To find what drives Chinese physicians' acceptance of AI.
papers.method: Nationwide survey of over 4,000 physicians using an extended UTAUT model, analysed with SEM and explainable machine learning (SHAP).
papers.result: Organisational support and expected performance mattered most (random forest AUC 0.84).
papers.tools: UTAUT, random forest, SHAP, survey, scikit-learn, Python
papers.gap: Intentions, not actual use; senior-heavy sample.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Online platform recruitment; self-report.
papers.methodologyDetail: Over four thousand Chinese physicians completed a validated questionnaire based on a technology-acceptance model, and the team analysed it both with structural equation modelling and with an explainable machine learning model to see which factors best predict acceptance of AI. Organisational support and expected performance mattered most. The combination of SEM with SHAP is a useful approach for the PhD's acceptance analysis.
papers.studyDesign: Nationwide cross-sectional survey of physicians in mainland China (Shuguang Hospital Shanghai, KINGYEE and Zhejiang University), January-April, distributed via Medlive.
papers.datasets: 4,024 in-service physicians from 29 provinces (77.4% tertiary hospitals; 72.9% senior titles).
papers.preprocessing: Stratified random sampling by province and hospital tier; questionnaire adapted from UTAUT with an added perceived-impact (PI) construct; exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis for psychometric validation.
papers.modelDetails: Extended UTAUT model (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, perceived impact) tested with structural equation modelling; random forest classifier with SHAP explanations to identify key predictors of acceptance.
papers.training: Random forest trained on survey features (scikit-learn).
papers.evaluation: SEM path coefficients and mediation; random forest accuracy and AUC; SHAP feature importance.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Random forest accuracy 85.6% and AUC 0.836; SHAP identified organisational and expectancy factors (e.g. facilitating conditions, performance expectancy) as key drivers of acceptance; SEM confirmed direct and mediated effects.
papers.statistics: EFA/CFA; SEM; chi-square, Fisher and Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction (Python).

papers.title: Barriers to and facilitators of clinician acceptance and use of artificial intelligence in healthcare settings: a scoping review
papers.authors: Scipion CEA, Manchester MA, Federman A, Wang Y, Arias JJ
papers.aim: To review barriers and facilitators of clinicians' acceptance of AI.
papers.method: Scoping review mapping findings to technology-acceptance constructs and factors outside the model.
papers.result: Beyond standard UTAUT factors, trust, transparency, liability and workflow fit are key, so acceptance models need refining for AI.
papers.tools: UTAUT, PRISMA
papers.gap: Mostly high-income settings; few real-world implementations.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: English only; no quality appraisal.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors mapped published evidence on what helps or hinders clinicians in accepting and using AI, classifying findings by technology-acceptance constructs and noting factors the standard model misses, such as trust, liability and workflow fit. This guides which constructs the PhD should measure and which implementation barriers to address in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR (Georgia State University and Icahn School of Medicine, USA).
papers.datasets: English-language studies of physicians, nurses and paramedical staff using hypothetical or real AI tools in healthcare settings (databases and numbers in paper).
papers.preprocessing: PICOST framework integrated with PCC for eligibility; studies on non-AI digital devices or robots excluded; protocol in supplementary material.
papers.modelDetails: Data extraction and mapping of barriers and facilitators to clinician acceptance and use of AI, organised against UTAUT constructs and additional context-specific factors.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Thematic mapping of barriers and facilitators.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Barriers and facilitators spanned performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions plus factors outside UTAUT (trust, transparency, liability, ethics, workflow fit); frameworks like UTAUT need refinement for AI.
papers.availability: Protocol and checklist as supplementary files.

papers.title: AI in Fracture Detection: A Cross-Disciplinary Analysis of Physician Acceptance Using the UTAUT Model
papers.authors: Breitwieser M, Zirknitzer S, Poslusny K, Freude T, Scholsching J, Bodenschatz K, Wagner A, Hergan K, Schaffert M, Metzger R, et al.
papers.aim: To measure physicians' acceptance of an AI fracture-detection tool before it was introduced.
papers.method: Baseline UTAUT questionnaire before a randomised trial, analysed with factor analysis and SEM.
papers.result: Expected usefulness and ease of use drove intention to use; acceptance varied by specialty and experience.
papers.tools: UTAUT, survey, Likert, R, RCT
papers.gap: Small sample; Alpine region only.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Exploratory SEM; pre-implementation attitudes only.
papers.methodologyDetail: Before an AI fracture-detection tool was introduced in a randomised trial, the physicians who would use it completed a technology-acceptance questionnaire, analysed with factor analysis and structural equation modelling suited to small ordinal samples. Expected usefulness and ease of use drove intention to use. Measuring acceptance at baseline before deployment is a step the PhD can copy for its clinician evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre cross-sectional baseline (pre-implementation) survey within the SMART Fracture Trial RCT (Paracelsus Medical University Salzburg and Nuremberg, Regional Hospital Hallein; Austria and Germany).
papers.datasets: 92 physicians (response rate 83.8%; mean age 41.1; 55.4% orthopaedics/trauma, 29.3% paediatric surgery, 13.0% radiology; 47.8% consultants, 44.6% residents).
papers.preprocessing: 21-item five-point Likert questionnaire covering UTAUT constructs; reliability with Cronbach's α and Spearman-Brown for two-item scales.
papers.modelDetails: UTAUT model (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, behavioural intention) for acceptance of an AI fracture detection tool on radiographs in emergency care.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: CFA with robust DWLS for ordinal data; trimmed exploratory SEM; comparisons across specialties and roles.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Performance and effort expectancy were key predictors of intention to use; acceptance differed by specialty and experience; implementation should focus on intuitive design, targeted training and clear communication of clinical benefits.

papers.title: Acceptance, Barriers, and Facilitators to Implementing Artificial Intelligence-Based Decision Support Systems in Emergency Departments: Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation
papers.authors: Fujimori R, Liu K, Soeno S, Naraba H, Ogura K, Hara K, Sonoo T, Ogura T, Nakamura K, Goto T
papers.aim: To evaluate acceptance, barriers and facilitators of an AI aortic dissection alert in the emergency department.
papers.method: Physicians used the tool on vignettes, then completed an acceptance questionnaire and framework-based interviews.
papers.result: High acceptance; failure and over-reliance were concerns, while local development and workflow fit helped.
papers.tools: UTAUT, semi-structured interviews, Likert
papers.gap: Tiny sample; vignette setting; developer-run study.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Convenience sampling; industry involvement.
papers.methodologyDetail: Emergency physicians used an AI alert system for aortic dissection on realistic vignettes, then completed an acceptance questionnaire and an interview structured by an implementation-science framework. They liked the tool but worried about failures and over-reliance, and valued that it was locally built and fitted their workflow. This mixed-methods design and the local-development finding support the PhD's approach in Sri Lanka.

papers.datasets: 14 physicians (6 transitional residents, 5 emergency medicine residents, 3 emergency physicians) recruited by convenience sampling.
papers.preprocessing: 1.5-hour sessions: introduction, hands-on use of the web-deployed CDSS with typical and atypical vignette cases, then questionnaire and interview.
papers.modelDetails: Real-time machine learning CDSS predicting aortic dissection from numeric and text chart data (e.g. chief complaint) with emergency alerts; evaluated with UTAUT questionnaire and CFIR-based semi-structured interviews.
papers.training: ML model developed previously by the team.
papers.evaluation: UTAUT Likert scores; qualitative CFIR-guided analysis of barriers and facilitators.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Physicians showed high acceptance; concerns about system failure and over-trust were barriers, while local development and design aligned with emergency workflows were facilitators.

papers.title: Diagnostic Performance, Triage Safety, and Usability of a Clinical Decision Support System Within a University Hospital Emergency Department: Algorithm Performance and Usability Study
papers.authors: Määttä J, Lindell R, Hayward N, Martikainen S, Honkanen K, Inkala M, Hirvonen P, Martikainen TJ
papers.aim: To evaluate a decision support system for emergency department triage.
papers.method: Patients filled in a symptom form while waiting; the system's urgency and diagnoses were later compared with two physicians' judgements, plus a usability survey (silent design).
papers.result: Triage was safe with high sensitivity for urgent cases, acceptable diagnosis and good usability.
papers.tools: System Usability Scale, survey
papers.gap: Silent mode only; excludes the sickest patients.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; vendor-affiliated authors.
papers.methodologyDetail: Emergency department patients filled in an online symptom form while waiting, and the decision support system's urgency and diagnosis suggestions were later compared with judgements by two physicians who reviewed their records, alongside a usability survey. The system was judged safe enough for further real-world testing. The prospective silent design, where outputs do not affect care, is a safe first-stage evaluation approach the PhD could use.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective algorithm performance and usability study at Kuopio University Hospital emergency department, Finland, 3 weeks in September 2020 (NCT04577079; ethics 347/2020); written consent.
papers.datasets: 259 patients completed the CDSS form; 248 analysed (49.2% female; mean age 46, range 18-82); power analysis required at least 246.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions: age ≤ 17, cognitive impairment, ambulance arrivals or immediate care, misuse or incomplete forms; patients completed the web form on tablets in the waiting room; data not used for care.
papers.modelDetails: Klinik Access CDSS web-based patient symptom questionnaire producing urgency triage and differential diagnosis suggestions.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial algorithm).
papers.evaluation: Sensitivity and PPV (95% CI) of CDSS urgency against two independent physicians' EHR-based assessments; diagnostic suggestion accuracy; triage safety (under-triage); usability questionnaire.
papers.baselines: Independent physician assessments and triage nurse.
papers.results: CDSS urgency evaluation was safe with high sensitivity for urgent cases and acceptable diagnostic performance; good usability; supports further real-world assessment and faster triage with patient-provided data.
papers.statistics: Sensitivity and PPV with 95% CI; inter-rater comparison.

papers.title: Usability assessments in clinical decision support systems
papers.authors: Cubukcu HC, Canbaz H
papers.aim: To review usability problems and assessment methods for decision support tools.
papers.method: Review of common usability issues and methods such as heuristic evaluation and think-aloud testing.
papers.result: Iterative user-centred design with user feedback improves usability and uptake.
papers.tools: SUS
papers.gap: No systematic search or AI-specific usability evidence.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Brief narrative review.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors summarise common usability problems in decision support tools and the methods used to find them, such as heuristic evaluation and think-aloud testing, and recommend iterative user-centred design. This provides a menu of usability evaluation methods for the PhD's escalation interface.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Turkish Ministry of Health, Hacettepe University, Yenimahalle Training and Research Hospital, Turkey).
papers.datasets: Published studies on usability of clinical decision support tools.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Overview of usability issues (graphical interface, user experience, terminology clarity, user control) and assessment methods (heuristic evaluation, think-aloud testing, cognitive walkthrough, surveys such as SUS).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Usability problems limit CDS uptake; incorporating user feedback, iterative user-centred design and addressing interface challenges improves usability and acceptance.

papers.title: Interruptive Versus Noninterruptive Clinical Decision Support: Usability Study
papers.authors: Blecker S, Pandya R, Stork S, Mann D, Kuperman G, Shelley D, Austrian JS
papers.aim: To compare interruptive pop-up and non-interruptive sidebar decision support.
papers.method: Providers used both versions of heart-failure advice in random order while thinking aloud, then were interviewed.
papers.result: Preferences varied by role: pop-ups risk alert fatigue, sidebars risk being missed.
papers.tools: semi-structured interviews
papers.gap: Lab setting; small sample; no outcome measures.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single institution; one CDS topic.
papers.methodologyDetail: Providers tried both an interrupting pop-up and a sidebar version of the same heart-failure prescribing advice in random order while thinking aloud, then were interviewed. Preferences varied by role, balancing alert fatigue against the risk of missing advice. This informs how the PhD's escalation messages should be delivered, interruptive for high-risk cases and passive otherwise.
papers.studyDesign: Laboratory usability study with randomised presentation order (NYU Langone Health, USA).
papers.datasets: 12 inpatient providers (9 medicine, others surgery or neurology; attendings, residents, NPs, PAs) recruited by purposive sampling.
papers.preprocessing: Providers randomly assigned (random number generation) to use the interruptive alert first (n = 7) or noninterruptive alert first (n = 5).
papers.modelDetails: Two versions of a CDS recommending ACE inhibitor prescribing for inpatients with heart failure: an interruptive alert at order entry and a noninterruptive alert in the EHR sidebar; think-aloud testing and semi-structured interviews.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative coding of think-aloud and interview data into themes mapped to the CDS Five Rights; preferences between versions.
papers.baselines: Comparison of the two alert designs.
papers.results: Four themes aligned with CDS Five Rights; preferences depended on provider role (those with global responsibility favoured noninterruptive display); interruptive alerts raised alert-fatigue concerns while noninterruptive ones risked being missed.

papers.title: Assessing the Usability of a Clinical Decision Support System: Heuristic Evaluation
papers.authors: Cho H, Keenan G, Madandola OO, Dos Santos FC, Macieira TGR, Bjarnadottir RI, Priola KJB, Dunn Lopez K
papers.aim: To check a decision support tool's usability with expert heuristic evaluation before deployment.
papers.method: Six usability experts rated the tool against ten design heuristics and scored problem severity.
papers.result: Problems with user control and error prevention were found and fixed before rollout.
papers.tools: RCT
papers.gap: Expert inspection without end users.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small expert panel; single system.
papers.methodologyDetail: Before a decision support tool was rolled out in a national trial, six usability experts inspected it against ten standard design principles using a checklist and rated how severe each problem was. Problems with user control and error prevention were found and fixed early. Heuristic evaluation is a low-cost step the PhD can run on its escalation interface before clinician testing.
papers.studyDesign: Heuristic evaluation case study (University of Florida and University of Iowa Colleges of Nursing, USA) before deployment in a national RCT.
papers.datasets: 6 HCI experts (4 nursing, 1 pharmaceutical sciences, 1 systems engineering) evaluating a nurse-facing CDS intervention.
papers.preprocessing: Systematic inspection using a checklist (Bright et al.) for Nielsen's 10 heuristics with yes/no items.
papers.modelDetails: Heuristic evaluation with severity ratings from 0 (no problem) to 4 (usability catastrophe) per heuristic, plus expert comments.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Mean severity scores per heuristic and qualitative comments.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Mean severity ranged from 0.66 (flexibility and efficiency of use) to 2.00 (user control and freedom; error prevention); issues were fixed before deployment; heuristic evaluation is efficient and supports transparent usability reporting required by regulation.

papers.title: Live Usability Testing of Two Complex Clinical Decision Support Tools: Observational Study
papers.authors: Richardson S, Feldstein D, McGinn T, Park LS, Khan S, Hess R, Smith PD, Mishuris RG, McCullagh L, Mann D
papers.aim: To test usability of two complex decision support tools during real primary-care visits.
papers.method: Observation of providers using two prediction-rule tools in live consultations.
papers.result: Short, flexible tools that fit each provider's workflow worked best.
papers.tools: survey
papers.gap: Very small sample.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single site; rule-based tools, not AI.
papers.methodologyDetail: Researchers watched primary care providers use two prediction-rule decision tools during real patient visits and analysed what made them easy or hard to use. Tools that were short and fitted each provider's workflow worked best. Testing in live clinical use, not just in a lab, is a lesson for the PhD's later deployment evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Qualitative observational live usability study within the iCPR2 trial (University of Wisconsin-Madison, USA), January 2017.
papers.datasets: 3 volunteer primary care providers (2 nurse practitioners, 1 physician) across 6 real patient care sessions.
papers.preprocessing: Convenience sample from the intervention arm; sessions observed and recorded in the real clinical environment.
papers.modelDetails: Two EHR-embedded CDS tools in Epic using clinical prediction rules: Centor score for streptococcal pharyngitis and Heckerling rule for pneumonia, triggered by visit reason with alerts and risk calculators.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Observation and think-aloud of live use; qualitative analysis of usability issues and workflow fit.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Usability issues related to workflow timing, length and flexibility; CDS can reduce provider strain by being short, flexible and customisable to individual workflows.

papers.title: Exploring Usability of a Clinical Decision Support System for Cancer Care: A User-Centered Study
papers.authors: Chyzhyk D, Arregi M, Errazquin M, Ariceta A, Sevilla M, Álvarez R, Alberich Inchausti M
papers.aim: To test usability of a cancer side-effect monitoring decision support app.
papers.method: Patients and clinicians completed set tasks with success and errors recorded, then rated usability (SUS).
papers.result: All tasks completed and SUS in the top 10% (grade A); only minor fixes needed.
papers.tools: System Usability Scale, SUS
papers.gap: Very small sample; non-clinical setting; company-run.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Vendor authorship.
papers.methodologyDetail: Patients and clinicians performed set tasks in a cancer side-effect monitoring app while their success and errors were recorded, then rated usability with standard questionnaires and gave feedback. Usability was excellent with only minor fixes needed. The combination of task completion, error logging and SUS is a simple protocol for the PhD's interface testing.
papers.studyDesign: Multi-method user-centred usability study of a CE-marked medical device app (Naru Intelligence Solutions, San Sebastián, Spain).
papers.datasets: Six oncology patients and six healthcare professionals.
papers.preprocessing: Realistic task scenarios for each user group; demographic data collected.
papers.modelDetails: Digital CDSS for monitoring and managing adverse events in cancer patients using electronic patient-reported outcome measures (ePROMs).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Scenario completion rates and errors, System Usability Scale, After Scenario Questionnaire and qualitative feedback.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: All participants completed 100% of tasks; two of six patients had login errors unrelated to safety; SUS in the 90th percentile (grade A) for both groups; minor improvements identified.

papers.title: Explainable AI in Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Meta-Analysis of Methods, Applications, and Usability Challenges
papers.authors: Abbas Q, Jeong W, Lee SW
papers.aim: To review explainable AI methods in clinical decision support and their usability.
papers.method: Review of 62 studies, classifying explanation methods, data, models and evaluation approaches.
papers.result: SHAP and Grad-CAM dominate, and most evaluations are technical rather than with clinicians.
papers.tools: SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM
papers.gap: Few clinician-centred or longitudinal evaluations.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Heterogeneous studies; limited quantitative pooling.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed 62 studies that added explanations to clinical AI, classifying which explanation methods were used for which data and models and how explanations were evaluated. Most studies tested explanations technically rather than with clinicians. This guides the PhD to evaluate any explanations in the escalation interface with clinicians, not only with technical metrics.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review / meta-analysis (Institute of Space Technology, Pakistan, and Sungkyunkwan University, South Korea).
papers.datasets: 62 peer-reviewed studies (2018-2025) on explainable AI in clinical decision support across radiology, cardiology, pathology, ICU, oncology, neurology, primary care and diabetes.
papers.preprocessing: Systematic search and screening (details in paper); extraction of XAI method, domain, model type, data and evaluation approach.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy and synthesis of XAI methods (SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM, attention, LRP, integrated gradients, counterfactuals, concept-based and causal methods) and how they are evaluated (fidelity, IoU of heatmaps, clinician feedback, usability ratings).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Pooled/quantitative summary of method use and evaluation practices; usability challenges.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: SHAP and Grad-CAM dominate; most evaluations are technical rather than clinician-centred; usability, workflow integration and trust remain challenges; longitudinal clinical validation, participatory design and standardised explanation evaluation are needed.

papers.title: Leveraging Dual Usability Methods to Evaluate Clinical Decision Support Among Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury: Mixed Methods Study
papers.authors: Rizvi RF, Faisal S, Sussman M, Mendlick P, Brown S, Lindemann E, Switzer S, Melton GB, Tignanelli CJ
papers.aim: To evaluate a brain injury decision support tool with two usability methods.
papers.method: Experts did a heuristic evaluation, then trauma providers used the tool on tasks with think-aloud and ease ratings.
papers.result: The two methods found different problems, so using both gives a fuller picture (ease score 5.9 of 7).

papers.gap: Small samples; pre-deployment only.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single health system.
papers.methodologyDetail: Usability experts first inspected a brain injury decision support tool against design heuristics, and then trauma providers used it on tasks while thinking aloud and rating ease of use. The two methods found different problems, so together they gave a fuller picture. This dual approach is a practical template for testing the PhD's neuro-oncology escalation interface.
papers.studyDesign: Mixed-methods usability study combining heuristic evaluation and end-user testing (University of Minnesota and Fairview Health Services, USA).
papers.datasets: 3 usability experts and 5 trauma providers.
papers.preprocessing: Realistic tasks in the EHR-integrated CDSS; data collected via think-aloud, observation and questionnaires.
papers.modelDetails: FHIR-based CDSS delivering a venous thromboembolism prophylaxis guideline for traumatic brain injury (modified Berne-Norwood criteria: low, moderate, high risk of haemorrhage progression), adapted from a COVID-19 CPG-FHIR CDSS (108 + 21 data elements).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Heuristic violations and severity (Nielsen heuristics); task success, Single Ease Questions, SUS and qualitative feedback from end users.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Mean Single Ease Question score 5.9 (SD 0.53) across tasks; expert and end-user methods identified complementary usability issues, supporting combined use.

papers.title: Implementing an Artificial Intelligence Decision Support System in Radiology: Prospective Qualitative Evaluation Study Using the Nonadoption Abandonment Scale-Up, Spread, and Sustainability (NASSS) Framework
papers.authors: Naicker S, Schmidt P, Shar B, Tariq A, Earnshaw A, McPhail S
papers.aim: To study implementation of an AI tool in radiology over time with the NASSS framework.
papers.method: Staff interviews before, during and a year after go-live, coded into NASSS domains.
papers.result: Barriers grew after go-live along with enablers; lasting adoption depended on fixing workflow and performance problems.
papers.tools: NASSS (Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread, Sustainability) framework guiding interview design and deductive coding of barriers and enablers…
papers.gap: Single site; commercial tool not named in detail.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Staff turnover limited longitudinal follow-up.
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiology staff were interviewed before, during and a year after an AI decision support tool was introduced, and their comments were coded into the domains of an implementation framework that explains why technologies succeed or are abandoned. Barriers increased after go-live even as enablers grew. This longitudinal NASSS approach is a strong model for the PhD's implementation evaluation in a Sri Lankan hospital.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective qualitative implementation study across three phases (Queensland University of Technology and Princess Alexandra Hospital, Australia), reported per COREQ.
papers.datasets: 43 one-on-one interviews with 7 radiographers, 20 radiology registrars and 16 consultant radiologists (26 male, 17 female); 9 interviewed at multiple time points.
papers.preprocessing: Baseline (12 months before deployment), peri-implementation (8-week rollout) and post-implementation (12 months after) phases; each interview treated as a discrete data point due to staff rotation.
papers.modelDetails: NASSS (Nonadoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread, Sustainability) framework guiding interview design and deductive coding of barriers and enablers to a regulator-approved commercial AI CDSS in radiology.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Counts and themes of barriers and enablers across NASSS domains and phases.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 56 barriers/18 enablers at baseline, 55/14 peri-implementation and 82/33 post-implementation; clinicians stayed willing to engage, but sustainable adoption depended on consolidating early positive experiences and addressing negative ones such as workflow and performance issues.
papers.statistics: Qualitative framework analysis with frequency counts.

papers.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Imaging Support Software for Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Mayo Clinic Telestroke Network
papers.authors: Smith BH, Wolfe JG, Karam A, Demarkschalk BM, Hrdlicka CM, Nasr DM, Chukwudelunzu FE, Nord CA, Pahl EA, Fernandez C, et al.
papers.venue: Mayo Clinic proceedings. Innovations, quality & outcomes
papers.aim: To evaluate AI stroke imaging software in a real telestroke network.
papers.method: Three months before and after introducing the software were compared for treatment rates, speed and transfers, plus a user survey.
papers.result: No significant clinical changes, but users were satisfied.
papers.tools: survey
papers.gap: Short periods; underpowered; no concurrent control.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Before-after design susceptible to secular trends.
papers.methodologyDetail: The stroke network compared three months of patients before and after introducing AI software that analyses brain scans, measuring treatment rates, speed and transfers, and surveying clinicians. Changes in outcomes were small and not significant, but users were satisfied. Real-world prospective evaluations can show smaller effects than lab studies, which the PhD should anticipate.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective before-after evaluation in the Mayo Clinic Telestroke Network (17 mainly rural sites in Minnesota and Wisconsin, USA); no control group.
papers.datasets: 907 telestroke patients: 444 pre-implementation (10 February to 9 May 2024) and 463 post-implementation (3 months); 291 acute ischaemic stroke and 88 TIA at discharge.
papers.preprocessing: Data from all video telestroke evaluations in each period; pre/post surveys of telestroke users.
papers.modelDetails: AI-driven stroke imaging support software (Brainomix e-Stroke type: automated CT, CTA and perfusion analysis) deployed in the network.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial software).
papers.evaluation: Primary: IVT and EVT treatment rates and times to treatment decision and delivery; secondary: transfer rates and times, user satisfaction survey.
papers.baselines: Pre-implementation period.
papers.results: IVT delivery rose from 26.6% to 35.0% of potentially eligible patients (p = 0.24); EVT stayed at 31%; time to IVT 47 to 41 min (p = 0.772); overall treatment 23.1% to 23.9% (p = 0.944); no significant clinical differences but good user satisfaction.
papers.statistics: Chi-square and comparison of medians between periods.

papers.title: Prospective Data Curation Enables High-Performance Artificial Intelligence for Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in a Resource-Limited Setting
papers.authors: Ashrafzadeh CM, Bahi M, Mostafa A, El Manhaly M, Ghoneim M, Al-Bayoumy B, Khamis E, Mostafa M, Aziz HA, Khaled N, et al.
papers.aim: To show that carefully curated local data can produce high-performing AI for diabetic retinopathy in a resource-limited setting.
papers.method: An Egyptian reading centre collected over 150,000 standardised, quality-controlled retinal images to train deep learning models.
papers.result: AUC 0.962 for referable retinopathy, showing curation alone enabled high-quality AI.
papers.tools: Grad-CAM, Inception
papers.gap: Single centre and camera type; external validation needed.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Convenience sample within study window.
papers.methodologyDetail: A screening reading centre in Egypt collected over 150,000 standardised wide-field retinal images graded under strict quality control, and used the curated data to train deep learning models for referable retinopathy and macular oedema. The models performed very well. This is strong evidence for the PhD's argument that a carefully curated local registry in an LMIC can itself enable high-quality AI.
papers.studyDesign: Cross-sectional diagnostic technology evaluation at the Alexandria iCare Retina Reading Center, Egypt, with Joslin Diabetes Center/Harvard (IRB 00012098; NCT04935749); informed consent.
papers.datasets: 152,025 ultra-widefield colour fundus images collected February 2022 to June 2024 during routine screening; 26,232 gradable on-axis images used (mean age 60.7; 58.1% female); 8,741 (33.3%) more-than-mild DR; training set 21,009 images.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised Optos 200° UWF acquisition with eyelid lifting; prospective ETDRS grading by Joslin-certified graders with 20% monthly ophthalmologist adjudication and ≥ 80% within-one-step agreement maintained; non-colour and ungradable images excluded.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning classifiers for more-than-mild DR (MTM) and diabetic macular oedema (DME) from UWF images, with Grad-CAM visualisation.
papers.training: Supervised training on curated labels (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUC, sensitivity and specificity on held-out test data; Grad-CAM inspection.
papers.baselines: Expert grading as reference.
papers.results: MTM model AUC 0.962 ± 0.003 with sensitivity 0.922; high DME performance; Grad-CAM showed focus on clinically relevant lesions; careful curation alone enabled high-performing AI in a resource-limited setting.
papers.statistics: Mean ± SD across runs; ROC analysis.

papers.title: Impact of Large Language Model Assistance on Radiologists' Diagnostic Performance for Brain Tumors by Experience Level
papers.authors: Song CW, Baek BH, Kim SK, Yoon W, Lee YY, Park I, Park JH, Park SB, Choi IW
papers.aim: To test whether LLM help improves radiologists' brain tumour diagnosis by experience level.

papers.result: LLM help mainly improved trainees, with smaller effects for experienced radiologists.

papers.gap: Selected images, not full MRI volumes; no uncertainty handling.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
